translations.text: Demonstration on Faith
I received your letter, my dear friend, and when I read it, it made me very glad that you had turned your mind to these inquiries. For this question that you asked me
is freely given and freely received. Whoever has something and wishes to withhold it from someone who asks for it will have that very thing he withheld taken away from him.
For whoever has received freely ought also to give freely. As for what you asked me, my dear friend, I will write to you according to what my humble understanding has grasped.
Even concerning what you did not ask me, I will ask God and explain it to you. Now listen, my dear friend,
and open to me the inward eyes of your heart and the spiritual senses of your mind, to attend to what I am saying to you.
For faith is composed of many things and is brought to completion in many ways.
It is like a building constructed through many kinds of work, whose structure rises upward. Know, my dear friend,
that stones are laid in the foundations of a building, and then the whole building rises upon the stones until it is completed.
So it is with all our faith. Its foundation is the solid stone, who is our Lord Jesus Christ, and faith is laid upon him, upon the stone.
Upon faith the whole building rises until it is finished. The foundation is the beginning of the whole building.
For when someone approaches faith, he is placed upon the stone, who is our Lord Jesus Christ, and his building is not shaken by waves,
nor harmed by winds, nor brought down by storms, because his building has risen upon the bedrock of the solid stone.
In calling Christ a stone, I have not spoken from my own thinking. Rather, the prophets called him a stone before me, and I will show you.
But for now, listen concerning faith, which is laid upon the stone, and concerning the building that rises upon the stone. For first a person believes,
and when he believes, he loves; when he loves, he hopes; when he hopes, he is justified; when he is justified, he is perfected; and when he is perfected, he is made complete.
When his whole building has risen and has been completed and perfected, then he becomes a house and a temple for Christ to dwell in, as Jeremiah the prophet said:
“The temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord—you are the temple of the Lord, if you make your ways and your deeds good.”
And again he said through the prophet, “I will dwell in them and walk among them.” The blessed apostle also said this: “You are the temple of God,
and the Spirit of Christ dwells in you.” Our Lord also said this to his disciples: “You are in me, and I am in you.”
When the house becomes a dwelling place, then a person begins to take care to provide what is needed by the one who dwells in the building.
It is just as when a king or an honored person takes up residence in a house that has been called by the king’s name:
the king requires all the royal furnishings and all the service required for the king’s honor.
For a king does not lodge or dwell in a house that is empty of every good thing. Rather, the king requires the house to be fully furnished,
with nothing lacking in it. If anything is lacking there in the house where the king is staying, the keeper of the house is handed over to death because he did not prepare the service for the king.
So too, a person who has become a house and a dwelling place for Christ should see what is needed for the service of Christ who dwells in him, and by what things he may please him.
For first he builds his building on the stone, which is Christ, and on this stone faith is laid, and on faith the whole building rises.
The inhabitant of the house requires pure fasting, and it is established through faith. He also requires pure prayer,
and it is accepted through faith. He needs love, and it is built up through faith. He needs acts of charity, and they are given through faith.
He asks for humility, and it is adorned through faith. He chooses virginity for himself, and it is loved through faith. He brings holiness near to himself,
and it is planted through faith. He also considers wisdom, and it is found through faith. He further seeks hospitality, and it is made more excellent through faith.
He requires sincerity, and it is mingled with faith. He also seeks patience, and it is perfected through faith.
He reflects on gentleness, and it is acquired through faith. He loves mourning, and it is manifested through faith. He also seeks purity,
and it is preserved through faith. Faith requires all these things, being laid on the bedrock of the firm stone, which is Christ.
These deeds are required by Christ the King, who dwells in people who have been built up through these deeds.
And if you say, “If Christ was laid as the foundation, how does Christ also dwell in the building when it is completed?”
For the blessed apostle said both these things. He said, “Like a wise master builder, I laid a foundation.”
There he explained the foundation and made it clear, for he said this: “No one can lay another foundation besides the one that has been laid,
which is Jesus Christ.” And as for Christ also dwelling in the building, this is the very statement written above: Jeremiah called people temples,
and God dwells in them. And the apostle said, “The Spirit of Christ passes through you.” And our Lord said, “I and my Father are one.”
Thus the statement is complete: Christ dwells in people who believe in him, and he is the foundation on which the whole building rises.
But let me return to my earlier statement, that Christ was called a stone by the prophets. For long ago David said about him,
“The stone that the builders rejected has become the head of the building.” And how did the builders reject this stone, which is Christ? They rejected him in this way:
before Pilate they said, “This man shall not be king over us.” And again, in that parable which our Lord told, a man of noble birth
went away to receive a kingdom and return to reign over them. But they sent messengers after him, saying, “This man shall not be king over us.”
By these things they rejected the stone, which is Christ. And how did it become the head of the building? By being raised over the building of the nations, with their whole building rising upon it.
And who are the builders but the priests and Pharisees? They did not build a firm building, but were tearing down what he was building, as it is written in the prophet Ezekiel:
“He was building a wall, but they were pushing it over so that it would fall.” And again it is written, “I sought among them a man who would build a fence
and stand in the breach on behalf of the land, so that I would not destroy it, but I found none.” Isaiah too prophesied beforehand about this stone.
For he said, “Thus says the Lord: Look, I am laying in Zion a chosen stone, a precious cornerstone, the chief stone of the foundation wall.”
And he said again there, “Everyone who believes in him will not be afraid. Whoever falls on that stone will be broken, and anyone on whom it falls, it will crush.”
For the people of the house of Israel fell on it, and it became their ruin forever. It also fell on the image and crushed it. The nations believed in him and are not afraid.
And he showed concerning the stone that it was made the capstone and the foundation. And if that stone was laid as a foundation,
how did it also become the capstone? It was because, when our Lord came, he established his faith on earth like a foundation, and ascended above all the heavens,
like a capstone. And the whole building was completed for him with stones from below and from above. And concerning the faith of which I said that he established his faith on earth,
David proclaimed this beforehand concerning Christ. For he said, “Faith will spring up from the earth.” And concerning his also being above, he said, “Righteousness looked down from heaven.”
Daniel also spoke concerning this stone, which is Christ. For he said, “A stone was cut from the mountain without hands,
and struck the image, and the whole earth was filled with it.” He showed this beforehand concerning Christ, that the whole earth would be filled with him. For with the faith of Christ,
look, all the ends of the earth have been filled, as David said: “The sound of the good news of Christ has gone out through all the earth.”
And when he sent out his apostles, he also said to them, “Go out and make disciples of all the nations, so that they may believe in me.”
The prophet Zechariah also prophesied concerning this stone, which is Christ. For he said, “I saw a chief stone of equality and love.”
And why did he say “chief”? Because he was with his Father from the beginning. And as for his also saying “of love,” it was because, when he came into the world,
he said to his disciples, “This is my commandment, that you love one another.” And again he said, “I have called you my friends.”
And the blessed apostle said, “God loved us with the love of his Son.” Truly, Christ loved us and gave himself up for us.
And he explained and showed concerning the stone: “Look, I am opening seven eyes upon this stone.”
And what, then, are the seven eyes that were opened upon the stone, if not the Spirit of God, who rested upon Christ in seven activities?
As the prophet Isaiah said, “The Spirit of God will rest and dwell upon him: of wisdom and understanding, of counsel and might, of knowledge and the fear of the Lord.”
These are the seven eyes that were opened upon the stone. And these are the seven eyes of the Lord that look upon the whole earth.
This too was said concerning Christ. For he said that light was given to all the nations,
as the prophet Isaiah said: “I have given you as a light to all the nations, so that you may be my salvation to the ends of the earth.”
And David also said, “Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths.” And the Word and utterance of the Lord is Christ.
As it is written at the beginning of the gospel of our Life-giver, “In the beginning was the Word.” And there he also testified concerning the light: “That light was shining in the darkness,
and the darkness did not comprehend it.” And what, then, does this mean, that the light was shining in the darkness and the darkness did not comprehend it, if not Christ,
who shone his light among the people of the house of Israel? And the people of the house of Israel did not comprehend the light of Christ because they did not believe in him.
As it is written, “He came to his own, and his own did not receive him.” And our Lord Jesus himself also called them darkness.
For he said to his disciples, “What I tell you in darkness, say in the light.”
“Let your light shine among the nations,” he said, because they received the light of Christ, who is a light to the nations.
And again he said to his apostles, “You are the light of the world.” And again he said to them, “Let your light shine before people,
so that they may see your good deeds and glorify your Father in heaven.” And again he made it known about himself that he is the light.
For he said to his disciples, “Walk while you have the light with you, before darkness overtakes you.”
And again he said to them, “Believe in the light, so that you may become children of light.” And again he said, “I am the light of the world.” And again he said,
“No one lights a lamp and puts it under a measuring basket or under a bed, or puts it in a hidden place. Instead, he puts it on a lampstand,
so that everyone may see the lamp’s light.” And the shining lamp is Christ, as David said, “Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths.”
And again the prophet Hosea also said, “Light a lamp for yourselves and seek the Lord.” And our Lord Jesus Christ said,
“What woman who has ten coins and loses one of them does not light a lamp, sweep the house, and search for the coin she lost?”
And who, then, is this woman, if not the congregation of the house of Israel, to whom ten commandments were given?
And they lost the first commandment, the one in which he warned them and said, “I am the Lord your God, who brought you up from the land of Egypt.”
And once they lost this first commandment, they could not keep the nine that followed it either, because the nine depend on the first.
For it was not possible for them to keep the nine commandments while worshiping Baal.
For they lost the first commandment, like that woman who lost one coin out of ten. And the prophet called out to them,
“Light a lamp for yourselves and seek the Lord.” And again the prophet Isaiah also said, “Seek the Lord,
and when you have found him, call on him, and when he is near. Let the sinner abandon his way, and the wicked man his thinking.”
For that lamp shone, but they did not seek the Lord their God by its light. And his light shone in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it. And the lamp was raised onto a lampstand,
but those inside the house did not see its light. And what, then, does this mean, that the lamp was raised onto a lampstand, if not his being raised onto the cross?
And through this the whole house became dark for them. For when they crucified him, the light became dark for them and shone among the nations.
For from the sixth hour, when they crucified him, until the ninth hour, darkness came over the whole land of Israel, and the sun set at noon.
And the land grew dark in broad daylight, as it is written in the prophet Zechariah: “On that day, says the Lord, I will make the sun set at noon, and I will darken the land in broad daylight.”
I return, then, to my earlier statement about faith, upon which all the fine works of the building rise. And as for the building that I spoke of,
I was not speaking of something unrelated. Rather, the blessed apostle wrote in the first letter to the Corinthians and said, “Like a wise master builder, I laid a foundation,
and everyone builds on it. Some build with silver, gold, and precious stones, and some build with reeds, hay, and stubble.”
And on the last day that building is tested by fire, for gold, silver, and precious stones are preserved in the fire.
Because they are a solid building. But fire overcomes straw, reeds, and stubble, and they burn.
And what are the gold, silver, and precious stones with which the building is raised, if not the good works of faith, which are preserved in the fire?
For Christ dwells in that solid building, and he is the one who preserves it from fire.
Let us look and learn from the example God has given us even in this world, so that the promises of that world may be confirmed for us.
Let us learn from those three righteous men who fell into the fire and were not burned: Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael, over whom the fire had no power.
For they built a solid building, rejected the command of King Nebuchadnezzar, and did not worship the image he had made. But those who transgressed God's command—
Fire quickly overpowered them, set them ablaze, and they burned without mercy. For the people of Sodom burned like straw, reeds, and stubble.
Nadab and Abihu also burned because they transgressed God's command. The two hundred and fifty men who were offering incense also burned.
The two captains and the hundred men with them also burned because they approached the mountain where Elijah was sitting, he who went up to heaven in a chariot of fire.
The accusers also burned because they dug a pit for righteous men. For this reason, my beloved, the righteous are tested by fire,
Like gold, silver, and precious stones. But the wicked burn in the fire,
Like straw, reeds, and stubble, which fire overcomes and burns. As the prophet Isaiah said, “The Lord judges by fire, and by it he tests all flesh.”

And again he said, “You will go out and see the corpses of the men who rebelled against me. Their worm does not die, and their fire is not extinguished, and they will be a spectacle of horror to all flesh.”
The apostle also explained to us about this building and this foundation. For he said, “Another foundation besides this one that has been laid
No one can lay, which is Jesus Christ.” The apostle also spoke about faith mingled with hope and love. For he said:
“These are the three that remain: faith, hope, and love.” And he showed that faith is laid first upon the solid foundation.
For Abel's offering was accepted because of his faith. And Enoch, because he was pleasing through his faith, was taken away from death. And Noah, because he believed,
Was sheltered from the flood. And Abraham was blessed through his faith, and it was credited to him as righteousness. And Isaac was loved because he believed.
And Jacob was protected because of his faith. And Joseph, because of his faith, was tested by the waters of strife and was delivered from the trial.
And his Lord established a testimony in him, as David said: “He established it as a testimony in Joseph.” Moses also performed many mighty deeds and wonders through faith.
And through faith he devastated the Egyptians with ten plagues. Again, through faith he divided the sea, brought his people across, and drowned the Egyptians in it.
And through faith he threw wood into the bitter water, and it became sweet. And through faith he brought down manna and fed his people to the full.
And through faith he stretched out his hands and defeated Amalek, as it is written: “His hands remained in faith until the sun set.”
Through faith he also went up Mount Sinai, fasting twice for forty days each time.
Again, through faith he defeated Sihon and Og, the kings of the Amorites.
This is astonishing, my beloved, and a great wonder that Moses performed at the Red Sea, when the waters were divided through faith.
They stood like lofty mountains and mighty cliffs, and remained still. They remained still and stood at the command, bound up as though in wineskins.

They were held in check above as they were below, and their fluidity did not pass beyond its boundary. They changed the nature with which they had been created, and creatures without perception became obedient.
The waves stood upright and awaited retribution, until the people should cross. The billows were astonished and waited, looking for the command and the retribution.
The foundations that had existed since ages past were exposed, and what had been wet from the beginning suddenly became dry. The gates lifted their heads, and the everlasting gates were raised.
The pillar of light entered and illuminated the whole camp, and the people crossed through faith. There was a righteous judgment against [?] Pharaoh, his army, and his chariots.
Likewise, Joshua son of Nun divided the Jordan through his faith, and the Israelites crossed as in the days of Moses.
Know, my beloved, that this crossing of the Jordan was divided three times: the first time by Joshua son of Nun,
the second by Elijah, and then by Elisha. For the words of Scripture make known that opposite that crossing at Jericho,
there Elijah ascended to heaven. For when Elisha returned after him, divided the Jordan, and crossed, the sons of the prophets of Jericho came out
to meet Elisha and said, “The spirit of Elijah has rested upon Elisha.” And when the people crossed in the days of Joshua son of Nun—
for it is written that the people crossed opposite Jericho. Joshua son of Nun also brought down the walls of Jericho through faith,
and they fell without effort. Again, through his faith he destroyed thirty-one kings and gave the land to the Israelites as an inheritance.
Again, through that same faith of his, he stretched out his hands toward heaven and stopped the sun at Gibeon and the moon in the valley of Aijalon.
They stopped and stood still in their courses. In short, all our righteous fathers triumphed through faith in everything they did,
as the blessed apostle also testified concerning them all, that they succeeded through faith. Again, Solomon said, “Many men are called merciful,
but who can find a faithful man?” Job also said this: “My integrity will not depart from me, and I will hold firmly to my righteousness.”
Our Life-giver also used to say this to everyone who approached him to be healed: “Let it be done for you according to your faith.”
When a blind man approached him, he said to him, “Do you believe that I can heal you?” The blind man said to him, “Yes, my Lord, I believe.”
And his faith opened his eyes. To the man whose son was sick, he said, “Believe, and your son will live.” He said to him, “I believe, my Lord;
help my little faith.” And through his faith his son was healed. When the king’s servant approached him, his servant boy was also healed through his faith,
when he said to our Lord, “Say the word, and my servant boy will be healed.” Our Lord marveled at his faith, and it was done for him according to his faith.
Also, when the leader of the synagogue pleaded with him about his daughter, he said to him, “Only believe, and your daughter will live.”
He believed, and his daughter came to life and rose. When Lazarus died, our Lord said to Martha, “If you believe, your brother will rise.”
Martha said to him, “Yes, my Lord, I believe.” And he raised him after four days. Simon, too, who was called Cephas,
was called a firm rock because of his faith. And when our Lord gave his apostles the mystery of baptism, he said to them:
“Whoever believes and is baptized will live, and whoever does not believe will be condemned.” Again he said to his apostles, “If you believe and do not doubt,
there is nothing you will be unable to do.” For when our Lord walked on the waves of the sea, Simon also walked with him through his faith.
But when he wavered in his faith and began to sink, our Lord called him a man of little faith. And when his apostles made a request of our Lord,
they asked him for nothing except this: “Increase our faith.” He said to them, “If you have faith,
even a mountain will move out of your way.” And he told them not to doubt and sink in the world, like Simon,
who began to sink in the sea when he doubted. And again he said, “This sign will be given to those who believe:
they will speak in new languages, cast out demons, and lay their hands on the sick, and they will recover.”
Let us therefore draw near, my dear friend, to faith, whose mighty deeds are so numerous. For faith has raised people to heaven and overcome the flood,
made the barren bear children, rescued people from the sword, brought them up from the pit, made the poor rich, released prisoners, and delivered the persecuted.
It has brought down fire, divided the sea, split the rock, given the thirsty water to drink, fed the hungry, and brought the dead to life.
It has brought people up from Sheol, stilled the waves, healed the sick, defeated armies, overthrown walls, and shut the mouths of lions.
It has quenched fiery flames, humbled the proud, and brought the humble to honor. All these mighty deeds were accomplished through faith.
For this is faith: that a person should believe in God, the Lord of all, who made heaven and earth and the seas and everything in them;
that he made Adam in his image; that he gave the Law to Moses; that he sent some of his Spirit into the prophets; and that he also sent his Messiah into the world;
and that a person should believe in the resurrection of the dead and also believe in the mystery of baptism. This is the faith of the church of God.
A person must also free himself from observing hours, weeks, months, and seasons, and from divination, omens, astrology, and sorcery;
from sexual immorality and singing; from empty teachings, the instruments of the Evil One; from the enticement of sweet words; and from blasphemy and adultery.
A person must not give false testimony, nor speak with a double tongue.
For these are the works of faith, which is founded on the firm rock that is Christ, on whom the whole building rises.
There is much more, my dear friend, about faith in the Holy Scriptures. But I have written these few things out of many to remind you, my beloved,
so that you may know and make known, believe and also be trusted. And when you have read and learned the works of faith,

you will be like that cultivated soil in which the good seed fell and which yielded fruit a hundredfold, sixtyfold, and thirtyfold. And when you go to your Lord, he will call you a good, diligent, and faithful servant,
who, because of his abundant faith, entered the kingdom of his Lord. The Demonstration on Faith is complete.
Demonstration on Love
Be assured, my beloved: the whole Law and the Prophets hang on two commandments, as our Savior said. For someone who will not be persuaded, the Law and the Prophets are too little to persuade him.
For our Savior said that the Law and the Prophets hang on these two commandments:
that a person should love the Lord his God with all his soul, with all his strength, and with all his possessions; and that a person should also love his neighbor as himself.
And when you enter into an examination of these two commandments, on which the entire force of the Law and the Prophets hangs:
For if these two commandments, on which the entire force of the Law and the Prophets hangs,
had been fixed in people's hearts and minds, there would have been no need even for the Law and the Prophets to be written.
As it is written, the law is not laid down for the righteous, but for the wicked. The law was laid down because of the wicked. And if righteousness had remained among human beings,
there would have been no need for the law. Again, if the law had not been laid down, God's power would not have been made known in every generation
and in all the wonders he displayed. Through the transgression of the commandment by Adam's household, death was decreed upon the world. And God's power is revealed
when all human beings rise at the end, at the time when death's authority is taken away. And because of the wicked in the days of Noah,
God's power was revealed in the waters of the flood. And because Abraham observed the righteousness prescribed in the law before the law was laid down,
God's power was revealed in him through righteousness, when he brought back the captives of Sodom by the power of his God and did not reach out his hand to take any of the plunder.
And after that day God said to him, “Your reward is very great because of your righteousness.” Though the law had not been laid down for him, he demonstrated the deeds required by the law,
and no law was needed for his righteousness. Likewise, his sons Isaac and Jacob had no need for a law to be laid down for their righteousness,
because their father commanded them to practice righteousness and justice, as it is written that the Lord said about Abraham:
“I know him: he will command his children after him to keep all my commandments.” Joseph also observed the righteousness prescribed in the law
when he did not obey his mistress. For he said, “How could I do this great evil and sin against God?” Moses, too, observed the righteousness prescribed in the law
when he refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter. For this reason the Lord deemed him worthy to give the law to his people through him.
For all these demonstrated the deeds required by the law, though no law had been laid down for their righteousness. They were a law to themselves.
For when the time of the law arrived, it was added because of transgression. And he showed that the law was an addition.
And why, indeed, was this addition made? It was because of the calling of the nations, which had already been promised before the law.
The law was a guardian and tutor until the offspring came through whom the nations were blessed. For the sworn promise made to Abraham
is the covenant of promise, in which God said to him, “Through your offspring all the nations will be blessed.” And this is the declaration that constituted that covenant,
which was promised to Abraham four hundred and thirty years before the law was laid down: that the nations would be blessed through his offspring.
who is Christ. The Law came four hundred and thirty years after these things. For when Abraham received this promise,
he was eighty-five years old. From that time until Jacob entered Egypt, there were two hundred and five years.
And from the time Jacob entered Egypt until the people came out under Moses, there were two hundred and twenty-five years.
The account of their stay was recorded: “The Israelites lived in the land of Egypt for four hundred and thirty years.” But why, my beloved,
when they lived there for two hundred and twenty-five years, were four hundred and thirty years recorded for them?
It was because, from the very moment he said to Abraham, “Know for certain that your descendants will be strangers in a land that is not theirs,
and they will make them work and enslave them for four hundred years”—for at that very time, when this statement was spoken to Abraham,
“You will have a child,” it took shape through faith in Abraham’s heart, as it is written: “Abraham believed God,
and it was credited to him as righteousness.” The statement about the slavery his children would endure in Egypt was also conceived in Abraham’s heart.
He began to worry about how his descendants would be in slavery, and his heart became enslaved in Egypt. In the same way, Isaac and Jacob also pondered that slavery,
and their thoughts were enslaved within Egypt. Slavery was promised to Abraham for his descendants before they were born.
For that statement preceded Isaac’s birth by fifteen years, and the promise of slavery preceded their entry into Egypt by
two hundred and five years. And the promise that all nations would be blessed through Abraham’s descendants preceded the Law by four hundred and thirty years.
The Law could not cancel the promise. Thus the Law became an addition to that promise until its time came.
That promise was kept for one thousand seven hundred and ninety-four years, from the time it was promised to Abraham until it came to pass.
That promise remained in safekeeping for one thousand three hundred and sixty-four years after the establishment of the Law. The promise preceded the Law by
four hundred and thirty years. When it came to pass, it abolished the observances of the Law. The Law and the Prophets were summed up in these two commandments,
about which our Lord spoke. For it is written: “The whole Law and the Prophets prophesied until John the Baptist.” And our Lord said,
“I have not come to abolish the Law and the Prophets, but to fulfill them.” Again it is written: “The confirmation of the Law came through Jesus.”
What, then, did the Law and the Prophets lack, that they needed to be fulfilled? It was because the covenant, which is the promise, was hidden within them.
For the covenant given to Moses was not brought to completion until this later covenant came, which is itself the first,
promised earlier and recorded afterward. The one who established the covenant died, and he dissolved the two covenants and made the two into one.
He abolished the law of commandments with its ordinances. For the requirements of the Law were abolished at the coming of our Life-giver.
He offered himself in place of the offerings prescribed in the Law, and he was led like a lamb to slaughter in place of the lambs of atonement. The fattened calf was killed for us,
so that we would have no need to offer young cattle. He came and went up on the cross so that offerings and sacrifices would no longer be demanded of us.
He gave his blood for all humanity, so that the blood of animals would not be required of us, and entered the sanctuary not made by human hands.
He became a priest and a minister of the sanctuary. For from the time he came, he abolished the observances prescribed in the Law.
From the time they bound him, their festivals were bound in chains. And because they wanted to condemn the innocent one, he removed their judges from them.
Because they rejected his kingship, he took the kingdom away from them, for the one to whom the kingdom belongs had come. He offered up a living sacrifice on our behalf,
and abolished their sacrifices. The Israelites remained without sacrifices and without an altar, without anyone to wear the ephod or offer incense.
He brought visions and prophets to an end among them because they did not listen to the great prophet. The first covenant was fulfilled by the later one,
and the practices prescribed in the Law grew old and aged, and became subject to decay. For from the time the new covenant was given,
the old one came to an end. And it was not only from the time of our Savior’s coming that sacrifices were rejected, but even long before,
their sacrifices did not please him, as it is written: “I do not eat the flesh of rams, nor do I drink the blood of goats.”
Rather, it says, “Offer thanksgiving as a sacrifice to God, and fulfill your vows to the Most High.” And again it says, “God does not reject a broken heart.” And again it says,
“You did not desire sacrifices, nor were you pleased with whole burnt offerings. The sacrifices of God are a humble spirit.” And the prophet Isaiah also said,
“I do not require your many sacrifices, says the Lord.” And again he said to them, “I hate and reject your festivals, and I will not savor the fragrance at your solemn assemblies.”
Furthermore, this saying spoken by our Savior, on which the Law and the Prophets hang, is beautiful, good, and fitting. For our Lord said this:
“Not one letter, not one yod, will pass away from the Law and the Prophets until everything comes to pass.” For he took the Law and the Prophets
and hung them on two commandments, and abolished nothing in them. And when you look carefully at this saying,
it truly is so: the observances prescribed in the Law, and everything written in it, come under this saying:
“Love the Lord your God with all your soul, with all your strength, and with all your heart.” And everything that was done under the Law
was intended to bring them to love the Lord their God, and for each person to love their fellow human being as themselves. These two commandments are above the whole Law.
When you pay attention and examine the Law, at the beginning of the whole Law it is written: “I am the Lord your God,
who brought you up from the land of Egypt. You shall not make for yourself any image or any likeness alongside me.” And when someone does not set up another god alongside him,
that person comes under the saying on which he hung the Law and the Prophets. Remember, my dear friend, that I wrote to you that the Law is not laid down for the righteous.
For whoever maintains righteousness is above the commandment, the Law, and the Prophets. And the saying spoken by our Lord is true:
“Not one letter, not one yod, will pass away from the Law and the Prophets,” because he sealed them and hung them on two commandments.
Now listen, my dear friend, to the explanation of this statement, in case someone asks why this is written: “The length of time the Israelites lived in the land of Egypt was
four hundred and thirty years,” whereas, when this promise was made, Abraham was told that it would be four hundred years.
And they received thirty more. But I will show you, my dear friend, how the matter stands. For when the time came for the completion of four hundred years,
Moses was sent to deliver them. When he killed the Egyptian, they rejected their deliverer, and Moses fled to Midian.
And wrath came upon them, so that they would remain in Egypt for thirty years. For they said to Moses, “Who appointed you ruler and judge over us?”
When they rejected their deliverer, God's wrath kept them in Egypt for thirty years, and Moses was in Midian for thirty years.
Then, when their oppression increased, he brought them out of Egypt. God showed this patience for two reasons: first, so that they would be disciplined
because they rejected Moses; and second, so that the sins of the Amorites would reach their full measure. Beyond what he had promised Abraham,
he added thirty years for the people, and he showed patience toward the Amorites for seventy years: thirty in Egypt and forty in the wilderness.
When four hundred and thirty-four years had passed, bringing the sins of the Amorites to their full measure, he brought them into the promised land.
But know, my dear friend, that God is not bound by a law. For sometimes he reduces what is great, and sometimes he adds to what is small.
For in the days of Noah, because of the wickedness of the sons of [?], he declared that the days of humankind would be one hundred and twenty years.
And he wiped them out in the six hundredth year of Noah's life. For he had said that they would remain on the earth for one hundred and twenty years,
but in the six hundredth year of Noah's life they were wiped out, and he reduced those years by twenty. And again it is written
that when the wickedness of the sinful kingdom of the house of Ephraim increased, when Jeroboam son of Nebat reigned over them—
he who sinned and caused Israel to sin—and when they had sinned, he pronounced a warning against them through the prophecy of Isaiah the prophet, who said to them,
“After sixty-five years, Ephraim will cease to be a people.” This pronouncement came in the first year of Ahaz. And in the fourth year of Hezekiah,
Shalmaneser king of Assyria came up against them, and from Tiglath-pileser [?], and he exiled them from their land. For Ahaz reigned over them
for sixteen years, and in the fourth year of Hezekiah the kings of Assyria gained power over them. There were only twenty years,
and Ephraim was cut off from the people of Israel. He reduced the years for them by forty-five. He had spoken beforehand and set a time, but did not carry it out according to what he had decreed.
It was not without knowledge that he declared to them that these things would happen in this way, and that afterward the years would be reduced or increased.
Rather, he did so with knowledge, for he knew that they would reach this measure. In his mercy, he gave them time to repent,
so that human beings would not lose heart. But those human beings despised God's patience, and when they heard
that there was a long time before the threatened wrath would come, they boldly sinned before him and said, “As for what the prophets say,
they are prophesying about a distant time.” Therefore, when this thought arose among them in the days of Ezekiel the prophet,
and they said, “What this man prophesies concerns a distant time,” he said to Ezekiel, “As I live, says the Lord of lords,
there will no longer be any delay in my words. For whatever word I speak, I will carry it out quickly.” And as for what he had previously decreed,
He gave people time for repentance, so that they might repent. But they were relying on God's patience
and were not repenting. He too goes back on the time he set and fixed for them. He does not act out of ignorance, but as it is written: “Woe to the plunderer!
You shall not plunder, and the deceiver shall not deceive you. For when you want to plunder, you will be plundered, and when you want to deceive, you will be deceived.”
Again, it is written in Jeremiah: “If I speak concerning a nation and a kingdom, to uproot, tear down, overthrow, and destroy, and that nation turns from its wickedness,
I too will go back on my word and turn away from them what I said against them.” Again, Jeremiah says: “If I speak concerning a nation and a kingdom,
to build and to plant, and that nation does evil before me, I too will go back on my word and withhold from it the good that I said I would do for it.”
Now I have written all these things to you, my dear friend, because earlier, in that first discourse on the subject of faith, I showed you
that through faith the foundation of this covenant in which we stand can be established. And in this second discourse I have written to you and reminded you
that the whole Law and the Prophets hang on two commandments, those of which our Savior spoke. And in these two commandments
the whole Law and the Prophets are contained. Faith is contained in the Law, and through faith true love is established,
the love that belongs to those two commandments: after a person loves the Lord his God, he also loves his neighbor as himself.
Now listen, my dear friend, concerning love, which is one of those two commandments. For when our Life-giver came,
he showed the zeal of love. For he said to his disciples, “This is my commandment, that you love one another.”
Again he said to them, “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another.” And again, when teaching about love,
he instructed them in this way: “Love your enemies, bless whoever curses you, and pray for those who mistreat you
and persecute you.” He also said this to them: “If you love those who love you, what credit is that to you?
For if you love someone who loves you, even the pagans do the same: they love whoever loves them.” Again our Life-giver said,
“If you do good to someone who treats you well, what credit is that to you? Look, even tax collectors and sinners do the same.
But you,” he said, “because you have been called children of God in heaven, should imitate him, for he has mercy even on the ungrateful.”
Again our Savior said, “Forgive, and you will be forgiven. Release, and you will be released. Give, and it will be given to you.” Again he spoke
and filled us with fear: “If you do not forgive people the wrongs they commit against you, neither will the Father forgive you.”
For he instructed us in this way, saying, “If your brother sins against you, forgive him. Even if he sins against you seven times in one day, forgive him.”
When Simon Peter heard this saying, he said to our Lord, “How many times should I forgive my brother if he sins against me?
Seven times?” Our Lord said to him, “Not only seven, but seventy times seven.
Even if,” he said, “he sins against you four hundred and ninety times, forgive him in a single day, and imitate his good Father, who has made his forgiveness abundant.”
Concerning Jerusalem. When he took the Israelites captive to Babylon, he disciplined them there for seventy years. And when his mercy was revealed,
he gathered them back to their land through Ezra the scribe, and generously granted them forgiveness for half of his day: seventy weeks of years,
four hundred and ninety years. But when they shed innocent blood, Jerusalem was no longer forgiven.
Instead, he handed it over to its enemies, and they uprooted it. They did not leave one stone upon another, nor did they leave its foundations for the Lord.
And he did not say that the descendants of Edom should receive retribution, because they did not cry out against Jerusalem, “Lay it bare! Lay it bare, down to its foundations!”
But God, during half of his day, forgave for four hundred and ninety years and bore with their sins. Then he uprooted Jerusalem itself
and handed it over to foreigners. In this way our Life-giver commanded them that a person should forgive his brother four hundred and ninety times in one day.
But do not be troubled, my dear friend, by what I wrote to you, that God forgave Jerusalem for half of his day.
For this is what is written in David, in the ninetieth psalm: “A thousand years in the eyes of the Lord are like yesterday, which has passed.”
The wise rabbis also say this: the world is appointed by God to last the equivalent of six days.
At the completion of six thousand years, the world will be dissolved, and God's Sabbath will come, like the Sabbath after six days.
As our Savior explained and showed us concerning the Sabbath, he said this: “Pray that your flight may not take place in winter or on the Sabbath.”
And again the apostle says, “God's Sabbath still remains. Let us therefore strive to enter his rest.”
Again, when our Lord taught his disciples to pray, he told them, “Pray in this way: Forgive us our debts, and we too will forgive our debtors.”
And again he said, “When you wish to present an offering and remember that you hold some grudge against your brother, leave your offering before the altar,
and go and be reconciled with your brother. Then come and present your offering.” Otherwise, when a person prays, “Forgive us our debts, and we too will forgive our debtors,”
he may be caught by his own words, and the one who receives prayers may say to him, “You do not forgive your debtor. How can you be forgiven?”
And your prayer will remain on the earth. Again, our Lord showed us the example of that man who began to settle accounts with his servants.
When his servant, who owed him ten thousand talents, came before him, his master pressed him to pay what he owed.
When he could not repay his debt to his master, his master ordered his release and forgave him everything he owed. But that servant, in his wickedness,
did not remember his master's forgiveness, or how generously he had forgiven him. When he went out, he found one of his fellow servants who owed him a hundred denarii.
He seized him and began choking him, saying, “Give me what you owe me!” He would not accept the plea that his fellow servant made to him,
but went and shut him up in prison. And because he did not forgive his fellow servant a little, though he himself had been forgiven much, he was handed over to the jailers to torture him
until he paid what he owed. And he told them, “This is what my Father in heaven will do to you unless each of you forgives his brother.”
Again, my dear friend, see how the blessed apostle also exalts love when he says, “If you are eager for the greater gifts,”
“I too will show you which gift is greater.” And he said, “If I have prophecy and know all mysteries and all knowledge,
and have all faith, so that I can move a mountain, but have no love, I have gained nothing. And if I give everything I have to feed the poor,
and even hand over my body to be burned, but have no love, again I have gained nothing.” For he said this: “Love is patient and kind,
and does not envy, does not boast, and is not arrogant. It does not seek only what pleases itself, but what benefits many.
Love hopes for everything and endures everything. Love never fails.” Again he said that love is greater than everything. The apostle showed and explained
that, after faith, love is superior, and through it the true building stands firm. He showed that prophecy is established through love, and mysteries are revealed through love,
and knowledge is brought to fullness through love, and faith is strengthened through love. Whoever has faith can move a mountain.
For without love there is no benefit. Even if someone gives everything he has to the poor, but his gifts are not given in love,
he gains nothing. Even if he has his body burned in the fire for the name of his Lord, he receives no benefit. He also showed
that patience, endurance, kindness, and not envying one's brother are found among those who practice love.
Endurance, humility, and fellowship are also established through love itself. For faith is laid on the rock of the building,
and love is the building's bonds, by which the walls of the house are held together. If a defect is found in the bonds of the house, the whole building falls.
So it is with love: when division is found in it, all faith collapses. Faith cannot remove jealousy and strife
until the love of Christ comes, just as a building cannot rise properly until its walls are held together with bonds.
I will also show you that love is greater than everything, and that through it the righteous people of old were made perfect. For it is shown concerning Moses
that he offered his own life for the people of his nation, to be erased from the book of life, provided that the people were not erased. Even when they rose against him to stone him,
he offered a plea before God on their behalf, so that they might live. David also demonstrated love when he was being persecuted by Saul,
who was constantly hunting him down to kill him. Yet David showed mercy with abundant love to Saul, his enemy,
who sought his life. Saul was delivered into David's hands twice, but he did not kill him. He repaid good for evil. Because of this,
goodness did not depart from his house. Because he forgave, he was forgiven. But Saul repaid evil for good, and evil did not depart from his house.
He called to God, but God did not answer him. He fell by the sword of the Philistines, and David wept bitterly over him. David fulfilled beforehand the command of our Savior, who said,
“Love your enemies,” and “Forgive, and you will be forgiven.” Thus David loved and was loved; he forgave and was forgiven.
Elisha also demonstrated this love when his enemies came against him to seize him and harm him.
He treated them kindly, set bread and water before them, and sent them away from him in peace. He fulfilled the written saying:
“If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him a drink.” So too the prophet Jeremiah, concerning those who imprisoned him in the pit and continually abused him,
But he even prayed for them before God. Our Savior taught us this same example of those of old: to love our enemies
and to pray for those who hate us. And if he commanded us to love our enemies and pray for those who hate us, what relief will there be on the day of judgment,
when we hate our brothers and our own members? For we belong to Christ’s body and are members of his members.
For whoever hates one of Christ’s members is cut off from the whole body, and whoever hates his brother is separated from the children of God.
In what our Savior taught us, he showed the earnestness of love. For first he fulfilled it himself, and then he taught those who heard him.
He reconciled our hostility with his Father because he loved us. He gave up his innocent self for the guilty, and he, the good one, was dishonored for the wicked.
He, the rich one, became poor for our sake, and he, the living one, died for the dead. Through his death he brought our dead state to life. And the Son of the Lord of all
took the form of a servant for our sake. He to whom everything is subject subjected himself, to free us from slavery to sin.
In his great love, he gave blessedness to the poor in spirit and promised the peacemakers that they would be his brothers
and would be called children of God. He promised the meek that they would inherit the land of the living, and promised mourners that they would be comforted.
He promised the hungry that they would be satisfied in his kingdom, and gladdened those who weep with his promise. He promised the merciful that they would receive mercy.
He said that those who are pure in heart would see God. He also promised those persecuted for righteousness
that they would enter the kingdom of heaven. To those persecuted for his name, he promised blessedness and rest in his kingdom.
In place of our nature of dust, he made us the salt of truth and rescued us from being food for the serpent. He called us the light of the world,
to rescue us from the power of death. He made us good instead of evil, and beautiful instead of ugly, and gave us love instead of hatred.
He joined us to the good man who brings good things out of his treasures, and rescued us from the one who brings evil things out of the stores of his heart.
Because of his overflowing love, he healed the wounds of the sick. He also healed the centurion’s son because of his faith.
By his power he stilled the sea’s storms for us, and by his grace he drove the demons of Legion away from us. In his mercy he brought the synagogue leader’s daughter back to life.
He also cleansed the woman from the impurity of her bleeding and opened the eyes of the two blind men who approached him. He also gave his Twelve power and authority
over every pain and sickness, and gave it to us as well through their hands. He kept us from the way of the Gentiles and the Samaritans.
In his mercy he gave us strength not to be afraid when we are brought before the rulers of the world. He cast division upon the earth
because of his great peace. In his compassion he forgave the sinful woman’s many debts. By his grace he made us worthy
to build a tower at his expense. He drove unclean spirits out of us and made us a dwelling place for his divinity. He sowed good seed in us,
so that we might bear fruit a hundredfold, sixtyfold, and thirtyfold. He was placed within the world like a treasure laid up in an estate.
He showed the power of his greatness when he was thrown from the height into the depth and was not harmed. He satisfied the hungry who were exhausted.
From five loaves and two fish, five thousand men, besides children and women; and he showed the greatness of his glory.
And because of his great love, he listened to the Canaanite woman and raised her daughter from her sickness. And by the authority of the one who sent him,
he loosened the tongue of a man who stammered and was hard of hearing. The blind saw his light, and through him they praised the one who sent him. And when he went up the mountain to pray,
the sun’s rays were outshone by his light. And he made his surpassing power known in that boy whom a spirit used to attack.
And the demon departed at his word. And he gave us an example and a pattern, that we should become like children and enter the kingdom of heaven.
And he spoke and taught concerning the little ones, that no one should despise them, because their angels always see the Father in heaven.
And again he showed his perfect healing in that man who had been sick for thirty-eight years. He showed him abundant compassion and made him well.
Again he gave us a command to leave the world and turn to him. And he revealed to us that whoever loves the world cannot please God,
through the example of the rich man who trusted in his possessions, and through that man who enjoyed his good things and came to ruin in Sheol.
And he asked for water on the tip of a finger, but no one gave him any. And he hired us as laborers to toil in his vineyard, which is the vineyard of truth.
Our Life-giver did all these things for us because of his great love. Let us too, my beloved, share in the love of Christ,
by loving one another and fulfilling these two commandments, on which the whole Law and the Prophets hang.
The Demonstration on Love is finished.
Demonstration on Fasting
Pure fasting is favored before God and is kept like a treasure in heaven. It is a weapon against the evil one and a shield that intercepts the enemy’s arrows.
I have not said this from my own thinking, but from the holy Scriptures, which have already shown us that fasting has always helped those who fasted sincerely.
For fasting, my beloved, is not merely abstaining from bread and water. Rather, there are many observances of fasting.
For one person fasts from bread and water until he grows hungry and thirsty. Another fasts by remaining a virgin: he hungers but does not eat, and thirsts but does not drink.
And this fasting is more excellent. Another fasts through chastity, and this too is fasting. Another fasts from meat, wine, and various foods.
Another fasts by putting a fence around his mouth so that he does not speak hateful words. Another fasts from anger and subdues his inclination so that he is not overcome.
Another fasts from possessions to free himself for his service. Another fasts from beds of various kinds so that he may stay awake in prayer.
Another fasts from the affairs of this world so that he may not be harmed by the enemy. Another fasts by mourning, so that through affliction he may please his Lord.
And another gathers all these together and makes them one fast, just as someone fasts from food while hungry.
When someone abstains from eating and drinking, he is called a person who fasts. But if he eats and drinks even a little, he has broken his fast.
So too, a person who fasts from all these things, if from time to time he breaks one or another of these observances,
Again, the fast of anyone who violates any one of all these things is not counted to his credit, just as the fast of someone who eats and drinks greedily is not counted.
If someone happens to break his fast because of hunger, his sin is not great. But if someone abstains from all these things and then proceeds to violate them one by one, his sin is great, not small.
Now listen, my beloved, to an example of pure fasting. For Abel first demonstrated pure fasting through his offering, and Enoch by pleasing his God.
And Noah, who preserved his integrity in a corrupt generation; and Abraham, by excelling in his faith; and Isaac, because of Abraham’s covenant;
and Jacob, because of Isaac’s oath, because he knew God; and Joseph, because of his compassion and his provision for others.
For all these, their purity was a perfect fast before God. If there is no purity of heart, fasting is not accepted. Remember and see, my beloved,
that it is an excellent thing for someone to purify his heart, guard his tongue, and restrain his hands from evil, as in the things I wrote to you above.
For a person should not mix honey with gall. If someone fasts from bread and water,
he must not mix insults and curses into his fast. For your house, which is God’s temple, has only one door.
And it is not fitting for you, O human being, that dung and filth should come out through the door by which the King enters.
For when someone fasts from all hateful things and receives the body and blood of Christ, he must guard his mouth, through which the King’s Son enters.
You have no right, O human being, to bring filthy words out of that same mouth of yours. Listen to what our Life-giver said:
“What enters a person does not defile him, but what comes out of his mouth—that is what defiles him.”
Moses too observed a pure fast when he went up the mountain and brought the law to his people.
He was strengthened in his fasting for periods of forty days, and he received surpassing glory when the skin of his face shone.
He turned wrath away from his people, and they were not wiped out. Following the example of Moses’ fast, Elijah, the mighty warrior, also fasted when he was persecuted by Jezebel.
He traveled as far as Horeb during his forty-day fast, to the place where God had spoken with Moses. And God revealed himself to him there.
He commanded him and said to him, “Go, anoint Jehu son of Nimshi, and Hazael, so that he may exact vengeance on the Israelites, and Elisha son of Shaphat,
to take your place.” Through his perfect fast he rejoiced in the revelation of his Lord, just as Moses rejoiced when he fasted twice, for forty days each time,

and turned the anger of his God away from his people, and brought down the tablets of the covenant, inscribed by the finger of God. Both of these men found their glory in their fasting, and through it they were made perfect.
Again, I will also show you an unacceptable fast of wickedness and bloodshed, which Jezebel decreed—she who stirred up Ahab and brought Israel to ruin.
For she wrote a letter in Ahab’s name and sent it to the inhabitants of Jezreel, wicked men who obeyed the wicked Jezebel.
In that wicked letter she wrote as follows: “Proclaim a fast and seat Naboth at the head of the people.
Seat two wicked men opposite him, and let them testify against him and say, ‘Naboth has reviled God and the king.’ Then let him be stoned to death.”
And this, my beloved, which Jezebel wrote to them—that two men should testify against Naboth—she sent to them as though it came from the holy law.
For it is written in the Law that someone deserving death must not be put to death on the testimony of one witness, but must die on the testimony of two witnesses.
And this is written: “The witnesses must be the first to raise their hands against him to stone him, and afterward all the people.” Again, she wrote to them
that they should testify against him in this way: “Naboth cursed God and the king.” This too she wrote to them as though drawing from the holy Law, in her wicked letter, for it is written:
“Whoever curses the name of God must be stoned,” because he pronounced the holy name and cursed it. But Jezebel was not concerned that God's name had been cursed.
Rather, she was concerned about Ahab's greed, because he coveted Naboth's vineyard. Ahab did not remember that it is written: “You must not covet anything that belongs to your neighbor.”
O Jezebel, you who brought Ahab to ruin, who is this God whom Naboth cursed? Is it the one whose altar you demolished, or the one whose prophets you killed?
Or which king did he curse? The one who set aside the Law and wanted to seize Naboth's inheritance? Why then, Jezebel,
did you not uphold what is written at the beginning of the Law's commandments? For it is written: “You must not worship another god.” Yet Jezebel worshiped Baal.
Again it is written: “You must not shed innocent blood in the land that the Lord your God gives you.” Should you not have remembered, O Jezebel, that it is written:
“No atonement can be made for the land in which blood has been shed, unless the blood of the one who shed it is shed there.”
Were you afraid of this, O Jezebel, and did you then show a wicked zeal, claiming that Naboth had cursed God when he had not cursed him?
Again it is written: “Whoever sheds human blood, his blood will be shed.” And Jezebel, who stirred up anger, shed Naboth's innocent blood.

Therefore, in the very place where innocent blood was shed during the wicked fast that had been decreed, Jezebel's blood was shed, and dogs ate her. As for Ahab, who listened to her advice, dogs licked up his blood there.
And if Jezebel selected and took from the Law what helped her do harm, although she did not observe the Law,
you wicked men, inhabitants of Jezreel, how could you accept a letter that prescribed a wicked fast and contained instructions for false testimony and bloodshed?
In what generations have you heard of people keeping a fast and shedding innocent blood? Why, then, did you not reject the wicked letter and the false testimony?
For this reason Ahab and Jezebel received just punishment for the innocent blood of Naboth that they shed. The inhabitants of Jezreel, who obeyed Jezebel, also received just punishment.
For Hosea prophesies and says: “In a little while I will hold the house of Jehu accountable for the blood of Jezreel.”
Jehu exacted payment for Naboth's blood from Jezebel and the house of Ahab, and he slaughtered the inhabitants of Jezreel in the temple of Baal.
Naboth's blood came upon them, as Jehu said on that day of retribution: “In the evening I saw Naboth's blood and the blood of his sons.”
Thus retribution came upon him, and the fast that the inhabitants of Jezreel kept brought condemnation.
The inhabitants of Nineveh, in contrast, kept a pure fast when Jonah proclaimed their overthrow to them. For this is written:
When they heard Jonah's proclamation, they decreed a sustained fast and earnest supplication, sitting on sackcloth and ashes.
They took off their luxurious clothes and put on sackcloth instead. They kept infants from their mothers' breasts, and sheep and cattle from grazing.
For this is written: “The news reached the king of Nineveh, and he rose from his throne and took off his crown.”
He sat on sackcloth and spread ashes beneath himself. He proclaimed in Nineveh, his city, saying, “By command of the king and his nobles:
Neither people nor livestock are to taste anything. They must not graze or even drink water. Instead, both people and livestock must be covered with sackcloth.
Let them cry out to God with lamentation, so that he may turn his fury and anger away from us, and we may not perish.” And this is what is written:
“God saw their deeds, that they turned from their evil ways, and he turned his fury away from them and did not destroy them.” It does not say:
That he saw their fasting from bread and water, or their sackcloth and ashes, but that they turned from their evil ways and from the wickedness of their deeds.
For this is what the king of Nineveh proclaimed: “Let everyone turn from his evil way and from the violence in their hands.”
Their fast became pure, and the fast that the Ninevites observed was accepted when they turned from their evil ways and from the violence in their hands.
The pure fast that the Ninevites observed was pleasing, and their fast was not like that of the people of Jezreel, during which innocent blood was shed.
For at all times, my dear friend, when someone fasts from evil, that fast is better than fasting from bread and water,
And better than humbling oneself, bending one's neck like a rush, and spreading sackcloth and ashes beneath oneself, as Isaiah said.
For when someone fasts from bread and water and from every kind of food, spreads sackcloth and ashes beneath himself, and mourns, this is lovely, fitting, and good.
But this is better still: when someone humbles himself, loosens the bonds of injustice, and cuts the fetters of deceit.
Then his light breaks forth like the sun, his righteousness goes before him, and he becomes like a flourishing garden and like a spring whose waters never fail.
He does not resemble the hypocrites, who darken their faces, disfigure their appearance, and make their fasting known.
For look: even the deceitful teachings, the instruments of the Evil One, fast and recall their sins, but they have no one to reward them.
For who will give a reward to Marcion, who does not acknowledge the Good One, our Maker? And who will repay Valentinus for his fasting, when he proclaims that his makers are many,
And says that the perfect God has not been spoken of by any mouth, nor has any mind fathomed him? Or who will reward the children of darkness, the teaching of wicked Mani,
Who dwell in darkness like snakes and practice Chaldean astrology, the teaching of Babylon? Look: all these fast, but their fasting is not accepted.
Listen again, my dear friend. I will show you an acceptable fast, the one observed by Mordecai and Esther. Their fasting became a protective barrier of deliverance for all their people.

They brought to nothing the arrogance of Haman, their oppressor. His injustice came back upon his own head, and his deceitful scheme turned against him. He was judged with the judgment he had wanted to impose.
The measure he wanted to use was measured out to him. What he planned to do was done to him, and he was bound with the cord of his sins.
The wealth in which he boasted did not accompany him, and his wisdom did not rescue him. Because he had devised evil, his pride was humbled, and his honor departed from him.
His beauty was ruined, and his strength was brought low. He was struck with the blow he had wanted to strike, and he was killed by the death he had wanted to inflict.
For he wanted to destroy all the Jews under the rule of King Ahasuerus. But the fasting of Mordecai and Esther became a protective barrier
And intercepted Haman's arrows. Haman was caught in his own injustice, and his destroying sword entered his own heart. His bow, which had been drawn for wrongdoing, was broken.
As it is written about the wicked, “Their sword will enter their own hearts, and their bows will be broken.” This was fulfilled in Haman.
For when he prepared a gallows for Mordecai and his sons, Haman and his sons were hanged on it. He was caught in the pit he had made,
and trapped in the snare he had hidden. His own net was spread over him, and he fell into his wicked snares. He came to his end forever.
But why, my dear friend, did Haman ask and petition the king that all the Jews should perish? It was because he wanted to take revenge for his own people,
and wipe out the name of the Israelites, just as the memory of Amalek had been wiped out from under heaven. Haman had remained as a survivor of the Amalekites.
For this is what is written: Haman son of Hammedatha, the Agagite, was held in honor in the palace of King Ahasuerus.
Mordecai used to sit at the king’s gate every day because Esther, whom he had raised, had been taken away and had pleased King Ahasuerus
more than all the young women who were her companions. She entered and took the place of Queen Vashti. And Mordecai himself, every day,
would come early and sit at the king’s gate. Haman ranked third under the king and was honored throughout his kingdom.
Everyone at the king’s gate, whenever they saw Haman, would fall down and bow before him. But Mordecai would not rise before him.
For this reason, he wanted to use this pretext to take revenge on Mordecai’s people and exact repayment from them for the disgrace of the Amalekites.
For Haman was descended from the house of Agag, king of Amalek, whom Saul brought back and Samuel cut to pieces before the Lord.
Mordecai was descended from the house of Saul, from the tribe of Benjamin, from the descendants of Kish. Because Saul had destroyed the Amalekites,
Haman wanted to exact vengeance for his people from Israel, and for the killing of Agag from Mordecai.
The senseless man did not know that it had been decreed against him, against Amalek, that his memory should be wiped out from under heaven.
For it is written in the holy Law that God said to Moses, “Tell Joshua son of Nun to choose men for himself and wage war against Amalek.”
Joshua armed himself and waged war against Amalek. Amalek was defeated by the sign of the cross, through the outstretching of Moses’ hands.
When those who had gone out to battle had been destroyed, a remnant of them remained in their homeland. Then the Lord said to Moses, “Write a book of remembrance,
and place it before Joshua son of Nun, because I will utterly wipe out the memory of Amalek from under heaven.” Yet he was patient with them, the Amalekites,
so that perhaps they would hear what was written in God’s holy book, where he said, “I will utterly wipe them out, the Amalekites,” and would turn back to him, and he would turn toward them.

For if they had repented, repentance would have been possible, just as repentance was possible for the Ninevites when he threatened them with destruction. They showed repentance, and he turned his wrath away from them.
And just as the Gibeonites were given a pledge of protection and did not perish with the Canaanites, and just as repentance was granted to Rahab, who believed,
so repentance would also have been granted to the Amalekites if they had believed, while he was patient with them for four hundred years. And after all this time,
when he saw that they had not repented, his wrath prevailed against them, and he remembered what Moses had recorded in his holy book. For when Saul became king, God said to Samuel,
“Tell him: ‘I remember what Amalek did to you when you came out of Egypt, how he met you with the sword. Now go and destroy the sinner Amalek.’”
Saul went and devastated the Amalekites. But because Saul showed mercy to Amalek, he was rejected as king, because he left a survivor among them.
Haman was a survivor of the house of Agag whom Saul had spared. Mordecai was descended from the house of Saul, who had devastated the house of Agag.
There are some people, my beloved, who bring accusations against Mordecai and say, “Why did he not rise before Haman?
After all, he was honored throughout the kingdom. What harm would Mordecai have suffered,” they say, “if he had shown him honor?”
They also say, “If Mordecai had risen before Haman, this evil would not have been planned against Mordecai and his people.”
But whoever says these things does not understand the significance of the matter. Mordecai did this as a righteous man who kept the law.
He did not rise before the wicked Haman because he considered Saul, his kinsman, who had been rejected as king because he showed mercy to King Agag, Haman’s kinsman.
Wrath came upon Saul. Likewise, if Mordecai had shown honor to the wicked Haman, wrath would have risen against him as it did against Saul.
But why, my beloved, did Amalek, rather than all the other nations, go out to meet Israel in battle?
For Amalek planned to go out and destroy the descendants of Jacob and nullify Isaac’s blessings.
He was afraid of being subjected to the descendants of Jacob, for Isaac had said to Esau, “You shall serve your brother Jacob.
But if you repent, his yoke will pass from your neck.” For this reason, you should know that Amalek was the son of the concubine of Eliphaz, the son of Esau.
He did not want to be subjected to the descendants of Jacob. But why, my beloved, did Isaac say to Esau, “You shall serve your brother Jacob”?
The text explains it this way: because Esau took his wives from the daughters of Canaan, who had been cursed by his father Noah.
For Noah had said to him, “You shall be a slave of slaves to your brothers.” Because Abraham and Isaac knew
that the Canaanites were cursed, they did not take wives from their daughters for their sons. Neither Abraham took one for Isaac, nor Isaac for Jacob,
so that the cursed offspring of the Canaanites would not be mixed with the offspring of Shem, who had been blessed by Noah.
For this reason Amalek, the son of Eliphaz, the son of Esau, wanted to nullify Noah’s curses and Isaac’s blessings and fight against the descendants of Jacob.
God also justly wrote concerning Amalek that his memory should be erased by the descendants of Rachel.
First Joshua son of Nun, from the tribe of Joseph, fought against him, and afterward Saul, from the descendants of Benjamin.
Mordecai destroyed their survivor through his fasting. For among all the descendants of Esau, it was Amalek who wanted to fight against the descendants of Jacob.
And it was his own memory that was erased. See how, through the fasting of Mordecai and Esther, Haman was overthrown from his high position, and the survivor of the Amalekites perished.
Mordecai received Haman’s honor and became great throughout the kingdom of Ahasuerus, and Esther became queen in place of Vashti.
Daniel, too, observed an acceptable fast for three full weeks on behalf of his people,
so that their time in Babylon would not be extended beyond seventy years. Through his fasting for twenty-one days, he was heard before his God.
And in those very days Gabriel rose to help him, for he was the one who always received prayers.
Michael, their prince, also helped alongside Gabriel, and they stood against the prince of Persia for twenty-one days.
And he helped Daniel in his fasting. Know, my beloved, that Gabriel is the one who receives prayers before God.
For when Daniel prayed, Gabriel himself came to him, strengthened him, and said to him, “Your prayer has been heard before God.”
“And I have come because of your words.” He encouraged him and said to him, “Be strong, greatly beloved man.” Again, it was he who came to him during the prayer of his fast.
It was also Gabriel himself who presented Zechariah’s prayer before God, when he brought him the good news of John’s birth. For he said to him, “Your prayer has been heard before God.”
He also presented Mary’s prayer before God and brought her the good news of Christ’s birth. For he said to her, “You have found favor with God.”
And how did Mary find favor, except through her fasting and her prayer? For Gabriel himself received pure prayers
and presented them before God. And Michael was the prince of the Israelites. This is the one about whom he said to Moses:
“Look, my angel will go before you and destroy the inhabitants of the land before you.” And this is the one who appeared to Balaam’s donkey when Balaam was going to curse Israel.
He also appeared to Joshua son of Nun, with his sword drawn, standing in the plain of Jericho. When Joshua saw him, he thought he was one of the enemies.
Joshua said to him, “Are you one of us, or one of our enemies?” Michael said to him, “I am the commander of the Lord’s armies, and now I have come.”
He brought down the walls of Jericho before Joshua son of Nun, and he also destroyed thirty-one kings before him.
He destroyed a million Indians before Asa. He also destroyed a hundred and eighty-five thousand in the Assyrian’s camp.
And when the Israelites went to Babylon, he too went with them and fought on their behalf.
But why, my beloved, did Daniel fast during those three weeks of days, petitioning God and pleading with him, when it is not written that he had fasted before that time?
For it is written that when the seventy years of Jerusalem’s desolation were completed, as Jeremiah the prophet had said,
he offered his prayer and pleaded before his God that they should not remain any longer than these seventy years, just as he had shortened the time for the generation in Noah’s days,
and just as he had extended it for the Israelites in Egypt, and just as he had shortened it for the descendants of Ephraim.
Daniel thought that, because of the people’s sins, he might keep them longer than these seventy years of which Jeremiah had spoken.
Gabriel and Michael, their prince, were helping him in his fasting. Michael himself would also find relief through them when they returned to your land.
And Gabriel helped alongside him so that the fruits of their prayers in the sanctuary might increase, and so that the offerings he presented before God every day might increase.
But the prince of the kingdom of Persia did not want the holy offspring of Israel to be separated from the sinful kingdom of Persia, which had been entrusted to him by God.
For as long as they were there, there were righteous people among them, and he too rejoiced in them.
And see how Daniel’s excellent fast prevailed and brought back his people from captivity at the completion of seventy years.
But the commander of our camp is greater than Gabriel, more exalted than Michael, and stronger than the prince of Persia.
He is our life-giver, our Lord Jesus Christ, who came and clothed himself in our humanity, suffered and was tempted in the body he took from us, and is able to help those who are tempted.
For he fasted on our behalf, defeated our enemy, and commanded us to fast and keep watch at all times, so that through the power of pure fasting we might reach his rest.
The Demonstration on Fasting is finished.
Demonstration on Prayer
Purity of heart is prayer, greater than all prayers offered aloud. And silence, when joined with a clear mind,
is better than a loud voice when someone cries out. Now, my beloved, give me your heart and your attention, and hear the power of pure prayer.
See how our righteous ancestors triumphed through it in their prayer before God, and how it became a pure offering for them.
For through prayer offerings were accepted. It also turned back the flood, healed barrenness, overthrew armies, and revealed mysteries.
It divided the sea, opened a way through the Jordan, held back the sun, and made the moon stand still. It destroyed the unclean, brought down fire, and shut up the heavens.
It brought people up from the pit, rescued them from fire, and saved them from the sea. Its power is exceedingly great, just as the power of pure fasting is great.
For just as I explained and showed you the matter of fasting in the discourse before this one, so too I will not grow weary of recounting and showing you what concerns prayer.
For at the beginning, because of the purity of Abel’s heart, his offering was accepted before God, while Cain’s was rejected. And how do we know
that Abel’s offering was accepted and Cain’s was rejected, and that Abel knew his offering had been accepted, while Cain also knew that his had been rejected?
I will explain this to you as well as I can. Now you know, my beloved, that an offering was distinguished in this way:
if it was accepted before God, fire would come down from heaven, and the offering would be consumed by it.
For when Abel and Cain presented their offerings together, the living fire that ministered before God came down
and licked up Abel’s pure offering, but did not approach Cain’s, which was not pure. From this Abel knew that his offering had been accepted.
Cain also knew that his had been rejected. The fruits of Cain’s heart themselves showed and testified against him that he was full of deceit,
