and to those who do God's will. The gate is open, the road is cleared, and the spring flows and gives drink to the thirsty. The table is set,
and the banquet is prepared. The fattened calf is slaughtered, the cup of salvation is mixed, delight is prepared, and the bridegroom is about to recline at table.
The apostles have issued the invitation, and those invited are very many. You who are chosen, prepare yourselves! The light shines, glorious and beautiful,
and garments not made by hands are ready. The shout is near, the graves are opening, and the treasures are being revealed.
The dead rise, and the living fly to meet the King. The banquet is set, the horn gives courage, and the trumpets urge haste.
The watchers of heaven run, and the throne is set for judgment. Whoever has labored rejoices, and whoever has been idle is afraid. Whoever has acted wickedly does not approach the judgment.
Those on the right rejoice, while those on the left weep and wail. Those in the light are glorious, while those in darkness groan,
that they might moisten their tongues. Grace passes away, and justice reigns. There is no repentance in that place. Winter draws near, and summer has passed.
The Sabbath of rest is coming. Labor ceases, night comes to an end, and light reigns. Death's sting is broken, and death is swallowed up by life.
Those who return to Sheol weep and gnash their teeth, while those who go to the kingdom are glad and rejoice, exult and offer praise.
For those who do not take wives are served by the watchers of heaven. Those who preserve chastity find rest in the sanctuary of the Most High.
The Only Begotten, who is from his Father's embrace, gives joy to all the celibates. There is neither male nor female there, neither slave nor free,
but all are children of the Most High. And all the pure virgins who are betrothed to Christ—
their lamps shine there, and they enter his bridal chamber with the bridegroom. All those betrothed to Christ are far removed from the curses of the law
and are freed from the punishment of Eve's daughters. For they do not marry men, so as to receive the curses and suffer pain.
They take no account of death, because they hand no children over to it. Instead of a husband who dies, they are betrothed to Christ. And because they bear no children,
they are given a name better than sons and daughters. Instead of the laments of Eve's daughters, they sing the bridegroom's songs.
The wedding feast of Eve's daughters lasts seven days, but their bridegroom never departs. The adornment of Eve's daughters is wool that wears out and decays,
but their garments do not wear out. Old age withers the beauty of Eve's daughters, but their own beauty is renewed at the resurrection.
O virgins who have betrothed yourselves to Christ, when one of the members of the covenant says to one of you, “Let me live with you, and serve me,”
Say this to him: “I am betrothed to a man who is a king, and it is him I serve. If I leave his service and serve you,
my betrothed will be angry with me, write me a certificate of divorce, and dismiss me from his house. And while you wish to receive honor from me, and I to receive honor from you,
harm may come to both you and me. Do not put fire in your lap, lest it burn your clothes. Rather, keep your honor on your own,
and I will keep my honor on my own. These are the things the bridegroom has prepared for the young men at his wedding feast. Prepare a [?] for yourself, and make yourself ready to meet him.
And I will prepare oil for myself, so that I may enter with the wise women and not be kept outside the door with the foolish virgins.”

Now listen, my dear friend, to what I write to you about the things that are fitting for those who live a single life, the members of the covenant, virgins and those who practice sexual abstinence. Before everything else,
it is fitting that a man upon whom the yoke has been laid should be firm in his faith, as I wrote to you in the first letter.
He should be diligent in fasting and prayer, fervent in his love for Christ, humble, meek, and sensible.
His speech should be gentle and pleasant. His attitude toward everyone should be sincere, and he should speak his words with care.
He should put a fence around his mouth against harmful words and keep himself from uncontrolled laughter. He should not love finery in clothing.
Nor is it fitting for him to grow his hair long and adorn it. It is not fitting for him to anoint himself with fragrant oils, nor should he recline at banquets.
It is not fitting for him to wear ornate clothing, nor should he be eager to travel on a donkey. He should keep a proud attitude far from himself.
It is not fitting for him to gaze at ornate clothing, nor should he wear fine wraps. He should rid himself of a deceitful tongue and put jealousy and quarreling away from himself.
He should cast deceitful lips away from himself. As for words spoken about someone when the person being spoken about is not present,
he should neither listen to them nor accept them, lest he sin before investigating. Mockery is an ugly fault, and it should not even enter his mind.
He should not lend at interest or love greed. Let him suffer wrong rather than do wrong, and let him also keep disorder far from himself.
He should not speak frivolous words. He should not ridicule someone who has repented of his sins, nor mock his brother who fasts.
He should not shame someone who cannot fast. Where his correction is accepted, let him rebuke; where he is not accepted, let him preserve his dignity. When his words are welcome, let him speak,
and otherwise let him remain silent. He should not degrade himself by begging for the sake of his stomach. He should reveal his secret to someone who fears God,
and guard himself against an evil person. He should not speak evil behind anyone’s back, not even his enemy’s. He should strive in such a way that he has no enemy at all.
When others envy him for his goodness, let him increase his goodness and not be harmed by their envy. When he has something and gives to the poor, let him rejoice;
and when he has nothing, let him not be distressed. He should have no dealings with an evil person and should not converse with an abusive man,
so that he does not expose himself to abuse. He should not argue with a blasphemer, lest his Lord be insulted because of him. He should keep far away from slander,
and should not curry anyone’s favor with flattering words. These things are fitting for those who live a single life, who accept the heavenly yoke
and become disciples of Christ. For it is fitting that Christ’s disciples should imitate Christ their teacher.
Let us take an example, my beloved, from our Life-giver: though he was rich, he made himself poor; and though he was exalted, he humbled his greatness.
Though his dwelling was on high, he had nowhere to lay his head. And though he was destined to come upon the clouds,
he rode on a colt and entered Jerusalem. Though he is God, the Son of God, he took the form of a servant. And though he was rest for all who toil,
he himself grew weary from the labor of the journey. Though he was the spring that quenches thirst, he grew thirsty and asked for water to drink.

Though he was fullness and satisfied our hunger, he grew hungry when he went out into the wilderness to be tempted. Though he was the wakeful one who never slumbers, he slumbered and slept in a boat in the middle of the sea.
Though he was served in his Father's tabernacle, he himself was served by human hands. And though he was the physician of all sick people,
nails were driven into his hands. Though his mouth brought forth good things, they gave him gall to eat. And though he hurt no one and quarreled with no one,
he received blows and endured abuse. Though he was the giver of life to all mortals, he surrendered himself to death on the cross.
Our Life-giver showed us all this humility in himself. Let us therefore humble ourselves too, my beloved. When our Lord came outside his own nature,
he walked in our nature. Let us remain in our nature, so that on the day of righteousness he may give us a share in his nature. Our Lord took a pledge from us and went away,
and he left us a pledge of his own and was exalted. It was not because he was in need, but because of our need, that this arrangement was devised.
What is ours was already his from the beginning. But who had given us what is his? For what our Lord promised us is certain:
“Where I am, you too will be.” For what he took from what is ours is with him in glory, and a crown is bound upon its head.
And what we have received of his, we ought to honor. What is ours is honored with him, though not in our nature. Let us honor what is his in its own nature.
If we honor it, we shall go to him who took our pledge and ascended. But if we despise it, he will take from us what he gave us. And if we stain his pledge,
he will take back what is his there and deprive us of what he promised us. Let us care well for the King's Son who is with us, because a hostage has been taken from us in exchange for him.
Anyone who treats the King's Son with honor receives many gifts from the King. What is ours sits with him in glory, and a crown is bound upon its head,
and he has seated it with the King. But we, who are poor—what shall we do for the King's Son who is with us? He requires nothing from us
except that we adorn our temples for him, so that when the time is completed and he goes to his Father, he may thank him on our behalf because we honored him. When he came to us,
he had nothing of ours, nor did we have anything of his, although both natures belong to him and to his Father.
For when Gabriel brought the good news to blessed Mary, who bore him, he took the Word from on high and came. And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.
And when he went to the one who sent him, he took away something he had not brought, as the apostle said: “He raised us up and seated us with him in heaven.”
And when he went to his Father, he sent us his Spirit and said to us, “I am with you until the world comes to an end.”
For Christ sits at his Father's right hand, and Christ dwells among human beings. Through his Father's wisdom, he suffices for those above and those below,
and he dwells in many, though he is one. He overshadows all believers, each with a portion of himself, yet he is not diminished, as it is written:
whom they distributed among many. Yet while he is distributed among many, he sits at his Father's right hand. He is in us, and we are in him.
As he said, “You are in me, and I am in you.” And elsewhere he said, “I and my Father are one.”
If someone whose understanding lacks knowledge disputes this and says, “Since Christ is one, and his Father is one,
how do Christ and his Father dwell in believing people? And how do righteous people become temples for God, so that he dwells in them?
Then, if this is so, and each believing person receives a Christ of his own, and God who is in Christ—if this is so,
there are many gods and countless Christs.” But listen, my dear friend, to a spiritual explanation appropriate to this matter.
Let the person who speaks this way gain assurance from something visible. For everyone knows that the sun is fixed in heaven, while its rays are spread over the earth.
Its light enters through many doors and the windows of houses. Wherever the sun's light falls, even on a patch the size of a palm, it is called “the sun.”
And when it falls in many places, it is called by the same name, while the sun itself is in heaven. Then, if this is so,
there are many suns! Likewise, the waters of the sea are abundant, but when you take a single cupful from them, it is called “water.”
And when you divide it among a thousand vessels, it is still called by its name, “water.” Likewise, when you kindle fire from fire in many places,
the fire from which you take it and kindle it is not diminished. It is called by the one name, “fire.” And merely because you distribute it to many places,
it does not acquire many names. And when you take dust from the earth and scatter it in many places, the dust is not diminished at all.
Nor can you call it by many names. So too God and his Christ, though they are one, dwell in many people.
They themselves are in heaven, and they are not diminished at all by dwelling in many people, just as the sun in heaven is not diminished at all
when its power rests upon the earth. How much greater, then, is the power of God, since even the sun itself stands by God's power!
Again, my dear friend, I remind you also of what is written. For it is written that when it became burdensome for Moses to lead the camp alone,
the Lord said to him, “Look, I will take some of the spirit that is upon you and place it upon seventy men, the elders of Israel.”
When he took some of Moses' spirit, and seventy men were filled from it, Moses was not diminished at all, nor did his spirit perceive
that anything had been taken from him. The blessed apostle also said that God distributed some of the Spirit of his Christ and sent it into the prophets, yet Christ was not diminished at all,
because his Father did not give him the Spirit by measure. Through this line of thought you can understand that Christ dwells in believing people,
while Christ is not diminished at all by being distributed among many. For the prophets received from the Spirit of Christ,
each of them according to what he was able to receive. And again, some of Christ's own Spirit is poured out today upon all flesh,
and sons and daughters, old men and young men, male slaves and female slaves prophesy. Something of Christ is in us, while Christ is in heaven,
at his Father's right hand. Christ did not receive the Spirit by measure; rather, his Father loved him and entrusted everything into his hands.
And he gave him authority over his entire treasury. For John said, “The Father did not give the Spirit to his Son by measure, but loved him and entrusted everything into his hands.”
Our Lord also said, “Everything has been entrusted to me by my Father.” Again he said, “The Father will judge no one, but will give all judgment to his Son.”
The apostle also said, “Everything will be subjected to Christ, except his Father, who subjected everything to him. And when everything has been subjected to him by his Father,
then he himself will also be subjected to God his Father, who subjected everything to him, and God will be all in all, and in everyone.”
Our Lord testifies about John that he is greater than the prophets. Yet he received the Spirit by measure, because in the same measure that Elijah received,
John received the Spirit. And just as Elijah lived in the wilderness, so too John was led by the Spirit of God,
and lived in the wilderness, in the mountains, and in caves. Birds fed Elijah, and John ate flying locusts.
Elijah had a leather belt tied around his waist, and John had a leather strap tied around his waist. Jezebel persecuted Elijah,
and Herodias persecuted John. Elijah rebuked Ahab, and John rebuked Herod. Elijah divided the Jordan, and John opened the way for baptism.
Elijah’s spirit rested twofold on Elisha, and John laid his hand on our Savior, who received the Spirit without measure.
Elijah opened heaven and ascended, and John saw heaven opened and the Spirit of God descending and resting on him, on our Savior.
Elisha received a double portion of Elijah’s spirit, and our Savior received John’s spirit and received the Spirit from heaven. Elisha received Elijah’s mantle,
and our Savior received the laying on of hands of the priests. Elisha made oil from water, and our Savior made wine from water.
Elisha fed only a hundred men with a little bread, and our Savior fed five thousand men with a little bread,
besides the children and women. Elisha cleansed Naaman the leper, and our Savior cleansed ten. Elisha cursed the children, and they were devoured by bears,
and our Savior blessed the children. Children insulted Elisha, and children praised our Savior with hosannas. Elisha cursed his disciple Gehazi,
and our Savior cursed his disciple Judas and blessed all his disciples. Elisha brought just one dead person back to life,
and our Savior brought three back to life. Through Elisha’s bones, one dead person came to life. And when our Savior descended to the abode of the dead, the dead—
he brought many of them to life and raised them up. And many are the signs performed by the Spirit of Christ, which the prophets received from him.
Therefore, my beloved, we too have received from the Spirit of Christ, and Christ dwells in us, as it is written that the Spirit said through the mouth of the prophet,
“I will dwell in them and walk among them.” From now on, let us prepare our temples for the Spirit of Christ, and let us not grieve the Spirit, lest it depart from us.
Remember what the apostle warns you: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit, with which you were sealed for the day of salvation.”
For through baptism we receive the Spirit of Christ. At the very moment when the priests invoke the Spirit, it opens heaven and descends,
and hovers over the water, and those who are baptized put it on. For the Spirit is far from all who are born of the flesh,
until they come to birth through water, and then they receive the Holy Spirit. For at their first birth they are born with a natural spirit.
which is created within a human being, and it too is not mortal, as he said: “Adam became a living soul.”
And at the second birth, which takes place in baptism, they receive the Holy Spirit, a portion of the Godhead, and it too is not mortal.
For when people die, the animating spirit is buried with the body, and sensation is taken away from it.
But the heavenly Spirit that they receive goes to its own nature, to Christ. The apostle made both these things known.
For he said: “The body is buried as a natural body and rises as a spiritual body.” The Spirit, in turn, goes to Christ, to its own nature. And again the apostle said:
“When we depart from the body, we shall be with our Lord.” For the Spirit of Christ, which spiritual people receive, goes to our Lord.
And the animating spirit is buried in its own nature, and sensation is taken away from it. As for anyone who has kept the Spirit of Christ in purity,
when it goes to Christ, it says to him: “The body to which I went, and which put me on from the water of baptism, kept me in holiness.”
And the Holy Spirit urges Christ to raise that body which kept it in purity. That Spirit asks to be joined to it again,
so that the body may rise in glory. But if anyone receives the Spirit from the water and grieves it, it leaves him before he dies.
It goes to its own nature, to Christ, and complains to him about the person who grieved it. And when the appointed time reaches its end,
and the time of the resurrection draws near, the Holy Spirit that was kept in purity receives great power from its own nature and comes ahead of Christ.
It stands at the entrance to the burial place where the people who kept it in purity are buried, and waits for the shout.
And when the Watchers open the gates of heaven before the King, then the horn sounds and the trumpets ring out.
The Spirit that is waiting for the shout hears it, and quickly opens the graves and raises the bodies and what was buried in them.
It clothes the body in the glory that came with it. The Spirit is within, to raise the body, and the glory is outside, to adorn the body.
The animating spirit is swallowed up in the heavenly Spirit, and the whole person becomes spiritual, with his body still in him.
Death is swallowed up in life, and the body is swallowed up in the Spirit. Through the Spirit, that person flies to meet the King
and welcomes him with joy. And Christ acknowledges the kindness of the body that kept his Spirit in purity.
This, my dear friend, is the Spirit that the prophets received, and that we too have received. It is not always present with those who receive it.
Rather, at times it goes to the one who sent it, and at times it comes to the one who received it. Listen to what our Lord said:
“Do not despise one of these little ones who believe in me, for their angels in heaven always see the face of my Father.”
This Spirit continually goes and stands before God and sees his face. And if anyone defiles the temple in which it dwells, it complains about him before God.
I will show you from what is written that the Spirit is not always present with those who receive it. For it is written:
“The Holy Spirit that Saul received when he was anointed departed from him because he grieved it, and God sent him a tormenting spirit in its place.”
And when he was tormented by the evil spirit, David would play the lyre, and the Holy Spirit, whom David had received when he was anointed, would come.
And the evil spirit that was tormenting Saul would flee before the Holy Spirit. But the Holy Spirit was not present—
the Spirit David had received—with him at all times, but only when he played the lyre; then the Spirit would come. For if the Spirit had been with him at all times,
the Spirit would not have allowed him to sin with Uriah’s wife. For when he prayed about his sins and confessed his offenses before God,
he would say this: “Do not take your Holy Spirit from me.” And concerning Elisha too, it is likewise written that only when he played his lyre,
then the Spirit came to him, and he prophesied and said, “This is what the Lord says: You will see neither wind nor rain,
and this valley will be made into pits upon pits.” And when the Shunammite woman came to him concerning her son who had died,
he said this to him: “The Lord has hidden it from me and has not made it known to me.” And when the king of Israel sent someone against him to kill him,
the Spirit informed him before the messenger came against him, and he said, “Look, this son of wickedness has sent someone to take off my head.”
And he also announced the abundance that would be in Samaria the next day. Again, the Spirit informed him when Gehazi stole the silver and hid it.
Therefore, my beloved, when the Holy Spirit departs from a person who has received the Spirit, while the Spirit goes away and comes back to him,
it is then that Satan does battle with that person, to make him stumble so that the Holy Spirit will leave him entirely.
For as long as the Spirit is with a person, Satan is afraid to approach him. And see, my beloved, that even our Lord,
who was born of the Spirit, was not tempted by Satan until he received the Spirit of baptism /at baptism/ from on high.
Then the Spirit led him out to be tempted by Satan. But a person has this opportunity: at the very moment when he senses within himself
that he is not fervent in the Spirit and that his heart has fallen into the cares of this world, he should know that the Spirit is not with him. He should rise, pray, and keep watch,
so that the Spirit of God may come to him and he may not be overcome by the enemy. For a thief does not break into a house until he sees that its owner has left it.
Likewise, Satan cannot do battle against this house, which is our body, until the Spirit of Christ departs from it.
But know, my beloved, that a thief does not actually know whether the owner of the house is inside it or not. Instead, he listens beforehand and watches
to see whether he hears the voice of the owner of the house, who is inside, saying, “I have a journey to make.” And when he investigates and sees that the owner of the house has gone away
to attend to his business, then the thief comes, breaks into the house, and steals. But if he hears the voice of the owner of the house
warning and instructing his household to stay awake and guard his house, and saying to them, “I too am inside the house,”
then the thief becomes afraid and flees, so that he will not be seized and caught. Likewise, Satan does not have foreknowledge
by which to know and see when the Spirit departs, so that he can come to plunder the person. Rather, he too listens, watches, and prowls about.
But if he hears a person in whom Christ dwells saying hateful words, or becoming angry and quarreling, or fighting,
Then Satan knows that Christ is not with him, and he comes and carries out his will in him. For Christ dwells among the gentle and the humble,
and he makes his home in them, in those who tremble at his word, as he said through the prophet: “On whom shall I look, and with whom shall I dwell,
except the gentle and the humble who tremble at my word?” And our Lord said: “Whoever walks in my commandments and keeps my love,
we will come to him and make our dwelling with him.” But if he hears of a person who is watchful and prays and meditates on the law of his Lord
day and night, then he turns away from him, because he knows that Christ is with him. But if you say, “How great is Satan,
that he fights against so many!” then listen and be convinced by what I explained to you above about Christ: how he is distributed among many,
yet he himself is not diminished at all. For a house into which a little sunlight enters through its window is entirely lit up. And a person into whom a little of Satan enters
becomes entirely dark. Listen to what the apostle said: “If Satan disguises himself as an angel of light, it is no great thing
if his servants also disguise themselves as servants of righteousness.” And our Lord also said to his disciples: “Look, I have given you authority
to trample the power of the enemy.” The Scriptures have made known that he has power, and servants as well. Job also said about him
that God made him to wage his war. So he sends these servants of his running about in the world to wage war.
But know that he does not fight openly, because authority over him has been given since the coming of our Life-giver. Instead, he seizes things by robbery and steals things secretly.
Let me explain to you, my dear friend, that saying spoken by the apostle, by which the teachings that are the weapons of the Evil One are brought down,
along with deceitful teachings. For the apostle said: “There is a natural body, and there is a spiritual body.” He says, “Thus it is written:
‘The first Adam became a living soul,’ and the second Adam a life-giving spirit.” And they say that there are two Adams.

And he said: “Just as we have put on the image of that Adam who is from the earth, so we shall put on the image of that Adam who is from heaven.” For the Adam who is from the earth is the one who sinned,
and the Adam who is from heaven is our Life-giver, our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore, those who receive the Spirit of Christ become like the heavenly Adam,
who is our Life-giver, our Lord Jesus Christ, because the natural is swallowed up by the spiritual, as I wrote to you above.
But a person who grieves the Spirit of Christ will have a merely natural existence at his resurrection, because the heavenly Spirit is not with him
for the natural to be swallowed up in it. Instead, when he rises, he remains in his own nature, stripped of the Spirit. Because he disgraced the Spirit of Christ, he is handed over to great disgrace.
But whoever honors the Spirit, so that it is sheltered within him in purity, will be sheltered by the Holy Spirit on that day. He will become entirely spiritual
and will not be found naked, as the apostle said: “Provided that, when we are clothed, we are not found naked.” And again he said: “We shall all sleep,
but at the resurrection we shall not all be changed.” And again he said: “This mortal must put on immortality, and this perishable must put on imperishability.
And when this mortal has put on immortality, and this perishable has put on imperishability, then the saying that is written will be fulfilled:
‘Death has been swallowed up by victory.’” Again he said that suddenly, in the blink of an eye, the dead will rise imperishable.
And we will be changed. Those who are changed will put on the image of that heavenly Adam and become spiritual.
Those who are not changed will remain in their natural state, in the created nature of Adam who came from dust, and will remain in their own nature on the earth below.
Then the heavenly ones will be caught up to heaven, and the Spirit in which they are clothed will carry them aloft. They will inherit the kingdom that was prepared for them from the beginning.
The natural ones will remain on earth under the weight of their bodies and will return to Sheol. There will be weeping and grinding of teeth there.
I have written these things as a reminder to myself and also to you, my dear friend. From now on, love virginity, the heavenly portion, fellowship with the watchers of heaven.
For nothing compares with it, and Christ dwells in those who are like this. Summertime has drawn near.
The fig tree has sprouted, and its leaves have come out. The signs our Savior gave have begun to be fulfilled. For he said that nation would rise against nation,
and kingdom against kingdom, and there would be famines, plagues, and terrors from heaven. Look, all these things have been fulfilled in our days.
Now read what I have written to you—you and the brothers who are members of the covenant, who love virginity.
Be on your guard against mockers. For whoever mocks and ridicules his brother fulfills the saying written in the Gospel,
when our Lord wanted to rid the greedy and the Pharisees of their way of thinking. For it is written that because they loved money, they mocked him.
Even now, all those who do not agree with these things mock in the same way. Read and learn, and be diligent in reading and putting it into practice.
Let the law of God be your meditation at all times. When you have read this letter, by your life, my dear friend, stand up and pray, and remember my sinfulness in your prayer.
The Demonstration on the Members of the Covenant is ended.
Demonstration on the Penitent.
There is only one victor among all those born who have put on a body: our Lord Jesus Christ, as he himself testified about himself.
For he said, “I have overcome the world.” The prophet also testified about him: “He did no wrong, nor was deceit found in his mouth.”
And the blessed apostle said, “He made the one who knew no sin to be sin for our sake.” And how did he make him sin?
It was because he took sin, though he himself had not committed it, and nailed it to his cross. Again the apostle said, “Many run in the stadium,
but only one receives the crown.” Moreover, there is no other among Adam’s descendants who has entered the contest without being struck and taking blows.
For sin has reigned since Adam transgressed the commandment. It took blows from many and struck many.
It killed many, and none of those many killed it, until our Savior came, took it, and nailed it to his cross.
Even while nailed to the cross, it still has its sting and stings many, until the end comes and its sting is broken.
There are medicines for all illnesses, and they can be healed when a skilled physician finds them. For those wounded in our contest, there is the medicine of repentance,
which they apply to their wounds and are healed. O physicians, disciples of our skilled Physician, take this medicine for yourselves.
Through it you will heal the wounds of the sick. For warriors who are wounded in battle at the hands of the one fighting against them,
when a skilled physician is found for them, he devises a way to treat them and heal the wounded. And when the physician heals someone wounded in battle,
he receives gifts and honor from the king. So too, my beloved, when someone struggles in our contest, and his adversary comes against him and strikes him,
it is right to give him repentance as medicine, provided that the wounded person's remorse is great, because God does not reject those who repent.
For the prophet Ezekiel said, “I do not desire the death of the sinner who dies, but that he turn from his evil way and live.”
Someone wounded in battle is not ashamed to place himself in the hands of a skilled physician, because the battle overcame him and he was wounded. And when he is healed,
the king does not reject him, but numbers and counts him among his army. Likewise, someone whom Satan has struck should not be ashamed
to confess his wrongdoing, turn away from it, and seek repentance as medicine for himself. For anyone ashamed to show his wound
develops gangrene, and his whole body is harmed. But someone who is not ashamed has his wound healed and returns to enter the contest again.
Someone who develops gangrene can no longer be healed and does not put back on the armor he took off. Likewise, someone defeated in our contest
has this means of being healed: to say, “I have sinned,” and seek repentance. But someone who is ashamed cannot be healed,
because he is unwilling to make his wounds known to the physician who received two denarii, with which he heals all who are wounded.
You too, physicians and disciples of our victorious Physician, must not withhold treatment from anyone who needs to be healed.
Give repentance as medicine to anyone who shows you his wound. And anyone ashamed to show his pain, encourage him not to hide it from you.
When he reveals it to you, do not expose him, lest because of him even the innocent be considered guilty by enemies and adversaries.
When men fall slain from a battle line, their enemies consider them all disgraced. And when wounded men are found among them,
those who have not been wounded treat their injuries and do not disclose them to their enemies.
But if they make them known to everyone, the whole camp acquires a bad reputation. And the king himself, the commander of the army,
is angry with those who expose his camp, and they receive blows from him worse than those received in battle.
But if those who have been wounded are unwilling to disclose their wounds, the physicians deserve no blame
for not healing the sick who were wounded. And if the wounded wish to hide their injuries,
they can no longer put on armor, because they have developed gangrene in their bodies. And if, while they have gangrene, they dare to put on armor,
when they enter the contest, their armor grows hot on them, their wounds rot and fester, and they are killed.
And when those from whom they hid their wounds find their corpses, then they laugh at all their schemes,
because they hid the pain of their wounds. They do not even give their corpses burial, and they regard them as foolish, wicked, and reckless.
And whoever reveals his wound and is healed should guard the place that was healed, so that he is not wounded there twice.
For someone who has been wounded twice is difficult even for a skilled physician to heal, because every wound that occurs in a scar
does not heal. And even if it does heal again, he cannot put on armor. And even if he dares to put on armor, he acquires a habit of defeat.
You who wear the armor of Christ, learn the tactics of battle, so that you are not defeated and brought low in the contest.
Our adversary is cunning and skilled, but his armor is inferior to ours. So we must not turn to his ways and take up his armor:
sleep in place of wakefulness. For he is invisible to us when he fights against us. Let us turn to the one who sees him, so that he may drive him away from us.
I also advise you who are wounded: do not be ashamed to say, “We have been brought low in the contest.” Take medicine for yourselves without payment,
and repent and live before you are killed. And you physicians, I remind you of what is written in the books of our wise Physician:
he did not withhold repentance. For when Adam sinned, he called him to repentance when he said to him, “Where are you, Adam?”
But he concealed his sin from the one who examines the heart, and blamed Eve for misleading him. And because he did not confess his wrongdoing,
he sentenced him and all his descendants to death. And Cain, who was full of deceit and whose offering he did not accept—
he also offered him repentance, but he did not accept it. For he said to him, “If you do well, I will accept your offering. But if you do not do well, your sin is your creditor.”
And in the deceitfulness of his heart he killed his brother and was cursed, and he became a trembling wanderer on the earth. To the generation in the days of Noah, too,
he gave a hundred and twenty years for repentance, but they were unwilling to repent. And at the completion of a hundred years he swept them away.
See, my dear friend, how excellent it is for someone to confess and turn away from his wrongdoing. Our God does not reject those who repent.
For the sins of the people of Nineveh had grown severe, but they accepted Jonah’s preaching when he proclaimed their overthrow, and they repented.
And God had mercy on them. But when the sins of the Israelites multiplied, he called them to repentance, and they did not accept it.
For he called to them through Jeremiah and said, “Return, backsliding children, and I will heal your backsliding.” Again he proclaimed in the hearing of Jerusalem and said to her,
“Return to me, backsliding daughter.” Again he said to the Israelites, “Repent and turn away from your evil ways
and from the wickedness of your deeds.” And he said this to the people: “If you return to me, I will restore you, and you will stand before me.” Again he spoke this way and rebuked them:
“I said that you should return to me with all your heart, inhabitant of Israel, but you did not return.” Again he told a parable about them,
and reminded them of what is written in the Law. He was willing to overrule the Law for the sake of their repentance. For he said, “When a man takes a wife,
and she leaves him and becomes another man’s wife, and the other man who married her dies or divorces her,
and she returns to her first husband, her first husband is no longer permitted to take her back after she has been defiled. But if he does take her back,
that land will indeed be defiled.” And he says, “Now I too took you for myself, Jerusalem, and you belonged to me, but you left me.”
You went away and prostituted yourself with stones and wood. Now, he says, return to me, and I will receive you. Because of your repentance, I set aside the law.
Do not be afraid, then, you who repent, of the loss of hope spoken of in the Scriptures, for it is fitting for the Spirit of God to give warnings in this way.
For he gave a fearful warning through Ezekiel the prophet when he said to him: If a person practices justice and righteousness all his days,
but practices wickedness at the end of his days, he will die in that wickedness. And if a person practices wickedness all his days,
but repents and practices justice and righteousness, he will save his life. With this one statement he warned the righteous person not to sin and lose the race he has run,
and gave the wicked person hope that he might turn away from his wickedness and live. Again he said to Ezekiel: Even if I cut off the wicked person's hope, you must certainly warn him.
Even when I encourage the righteous person, you must set fear before him so that he takes care. When I say to the sinner, ‘You will surely die,’
and you do not warn him, the sinner will die in his wickedness, but I will demand his blood from your hands because you did not warn him. But if you warn the sinner,
that sinner will live because you warned him, and you will save your own life. And when you tell the righteous person, ‘You will surely live,’ and he relies on this,
it is your responsibility, and it is fitting for you, to warn him not to become proud and sin. He will live because he takes care, and you will save your own life.
Listen again, you who repent, to the hand that is stretched out and calls you to repentance. For he also spoke through Jeremiah the prophet and offered repentance.
For this is what he said: If I declare concerning a nation and a kingdom that I will uproot, tear down, overthrow, and destroy it, and that nation turns from its wickedness,
I will turn away from it the disaster that I decreed against it. And if I declare concerning a nation and a kingdom that I will build and plant it, and it relies on this
and does what is evil in my sight, I too will turn away from it the good that I promised it, and I will destroy it because of its wickedness and its sins.
Listen again, you too who hold the keys to the gates of heaven, and open the gates to those who repent. Be persuaded by what the blessed apostle said:
If any of you becomes involved in wrongdoing, you who are spiritual must restore him in a gentle spirit.
And be watchful, he says, lest you too be tempted. For the apostle was afraid and warned them. For he said about himself:
Lest I, who have preached to others, should myself be rejected. As for anyone among you who becomes involved in wrongdoing, he says, do not treat him as an enemy,
but advise and admonish him as a brother, because when you separate him from yourselves, he is swallowed up by Satan.
Again he said that we who are strong ought to bear the weakness of the weak. Again he said that the one who is lame should not be overthrown, but rather be healed.
And I also say to you who repent: Do not deprive yourselves of this opportunity that has been given for healing. For it says in Scripture:

God has mercy on the one who confesses his sins and turns away from them. Look at the son who squandered his possessions: when he returned to his father, his father rejoiced over him and received him.
He slaughtered the fattened calf for him, and his father rejoiced at his repentance. He also called his friends to rejoice with him. His father embraced him and kissed him,
and said: This son of mine was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found. His father did not reproach him for the possessions he had squandered.
Our Lord encouraged those who repent and said: I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.
And he said again, “There will be joy in heaven over one sinner who repents, more than over ninety-nine righteous people
who have no need of repentance.” The shepherd is more concerned about the sheep lost from the whole flock than about those that have not strayed.
For Christ died for sinners, not for the righteous, as he said through the prophet: “He bore the sins of many.” And the apostle said,
“If, while we were sinners, God was reconciled to us through the death of his Son, how much more now, through reconciliation with him, shall we live by his life!”
God forgives whoever confesses his wrongdoing. For when David sinned, Nathan the prophet came to him and made known to him his wrongdoing and the punishment he would receive.
Then David confessed and said, “I have sinned.” The prophet said to him, “The Lord has also taken away your wrongdoing, because you have confessed.” And when he prayed, he said this:
“Against you alone have I sinned, and I have done evil before you.” And again he pleaded with God and said, “Do not bring your servant into judgment,
because no one living is innocent before you.” Solomon also said this: “Who can say, ‘You are pure, my heart, and I have been cleansed of sins’?”
It is also written in the Law that Moses prayed before God and said, “You forgive wrongdoing and sin, yet you certainly do not acquit.”
And when he wanted to wipe out his people because of their sins, Moses spoke this way as he pleaded and begged for mercy, saying to him, “Forgive your people their wrongdoing,
as you have forgiven them from Egypt until today.” And God said to him, “I forgive them, as you have asked.”
You who seek repentance, imitate Aaron, the chief of the priests, who confessed his sin after he had led the people into sin through the calf,
and his Lord forgave him. David too, the chief of Israel’s kings, confessed his wrongdoing and was forgiven.
Simon too, the chief of the disciples, denied Christ, saying, “I have not seen him,” and invoked a curse and swore, “I do not know him.”
But when he approached him with a repentant soul and shed many tears in his weeping, our Lord accepted him, made him a foundation, and called him the rock for building the church.
Do not be foolish like Adam, who was ashamed to confess his wrongdoing. Nor should you imitate Cain, who, when accused of killing his brother,
said, “I do not know where Abel is, because I was not his keeper.” And do not persist in an arrogant attitude,
like the corrupt generation. Do not heap wrongdoing upon wrongdoing and multiply your sins by declaring yourselves innocent
when you are guilty. Listen to our forefathers, who, even though they were righteous, humbled themselves.
For Abraham said, “I am dust and ashes,” and he placed himself in a lowly position. David also said,
“A human being’s days are like a breath.” And Solomon gave this warning: “If the righteous person is barely saved, where will the sinner and the wicked person be found?”
I beg you, my dear friend, by the mercies of God: just because I have written to you that God does not reject those who repent,
do not slacken your diligence and come to need repentance. Repentance is given only to those who need it.
But let this be true of you: that you have no need of repentance. This hand is stretched out to sinners, and the righteous do not seek it.
For alms are given to the poor, and the rich have no need of them. It is the man stripped by robbers who is given something to wear.
to cover the nakedness of someone who is ashamed. Do not lose what you have, lest you wear yourself out searching for it again, whether you find it or not.
Even if you do find it, it is not the same as what was yours. For someone who sins and repents is not equal to someone from whom sin is far removed.
Love the higher portion, and keep away from everything inferior. Equip yourself well with your armor, so that you will not be wounded in battle.
Do not put yourself in need of seeking medicine and wearing yourself out going to a physician. Even if you are healed, the scars remain visible.
Do not rely on the fact that healing is available and give yourself a dishonorable name. Rather, rise above the need for repentance.
Someone whose garment is torn needs to have it patched, and even if it is sewn up, everyone can tell. Someone whose fence is breached rebuilds it with toil.
Even if he rebuilds it, it is still called a breach. When thieves break into someone's house, it is broken into from within, and the hole they made is visible.
With great toil he acquires what he lost. Someone who cuts down his fruit tree must wait a long time until it sprouts again and bears fruit.
Someone whose irrigation spring breaks through toils and labors until he dams it up. Even after he dams it up, he fears that the water may increase and break through it.
Someone who strips his vineyard while it is in blossom is deprived of grapes to eat. Someone who steals has a shamefaced look.
He labors and toils until he is shown mercy. Someone whose work in the vineyard is poor receives his wages with his head bowed and cannot demand more.
Someone who subdues the force of his youth rejoices in the presence of the Ancient of Days. Someone who does not drink stolen water rests beside the spring of life.
You who have prepared yourselves for the contest, listen to the sound of the horn and take courage. I also speak to you who hold the horns:
Priests, scribes, and wise men, proclaim to all the people: Whoever is afraid should turn back from the contest, so that he does not make his brothers' hearts fail like his own.
Whoever has planted a vineyard should return to his work, so that he does not think about it and suffer defeat in battle. Whoever has become engaged to a woman and wishes to marry her should return
and rejoice with his wife. Whoever has built a house should return to it, lest he think about his house and fail to fight wholeheartedly. The contest is fitting for the single-minded,
because their faces are set toward what lies ahead, and they do not think about anything behind them, because their treasures are before them.
Everything they take as plunder becomes their own, and they receive their gain from the abundance [?]. But I say to you who sound the horns:
When you have finished giving the warning, look at those who turn back and inspect those who remain. Bring them down to the water of testing,
those who offer themselves for battle. The water tests everyone who is ready, and those who are lazy are separated out there.
Now hear, my beloved, this mystery that Gideon foreshadowed and whose likeness he displayed. When he gathered the people for battle, the scribes proclaimed the words of the law
and the sayings that I wrote to you above. Then many people turned back from the army. When those chosen for battle remained,
the Lord said to Gideon, “Bring them down to the water and test them there.” Whoever laps water with his tongue is eager and courageous about going into battle.
Whoever falls on his belly to drink water is weak and feeble about going into battle. Great indeed is this mystery, my beloved,
in which Gideon foreshadowed and displayed the pattern of baptism, the mystery of the contest, and the likeness of the single-minded. For he first warned the people.
At first, in the testing by water, when he tested them with water as well, only three hundred men were chosen out of ten thousand,
to take part in the contest. This agrees with the words of our Lord, who said, “Many are called, but few are chosen.”
Therefore it is fitting for the trumpet-blowers, the heralds of the church, to call out and warn all God’s covenant community,
before baptism—those who have dedicated themselves to virginity and holiness, the troops [?] \and the virgins,
the holy men; let the heralds warn them /and the virgins and the holy men, and let them warn them/ and say, “Whoever has his heart set on the natural union of marriage,
let him marry before baptism, lest he fall in the contest and be killed. Whoever is afraid of this part of the struggle, let him turn back,
lest he break his brothers’ hearts as his own heart is broken. Whoever loves possessions, let him turn back from the army, lest, when the battle overcomes him,
he remember his possessions and turn back. Whoever turns back from the contest brings disgrace upon himself. Whoever has not committed himself
and has not yet put on his armor is not blamed if he turns back. But anyone who commits himself and puts on his armor, if he turns back from the contest,
becomes an object of ridicule. The struggle is fitting for someone who strips himself of everything, because he will not remember anything behind him and turn back to it.”
Once they have proclaimed, announced the good news, and warned all God’s covenant community, let them bring to the baptismal water
those who have been chosen for the contest, and let them be tested. After baptism, let them see which are courageous and which are weak.
It is fitting to encourage the courageous, but let them openly turn the slack and weak back from the contest, lest, when the battle reaches them,
they conceal their weapons, flee, and be defeated. For he said to Gideon, “Bring down to the water those who have volunteered.”
When the people went down to the water, the Lord said to Gideon, “All those who lap water as a dog laps with its tongue—
these shall go with you into battle. But all those who fall down to drink water shall not go with you into battle.”
Great is this mystery, my dear friend, whose sign he showed beforehand to Gideon. For he said to him, “Whoever laps water like a dog is fit to go into battle.”
Of all the animals created along with humanity, none loves its master like a dog, which keeps watch for him by day and by night.
Even when its master beats it repeatedly, it does not leave his side. When it goes hunting with its master and a powerful lion encounters its master,
it gives itself over to death for its master’s sake. Such are the courageous ones who are set apart through the water: they follow their Lord like dogs
and give themselves over to death for his sake. They fight his battle courageously and keep watch for him by day and by night.
They bark like dogs as they meditate on the law day and night. They love our Lord and lick his wounds when they receive his body
and place it over their eyes and lick it with their tongues, as a dog licks its master. Those who do not meditate on the law
are called mute dogs that cannot bark. All those who are not diligent in fasting are called dogs with greedy appetites
that never know satisfaction. As for those who diligently seek mercy, the children’s bread is taken and thrown to them.
The Lord again said to Gideon, “Those who fall down to drink water must not go with you into battle, lest they fall and be defeated in battle.”
For they had already shown a sign of their downfall by drinking water lazily. Therefore, my dear friend, this is how those who enter the contest should conduct themselves:
They must not imitate those lazy men, lest they turn back from the struggle and become a disgrace to all their companions.
But listen to this, my dear friend: just because I have convinced you from the Scriptures that God does not reject those who repent, you must not become complacent and dare to sin.
Nor, because I have told you these things, should someone who has been wounded give up and fail to seek repentance. For this is how he should conduct himself:
He should mourn all his days, so that he does not become proud and bring condemnation on himself. A servant who wrongs his master changes his clothing so that his master may be reconciled to him.
He attends him early and late, hoping that he may receive him favorably. When his master sees that he is constantly attending him, he forgives his wrongdoing and is reconciled to him.
For if he says to his master, “I have wronged you,” his master has mercy on him. But if, after doing wrong, he tells his master, “I have not sinned,” he only increases his master's anger.
Remember, my dear friend, the son who squandered his possessions: when he confessed to his father, his father forgave his offenses. And likewise the sinful woman, whose offenses were many:
When she approached our Lord, he forgave her many sins and showed her mercy. Zacchaeus the tax collector was also a sinner, but he confessed his sins, and our Lord forgave him.
Our Savior also said this: “I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.” For our Lord died for sinners.
His coming was not in vain. The apostle also said of himself, “I was a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an abusive man, but God had mercy on me.”
Again he said this: “Christ died for us.” For the sheep that was lost from the whole flock—its master sought it, found it, and rejoiced over it.
And the watchers of heaven rejoice when a sinner turns back from his wrongdoing. For the Father in heaven does not want one of these little ones to perish,
those who have sinned and need repentance. Our Lord did not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.
Whenever any one of us becomes weak, let us share his suffering; and when someone stumbles, let us burn with anguish for him.
When pain strikes one of our limbs, let us work to treat its wound until it is healed. When one of our limbs is honored, the whole body is splendid and beautiful.
And when pain strikes one of our limbs, fever overtakes the whole body. Whoever causes one of these little ones to stumble falls into the sea,
with a donkey-driven millstone around his neck. Whoever rejoices at his brother's misfortune will soon suffer that same ruin himself. Whoever tramples his brother underfoot will not be forgiven.
There is no cure for the scoffer's wound, and the mocker's sins are not forgiven. For whoever digs a pit falls into it,
and whoever rolls a stone will have it roll back on him. Someone who slips and falls should not say, “Let everyone become like me.” And a rich person who has fallen into poverty
should not say, “Let all the rich become like me.” For if his request is granted, who will make up his own loss?
I have written all these things to you, my dear friend, because in our generation there are some who choose to become celibates,
members of the covenant and holy people. We engage in a contest against our adversary, and our adversary fights against us,
to turn us back to the natural condition that we left of our own free will. Some of us are defeated and wounded, yet, though guilty, they declare themselves innocent.
And although we know their faults, these people persist in the same attitude and are unwilling to approach repentance.
Because of their shame they die the second death, and they do not remember the [?] of their consciences. There is also someone who confesses his fault,
but they do not grant him repentance. O steward of Christ, grant repentance to your fellow servant, and remember that your Lord did not reject those who repent.
Weeds are sown in the field, and the owner of the crop did not allow his servants to clear the weeds from among the wheat until harvest time.
The net is spread in the sea, and the fish are not sorted until it is brought up. The servants received money from their master,
and the worthless servant is judged by his master. Wheat and straw are mixed together, and the owner of the threshing floor separates and cleans them. Many are invited to the banquet,
and the one who has no proper clothing is sent out into the darkness by his master. The wise women and the foolish women stand together, and the master of the bridal chamber knows whom he will admit.
O shepherds, disciples of our Lord, tend the flock and guide it well. Strengthen the weak and support the sick.
Bandage the injured, heal the lame, and guard the well-fed sheep for the owner of the flock. Do not resemble the ignorant and foolish shepherd,
who in his foolishness could not tend the flock. His arm withered and his eye went blind because he said, “Let the dying sheep die, and let the lost sheep perish.
And let the one that remains eat the flesh of its companions.” When the chief shepherd comes, he will condemn the ignorant and foolish shepherd,
because he did not care well for his fellow servants. But whoever tends the flock and guides it well is called a good and diligent servant, because he presented the flock to the shepherd intact.
O watchmen, keep a good watch and warn all the people about the sword, lest the sword come and take a life. That person is taken away because of their sins,
but you will be held accountable for their blood. If, however, a life is taken after the warning, that person is taken away because of their sins,
and you are not blamed. O well-fed sheep, do not gore the weak, lest you be condemned by our great shepherd when he comes.
Accept this appeal, my beloved, which draws near to those who repent and warns the righteous. This world is a world of grace, and until it ends there is repentance in it.
The time is approaching when grace will pass away and justice will reign, and there will be no repentance at that time. Justice is silent because grace has prevailed in its strength.
When the time of justice approaches, grace is unwilling to receive those who repent, because a limit has been set for its departure.
After that there is no more repentance. Read, my beloved, and learn, understand, and see that everyone needs this, to a greater or lesser extent.
For many run in the stadium, but the victorious contestant takes the crown, and everyone receives a reward according to their labor.
The Demonstration on Those Who Repent is completed.
The Demonstration on the Resurrection of the Dead.
For disputes continually arise about this: “How do the dead rise, and with what body will they come?”
They say, “Look, the body wears away and decays. Even the bones, after a long time has passed, crumble and are no longer recognizable.
And if you enter a tomb in which a hundred dead people are buried, you will not find a fistful of dust there.”
Those who hold these views say this: “We know that the dead rise, but they put on a heavenly body
and spiritual forms. If this is not so,” they say, “consider these hundred dead people buried in one grave.
After a long time has passed, there is nothing at all there. And when the dead come to life and put on a body and rise,
it is a heavenly body that they put on. Where did that body come from? For look, there is nothing in the grave.”
But anyone who thinks these things is foolish and without knowledge. When the dead entered, however, they were something,
and after a long time they became nothing. When the time comes for the dead to rise, that nothing becomes something,
in accordance with its original nature, and a transformation is added to its nature. You senseless person who thinks these things, listen to what the blessed apostle says
when he reasons with a fool like you: “Fool! The seed you sow does not come to life unless it dies. And what you sow
is not like what grows up as a plant, but a single bare grain of wheat or barley or one of the other seeds.
Each seed is given its own body. God clothes your seed with its body as he wishes.”
Now, fool, be convinced by this: each seed puts on its own body. You never sow wheat and reap barley,
and you never plant a vine and have it produce figs. Rather, everything proceeds according to its nature. So too, the very body that fell into the earth is the one that rises.
As for the body decaying and wasting away, you ought to be convinced by this same example of the seed: just as the seed, when it falls into the earth,
rots and decays, yet from its very rottenness sprouts, shoots up, and bears fruit. For plowed ground into which no seed has fallen
bears no fruit, even if that ground drinks up all the rain. And a grave in which no dead people are buried—
no people will come out of it at the resurrection of the dead, even if the full blast of the trumpet sounds within it. But if, as they say,
the spirits of the righteous ascend to heaven and put on a heavenly body, they are in heaven, and the one who raises the dead dwells in heaven. So when our Life-giver comes,
whom does he raise from the earth? And why is it written for us that the hour will come, and is already here, when even the dead will hear the voice of the Son of Man
and live and come out of their graves? For a heavenly body does not come, enter the grave, and then come back out of it.
For this is what foolish people say: “Why did the apostle say that the body in heaven is one thing and the body on earth another?”
But whoever hears this should also hear the other thing the apostle said: “There is a natural body, and there is a spiritual body.”
And again he said: “We shall all sleep, but we shall not all be changed.” And again he said: “This mortal thing is destined to put on immortality,
and this corruptible thing to put on incorruptibility.” Again he said: “We must all stand before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each person may receive repayment in his body
for what he previously did, whether good or evil.” Again he said: “What will those who are baptized on behalf of the dead do?
For if the dead do not rise, why are they baptized on their behalf?” Again he said: “If there is no resurrection of the dead, then Christ has not risen either.”
And if Christ has not risen, your faith and our preaching are useless. And if that is so, we are found to be false witnesses,
because we testified about God that he raised Christ, whom he did not raise. So, if the dead do not rise, there is no judgment either. And if there is no judgment,
then let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die. He says, “Do not be deceived: bad conversations corrupt good minds.”
As for what the apostle said, that the body in heaven is one thing and the body on earth another, you should understand this statement as follows:
when the body of the righteous rises and is transformed, it is called heavenly. But the one that is not transformed is called earthly in its nature.
Now listen, my dear friend, to a statement like this, which the same apostle also made. For he said, “The spiritual person judges everything,
but is judged by no one.” And again he said, “Those who belong to the Spirit think about the things of the Spirit, and those who belong to the flesh
think about the things of the flesh.” And again he said, “When we were in the flesh, sinful passions were at work in our bodily members,
so that we would bear fruit for death.” Again he said, “If the Spirit of Christ is in you, you belong to the Spirit.” The apostle said all these things
while he was clothed in flesh and was doing the works of the Spirit. So too, at the resurrection of the dead, a transformation takes place for the righteous,
and the earthly form is swallowed up by the heavenly, and the body is called heavenly. But the one that is not transformed is called earthly.
Now, my dear friend, I will persuade you about this resurrection of the dead as far as I can. For in the beginning God created Adam; he formed him from dust and made him stand.
For if, when Adam did not exist, he made him out of nothing, how much easier it is for him to raise him now, since he is already sown in the earth!
For if God were to do things that are easy for us, his works would not seem great to us. For among human beings there are
skilled craftsmen who make astonishing things. And those who were not the makers of these works stand and marvel,
saying, “How did these things come to be?” The work of their fellows seems difficult to them. How much more, then, should God's works be counted among wonders!
But for God, bringing the dead to life is no great thing. When no seed had been sown in the earth, the earth brought forth what had not fallen into it.
And when it had not conceived, it gave birth in its virginity. How, then, is it difficult for the earth to bring forth again what has fallen into it?
It is pregnant and will give birth, and its labor pains are near, as Isaiah said: “Who has seen anything like this, and who has heard anything like these things:
that the earth goes into labor in a single day, and a people is born in a single hour?” For Adam was not sown, yet he sprang up; he was not conceived, yet he was born.
But now his children have been sown, and they await the rain and will spring up. The earth is pregnant with many, and the time for it to give birth is near.
For all our fathers waited and ran in the hope of the resurrection and the coming to life of the dead, as the blessed apostle said:
“If the righteous had been looking forward to that city from which Abraham departed, they would have had time
to return and go back to it. But they show that they are looking forward to a better one, the one in heaven.”
And they were waiting to be released and go there soon. From what I have written to you, understand and see that they were awaiting the resurrection.
For when our father Jacob was dying, he made his son Joseph swear an oath and said to him, “Bury me in the tomb of my ancestors,
beside Abraham and Sarah, and Isaac and Rebekah.” But why, my beloved, did Jacob not want to be buried in Egypt,
but with his ancestors? By this he showed beforehand that he was awaiting the resurrection of the dead, so that when the shout and the sound of the trumpet came,
his resurrection would be close to that of his ancestors, and at the resurrection he would not be mixed with the wicked who return to Sheol and to torment.
Likewise, Joseph also made his brothers swear an oath and said to them, “When God remembers you, take my bones up from here with you.”
His brothers did as Joseph had said and kept the oath for one hundred and twenty-five years. At that very time,
when the Lord’s armies went out from the land of Egypt, Moses took Joseph’s bones and went out.
The bones of the righteous man were precious to him, and he valued them more than the gold and silver that the Israelites took from the Egyptians
when they plundered them. Joseph’s bones remained in the wilderness for forty years, and at the time when Moses died,
he passed them on to Joshua son of Nun. For the bones of his ancestor Joseph were more valuable to him than all the plunder of the land he conquered.
But why did Moses give Joseph’s bones to Joshua? It was because he was from the tribe
of Ephraim, Joseph’s son. He buried them in the promised land, so that there would be a treasure in that land, where Joseph’s bones were buried.
Also, when Jacob was dying, he blessed his tribes and showed them what would happen to them in the last days.
He said to Reuben, “Reuben, you are my firstborn, my strength and the first of my vigor. You went astray; like water, you will not remain, because you went up to your father’s bed.
Truly, you defiled my bed and went up.” From the time Jacob died until Moses died, there were two hundred and thirty-three years.
Then Moses wished, through his priesthood, to make atonement for Reuben, who had done wrong and sinned by sleeping with Bilhah, his father’s concubine,
so that when his brothers rose, he would not be excluded from their number. For at the beginning of his blessings he said, “Let Reuben live and not die, and let him be included in the number.”
And when the time came for Moses to sleep with his ancestors, he was distressed and grieved, and he pleaded with his Lord and begged
to cross over into the promised land. But why, my beloved, was Moses, a righteous man, grieved that he had not entered the promised land?
It was because he wanted to go and be buried with his ancestors, rather than be buried in the land of his enemies, in the land of Moab.
For the Moabites had hired Balaam son of Beor to curse Israel. This was why Moses wanted not to be buried in that land,
so that the Moabites would not come and take revenge on him, uncover the righteous man’s bones, and throw them away.
His Lord showed kindness to Moses: he brought him up Mount Nebo and showed him the whole land, making it pass before him.
When Moses looked over the whole land and looked at the mountain of the Jebusites, the place where the Divine Presence was destined to dwell, he grieved and wept,
when he saw the tomb in Hebron, where his ancestors Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob were buried, because he would not be buried beside them.
And his bones would be thrown upon their bones, and he would rise with them at the resurrection. And when he had seen the whole land, his Lord encouraged him and said to him:
“I will bury you and hide you, and no one will know your grave.” And Moses died at the word of the Lord’s mouth, and he buried him in the valley in the land of Moab,
opposite Beth-peor, the place where Israel sinned. And no one has known his grave to this day. Now there were two good things
that his Lord did for Moses by not revealing his grave to the Israelites. The first was so that his enemies would not know it
and throw his bones out of his grave. The second was so that his own people would not know it and make his grave a house of worship,
because he was regarded as a god in the eyes of his people. Understand this, my dear friend, from the fact that when he left them and went up the mountain, they said:
“As for this Moses who brought us up from the land of Egypt, we do not know what has happened to him.” And they made themselves a calf and worshiped it.
They did not remember God, who had brought them up from Egypt through Moses, with a mighty hand and an uplifted arm.
For this reason God protected Moses and did not reveal his grave, so that, if his grave became known, his people would not go astray
and make themselves an image, worship it, and offer sacrifices to it, and through their sins disturb the bones of the righteous man.
Moses himself also openly proclaimed the resurrection of the dead. For he spoke as though from the mouth of his God: “I put to death,
and I bring to life.” Hannah also said this in her prayer: “The Lord puts to death and brings to life; he brings down to Sheol and brings up.”
The prophet Isaiah also said this: “Your dead will live, Lord, and their bodies will rise. Those who lie in the dust will awake and give praise.”
David also proclaimed and said: “Look, you perform wonders for the dead, and the mighty ones will rise and give thanks to you,
and those in the graves will recount your grace.” And how do they recount God’s grace in the graves? It is when they hear the sound of the trumpet calling,
and the horn sounding from on high, and the shaking that takes place, and the graves opening, and the mighty ones rising with praise.
They speak to one another in the graves and say: “Great is the grace that has been shown to us! Our hope had been cut off, but now we have hope.
We were imprisoned in darkness, and we have come out into the light. We were sown in decay, and we have risen in glory. We were buried as natural beings,
and we have risen as spiritual beings. We were also sown in weakness, and we have risen in power.” This is the grace they recount in the graves.
And it was not in words alone, my dear friend, that God said, “I bring the dead to life.” He also showed us through deeds, with many testimonies.
So that we would have no doubt, he showed us clearly beforehand. For through Elijah the wonder was revealed that the dead come to life
and those who lie in the dust rise. For when the widow’s son died, Elijah brought him to life and gave him to his mother. And Elisha, his disciple, also
brought the Shunammite woman’s son to life, so that the testimony of two might be established and confirmed for us. And upon the bones of Elisha, too,
the Israelites threw a dead man, and that dead man came to life and rose, and the testimony of three was confirmed.
And through the prophet Ezekiel, too, the resurrection of the dead was clearly revealed, when God brought him out into the valley and showed him many bones.
He led him all around them and said to him, “Son of man, can these bones live?” Ezekiel said to him, “You know, Lord of lords.”
The Lord said to him, “Son of man, prophesy over these bones. Prophesy and say to the dry bones, ‘Hear the word of the Lord of lords.’”
When he made them hear these words, there was a shaking and a noise, and the bones gathered together, even those that had been crushed to pieces
and broken. The prophet saw them and marveled as they came from every direction, and each bone received its companion.
Each joint approached its matching joint, and they were fitted together. Their dryness became moist, and the joints were wrapped in sinews.
Blood surged in the arteries, skin spread over the flesh, and hair grew naturally. They lay there, but there was no breath in them.
Then he again commanded the prophet and said to him, “Prophesy to the breath and say to it, ‘Come, breath, from the four winds,
and breathe into these slain people so that they may live.’” When he made them hear this other word, breath entered them, and they lived and stood on their feet—a very great army.
But why, my beloved, did these dead people not rise through Ezekiel at a single word, with their resurrection completed in both bones and breath?
For the bones were fitted together at one word, and the breath came at another. It was so that perfection would remain with our Lord Jesus Christ,
who, with one voice and one word, will raise Adam’s entire body at the end. For it was not the word that was deficient,
but its bearer was small. Understand and see from this that Elijah and his disciple Elisha, too, when they brought the dead to life,
did not raise them with a single word. Rather, only after they had prayed and pleaded and spent no little time did the dead rise.
Our Lord, too, at his first coming, brought three dead people to life so that the testimony of three would be established. He raised each one of them with two utterances.
For when he brought the widow’s son to life, he called him twice, saying to him, “Young man, young man, rise!” And he came to life and rose.
Again, he called the synagogue leader’s daughter twice, saying to her, “Girl, girl, rise!” And her spirit returned, and she rose.
When Lazarus died and he went to the tomb, he prayed earnestly and called out in a loud voice, saying, “Lazarus, come out!” And he came to life and came out of his tomb.
All this I have explained to you—that these dead people rose at two utterances each—because two resurrections were to take place for them.
One is this resurrection, and the second is the one to come, because in that resurrection, in which all human beings will rise, there will be no falling again.
At a single word from God, sent through his Messiah, all the dead will rise swiftly, in the blink of an eye.
For its bearer is not small and deficient, since with a single word that he calls out, he makes all the ends of the earth hear.
All who lie down will leap up and rise, and the word will not return empty to the one who sent it. Rather, as it is written in the prophet Isaiah,
he compares the word to rain and snow. For he says, “Just as rain and snow come down from heaven and do not return there,
but make the earth sprout and bring forth, giving seed to the sower and bread to eat, so will the word that goes out from my mouth be.
It will not return to me empty, but will do what I desire and accomplish what I sent it to do.” For rain and snow do not return to heaven.
For they carry out the will of their sender on earth. And the message sent through his Messiah, who is his Word and his message, returned to him with great power.
For when he comes and brings it, it descends like rain and snow. Through it all the seeds sprout, and through it they bear righteous fruit.
And the message returned to its sender, and its journey was not fruitless. Rather, it spoke this way before its sender:
“Here I am, and the children whom the Lord has given me.” This is the voice through which the dead live. Our Savior testified about it when he said, “The hour will come
when even the dead will hear the voice of the Son of Man and come out of their graves.” As it is written, “In the beginning was the voice, which is the Word.”
Again he said, “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us.” This is the voice of God, crying out from on high and raising all the dead.
Our Lord also explained the resurrection of the dead to the Sadducees when they brought him the example of a woman who had been married to seven men. They said to him,
“Look, she was the wife of all of them. At the resurrection of the dead, whose wife will she be?” Then our Lord said to them, “You are greatly mistaken,
and you do not know the Scriptures or the power of God. For those who are worthy of that world and of the resurrection from the dead—
the men do not take wives, nor do the women marry men, because they cannot die, for they are like the angels of God
and are children of the resurrection. But concerning the resurrection, that the dead will rise, have you not read in Scripture what God said to Moses from the bush:
‘I am the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob’? Now God is not the God of the dead, for they are all alive to him.”
Yet there are some who, even while alive, are dead to God. He gave Adam a commandment and said to him,
“On the day you eat from the tree, you will surely die.” After he transgressed the commandment and ate, he lived nine hundred and thirty years.
But to God he was considered dead because of his sins. I will demonstrate to you, so that you may be certain, that a sinner is called dead even while alive.
For this is written in the prophet Ezekiel: “As I live, says the Lord of lords, I do not desire the death of the dead sinner.”
Our Lord also spoke to the man who said to him, “Let me go and bury my father, and then come to you.” Our Lord said to him, “Let the dead bury their dead.
But you, go and proclaim the kingdom of God.” How do you understand this saying, my dear friend? Have you ever seen dead people burying their dead?
Or how can a dead person get up to bury another dead person? Rather, accept this explanation from me: a sinner, while alive, is dead to God,
