We too observe the feast of Unleavened Bread, the festival of our Savior. They eat unleavened bread with bitter herbs, but our Savior rejected that cup of bitterness.
He took away all the bitterness of the nations when he tasted it and did not wish to drink. But the Jews call their sins to remembrance against themselves from time to time,
while we commemorate our Savior’s crucifixion and humiliation. For at Passover they came out from slavery to Pharaoh,
and on the day of the crucifixion we were delivered from slavery to Satan. They slaughtered a lamb from the flock and were rescued from the destroyer by its blood.
And we have been redeemed by the blood of the chosen Son from the destructive deeds we used to do. They had Moses as their leader.
And we have Jesus as our guide and Savior. For them Moses divided the sea and brought them across, while our Savior divided Sheol and broke its gates,
when he entered it and opened them. He cleared a path before all who believe in him. They were given manna to eat,
while our Lord gave us his body to eat. For them he brought water out of the rock, while for us our Savior made living water flow from his belly.
To them he promised the land of the Canaanites as an inheritance, while to us he pledged the land of the living. For them Moses lifted up a bronze serpent,
so that everyone who saw it would recover from the serpent’s bite. For us Jesus lifted himself up, so that when we look toward him we may be delivered from the bite of the serpent, who is Satan.

For them Moses made a temporary tabernacle, where they could offer sacrifices and offerings to receive forgiveness for their sins. And Jesus raised up David’s tabernacle, which had fallen and rose again.
And he also said to the Jews, “When you tear down this temple that you see, I will raise it up in three days.”
His disciples understood that he was speaking about his body: when they tore it down, he would raise it up in three days. In this very tabernacle he promised us life,
and in it our sins are forgiven. He called theirs a temporary tabernacle because it serves for only a short time, while ours is the temple of the Holy Spirit forever.
Now understand, my beloved, concerning this Passover lamb, how the Holy One commanded that it be eaten in one house and not in many houses.
The one house is the church of God. He also said that hired workers and resident foreigners must not eat any of it. And who are the hired workers and resident foreigners,
if not the teachings of the Evil One, which are not permitted to eat the Passover? Our Savior said about them,
“The hired worker, who does not own the sheep, leaves the sheep and runs away when he sees the wolf coming.” And he said, “Do not eat any of it raw,
nor boiled in water.” This is clear and plain: the offering that is presented in the church of God is roasted over fire,
and is not boiled, nor is it offered raw. And he said, “This is how you are to eat it: with your belts fastened around your waists,
your sandals on your feet, and your staffs in your hands.” These mysteries are very great. Whoever eats of the true Lamb, Christ,
fastens faith around his waist, puts the readiness of the gospel on his feet, and takes in his hand the sword of the Spirit,
which is the word of God. He also said, “Not a bone in it is to be broken.” This was fulfilled on the day they crucified him,
when they broke the legs of those who were crucified with him but did not break his. And he said that the written word was fulfilled:
“Not a bone in him will be broken.” And he said that a slave bought with money may eat the Passover only after the flesh of his foreskin has been circumcised.
For the slave who is purchased is the sinful person who repents and is purchased by the blood of Christ. And when he has circumcised his heart, cutting away evil deeds,
he then approaches baptism, the fulfillment of true circumcision. He joins the people of God and shares in the body and blood of Christ.
As for his saying, “Eat it in haste,” this is practiced in the church of God: they eat the Lamb in haste,
with fear and trembling, standing on their feet, because they are eager to eat life from the gift of the Spirit that they have received.
For Israel was baptized in the sea on that night of Passover, on the day of deliverance. And our Savior washed his disciples’ feet
on the night of Passover—a mystery of baptism. And know, my beloved, that it was only on that night that our Savior gave the true baptism.
For as long as he was going about with his disciples, they were administering the baptism of the law, with which the priests baptized:
a baptism according to what John said, “Repent of your sins.” But on that night he showed them the mystery of baptism into the suffering of his death,
as the apostle said: “You were buried with him through baptism into death, and you rose with him through the power of God.”
But know, my beloved, that John’s baptism did not bring forgiveness of sins, but repentance. The Acts
of the twelve apostles proclaims this, when the disciples question those who had been called from the nations and from Israel, saying to them,
“Have you been baptized?” They said, “We were baptized with John’s baptism.” Then they baptized them with the true baptism,
the mystery of our Savior’s suffering. Our Savior also testified to this when he said to his disciples, “John baptized with water,
but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.” For our Savior took water and poured it into a washbasin, took a linen cloth and tied it around his waist,
and began to wash his disciples’ feet. When he came to Simon Peter, Simon said to him, “Are you, my Lord, washing my feet?
You will never wash my feet!” Jesus said to him, “Unless I wash you, you have no share with me.”
Simon said to him, “Then, my Lord, wash not only my feet, but also my hands and my head.” Jesus said to him,
“Someone who has bathed needs only to wash his feet.” When he had washed his disciples’ feet, he took his clothes, reclined at the table, and said to them,
“You call me ‘our Teacher’ and ‘our Lord,’ and that is what I am. If I, then, your Teacher and your Lord, wash your feet,
how much more ought you to wash one another’s feet! I have shown you this example, so that you may do as I have done.”
After he had washed their feet and reclined at the table, he gave them his body and his blood. This was unlike Israel, who, after eating the Passover,
were then baptized in the cloud and in the sea, as the apostle said: “Our ancestors were all under the cloud, and they all passed through the sea.”
I have written these few words of persuasion to you so that you may go out in spirit against the Jews, because they observe the appointed time of the Passover feast

in violation of the commandment, although they have no authority to do so. They make a chest and an ark of the covenant, although they have not been commanded to do so. They do not understand the prophet who said,
“They will no longer say, ‘The ark of the covenant of the Lord.’ It will not come to mind. They will not remember it or attend to it, and it will not be made again.”
Since he said that it would not be made again, would not come to mind, and would not be attended to, know, my beloved, that whoever makes it has violated the commandment.
Jeremiah also said, “The people of Israel and the people of Judah have broken my covenant.” Concerning the covenant that would be given to the people, he proclaimed:
“I will establish a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah, not like the covenant that I gave their ancestors
on the day when I took them by the hand and brought them out of the land of Egypt. Because they broke my covenant, I too rejected them.”
And if they say, “Look, it was to Israel and Judah that he said he would give a new covenant”—for the one who called Israel “rulers of Sodom” and “people of Gomorrah”
is the one who called Abraham and made him a promise when he blessed him and said to him, “Your name shall no longer be called Abram, but your name shall be Abraham,
because I have made you the father of a multitude of nations.” And again he said to him, “Through your offspring all the nations of the earth shall be blessed.”
So that you may be convinced and convince the brothers who belong to your church and dispute about this date of Passover: these things are not difficult for those of sound understanding to know.
For if the day of the Passover of our Savior’s suffering falls for us on Sunday itself, according to the law we ought to observe it on Monday,
so that its entire week may be observed with its commemoration of the suffering and its unleavened bread, because after Passover there are seven days of unleavened bread,
until the twenty-first. And if the commemoration of the suffering falls on another day, on any one of the days of the week, we have no reason to dispute about these things.
But our great day is Friday. And although, in the reckoning of the month, the day of the crucifixion, on which our Savior suffered
and was among the dead for its night and day, is the fifteenth—from the sixth hour on Friday until the dawn of Sunday—
he rose on Sunday, the sixteenth. For at the beginning of the fourteenth he ate the Passover with his disciples, according to the law of Israel.
And on that same Friday, the fourteenth, he was on trial until the sixth hour, and he was crucified at the third hour.
He descended to the abode of the dead on the night leading into the fifteenth. On the Sabbath day, which was the fifteenth, he was in the abode of the dead.
And on the night leading into Sunday, which was the sixteenth, he rose and appeared to Mary Magdalene and to two of his disciples as they were walking along the road.
From now on, let anyone who falls into disputing about these days understand that at the beginning of the fourteenth our Lord celebrated the Passover and ate and drank with his disciples.
But from the time the rooster crowed, he neither ate nor drank again, because they seized him and began to put him on trial.
And as I explained to you above, he was in the abode of the dead on the fifteenth, throughout its night and day.
But this is what is required of us: to observe the feast at its proper time, from year to year; to fast in purity and pray continually;
to offer praise diligently and sing hymns fittingly; to give the sign, administer baptism properly, and offer the blessings of consecration at their appointed times;
and to fulfill all the observances of the feast. For our Lord suffered and rose, and from now on he no longer dies, and death has no power over him.
For the death he died, he died to sin once; but the life he lives, he lives to God. And us also, who were dead, he brought to life with him. For if we dispute about these things
and concern ourselves only with the fourteenth, and not with the feast that comes from year to year, we would be obliged to observe the fourteenth of every month
and mourn on the Friday of every week. Yet it is fitting that all the days of the week should be for us
an opportunity to do what is good before the Lord our God. So be persuaded by this little that I have written to you. You are not commanded to engage in contentious disputes over words,
in which there is no benefit, but to have a pure heart that keeps the commandment and the feast and the appointed times of the watches of the day.
The Demonstration on Passover is ended.
Demonstration on the Sabbath
The Lord commanded Moses his servant concerning the Sabbath day, that the Israelites should observe it. For this is what he said to them:
“For six days you shall do your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath of rest, holy to the Lord your God.
For in six days the Lord made heaven and earth, the seas and everything in them, and he stopped and rested on the seventh day.
Therefore God blessed the seventh day and made it holy, because on it he rested from all the works he had done.”
And he instructed them in this way: “You shall rest, along with your male servant, your female servant, your oxen, and your donkey.” He went further and instructed them:
“The hired worker, the resident foreigner, and every animal that grows weary and toils in servitude shall rest.” Now, my dear friend, concerning this Sabbath day,
in which the Jewish people take pride and boast, saying, “By this we live, because we observe the Sabbath and the festival,”
I will explain it to you as well as I can in a few words, just as I explained circumcision and Passover to you.
For the Sabbath was not established as a dividing line between death and life, nor between righteousness and sin, but was given for rest,
unlike other commandments by which people live, but die if they do not carry them out. For when the Sabbath was observed,
it was as something given for the people's rest—not only for human beings to rest, but also for animals. For he said, “Your ox and your donkey and all your livestock shall rest.”
For if the Sabbath was established as a dividing line between death and life, and between righteousness and sins, what benefit is there for an animal that observes the Sabbath?
Or what harm will it suffer if it does not observe it? For we see that on the other days, when an animal performs servile work and strenuous labor,
it is more righteous, far more than on the Sabbath day. For on working days the animal works and grows weary
with burdens and loads, and the oxen pull the plow. Because they are weary, they have no opportunity to commit sins. But on the Sabbath day,
when donkeys, oxen, and all animals of every kind are idle, they are not prevented from mating with their mothers, their sisters, or any of their close relatives,
and they are not charged with sin for committing these sins on the Sabbath day.
For this is the law of all animals. And know that just as an animal incurs no sin by engaging in these things, neither does it gain righteousness.
For the reward for righteousness comes in the new world, at the resurrection of the dead, to those who do righteous deeds.
But an animal will have no resurrection in which to receive a reward for observing the Sabbath, nor will it come to judgment.

And just as the law has not imposed any other commandment on an animal for it to observe, neither does the Sabbath benefit it in any way. For the Holy One commanded in his law, “You shall not commit adultery.”
Yet animals commit adultery publicly and engage openly in sexual immorality. And the law commanded and warned, “Cursed is anyone who takes his sister,” along with all the rest of his close relatives.
Animals do all these things. Again, it is written, “You shall not kill.” Yet an animal, because of its lack of understanding, kills its mate and eats its flesh.
Again, it is written, “Slaughter and eat anything, but do not eat blood.” Yet an animal licks up its own blood.
And unclean meat is more pleasant for it to eat. For if an animal gains any benefit by keeping the Sabbath,
the law should first have forbidden it these unclean things, and then it would have been justified by keeping the Sabbath.
And this is the argument I have written: the Sabbath was given for rest to every creature that is full of weariness. For if it had not been given for rest to every body that grows weary,
then creatures that do not grow weary should also have kept the Sabbath from the earliest times, so that they too might be justified.
But we see that the sun travels, the moon moves along, the stars run, the winds blow, and the clouds fly,
and birds travel, springs surge with their flowing waters, waves rise up, and lightning flashes race along and illuminate creation,
and thunderclaps thunder repeatedly in their season, trees bring forth their fruit, and the growth of everything gains strength.
And we see nothing that rests on the Sabbath day except human beings and livestock, who are subject to the bondage of labor.
For if the Sabbath had been given for righteousness, it should have been given to Adam before Israel, so that he might keep it and be justified through it.
And God would not have given him the command not to eat from the tree of the knowledge of evil and good, so that he would not die.
But because Adam had not been subjected to labor before he transgressed the commandment, he did not give him the Sabbath. Rather, after he transgressed the commandment,
he then received the sentence of exhausting labor: to toil on the earth as a guilty offender. And he sentenced him to death.
For if righteousness had depended on the Sabbath, Enoch would have found favor through it, as would all the generations after him.
Nor did Noah keep the Sabbath so that through it he might be called blameless and free of sins. Rather, God said this to Noah:
“I have seen that you are righteous and blameless in this generation.” He was not justified by keeping the Sabbath, but by maintaining his integrity in a corrupt generation,
as the course of the account makes clear. For it is not even written that he had intercourse in the world. “Noah,” it says, “was five hundred years old,”
when God spoke with him and said to him, “I have seen that you are righteous and blameless before me in this generation.”
And his integrity, as it appears to us, consisted in this: when he saw that the descendants of Seth had intermingled with the household of Cain, who were cursed,
he resolved not to take a wife or father children, so that they would not intermingle and become cursed along with the household of Cain, the cursed offspring.
And when God saw that his heart was pure and blameless, he wished a replacement for the world to come from him, since he had decided to wipe them out because of their wickedness.
Then he spoke with him when he was five hundred years old and said, “I have seen that you are blameless before me in this generation,”
when he still had no son. For, as the account itself indicates to us, just as I noted above, Noah had not taken a wife
during all that time, until God spoke with him and said to him, “I have seen that you are blameless before me in this generation.
Now,” he said, “make yourself an ark of wood in which you may take shelter.” When Noah heard these things—that God had commanded him to make an ark
and had said to him, “I will utterly wipe humankind from the face of the earth, because they have corrupted their ways”—then, in his five hundredth year,
Noah took a wife from the daughters of Seth, the blessed line of the righteous, and fathered Shem, Ham, and Japheth, these three.
Noah warned his sons not to take wives from the daughters of Cain. Instead, he gave them wives from the line of the righteous,

so that offspring from them might be preserved on the face of the earth, and the world might be sustained through them. To let you know that these things are so, I will show you from the reckoning of the years.
For Shem, Noah’s firstborn, had a son, Arpachshad, two years after the flood. Shem was a hundred years old when he fathered Arpachshad,
two years after the flood. From these facts we learn that Noah was five hundred and two years old when he fathered Shem.
Understand from this reckoning that Noah did not take a wife before God spoke with him, nor did he take wives for his sons
until the time when he was about to enter the ark. For if he had taken a wife in his youth, he would also have fathered children,
like Adam, who was a hundred and thirty years old when he fathered Seth. Seth was a hundred and five years old when he fathered Enosh, and Enosh was ninety years old when he fathered Kenan.
Kenan was seventy years old when he fathered Mahalalel, and Mahalalel was sixty-five years old when he fathered Jared.
Jared was a hundred and sixty-two years old when he fathered Enoch, and Enoch was sixty-five years old when he fathered Methuselah.
Methuselah was a hundred and eighty-seven years old when he fathered Lamech, and Lamech, Noah’s father, was a hundred and eighty-two years old when he fathered him.
He too, if he had taken a wife before God spoke with him, would have fathered children like his ancestors, for infertility had not held sway over him.
For at that time human beings were blessed to increase and multiply through their offspring, so that the world might be filled with them.
For Noah, who kept his integrity, was not afraid for himself, that he might mingle with the cursed line of Cain’s household,
but rather that, when he took a wife and fathered sons, his sons might transgress the law and take wives from that line.
But when he saw that God spoke with him and said to him, “I will wipe humankind from the face of the earth, and you alone I will save,”
then he took a wife so that he might have offspring through whom the world would be sustained, and so that he might become a father of the upright and the righteous.
The Holy Spirit chose him so that even Christ, who gives life to the world and abolishes Adam’s curses, would be born from his line.
Then he diligently took a wife from the blessed line and fathered Shem, the father of the righteous, in the five hundred and second year of his life,
and in the second year after God spoke with him. When he had fathered three sons, he began to build the ark, and he warned his sons not to take wives
until the time when they would enter the ark, lest they have children who would corrupt their ways
and, because of their sins, not be saved from the wrath that was to come. He kept watch over his sons for ninety-seven years
and took wives for them from the blessed line of his ancestors. Then, in the six hundredth year of Noah’s life, God spoke with him and said to him,
“Enter the ark, you and your wife, and your sons and your sons’ wives with you.” Noah entered the ark at six hundred years of age.
His son Shem was ninety-seven years old when he entered the ark. Then the flood came, and the corrupt generation perished.
Noah and his sons remained in the ark for twelve months and ten days before they came out. From Noah the second world came into being.
For he maintained his integrity in a corrupt generation. He did not observe the Sabbath, nor was he justified by circumcision, but by what I have explained to you.
From Noah was descended Abraham, a faithful man and leader of the righteous, who kept the law when no law had been laid down for him.
He fathered Isaac, the son of the promise, and Jacob, the head of the people. These righteous fathers did not observe the Sabbath.
Rather, they were justified by faith, as it is written: “Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness.”
Isaac and Jacob, his sons, followed their father's commandment and law, and they were justified by faith, not by the Sabbath. And Joseph, in the land of Egypt,
was not justified in his righteousness by observing the Sabbath. When his master's wife set her eye on him, intending to commit an impure act with him,
he spoke and said to his mistress, “How could I do this great evil and sin against God?” By this Joseph was justified, and not by the Sabbath.
For if it had stood between death and life, and between wickedness and righteousness, then to those righteous people whose names I mentioned above,
the Sabbath would have been given for them to observe and live. But the Sabbath was given to be observed for this reason:
so that male and female slaves, hired workers, resident foreigners, and speechless livestock might rest, and those worn out by toil might find rest.
For God cares for his entire creation, including animals and livestock, birds and wild animals. For Moses said,
when he repeated the law to the people, “For six years you shall sow your land and gather its crops, but in the seventh year you shall plow it and leave it,
so that the poor of your people may eat, and the wild animals may eat what remains.” The Holy One also gave this command about birds through Moses his servant:
“When you find a bird's nest before you in any tree or on the ground, with a mother and young or chicks in it,
and the mother is crouching over the young or the chicks, you shall not take the mother with her young. Instead, you must let the mother fly away, but you may take the young for yourself,
so that the Lord your God may bless you for these things.” And David said, “He feeds the young ravens that call to him.” David also said,
“You save human beings and livestock, Lord.” Job also said, “Who set the wild donkey free and removed the yoke from it,
making the plain its home and the salt land its dwelling?” Job also said, “He prepares food for the young eagles.”
And again he said, when speaking of birds and livestock, “They all look to you to give them their food at the proper time.
You give to them, and they are fed; you open your hand, and they are satisfied. But if you turn your face away, they are troubled.” Isaiah also said,
“There the kites gathered, each with its mate. He himself commanded it with his mouth, and his Spirit gathered them. His hand allotted them measured portions as an inheritance.”
See from these things that God cares for his entire creation and forgets nothing. For this very reason he instructed and commanded that the Sabbath day should be a time of rest.
Listen again to what he says: “In six days God made heaven and earth, and he ceased and rested from all his works.
For this reason God blessed the seventh day and made it holy.” What shall we say about this statement, that God rested on the seventh day?
Now listen and be convinced of this: God did not grow tired like a workman in the work of those six days.
Nor did he rest on the seventh day because he was tired. Far be it from us to say that God grew tired! Rather, this is the meaning of the statement:
God completed all his works in six days, and on the seventh day he ceased from all the works he had done.
And listen to the evidence that God does not grow tired. For David said, “The keeper of Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps.” And one who neither slumbers nor sleeps
does not grow tired either. And Isaiah said to the Israelites, “This is what the Lord says: Because thoughts have arisen in your hearts,
‘God is quite unable to save us,’ he said to them through Isaiah, ‘Has my hand been cut short and grown weak? Or have I no power to deliver?
Look, by my rebuke I dry up the sea and turn rivers into a desert. Their fish rot for lack of water and die.
I clothe the heavens in darkness and make sackcloth their covering, just as I dried up the Red Sea in the days of your ancestors
and split the Jordan and brought them across. Even now my hands have been able to save you, but you were sold because of your sins,
and your mother was sent away because of your wickedness. Though I do not grow tired, you have wearied me.’” As the prophet Malachi said, “You have wearied the Lord with your words.”
Now listen and be convinced that God created all his works without growing tired or toiling. For it says, “By the word of the Lord the heavens were made,
and by the breath of his mouth all their hosts.” Adam alone he made with his hands, and it is not written that he grew tired when he made him.
And when he made all created things, he spoke by the word of his mouth and they came into being, without toil and without weariness.
Rather, this is how the statement is to be understood: God ceased from all his works, and God rested on the seventh day.
For if God, who does not grow tired, ceased and rested from his works, how much more fitting is it for someone subject to toil and servitude to rest!
Isaiah also said this about God: “He neither grows tired nor sleeps, and his understanding cannot be fathomed.” Yet elsewhere, because of the people's sins, he said,
“You have enslaved me with your wickedness and wearied me with your sins.” See how in one place it is written that he neither grows tired nor sleeps,
while because of their wickedness he said to Israel, “You have enslaved me and wearied me.” All these words are well written, and the wise understand them with discernment.
As the apostle said, “The law is good if someone reads it with discernment.” And again the prophet said, “The ways of the Lord are straight,
and the wicked stumble in them, while the righteous travel and walk in them without difficulty.” Now this statement that God rested from his works
—which fools understand to mean that he grew tired like a workman—is like the statement he made when he wished to wipe out human beings because their sins had multiplied:
“I regret that I made them.” Otherwise, listen to the apostle, who says, “If it were not so, how would God judge the world?”
Now listen, my dear friend, concerning the Sabbath, and be convinced, just as I convinced you concerning circumcision, in which the people of Israel boast in vain.
Be convinced concerning the Sabbath too, that they take pride in vain in keeping it. For Joshua son of Nun did not let them rest on the Sabbath when he was waging war at Jericho,
as the triumphant apostle said: “If Joshua son of Nun had given them rest, there would have been no further mention of the Sabbath day.”
But God's Sabbath still remains. And again, when the Maccabees' enemies came against them to fight them on the Sabbath day,
they wanted to observe the Sabbath according to the Law. While they were observing it, their enemies came against them on the Sabbath
and killed many of them. When they saw that their enemies had plotted to fight them again while they were observing the Sabbath,
they profaned the Sabbath, fought on it, and defeated their enemies. They were not blamed for breaking the Sabbath. Nor were they alone in breaking the Sabbath,
but the priests in the temple also profaned the Sabbath and were without sin. For on the Sabbath day the priests offered sacrifices:
they slaughtered and skinned animals, split wood, and lit fires. Yet they were not blamed for breaking the Sabbath,
because they had been commanded to do this. For if the priests, who warned the people against sins, profaned the Sabbath—
and was this in some insignificant place? Rather, it was the place where all sins are forgiven—and they committed no offense and incurred no sins,
why are they so proud of observing the Sabbath, which was given for rest, as I have explained to you?
But listen now to what the Sabbath that God desires is. For Isaiah said to them, “This is my rest: give rest to the weary.”
And again he said, “Whoever observes the Sabbath without profaning it.” These are the ones who hold firmly to my covenant and choose what I desire.
To those who do not profane the Sabbath, which is God's rest, he spoke and promised to give them a gift.
For he said, “I will give them in my house and within my walls a name better than sons and daughters.” For the Sabbath is of no benefit to the wicked,
nor to murderers and thieves, but to those who choose what God desires and keep their hands from evil.
God dwells in them and lives among them, as he said, “I will dwell in them and walk among them.” For in Isaiah's days they observed the Sabbath,
yet followed the practices of the unclean nations and acted like Sodom and Gomorrah. They would say to the nations, “Keep away, for I am holy.”
It was about these people that Isaiah said, “These have become smoke in my anger, a fire burning all day long.” He took them and cast them out of his land
and scattered them among all the nations, because they did not observe God's rest but observed the Sabbath only bodily. But let us observe God's Sabbath,
doing what pleases his will, so that we may enter his Sabbath of rest, in which heaven and earth cease their work and all creatures are quiet and at rest.
Let us not be fleeing then, as our Savior said, “Let your flight not be in winter or on the Sabbath.” And the apostle said,
“God's Sabbath still remains.” I have written this brief explanation to you about the Sabbath, against those who boast about it.
The Demonstration on the Sabbath is finished.
Demonstration on Exhortation
All of us, gathered together, resolved to write this letter to all our brothers, the members of the church in every place: the bishops, priests, deacons, and the whole church of God,
together with all her offspring in every place who are with us.

To our dear and beloved brothers, the bishops, priests, and deacons, together with all the children of the church among you and all the people of God in Seleucia, Ctesiphon, and every place: abundant peace in our Lord, our God, and our Life-giver, who through Christ gave us life and brought us near to himself.

We inform you, our brothers and beloved friends—and as we inform you, we also remind ourselves—about what has happened in our days because of our sins, which have multiplied, grown strong, and provoked anger.
Our minds have been darkened and deprived of understanding, and we do not rouse ourselves so that God may turn toward us, as he said through the prophet:
“Turn to me, and I will turn toward you.” Hosea also said, “Take words with you and turn to the Lord.” And Isaiah said:
“Seek the Lord, and when you find him, call upon him. When he is near, let the sinner abandon his way, and the wicked man his thoughts.”
Again it is written, “If you seek the Lord, he will be found by you; but if you abandon him, he will abandon you.” And in David it is written, “The Lord looked down from heaven
to see whether there was anyone who understood and sought God. They have all turned aside and together become corrupt. There is no one who does good, not even one.”
Jeremiah said, “I sought among my people a man who would build a wall and stand in the breach on behalf of the land, so that I would not destroy it, but I found none.”
Again his Lord said to Jeremiah, “Go and say to the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem:
‘How long will you refuse to accept correction?’” Again he said through the prophet, “I called you, but you did not answer.
You will cry loudly in my ears, but I will not listen to you.” Again it is written, “There is no one who regrets his wickedness and says, ‘What have I done?’”
For leaders have arisen among our people who abandoned the law and boasted of injustice. They acquired property, and greed overcame them.
They lent at interest and took usurious profits. No one remembers that it is written, “Do not take usury or interest.” And whoever wishes to dwell in the Lord’s tent
“does not lend his money at interest.” Again he said that whoever does not take interest, does not lend at usury, and does not commit any of the abominations
that Ezekiel listed—God delights in him. In this present time there are people who have acted coercively, perverted justice, and shown partiality.
They acquitted the guilty and condemned the innocent. They loved the rich and hated the poor. They fed themselves and scattered the flock, and the world blinded them.
They loved bribes and drove out truth. They hated correction and loved wickedness. They hated the humble and loved the haughty, the proud, and the boastful.
In their days the light grew dark, the salt lost its flavor, teaching became obscured, and the law lost its strength. The vineyard was laid waste, and thorns sprang up.
People fell asleep, and the evil one sowed his weeds. The waves rose, and the storms grew fierce. The charioteers fell, and the chariots were thrown into confusion.
The sailors slumbered, and their ships sank. The law is bound up, and the testimony is sealed. The priest has become like the people. The ruler asks for gold,
and the judge says, “Give a bribe.” The great man declares his own desire. They despise the poor and deprive the afflicted of the land of their rights.
They bite with their teeth and proclaim peace, but against anyone who puts nothing into their mouths they proclaim war.
They despise justice and pervert everything that is right. They build Zion with blood and Jerusalem with injustice. Her leaders judge for bribes,
her priests teach for wages, and the prophets practice divination for money. Yet they rely on the Lord and say, “Look, the Lord is among us!”
Therefore it is night for them, and they will have darkness instead of divination. They are full of wrath and swollen with resentment. They love mockery and delight in missteps.
They delight in tales about one another, like someone eating honey and licking a honeycomb. Truth has stumbled, and rebuke has fled.
The honored have been debased, and teachers have been despised. They have called good people evil and evil people good. They have made light into darkness and darkness into light.
They have called bitter sweet and sweet bitter. They are wise in their own eyes and discerning in their own estimation.
They acquit the guilty because of his bribe and deprive the innocent of their innocence. Visions are cut off, and prophecy is hidden.
These things we have done, and these things have happened to us. We are plundered, persecuted, and scattered. Those who had no compassion to give now ask us to give them still more.

Because we hated one another, those who hate us without cause have multiplied. Because we mocked, we have been mocked. Because we despised, we have been despised. Because we lied, we have been lied to.

Because we exalted ourselves, we have been brought low. Because we oppressed, we have been oppressed. Because we wronged others, we have been wronged. My beloved, some among us have followed these ways.
They do not administer justice or seek righteousness. No one remembers the prophet who said, “Seek justice and do good to the oppressed.”
For our God, in his abundant mercy, repeatedly gave human beings an explanation when they sinned, and he entered into judgment with humanity.
Although he had the power, he did not act by force. For Isaiah the prophet said, “The Lord stands up to judge; he stands up to judge his people.” He says, “The Lord will enter into judgment
with the elders of his people and their leaders, because they burned the vineyard, stored up what they plundered from the poor, and overpowered and shamed the weak.”
Jeremiah said, “I will enter into judgment with you, says the Lord, as I entered into judgment with your ancestors.” And Micah said, “The Lord enters into judgment with his people
and rebukes Israel.” Isaiah said, “Present your cases, says the Lord; present your arguments, says the King of Jacob.”
Moses said to Israel, “Appoint judges and scribes for yourself in all your tribes, and let them judge the people with righteous judgments.
Do not accept a bribe or show partiality. Instead, listen to the small just as to the great, so that the Lord may bless you.”
Even concerning the dreadful judgment of Sodom, our good God was patient and gave an explanation to Abraham his friend, saying to him
that judgment is not carried out in anger. Again, he came forth in the Spirit to Ezekiel concerning the severe judgment, when the destroyer went out to destroy Jerusalem.
The prophet began to protest, “Why are you bringing an end to everyone who remains of Israel?”
He gave an explanation by showing him the defilement of twenty men, and the prophet was persuaded that the wicked were justly receiving punishment.

He also persuaded Jonah through the growth of the gourd, when Jonah grieved because it had withered. He said to him, “You had pity on the gourd’s shoot, which sprang up in one night and withered in one night.
Should I not have pity on Nineveh, the great city, in which there are more than a hundred and twenty thousand people,
besides the children and infants who do not know their right hand from their left, and the many animals?” Again, when he wished to uproot his vineyard,
because it had produced carobs instead of grapes, he seated the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem in judgment and said, “Judge between me and my vineyard.”
See, my beloved, the compassion of our good Maker: when he destroys the wicked in anger, he saves and rescues the innocent.
For he swept away the generation in Noah’s days because they acted wickedly, but in his mercy he saved Noah and his household.
He overthrew Sodom and its neighboring cities and rescued Lot from the midst of the destruction. In Egypt too, when he killed the Egyptians’ firstborn, he kept the firstborn of the Israelites alive.
In the days of Ezekiel, when he destroyed the city, he placed a mark between the eyes of the righteous men and rescued them. God did not condemn anyone without judgment.
But today there have appeared among our people wise judges who possess foreknowledge: before bringing people to trial, they judge and condemn them.
But one thing is grievous: although they possess foreknowledge, in their judgment they condemn not only people who know their right hand from their left,
but also newborn children and the many infants still in their mothers’ wombs, not yet born, the poor, the wicked, and members of the holy covenant—many tens of thousands.
There appeared among you one of our brothers who assumed the crown, though his own country took no notice of him. When his country was unwilling to accept him,
he went off to other kings, those far away from him, and asked them for chains and fetters. Then he began distributing them to his country and his city.
We suppose that what that king who assumed the crown requested from his fellow kings were gifts rather than chains—though he ought not to have asked them—
and that he distributed them to his nobles and the people of his country and city instead of chains and fetters. Let the wise person listen and understand.
This is why we have written these things, my dear friends: when a king assumes the crown, he receives kingship within his own city and among his nobles.

When they all approve of him, he then enters the treasury, takes many presents and gifts, and distributes them to all his nobles. He grants clemency throughout his kingdom and breaks the chains in all the prisons throughout his dominion.
He releases prisoners, brings out those confined, and gives relief to the distressed, because he has newly received kingship. Then people are confident that he will grow strong in his kingship
and become king over all the people. But this folly is worse than Rehoboam’s, and these judges are more childish in their understanding than the young men who were Rehoboam’s counselors.
Listen again, dear friends. Suppose there is a great king who appoints a steward over all his possessions and his entire household.
Suppose that steward foolishly goes and exalts himself over his fellow servants, raises himself above the king’s attendants, and seizes and imprisons them without trial and without authority.
He beats and insults them, without investigating their case or knowing whether they are guilty or innocent.
Then, from confinement and prison, the servants cry out and inform their master: “This steward of yours, our fellow servant, has imprisoned us without any wrongdoing.
He has neither tried us nor questioned us nor brought an accusation against us.” What do you say, our brothers? Will his master really praise that steward?
We know this: the king removes from office a steward who has imprisoned and insulted his fellow servants without trial, and what he did to his fellow servants is done to him.
For the King has written to us as follows: “With the judgment you pronounce, you will be judged.”
He admonished and warned them, saying, “Pay attention to what you have heard: with the judgment you pronounce, you will be judged.”
For pride and arrogance have brought many down. Through his pride Adam left Paradise and became dust, food for the serpent.
In his pride Cain killed his brother and became a trembling wanderer on the earth. Because Ham exalted himself and mocked his father, he was cursed and became a slave of slaves to his brothers.
Because of his pride Esau lost his birthright as the elder son. Because Pharaoh grew stubborn and exalted himself, he and his army drowned in the Red Sea.

Because the sons of Eli the priest exalted themselves over the people, they were rejected from the priesthood of the Holy One. Goliath the Philistine, in his arrogance toward David, was humbled and put to shame, and fell through his pride.
Abimelech son of Gideon, who exalted himself over his brothers and killed them, was overtaken by the curse of his brother Jotham.
Absalom, who exalted himself and seized the kingdom, fell and was humbled before David’s servants.
Adonijah son of Haggith, who stole the kingdom, neither succeeded nor prospered in his greatness. And Ahithophel, who counseled hateful things, had his pride humbled by his own hands.
Jeroboam son of Nebat, Solomon’s servant, who stirred up division among the people, left an evil memory in Israel.

Ahab son of Omri was overcome by greed and received punishment in the inherited property at Jezreel. And the king of Edom, who exalted himself against Ahab, found that one who straps on his armor is not like one who takes it off.
Haman, who exalted himself against Mordecai, received punishment on the gallows, both he and his sons. And the Babylonians who slandered Daniel had their bones crushed by the lions.
Judas, who betrayed our Savior, fell into the sea with a millstone around his neck. All these were humbled by their pride.
As it is written: “A person’s pride will humble him, but one whose spirit is humble will gain abundant honor.”
Now see, my beloved, how in every age and every generation God has granted great victories through wise people, so that they might reconcile those who are divided and make peace between them.
And not through men alone, but also through women. A woman from Tekoa reconciled Absalom with David at Joab’s counsel.
And through a woman there was peace in Israel when Shammua son of Bichri rebelled against David. A wise woman spoke with Joab from the wall and said:
“Listen, Joab, listen!” He said, “I am listening.” She said to Joab, “In former times they used to say that they would first consult the prophets, and only then destroy.
I am one who makes good the damage done to Israel. Yet you seek to destroy a child and his mother in Israel.” Joab said to her, “Far be it from me!
I will neither ruin nor destroy, for that is not the matter. Rather, one man, Shammua son of Bichri, has raised his hand against King David. Hand him over to us, and we will leave.” She said to him:
“His head will now be thrown to you from the wall.” She went and spoke with all the people. She cut off the head of Shammua son of Bichri, and they threw it from the wall to Joab.
And through a woman there was peace in Israel. Deborah became a mother and administered justice in Israel.
And Jael [?], the wife of Heber the Kenite, cut down and cast away the pride of Sisera, the commander of the army of Jabin [?], king of Hazor, when she drove a peg into his temple.
These Kenites belonged to the household of Moses’ father-in-law. Balaam son of Beor spoke prophetically about them: “Your dwelling is strong, and your nest is set in the cliff.”
And Rebekah, the mother of the righteous, brought about peace between Esau and Jacob when she sent him to Laban.

And our Savior, the great King who reconciled the rebellious world with his Father, took away the guilt of us all while we were guilty, and became the messenger of reconciliation between God and his creation.
While we were guilty and bitter, he asked us to be reconciled to him, as the apostle said: he became the messenger of reconciliation.
And he reconciled us with his Father. Though it was fitting that we, who had done wrong and sinned, should ask and plead for our Maker to be reconciled to us, he asked us to be reconciled to him.
For whoever initiated evil himself received the punishment of evil retribution.
Through the counsel of the serpent, who advised Eve, Adam left Paradise. The serpent’s punishment was severe and harsh.
He took away its food and gave it dust. It fell to the ground and went about on its belly, and he made it without legs.
who sinned through them and rushed against Adam, and ate dust all his days forever because he led Eve astray with food. He was made an enemy, and his head was handed over to be trampled.
For, like the serpent that led Adam astray, people have arisen among us who are deceivers, troublemakers, wicked, insolent, treacherous, and unjust.
They build up injustice and tear down righteousness. They plant wickedness and uproot goodness. They cultivate weeds and destroy the wheat.
They insult the righteous and bless the unjust. They love the proud and hate the humble. They praise and acquit liars, but despise the truthful and call them liars.
They vow injustice and carry out ruin. They conceive and give birth to destructive words. They twist their tongues and speak emptiness.
They are empty of goodness and puffed up with falsehood. They have no fruit to eat, for they are tainted with the serpent’s venom.
For what good has strife done, and what benefit has envy brought those who practice it? It separated Cain from his beloved Abel, for strife cursed Cain,
and sold Joseph, destroyed Pharaoh, drove Jacob away, swallowed Korah, destroyed his companions, killed Zimri, and stoned Achan.
It destroyed the world, brought down Sisera, laid waste to Jabin [?], threw Saul into turmoil, buried Goliath, trampled Amalek, cut down Absalom, and troubled Adonijah.
It led Jeroboam into sin, divided the people, destroyed Gibeah, laid waste to its inhabitants, threw Sennacherib into turmoil, and destroyed his army.
It brought Haman down, made a mockery of slanderers, uprooted Israel, and scattered it among every nation. Envy and strife destroyed all these.
Let us turn to our Savior, who said to us, “This is my commandment: that you love one another.” And the apostle said, “Owe nothing to anyone
except to love one another.” He exalted love still further and said, “Even if I do every good and noble deed, but have no love in me, I am nothing.”
Love covers shameful deeds. Love covers sins. Love is far from boasting. Love is devoid of arrogance. Love is free from strife.
Love is above envy. Love rises above division. Love has nothing to do with greed. Love is a stranger to causing distress.
Love is free from evil, for its fruits are lovely, desirable, splendid, and beautiful. Love saved Noah from the flood,
and rescued Rahab from Joshua’s sword. It exalted David and covered his sins, and delivered Hezekiah from the hands of his enemies.
It vindicated Asa and forgave Josiah. Love quenched the furnace’s fire for Hananiah and his companions in the land of Babylon,
and brought Daniel up from the pit. It saved Esther and Mordecai from Haman’s hands. Love conquers hatred and covers sins,
keeps injustice far away, removes envy, puts an end to strife, dissolves hostility, reconciles the angry, and breaks evil impulses.
Love’s compassion is great, and its kindness is abundant. Love is reproached. Love is insulted. Love is patient. Love reconciles enemies
and brings peace among those who are divided. Love is mistreated. Love loves silence. It loves the humble. It loves those who practice self-denial.
It loves the wise. It loves fasting. It loves prayer. It loves charitable giving. It loves the sincere. It loves the blameless. It loves the modest. It loves the repentant.

It loves peacemakers. It shows compassion and tender care. It gathers people and brings them near. It encourages and gladdens. When love is insulted, it controls its impulses, is patient, and remains calm,
and is silent and mistreated. Love takes no pleasure in anger. It does not rejoice in division. Envy gives it no delight. It does not worry about the days to come.
And it does not dwell on hateful things. For love is patient and kind, calm and broad-minded, and generous in its thinking.
Its senses are at rest. Love is not mocked / does not mock /. It does not reproach, ridicule, boast, show off, exalt itself, or lift itself up.
Love sees itself and knows its own condition. It is quiet, silent, and patient. It loves everyone and is loved by everyone. Love conceives harmony,
gives birth to peace, practices good things, and reflects on beautiful things. For love is not overcome by evil. Love is light; love is salt.
Love is a spring of good things. Love is a good seal, a precious pearl and a treasure, the seal of all love. It reflects on wisdom,
and its conduct is delightful. Love is a sound mind, an excellent thought, a disposition of hope, a perfect understanding, and a faithful conscience.
Blessed is the soul of the person who has acquired love, for through it lovely fruits reach maturity. For love is far from [?], which damages peace.
[?], King of the ages, we worship you, for you are patient with your whole creation, and all who do works of darkness are at ease before you.
You know the thoughts of all human beings. Many deny you while receiving your provisions, and wrong you through your own works.
But you, being good and patient toward human beings, have not judged us before your judgment, nor accused us, nor condemned us.
Your kindness is not withheld from the wicked. You make your sun rise, send down your rain, and cause your wind to blow. You feed and sustain,
give growth and grant relief. The wicked are left with the good in the world, the weeds with the wheat, and sinners with the righteous,
and the guilty with the innocent. For the sake of the wheat, the weeds are preserved until the harvest; and for the sake of the good, the wicked are left until the end.
For the sake of the upright, the unjust are allowed to remain until the end; and for the sake of the righteous, unbelievers are not judged until the judgment.
For if ten righteous people had been found, five cities would have been saved for their sake. For Lot's sake, Zoar was not overthrown. And in the days of Jeremiah,
if someone had been found to stand in the breach and build up a wall, perhaps Jerusalem would not have been destroyed, just as Moses stood in the breach for his people,
and Joshua son of Nun built up a wall, Hezekiah offered prayer, Asa presented supplication, Josiah purified the land, and Daniel brought back the captives.
Mordecai displayed victory. Each of the righteous, in his own time, stood in the breach for his people, offered supplication, and appeased the compassion of the Most High.
And at this time, who is the wise physician who will stand in the breach and build up a wall, so that the prophet's saying may not also be fulfilled against us,
when he rebukes the false prophets of his people and says to them, “Your prophets, Israel, have become like foxes among ruins.
You have not gone up into the breach or built up a wall around the people of Israel.” Blessed is the wise physician who takes medicines and labors among the sick.
Let the excellent watchman warn the people about the drawn sword. Let the diligent athlete triumph in the contest and not be weak in the contest.
Let the wise builder lay a deep foundation so that his building does not fall because of the waves. Let the diligent farmer gather his crops during the summer,
so that he will not be in need during the winter. Let the watchful gatekeeper not be overcome by sleep, so that when his master knocks, he may quickly open for him.
Let the discerning merchant sell his possessions and buy himself a pearl so that he may become rich. Let the vigilant helmsman watch his rigging so that his ship does not sink.
and lose his merchandise. Let the wise charioteer secure his chariot so that he does not fall and become a laughingstock. Let the victorious athlete compete in the stadium,

so that he does not lose his crown and become a laughingstock to his companions. Let the good steward provide for his fellow servants and not say in his heart, “My master is taking a long time to come.”
Let the hired workers labor in the vineyard so that they can ask for more without shame. Let the bridegroom’s attendants prepare their clothes,
so that when their master comes, they may enter his bridal chamber. Let those who provide for the poor distribute their possessions and send their treasures ahead to the place before them.
Let the children of peace extinguish strife so that they may be worthy to become children of the Father in heaven. Let those who sound the horns warn the people,
lest they be held accountable for a life taken through their fault. Let the prisoners of the congregation remain in the fortress and wait in silence for the recompense that is to come.
Let those who hold the keys open to those entering, so that the gate of the kingdom is not shut in their faces. Let those who are dead to the world and have put an end to their desires
silence [?] the world with all its storms. Let those born of water and redeemed with precious blood
beware of the fire and the outer darkness. Let those wearing armor exert themselves vigorously so that they do not become a laughingstock to all their companions.
Let those awaiting the shout prepare their lamps so that they are not left in need like the foolish virgins.

Let those building a tower calculate its cost so that they do not become a laughingstock to passersby. Let the excellent shepherds care for their flocks so that they may receive their reward from the chief shepherd.
Let those who have received money show a profit so that they do not go out into the darkness with the wicked servants.
Let those sound in mind cast off weakness and not fear the upheavals and the towering waves.
Let those reclining at the banquet prepare an offering [?] and put on clothes worthy of the bridal chamber.
Let those who have taken up the yoke endure reproach, and let the wise virgins prepare their lamps.
My beloved, let us train ourselves through toil and weariness, through keeping watch and petition, through fasting and prayer and earnest supplication,
lest we suddenly be taken from this world and be condemned at God’s righteous judgment. Let us not despise the service of the Holy One, lest we ourselves be rejected by him,

as he said through the prophet: “Because you have rejected the law of God, I will reject you from the priesthood.” And again it is written: “Those who honor me I will honor, and those who despise me will be disgraced.”
Consider what recompense the priests who despised his service received: Nadab and Abihu, holy priests, wearing the ephod and wrapped in the robe,
girded with fine linen and adorned in purple, wearing crowns, caps, and turbans, offering sacrifices and making atonement for Israel,
teaching the people and sanctifying the congregation. When a little blindness came over them, they despised the service of the Holy One and brought in unauthorized fire at the wrong time.
Fire flared up from their censers and burned them up. They were carried out and thrown outside the camp. And not only Nadab and Abihu,
but also Hophni and Phinehas, the sons of Eli the priest, because they honored themselves above the service entrusted to them and greedily took their due from the people,
and dishonored the women who prayed at the tent of meeting. Their father Eli did not rebuke them sternly and forcefully, but reproved them weakly and feebly,
when he heard from all the people, who were complaining that the priests, their teachers, were behaving wickedly. Then he called them and said to them:
My sons, what is this report I hear about you from all the people—that you are mistreating the people of God? No, my sons!
This report I hear about you is not good. If someone sins against another person, he can appeal to the Lord. But if someone sins against the Lord, to whom can he appeal?
This was the feeble rebuke with which Eli rebuked his sons, and then he fell silent. They accepted no correction from his rebuke. Woe to Eli the priest, the leader of the people!
When your sons, wicked men, would not listen to you, it was not fitting for the priesthood you exercised that you should share in the sins your sons were committing.
But it is clear that he rebuked them before the eyes of the people, and not with his whole heart.
For this reason our Savior warned us: If your eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out and throw it away from you—or your hand or your foot. These are the body's valued members:
the eye that sees, the hand that works, and the foot that walks. Yet even if these members cause you to stumble, cut them off and throw them away from you,
provided that you yourself are not excluded from life. Moses also warned, as our Savior did: If your son or your daughter, or the wife of your covenant, or your friend who is like your own self—
if one of these entices you and says to you, 'Abandon the Lord, and come, let us go and serve other gods,'
do not listen or consent. Do not pity them or cover up for them. Rather, they are to be stoned to death.
For a son, a daughter, and the wife of one's youth are beloved members: the eye, the hand, and the foot, which are valued and beloved within the whole body.
Our Savior also taught: Whoever does not love me more than his father and mother, and more than his own life, cannot be my disciple.
And Moses said: Love the Lord your God with your whole soul, with all your strength, and with all your possessions.
The Holy Scriptures taught us these things so that we might apply ourselves to them, so that God might love us and bring us into his glorious kingdom.
For because of their wickedness, Aaron's sons, who were clothed in holiness, were thrown without pity outside the camp, into an unclean place.
And because of the wickedness of Eli's sons, the people of Israel fell by the sword of the Philistines, and the ark of the covenant was taken captive.
They brought it into Ashdod, into the temple of Dagon, an unclean house. Again, because Uzzah the priest treated the service of God's ark with contempt, the Lord struck him down, and he died.
And what, dear friends, was Uzzah's contempt, except that he carried the ark on a cart, transgressed the law, and did something that Moses had not commanded?
For when the leaders of Israel presented offerings for the dedication of the tent of meeting—
oxen and carts—the Holy One commanded Moses his servant, saying to him: Take these from them and give them to the Levites, so that they may use the carts to perform their work at the tent of meeting
and carry all the equipment of the tent of meeting on the carts. For he told him: Give to the sons of Gershon according to the needs of their work, but do not give any to the sons of Kohath,
because the service of the holy things is entrusted to them; they must carry them on their shoulders, with honor, splendor, and glory. You know, our brothers,
that the ark of the covenant had never been carried on a cart until the time when the leaders of the Philistines sent it away
and placed it on a cart drawn by two cows whose calves were kept back behind them.
When the Israelites received the ark, the Levites took it down from the cart on which the Philistines had sent it, and placed it in the house of Abinadab, which was on the hill.
They wanted to carry it in that same customary way, and not on their shoulders as the Holy One had commanded Moses, and Moses had commanded the priests. But Uzzah did not understand.
For when Joshua son of Nun crossed the Jordan, God likewise commanded him that the priests should carry the ark and go ahead of the people, and that the Jordan should divide.
And all the people set out. From this Uzzah understood. For this reason he justly received judgment in wrath.
When David saw that the Lord had struck Uzzah down, he was afraid to bring the ark of God to himself.
Then they brought it into the house of Obed-edom the Gittite, for Obed-edom was from Gath of the Philistines, from an unclean people, and not from Israel.
He knew this: whoever does not honor the ark of God is struck with bitter pains and terrible plagues.
So the Philistines were struck with hemorrhoids, and the people of Ekron wailed and said, “Let the ark go to Gath.”
Obed-edom had known this since that time when the Philistines carried it away, at the time when they made an offering to the ark.
And Eli’s sons, Hophni and Phinehas, the priests who dishonored the sacred service, were killed. The Philistines became afraid and honored the ark of God.
Even when they sent it away, they sent it with offerings. In their eyes it was regarded as a great god, for earlier, when they saw it coming into the camp, they said:
“Woe to us! For look, God has come into the camp of the Hebrews! Take courage, Philistines, for this is the God who destroyed Egypt with every kind of plague.”
And see, beloved, that Obed-edom the Gittite was blessed because the ark of God entered his house.
When David brought it up from the house of Obed-edom to the city of Zion, he commanded the priests, and they carried it on their shoulders.
And as he went along on foot, he rejoiced and danced before the ark, while Michal daughter of Saul mocked him.

These are the things, beloved, that we felt compelled to write, to remind ourselves and you as well that all these things have happened to us at this time because we have treated the service of the Holy One with contempt.
Because we did not honor him, he handed us over to mockery before our enemies and treated us with contempt, as he said: “Those who despise me will be dishonored.”
For our minds have been darkened by pride, and greed has overcome us and blocked the springs of wisdom. The roots of learning have been darkened by greed and pride.
Sin entered the world through the enticement of greed, when Adam sinned by eating from the tree and left Paradise.
For the Holy One placed before Adam all the trees of Paradise, bearing blessed fruit, and said to him:
“You may eat from all of them. But do not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, so that you do not die.”
Yet all of Paradise did not satisfy his greed, though it is more spacious and excellent than the whole earth in which human beings are now sown.
In the end, all the righteous are destined to rest there, when the dominion of greed is taken away, as our Savior said to the man on his right: “Truly I tell you,
today you will be with me in the Garden of Eden.” And again it is written in the prophet: “The righteous will inherit the earth and dwell on it forever.”
But they will not inherit it [?], because it will certainly pass away, as it is written: “The heavens will pass away like smoke, and the earth will wear out like a garment.”
Our Lord also said: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.” These heavens above us, which are called the firmament, will pass away.
And this earth, which is dry land, wears out. But the land of the living and the heavens above the firmament do not wear out or pass away.
And the whole earth and the whole of Paradise were not enough for the greed that entered Adam, until he desired to take and eat even from what he had been commanded not to eat.
And because of greed Esau sold his birthright and was also rejected from the blessing.
And because of Pharaoh’s greed the land of Egypt was devastated. All the people he ruled were not enough for his greed, but he also wanted to subjugate Israel in slavery.
And Aaron’s sons, who became greedy, were rejected from the priesthood. And the Israelites, who greedily craved food time after time—
wrath rose against them: pestilence, snakes, and other plagues of every kind.
And Achan, too, because of his greedy desire, was stoned to death and perished from among his people. And the wicked priests, Eli’s sons—

greed deprived them of their lives. And King Saul, the chosen one of the people, because he coveted the things of Amalek devoted to destruction, fell from his high position, and his kingdom was torn away.
And Ahab son of Omri, king of Israel, coveted and took Naboth’s vineyard, and he fell in battle at Ramoth-gilead.
And again, Gehazi, Elisha’s disciple—his greed clothed him in leprosy. Greed has killed many and stripped them of their lives.
Judas Iscariot, one of the Twelve, did not satisfy his greed by stealing, until he took the price of the precious one. And through that very greed he was separated from his fellow disciples.
Greed also overcame Ananias, and an astonishing event befell him before the apostles’ feet.
The whole world is not enough for greed. For among the kings of every nation and language, each one finds his own country insufficient.
They gather armies and wage battles; they devastate cities and plunder countries.
They take captives and acquire possessions for themselves, and nothing is enough. They toil and wear themselves out and train for war. They demolish fortresses and carry out slaughter.
They climb and reach the heights and descend into the depths, in the hope that greed might be satisfied, but it is never filled. As wealth increases, greed grows.
And as possessions multiply, stinginess grows stronger. A poor person is satisfied with a day’s bread, while a rich person plans for years he will not live to see.
Patched clothing satisfies the poor, but amid splendid clothing from every country, greed stands naked.
The poor person’s bed is on the ground, and it is enough for him. But the rich person’s sleeping place has beds of every splendor and bedding of every kind, yet it is too little for greed.

The poor person drinks water and is satisfied, while the rich person drinks aged wine and still thirsts. The rich acquire gold and silver, and it becomes a stumbling block to them, and through it they are killed.
The sleep of all who love greed is disturbed, while the sleep of poverty is quiet and restful. The poor person thinks of breaking off some of his bread for someone in need.
But the rich person plans to swallow up someone who has less than he does. Blessed is the one who has not served the tyranny of the belly,
and the man whom greed has not overcome. And blessed is the person who reflects with understanding, through which the roots of greed are cut off.

And concerning these things we have written to you, beloved, you also know that because of greed those who hold the law and authority among our people have looked on us with hostility and envy. While our teaching agreed with our conduct, we walked in keeping with our calling,

and conducted ourselves in keeping with our calling. For even the holy laying on of hands, which some among us receive—they contend over it merely for [?]. And in our time one does not readily find anyone asking who fears God, but rather who is senior in the laying on of hands.
And when they say, “So-and-so is an elder,” they call him that, not so that he may recline in the place of honor.

And no one remembers the words of the Savior, when he pronounced woe upon the scribes and Pharisees and said to them, “Woe to you, because you love the seats in the synagogues and the places of honor at dinners, and you love people to call you ‘Rabbi, Rabbi.’”
Our brothers, titles do not bring anyone into life or deliver anyone from death, just as they did not deliver Nadab and Abihu or save Hophni and Phinehas.
Rather, good deeds are required along with titles, because deeds without titles deliver those who labor at them.
But titles without good deeds bring no benefit or help at all, as we wrote to you above.
And our brothers boast of the titles they receive, using them to bind and destroy and to receive honor. “I have authority,” each says.

And today what the prophet said has been fulfilled: “The great man speaks what his own soul desires.” And he said, “My flock was scattered for lack of a shepherd.” And again he said, “The shepherds fed themselves,”
“but they did not feed my flock.” And again he said, “O shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture!” And again he said to the shepherds,
“You graze on good pasture, but what you leave over you trample with your feet. And you drink sweet water,”
“but what you leave over you muddy with your feet. And my sheep graze on what your feet have trampled and drink the muddy water you have left over.”
And again he said to the shepherds, “You eat the fat sheep and clothe yourselves with wool, but you do not tend the sheep. Instead, you have subjected them by force.”
O shepherd who does not know his own dignity, who are you to judge a servant who is not yours? If he stands, it is before his own master that he stands.
And if he falls, it is before his own master that he falls. Yet he will indeed stand. If you cannot justify him, why have you condemned him?
But if you exalt yourself over me in your mind and say, “I am a teacher and king over you,” and I do not accept you, you bind me.
For how can you teach me humility when you are exalted, arrogant, and boastful? And how can you teach me to love one another when you are full of hatred and anger?
And how can you teach me, “If someone takes what is yours, do not demand it back,” when you demand what is yours and charge interest?
And how can you teach me to be modest when you are shameless, frivolous, and vainglorious? And how can you teach me to leave this world when you have fallen into it and are choking in it?

And how can you teach me to give relief to the poor when you persecute the poor who are your fellow servants? And how can you teach me to let go of what is in my heart when you keep old leaven stored within you?
And how can you teach me to make peace with my brother when you throw so many people into turmoil?
For if I see unfitting fruit in you, you say to me, “Whether you are unjust or wicked, follow my words.”

The one who teaches and acts is called great, and the one who breaks the commandments and teaches is called least. You received money and tied it up. A key was entrusted to you, and you shut the door.
You did not enter, and you do not allow those who come to enter. You are the eye of the body, but you have become blind, and the body has grown dark for lack of an eye.
You have become blind, and the body has become sightless. It is a case of a blind man leading a blind man, and you seek to throw your whole body into a pit.
When salt loses its flavor, it is thrown outside. And the servant who tied up the money goes into darkness. And the servant who beats his fellow servants is called to account by his master.
And the foolish shepherd’s eye is blinded, and his arm withers. The priests did not say, “Where is the Lord?” Those who handle the law did not know him, and the shepherds were false to him.
From the prophets of Jerusalem godlessness has spread throughout the land. The rulers of my people ravage it, and women rule over it.
Now we do not fear the Lord. What can a king do for us? Alas for us! What has happened, that the law is abandoned and some among us boast of wrongdoing?
Are we to sit in silence and amazement? You tell me, “Come, be our partner in everything I do.”
Now, teacher, the saying that our Lord spoke has been fulfilled in you: “You travel over sea and land to make one convert.”

“And when he becomes one, you make him a child of hell.” A prophet led his fellow prophet astray and lied to him. Because he listened to his words, he was delivered into the paws of a lion, which tore him apart.
When many priests and prophets went astray in the days of Ahab, seven thousand remained faithful to God: those who had not bent their knees or worshiped Baal.
Even Elijah did not know about them. They did not follow evil priests and blind guides to destruction.
If Rehoboam divided the kingdom, am I to follow him? Far be it from me! If Jeroboam abandoned his God, am I to walk in his footsteps? My God, save me from these things!
You tell me, “I am handsome and good-looking. God chose me and anointed me to reign over my people.”
Be convinced, then, O man: God swore and promised Phinehas son of Eleazar that he and his sons would have a covenant of priesthood forever.
Phinehas served as priest throughout the days of the judges, about three hundred and sixty-five years. Afterward Eli arose in his place.
When Eli and his sons transgressed the law, the Holy One revoked his promise. He said to Eli through a prophet, “I did indeed say that you and your father's household would serve before me forever.”
“But now, far be it from me, says the Lord! Those who honor me I will honor, and those who despise me will be disgraced.” Our father Isaac also wanted to bless Esau, his firstborn.
But Jacob was chosen from his mother's womb and received his blessings, as he said to Rebekah: “The older will serve the younger.” And the Holy One chose Saul to be king.
But because he did not do his will, he chose David and rejected Saul. Our brothers embellish and bring us a feeble spiritual interpretation that does not hold together:
They say, “Because of the evil times, we have appointed a leader for God's people, like Jehu, who was anointed in an inner room.”
But if someone asks you, O wise scribe, when the promise was made that Jehu would be anointed, and when the anointing actually came to him,
what will you tell him? Elijah received a command on Mount Horeb. He said to him, “Go and anoint Jehu to reign over Israel
and destroy the house of Ahab.” Elijah received the command and served for many years until he was taken up, and after him Elisha served. When Jehu's time came
and the measure of the sins of Ahab's house overflowed, then Elisha sent one of the company of prophets, who went and anointed him as commanded.
But if they compare the matter to Jehu, was such a command, then, given concerning the priest who was to arise among the people:
that when he arose he should destroy all his brothers, imprison them, and wipe them out, just as Jehu devastated and destroyed the house of Ahab?
This spiritual interpretation resembles Jezebel's. When she saw that Jehu had become king and was coming, she adorned herself, looked down at him from the window, and said to him,
“Welcome, Zimri, murderer of his master!” Her spiritual interpretation condemned her, and Jehu killed her too, tore her apart, and threw her to the dogs.
If he was chosen from his mother's womb like Jacob, let them tell us. And if he was consecrated from the womb like Jeremiah,
Even if he was appointed to kingship and called a son of God, like Solomon; and even if he was chosen before his conception, like Josiah;
and even if he built the temple, like Cyrus. Be convinced, O mortal, that Aaron did not glorify himself to become high priest.
And Moses too, when his Lord wished to make him a god to Pharaoh and a leader of his people,
begged to be excused many times, until, under great pressure, he sent him to Egypt and performed wonders and signs through him.
Or should one look at his great height, as with Saul, or at his handsome appearance, as with Eliab, or at his perfect beauty, as with Absalom?
The Lord takes no pleasure in appearance, nor in the lofty and arrogant. Samuel said, “The Lord examines the heart, while a man sees with his eyes.”
And the apostle said, “God chose the foolish of the world to shame the wise through them, and he chose the weak to shame the strong through them.
And he chose those of low birth, the insignificant, the despised, and those who are nothing, to bring to nothing those who are something,
so that no mortal may boast before God, from whom you have your being.” And Jeremiah also said, “Let not the powerful boast in their power, or the rich in their riches,
or the mighty in their might. Rather, let whoever boasts boast in the Lord.” For all human beings are God's creation.
Before him there is no distinction between slave and free, rich and poor. Rather, all who serve him are equal before him.
And if people boast of their abundance of speech and their great knowledge, they cannot prevail by this.
For it is written, “A multitude of words receives no answer, nor is a talkative man justified by his statements.”
And again it is written, “He takes speech away from the trustworthy and removes the discernment of the elders,” along with many other things that are written.
But you, our brothers, run in harmony and labor in peace. Extinguish evil, put away hostility, and reconcile the rebellious.
For truth is not overcome by injustice, nor is righteousness condemned by wickedness, nor is peace silenced by strife.
