Truth is not proved false by deceit. The just are not in harmony with the unjust, nor the righteous with the wicked, nor good with evil, nor sweetness with bitterness,
nor darkness with light, nor brightness with gloom, nor what is bland with what is salty, nor old leaven with fresh dough,
nor fire with water, nor peaceful people with troublemakers, nor believers with mockers, nor those crowned with those imprisoned,
nor the children of the right hand with the children of the left, nor the children of the kingdom with the children of Gehenna, nor those who fear God with those who disturb his flock,
nor the church of the Holy One with the teachings of the evil one. Injustice cannot be concealed, nor can deceit be hidden.
For whoever wishes to run and labor in harmony and peace receives the blessing our Savior gave: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God.”
Who does not long to be a son of the Father in heaven and a brother of Christ the King?
See, then, our brothers, how worthy of a good remembrance are those who labor for the harmony and peace of the people. For what did our Savior owe to death,
and what had he borrowed from Sheol, that, though he was alive, he died for the rebellious and reconciled them with his Father?
He entered Sheol and brought out its prisoners. He fought with the evil one and defeated him, trampled him, broke down his [?], and plundered his possessions.
He broke his gates and cut through his bars. He took his thorns and placed them on his own head. He sealed our souls with his own blood.
He freed the prisoners from the enclosed pit. He broke through the barrier and the sword’s edge. He took the curse and nailed it to his cross.
He gathered the scattered and reconciled the rebellious. He fed the hungry and gave the thirsty something to drink. He gave sight to the blind and healed the sick.

He straightened those who were bent over and made the lame walk. He took away our pains and healed our wounds. He cured our sickness, brought us near when we were far away, and gathered us when we were scattered.

He made us members of his household. He enriched us through his poverty, and through his sickness he made us well. He healed us through his crucifixion, and through his afflictions he brought us relief.
Because he endured all these things for us, his Father gave him a name more excellent than every name, so that at this name of Jesus every knee should bow,
not only those on earth but also those in heaven. As they bow and worship, they will say that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God his Father.
He became judge and Lord of the dead and the living, as he said in his Gospel: “The Father will judge no one, but will give all judgment to his Son.”
For this is the reward for our Savior’s labor: a great and excellent name, because he brought peace to a rebellious land.
Those who join with him and bring about harmony and peace become his brothers and children of God.
They inherit the kingdom, serve, and are served by the watchers of heaven, who neither envy nor become jealous, neither grow weary nor sleep, and rejoice over sinners who repent of their sins.
Beloved, it is not enough for us to learn to read the Scriptures of God; we must also put them into practice.
Thus it is clear to us that as long as a person lives in strife and contention, his prayer is not accepted and his petition is not heard.
His offering does not rise from the earth, and his alms do not bring forgiveness of sins. For as long as there is no harmony and peace,
the door stands open to the wicked / to the evil one /, to strife and rebellion. There is no judgment or investigation. The wheat is sifted; the weeds are mixed in.
Thorns spring up. Disturbances multiply. Scoffers grow strong. Mockers gain the upper hand. There is no correction, no guidance, no discernment.
The salt has lost its taste. The eye is dark. The body is dim. Trade has been taken away. There is no peace for anyone going in or coming out. These are the fruits that contention produces.
For now the champions become known, the diligent are distinguished, and all the valiant are recognized: those who run in harmony and labor in peace.
The reward is assured, and the recompense is great. These are the ones who stand in the breach, build up the wall, and devote themselves to labor,
[and stand] on behalf of their people. They are recorded for a good remembrance alongside the champions and diligent workers.
Beloved, in every generation and in every age, as it pleased the Good One, our Maker, he has made the small great, brought down the lofty, raised the lowly, and humbled the proud.
He has made the rich poor, exalted the poor, brought down the powerful, strengthened the weak, subdued the mighty, and made the insignificant strong.
He raised up Seth, the younger, in place of Cain, the firstborn; Noah in place of Adam as father of the second world; and Isaac in place of Ishmael;
Jacob in place of Esau; Joseph in place of Reuben; Ephraim in place of Manasseh; and Eleazar and Ithamar in place of Nadab and Abihu.
And Joshua and Caleb in place of the ten spies, their companions; and Samuel in place of Eli; and David in place of Saul; and Solomon in place of Adonijah;
and Jeroboam in place of Rehoboam; and Jehu in place of Ahab; and Mordecai in place of Haman; and Daniel and his brothers in place of the wise men of Babylon;
and the nations in place of the people. Likewise with women: he exalted Sarah in place of Hagar, who bore the firstborn, and Rachel in place of Leah;
and Hannah in place of Peninnah; and Esther in place of Vashti. Prophecy and judgment were also entrusted to women at various times, whenever the one who exalts the lowly wished.
Miriam the prophetess; and Hannah the prophetess; Huldah the prophetess; Elizabeth the prophetess; and Mary the prophetess, who bore the great prophet.
And Deborah the prophetess judged Israel in the days of King Barak son of Abinoam. No one finds fault with the will of our good God,
because no one can probe his judgments, and his ways cannot be traced. His judgments cannot be bounded, nor can his mind be measured.
For the works of God are great, and his thoughts are deep and wonderful. He suspended heaven without pillars and spread out the earth without columns.
He gathered the waters into hollows. He confined winds and storms in the storehouses of his will. He stretched out the firmament in the middle as a division between the waters and the waters.
He separated dry land from the sea. He fixed the lights in the firmament. He raised mountains upon the earth. He separated day from night, and light from darkness,
and summer from winter. He established the sand as a boundary for the sea and confined the seas within the ocean. The towering waves do not cross the boundary.
The sun travels without feet, and the moon moves through its changes. The clouds race without wings, and the wind blows without pinions.
The waters flow without a soul. The earth is suspended upon the waters, and the waters are gathered in the foundations. The wind cannot be seen.
The air cannot be touched. Heaven has no likeness, and the clouds cannot be understood. The creatures of the sea are mighty, and the sea monsters within it are wonderful.
The wings of the mind are extended, and the pinions of thought are spread. The senses of the intellect probe, and the eyes of the conscience peer intently.
The pupils of understanding fly about to see and discover the outcome, but not all the limits can be reached.
Who has perceived the place of knowledge? Who has reached the roots of wisdom? Who discerns the place of understanding? It is hidden from all the living and from the thoughts of all flesh.
It cannot be bought with gold by any of the idle. Its treasury stands open and accessible to those who ask. Its light surpasses the sun, and its radiance is more beautiful and splendid than the moon.
The recesses of the mind probe it, and the senses of thought acquire it. The strings of the intellect inherit it. Whoever has the door of his heart open finds it.
Whoever spreads the wings of his mind inherits it. It dwells in the diligent person and is planted within the heart of the wise. His roots are made firm at its springs,
and in it he acquires a hidden treasure. His thought flies to every height, and his meditation descends into every depth.
It depicts wonders within his heart, and the eyes of his senses see beyond the seas. All created things are contained in his thought,
and his nature is spacious enough to receive them. He is a great temple of his Maker, and the King on high enters and dwells in him. He raises his mind to the heights
and makes his thought fly to his sanctuary. His sanctuary. He shows him a treasury of every kind, and his intellect is amazed at the sight.
His heart carries all his senses away and shows him what he did not know. He gazes upon that place and examines it, and his intellect marvels at everything he sees.
All the Watchers hurry in his service, and the seraphim proclaim the holiness of his glory. They fly swiftly on their wings, and their garments are white and splendid.
They cover their faces from his radiance, and their movements are swifter than the wind. There the royal throne is established, and judgment is prepared in the court.
Thrones are set up for the righteous, who will judge the wicked on the day of judgment. When the wise man sees in his mind the place of his many treasures,
then his thought rises high, and his heart conceives and gives birth to every good thing. He reflects on everything that his likeness and appearance on earth have been commanded to do.
The perceptions of his mind range above and below. His thought is swifter than the sun, and its rays fly faster than the wind.
Like a light feather in every direction, the wise man is steadfast in his thought. He is small and insignificant in appearance, yet he is poured full from a mighty treasury.
In the dark night he is enlightened and sends his thoughts in every direction. His mind probes all the foundations and brings him a treasure of knowledge.
He sees what his ears have not heard, and perceives what his eyes have not seen. His meditation crosses every sea,
and the mighty waves count for nothing to him. His mind has neither ship nor sailor. Great and abundant is the treasure of his trade.
When he gives from what is his, he suffers no loss, and the poor grow rich from his treasury. There is no limit to his thought, which is gathered together and dwells within his breast.
It is a place where the king dwells and works. Who can count its treasures for you? Its revenues and expenditures are abundant, like those of a king who lacks nothing.
Now listen, beloved, as we remind ourselves and you how all God's creatures do his will and do not disobey his command.
Each one of them readily carries out his will, just as it has been commanded. But human beings disobey time after time and do not do his will.
They neither see nor hear nor understand. For the Holy One rebuked the children of Israel through Jeremiah and said to them:
“Will you not fear me, says the Lord, and will you not tremble before me? I have set the sand as a boundary for the sea, an everlasting ordinance that it cannot cross.
It struggles but cannot prevail; its waves rise but do not cross it. Yet this people has a rebellious and defiant heart,
and they have refused to obey my commandments.” Look at these astonishing wonders: the sea is bound by sand, and the waves are confined by a command.
All the surging waves are restrained by a word. They rise and rear up as far as heaven, and they are held back and subside as far as the deep.
They do not cross the boundary appointed for them. If anyone says that they are restrained by their own nature, let him understand from what happened in the days of Noah:
when he brought wrath through the waters of the flood, he withdrew his word from the grasp of the deep and lifted his command from the sand that held it bound.
The waters broke through and crossed the boundary, and the floodgates of heaven were opened. The firmament was split apart—the boundary between water and water.
Judgment was carried out against the wicked. For the firmament is set as a boundary between the waters above the firmament and the waters below,
as it is written that God made the firmament in the midst of the waters to separate water from water. He fixed the heavenly lights in it
and called it heaven. He gathered the waters from the surface of the dry land into one place. He called the gathering of the waters seas, and he called the dry land earth.
When he had carried out judgment against the wicked and destroyed the corrupt generation that transgressed the commandment, then the lower waters returned to the deep.
The sand stood firm to keep the command. The channels of heaven were shut, and the upper waters were held back by the firmament at his command.
The world rested between the waters above the firmament and the waters beneath the earth, with abundant waters confined in the clouds.
All of them are held back and set upon the foundation of his will. Not only did the waters do his will, but all his creatures also readily obey his command at all times.
The waters did so in the days of Noah, as did the waters, fire, darkness, swarms of flies, locusts, hail, and all the plagues in Egypt through Moses.
The sun, moon, and hailstones obeyed the command of Joshua son of Nun when he said, “Sun, remain over Gibeon, and moon, in the valley of Aijalon.”

Why did the sun remain over Gibeon? It was because the Gibeonites had taken refuge in the God of Israel /Israel/, and the kings of the Amorites had come up against them, until Joshua destroyed them while the sun stood still and the moon remained.
The stars of heaven did his bidding. They fought from their stations and waged war against Sisera and Midian,
in the days of Deborah and Barak son of Abinoam. The fanged beast also did his will: a bear tore apart the children, the offspring of the wicked.
The lions protected Daniel at his command. The fish in the sea also did his will when he commanded it and it swallowed Jonah.
When he told it to, it cast him out onto dry land. The worm also did his will in the stalk of the gourd that shaded Jonah,
when he commanded it and it cut through the stalk. The scorching wind dried it up at his command. The ravens, winged birds, also did his will,
and fed Elijah at the Wadi Cherith. The many fish also did his will when they were miraculously caught by the apostles of our Savior.
Another fish provided the poll tax for our Savior and Simon his disciple. Heaven and earth and [?] creatures do his will at all times, and not one of them disobeys his will.
But lawbreaking was found in Adam. From the first day, and even forever, he is a lawbreaker. Beloved, what rebellion is greater than this?
For through contentiousness, disorder, and strife, insolent, wicked, rebellious, and contemptuous people have arisen among our people:
people who insult and curse, who are jealous and envious, who cause disturbances and love greed, who rejoice in calamity and delight in others’ downfalls;
who hate truth and drive away righteousness, who rob and oppress, who deceive and despise their companions, who persist in falsehood;
who conceal themselves in wickedness, ridicule the good, amass profit, mock the righteous, and love disputes;
who disturb the peaceful and stir up quarrels, who conceive injustice and give birth to falsehood, who twist words and reject correction;
who are full of anger and deficient in understanding, who insist on their own will and hate the poor, who are boastful and arrogant, plunderers and oppressors;
who flatter and gather gossip, who are greedy and filthy, who entice others to destruction, drunkards and debauchees, deceitful people and liars;
who harbor grudges and love evil injuries, who take revenge for grudges and stir up strife, who are full of deceit and empty of kindness;
who lend money and sell at interest, evil workers and lazy hired hands. They eat in the name of our Lord, are honored in his name, and invoke his name,
yet they are empty of his words. These are the deceitful workers who tie up money and gain nothing from it.
These are the wicked servants who choke their fellow servants, and the weeds among the wheat. These are darkness amid the light.
False prophets and false messiahs. These are the children of the left hand, the heirs of darkness, who ask the righteous for water.
These are the thorns in the vineyard, the builders on sand whose building falls. These are those who turn back from battle.
Their god is their belly, and their glory is their shame. These are the whitewashed wall, the army of the Evil One and the offspring of Satan.
These are deaf serpents, mute dogs that cannot bark. These are those who justify themselves.
They are skilled in evil but have no understanding. These are those who sow strife, who rejoice in division and delight in stumbling.
These are those who sleep when it comes to good deeds, stay awake for evil deeds, and give rise to conflicts. These are lovers of themselves.
Fattened enemies, haters of Christ. These are the old yeast, worn-out wineskins, and torn garments.
These are the seeds /a seed/ among thorns, rocky ground for seed, and sand for building. These are those left out of the kingdom.
Dust for the serpent, and a lamp under a measuring basket. These are the tasteless salt that is thrown outside and is of no use.
These are those devoid of good deeds, counterfeit silver, and broken vessels. These are a vineyard of carob trees.
A vine of bitter grapes and a planting of Gomorrah. These are the rejected silver that the Lord rejected, and he called them unclean.
Perverted love, foolish virgins, sleeping gatekeepers. These are those who acquit the guilty and condemn the innocent.
The sons of [?]. These are those who hate rebuke and [?] words, who eat bread through deceit.
These are those who [?] speech, who whisper in hiding and strike in secret. These are those who are foolish in their words.
Those intent on “Give me!” who sow discord among brothers. These are lying tongues, a heart that devises injustice and malice.
These are those whose words are sweet, yet more bitter than wormwood and pleasing to [?]. These are defeated athletes.
Sailors who sink ships, hunters bent on destruction. These are treacherous scouts who look for a downfall and stir up wars.
These are messengers who cause turmoil, who lay stumbling blocks and provoke kingdoms. These are deadly poison.
The serpent’s gall and the viper’s venom. These are enemies of the Crucified One, a stumbling block to the cross.
Haters of Christ. These are children who give rise to strife, and these are the fruits of division.
Beloved children of peace, disciples of Christ, you are the light of the world, the salt of the earth, and the eye of the body.
You are the wedding guests, the good seed, and the building on rock. You are wise master builders who dig the foundation and uncover solid ground.
You are diligent farmers who fill storehouses and gather crops. You are wise merchants who receive money and show a profit.
You are hired workers who receive wages and ask for more. You are the holders of the keys.
Faithful messengers and blowers of horns. You are household managers who provide for others, new wineskins, and garments of glory.
You are the apostles who betroth the adorned bride, and the light in the darkness. You are the children of peace, the brothers of Christ, and the temple of the Spirit.
You are those who run in the contest, who labor in the stadium and receive crowns.
You are the vines in the vineyard, the seed of good wheat, yielding fruit a hundredfold.
You are those who light lamps and enter through the narrow gate of the kingdom. You are the children of the right hand, who travel along the narrow and constricted road.
You are those redeemed by the cross, purchased with the blood and body of Christ. You are Christ’s messengers, faithful heralds, born of water.
You are a sweet fragrance; your scent spreads everywhere. You are the new batch of dough in which there is no old yeast.
You are those invited to the bridegroom, dressed in clothes suitable for the banquet. You are those who have taken up the yoke,
who sit in silence and are bound to the congregation. You are the offspring of the church, those who raise her children and gather the flock.
You are the excellent shepherds who lead their flocks about in good pasture. And our Savior Jesus, the chief shepherd, is the light in the darkness
and the lamp on the lampstand, who illuminated the world and forgave their sins. For he is the precious pearl,
and we are the merchants who sold our possessions and bought him. He is the treasure of the village, and when we found him, we rejoiced in him and acquired him.
For he is the fountain of life, and we who were thirsty drank from him. He is the table filled with rich food and abundance,
and we who were hungry ate and were delighted. He is the gate of the kingdom, which has been opened before all who enter.
He is the wine that brings joy: mourners drink from it and forget their pains. He is the clothing and robe of glory in which all the victorious are wrapped.
He is the true vineyard, and his Father is the cultivator, and we are the vines planted within it. He is the tower in which many build.
Let us calculate its expenses so that we may build and finish. He is the bridegroom, the apostles are the matchmakers, and we are the bride. Let us prepare for ourselves [?].
He is the ladder that leads up to the heights. Let us labor and struggle so that we may ascend by him to his Father. He is the narrow and constricted road.
Let us follow in his footsteps so that we may reach the harbor. He is the priest, the holy minister. Let us labor to become members of his household.
He is the king of noble lineage who went to receive a kingdom. Let us honor his lowliness so that he may give us a share in his greatness. He is the herald and apostle of the Most High.
Let us listen to his words and become his confidants. He is the seed that bears much fruit, which was sown when it was small and became a mighty tree.
He is the firstborn Son, the child born of Mary. Let us welcome his lowliness so that we may rejoice in his greatness. He is the one who suffered, came to life, and ascended to the heights.
Let us truly believe in him so that we may welcome his coming. He is the judge of the dead and the living, who sits on the throne and judges the generations.
He is the one who grants the kingdom as an inheritance and sends people to torment, showing no favoritism and accepting no bribe. Therefore, through him let us give thanks to his Father.

Through him let us worship the one who sent him. Through him let us glorify as holy his sender, who delighted in us and chose us in him, made us rejoice in him and called us in him, and reconciled our lowliness with his greatness.
For we have nothing with which to repay these mercies except thanksgiving and worship, and loving one another. Let us labor to produce these fruits, which lead to eternal life.
It is fitting for us, beloved, to turn to God and offer heartfelt repentance before him, and not to share in Pharaoh’s hardness or Rehoboam’s foolishness.
Let us keep away from quarrels and divisions, which satisfy Satan’s will, for he approaches human beings subtly.
He makes them [?] in their lives and brings them down through his many desires. Through desire for one thing after another, he approaches Adam’s children.
He empties them like empty vessels, just as he began with their first father. His temptation does not take just one form, so that we could recognize it and flee from him.
For the deceitful one has many tricks. Through desire for food, he drove Adam out of Paradise, and through the desire to kill, he separated Abel from his brother Cain.
Through the desire to mock, Ham became a servant to his two brothers. Through greedy desire, he deprived Esau of the blessings and the birthright.
Through filthy desire, Shechem son of Hamor fell by the sword, together with all his people. Through hatred and envy, Jacob’s sons sold their brother Joseph to the Arabs.

Through filthy desire, Joseph’s master’s wife tried to seduce him, but he escaped its bondage. Through their lustful recklessness, the Sodomites perished. They rushed toward the fire, were consumed, and burned in the furnace.
Through the desire born of Pharaoh’s insolence, the king of Egypt drowned in the sea with his army. Through desire for the meat of Egypt, Jacob’s children perished in the desolate wilderness.
Through greedy desire for possessions, the descendants of Reuben, Gad, and Manasseh were held back and did not enter the promised land with their brothers.
Through the desire for gluttony and drunkenness, Nadab and Abihu were burned in the tent of meeting. Through the desire for greed and theft, the Lord brought trouble upon Achan by Joshua’s hands.
Through the lustful recklessness of Zimri son of Salu, twenty-four thousand Israelites fell in a single hour.
Because of contentiousness and wickedness, Abimelech son of Gideon killed his seventy brothers.
Through desire for Delilah, a prostitute, Samson was stripped of his strength, and his Nazirite consecration departed from him.
Through the impure desire of the men of Gibeah, sixty-five thousand from Israel and Benjamin fell by the sword.
Through the greedy desire of Eli’s sons, they were rejected and removed from the priesthood of the Holy One. Through the desire to show mercy to Amalek’s friends, Saul’s kingdom was torn apart.
Through desire for Tamar, Absalom’s sister, Amnon, David’s firstborn, was killed. Through his arrogant ambition, Adonijah son of Haggith failed to secure the kingship of David’s house.
Through desire for many women, Solomon’s heart turned away from his God. Through Rehoboam’s foolish desire, the Lord divided and diminished his kingdom.
Through Jeroboam son of Nebat’s contentious desire, five hundred thousand Israelites fell in one day at the hands of Abijah son of Rehoboam.

Through desire for Naboth’s vineyard, Ahab advanced and went up, and fell in battle at Ramoth-gilead. Through desire for Naaman’s silver, which Gehazi took, he and his descendants were clothed with leprosy forever.

Through desire for his treasure, Hezekiah became boastful, and his possessions, together with his sons, were carried away to Babylon. Through Sennacherib’s blasphemous desire, his army fell by the sword of the Most High.
Through the desire of his heart, Nebuchadnezzar was driven away from human beings to live with the wild animals. In his desire to give his wealth, Haman sought to destroy the Jewish people.
Through desire for a wicked decree, the Chaldeans slandered Daniel. Through his desire to steal, Judas became the betrayer of Christ the King.
Through Israel’s rebellious desire, they rejected Christ and denied his kingship.
Many such things are recorded in various forms. The deceitful one’s snares are planted, and he spreads his net like a skilled hunter.

He takes captives, leads them away, and brings them to destruction as he wishes. His desires are pleasant, and he leads not by force but by enticement. He appears sweet, although he is more bitter than wormwood.
When someone who is angry makes peace with his companion, he laments and weeps because that person has escaped his domination. Peace grieves him, and he loves turmoil.

On one pretext after another, he casts his bait to catch his prey. He hides his traps like a hunter, a skilled and clever craftsman. He lures and gathers to himself all the inhabitants of his dwelling.
His roads are broad and his paths spacious. All who belong to turmoil travel toward him, but the wise see him and flee from him.
They do not do his will, because they know that he is deceitful. The wise see his hidden traps
and his outspread net lying before them. They do not trust his enticements, and they spit out all his bitter morsels.
These things we write to you, our beloved, also serve to remind ourselves. It is not because you need to learn from us,
but as counselors and helpers. As it is written, a brother helped by his brother is like a city strengthened by its fortress.
The apostle says, “We are helpers of your joy.” And again he says, “They became helpers to us in the kingdom of God.”
Again, in another letter it is written: “Is there not even one wise person among you who can settle a dispute between one brother and another?”
For the wise and those who fear God—even when a saying comes from an uneducated person, the wise and helpful accept it and do not reject it.
Moses, the prophet, the great leader of all the people of Israel, accepted good advice from Jethro, the priest of Midian. Jethro’s name was written in his holy book,
and his advice was established in Israel forever. But if anyone disputes this advice of ours and does not pursue peace,
let him understand that such things have happened before. In every generation there have been foolish people who did not listen to good advice, and their end was disastrous.
When Adam sinned, his Lord called him to repent, but he refused. He hid behind an excuse, saying, “Eve led me astray.” He felt no remorse and did not repent.
When Cain killed his brother, he spoke with him so that he might feel remorse and repent. But he hid behind a lying excuse, saying, “He did not see me.”
He tested the people of Sodom through his angels, so that perhaps they would repent. But they persisted in their insolence and perished. They were utterly destroyed and burned with fire and sulfur.
King Pharaoh’s officials advised him, saying, “You have destroyed Egypt through your quarrels.” But he did not listen to the advice of his wise men.
The elders who had governed the kingdom with his father advised Rehoboam. But he rejected the advice of the wise and took counsel with young men. His kingdom was divided, and he fell into disgrace.
But you, our brothers, are wise, taught by God. Let us not refuse or be ashamed to seek peace and pursue harmony.
For jealousy and strife have thrown kingdoms into turmoil, laid cities waste, wiped out peoples, overthrown fortresses, and brought about many killings. Through them the sword has become widespread.

Envy and strife have separated brothers from their loved ones, driven them from city to city, and made them strangers and fugitives from their own lands. Though alive and walking on the earth, they were regarded as dead by their own kin. Jealousy has separated women from their husbands.
Through it, children have risen against their fathers. It has divided friends against their friends and made loved ones enemies of those dear to them.
It has stirred up trouble and set one person against another. It has divided two against three and three against two. A person kills his companion with his tongue and destroys him with his mouth,
showing no pity. Jealousy produces sighs in a person day after day. Evil thoughts smolder in those who love strife.
The old leaven has fermented and aged within them. It conceives foul deeds and produces bitter fruit.
He drives sleep away through the long night. And, my beloved, he becomes someone who insults his friend. If a good thought should happen to enter his heart,
the evil one drives it out of his heart. He plants his roots in the folds of his mind and drives his pegs into the thoughts of his heart.
He gathers many thoughts and brings them upon him. They enter and settle within his mind. The offspring of the evil one creeps in and is sown within him.
The sayings of the wise are foreign to him. The good seed is choked within him, as wheat is choked by thorns.
Good fruits diminish in his mind. He uproots the good seed and throws it out of his heart. The evil one stations his guards at the gates of his thought,
and they confuse his mind with many enticements. They enter him gently, like water, and water his heart as though it were solid rock,
so that when good seed falls into it, it quickly receives it, but its roots dry up and it produces no fruit. He stands and prays according to his daily habit.
He begins, completes, and concludes his prayer, but his heart is unaware of what his lips have uttered. His mouth recites what it has learned by habit,
while his heart is empty of good things. He puts the teaching of the Spirit out of his mind, and his mind forgets what it learned yesterday.
When his mind remembers, he sighs time after time. But the evil one emboldens him and fills his heart. A deceitful thought is firmly fixed within him,
and his heart floats as though in a sea of deep waters. His heart is clouded, his mind is dark, and his understanding is blind. He gropes and stumbles.
The evil one takes him by the hand and makes him run. He leads him along his paths into a trackless wilderness. He flings all good thoughts away from before him
and makes him ponder his own foul deeds. He emboldens him, saying, “Do not listen to persuasion, and do not humble yourself to make peace.”
The evil one laughs at him as he entices him, for he has acquired him as a slave who does his will. Yet the man does not realize that he has been sold for nothing,
nor does he see that his mind is blind. The evil one devises schemes and entices him with every kind of trick. He scatters bait for him as for a bird.
A foolish winged bird rejoices in its heart when it sees the bait hidden at the mouth of the trap. In its foolishness it approaches to pick it up, and the trap snaps shut on it,
and it comes out being carried away. The skilled hunter rejoices in his catch, because his time has not been spent in vain. So too with the person who loves contention and jealousy:
the evil one puffs him up and fills him with his bitter fruits. He entices and lures him as he would a bird. He scatters bait for him and springs the trap on him.

Once he has caught him through the sweetness of his enticements, he teaches him arguments he has never heard. The man learns disputation, becomes practiced in words, and stores harmful arguments in his mind.
He happens to forget the good things he learned, and they pass out of his heart. But the evil one’s teachings are kept within him like a hidden treasure, and evil roots grow firm in his mind.
Only with great effort are his claws finally torn out, like a lion’s claws from its prey. A wise physician, using many medicines, tears his claws out of the man’s heart.
For the longer evil thoughts remain in a person, the more his heart produces evil fruit and his tongue multiplies arguments that stir up trouble.
Desire for evil is sweet and entices his mind, but its outcome is more bitter than a snake’s gall. For anyone who holds a grudge in his heart, there is no medicine to heal him except peace.

Let a person lower himself before his brother and accept defeat before his friend. While the fruits of peace are near at hand, let jealous thoughts pass away, never to be remembered or rise into the heart again.
Beloved, our own sins are enough for us. Let our stumbling blocks not cripple many others. For a brother meets someone dear to him, lowers his face, and withholds a greeting.
But if he happens to meet a wicked pagan, he is the first to greet him. Oh, the blindness that darkens the mind! Oh, the slumber that is the sleep of death!
What relief will there be for us? For if an unjust man meets us, wicked and rich, we bow before him and greet him.
But in his envy the evil one has robbed us of the greeting of our brothers and loved ones. Our Lord commanded, “Love one another,” and the blessed apostle urged us to love.
And Moses, the foundation of the prophets, said, “Do not hate your brother in your heart, so that you do not sin.” Yet some of us hate in our hearts and flatter with our lips.
Our Lord opened before us his great treasury, which is full of every good thing. In it are love, peace, affection, healing, and purity.
And in it are all kinds of good, beautiful, and excellent things. He gave his stewards authority over his entire treasury. His treasury.
He also placed in the hands of the stewards chains, a prison, and prisoners, and gave them authority to bind and to release.
But the stewards abandoned love, peace, affection, and the whole treasury in its entirety. They chose instead to take chains and bonds.
They became jailers, executioners, and torturers instead of stewards of the treasury of every good thing.
Whoever enters is bound, and whoever leaves is imprisoned. Someone sins and offends against God, but does a favor for the jailers,
and they release him from his chains and say to him, “God is merciful and forgives sins. Come in to prayer.”
But to someone who offends against them, even over a trivial matter, they say, “You are bound and cut off from heaven and earth.
Woe also to anyone who speaks with him!” We think, brothers, that when the king sees that his stewards have transgressed the law
and violated the commandment he gave them, and are enforcing their own will, he will bind them with the bonds they loved and demand from their hands the blood of his servants.
He will deprive them of his treasury, which they did not love. Our Lord taught, “If your brother sins against you, rebuke him between you and him alone.
If he repents, forgive him. If he does not listen to you, take one or two others, so that every matter may be established before two or three witnesses.
If he does not listen to them, tell the church. If he does not listen to the church, then let him be to you like a pagan and a tax collector,”
because he did not accept persuasion. But we do not rebuke privately, or before two or three, or in the church. There is neither a hearing nor an accusation,
but only the declaration, “He is bound and cut off!” Our Lord also said, “If an offender sins against you seventy times seven in a single day, forgive him.”
What person has so many offenses that he would offend against his neighbor four hundred and ninety times in a single day?
Even if he commits all these offenses, our Lord commanded us to forgive. But we do not forgive even one offense in four hundred and ninety days.
And we die in our sins through holding a grudge, besides our other offenses.
My brothers, we have written these few words of reconciliation and peace to you because of this turmoil that has arisen among us at this time,
so that we may share in your peace, and also with our brothers in every place whom this dispute and division have reached.
And if anyone does not accept these words, we are neither wronged nor deprived, for the world was not worthy even of them.
Time after time, during their teaching, wicked people arose who opposed them, insulted them, and disputed their words.
A crowd of wicked people insulted Moses and rose against him. Jeremiah, too, was hated even by his own brothers, and they threw him into a pit.
When he rebuked his people for their sins, they spoke against him, saying, “This man does not desire the welfare of this people,
and he weakens the hands of the fighting men.” False prophets also sent word from Babylon to the priests in Jerusalem to stop Jeremiah from prophesying.
When the illustrious man saw that they would not accept his rebuke, he said, “I said that I would not speak in the Lord’s name or mention his word.
But it became in my mouth like a burning fire, shut up in my bones. I tried to endure it, but I could not.”
And at one time his Lord also commanded Ezekiel and said to him, “Look, they are putting chains on you and binding you with them.
When they do this to you, you will be silent and will not rebuke them, because I will make your tongue stick to the roof of your mouth.”
At another time he said, “My mouth was opened and was never closed again.” They also said to Amos, “Do not prophesy in the Lord’s name,
and do not teach the house of Isaac.” Yet he did not stop prophesying. And when Baruch son of Neriah wrote down the holy words from Jeremiah’s mouth,
and King Zedekiah heard them, he burned them in the fire because they contained a rebuke. But Jeremiah wrote them down and added to them.
They did not accept correction or repent of their sins, and through the king of Babylon they received the punishment that lawbreakers deserve.
God also said concerning all the prophets, “I cut down my prophets and killed them by the utterance of my mouth, but the Israelites did not repent of their sins.”
Our Savior’s own people even called him a Samaritan, gave him the name Beelzebul, and said that he had a demon.
When Paul taught, they called him a babbler. Not only did they refuse to accept their words,
but they also tormented them with blows and floggings, even to the point of death. Moses’ people rose against him to stone him.
Ahab sent Micaiah to prison. They threw Jeremiah into a muddy pit. They put chains on Ezekiel.
They seized our Savior, insulted him, condemned him unjustly, and hung him on a tree. Paul was at times imprisoned and at times stoned.
On one occasion they lowered him from the wall in a basket. They endured all these insults at the hands of their own people.
Yet they were not disheartened by their afflictions, because their building was set on a firm foundation.
A few rejected them, but many accepted them and lived by their words, and their good name endures for all generations.
Our Lord is the sower, and we are the soil that receives the seed. The sower filled his hand and scattered seed on his land. Some fell among thorns, and some on rock.
Birds picked up some of it, and some fell on good, cultivated soil, where it grew, sprang up, and yielded fruit—a hundredfold, sixtyfold, and thirtyfold.
See that the seed survived in one of the four portions and yielded fruit. One portion fell among choking thorns.
One portion fell on rock, and the sun dried it up when it rose. Another portion was picked up by a bird, which is an evil, ravenous bird.
Another portion fell on cultivated ground that receives water, and it bore fruit.
And we, our beloved, although we are sinful and deficient, are nevertheless built on this foundation, and we have received some of that leaven.
The seed of our Lord has fallen in our soil, and we have received silver from the rich merchant. His Spirit is poured out on all flesh,
and his grace is withheld from no one. If someone should happen to mock [?] and refuse to accept what we have written, he does us no harm,
and he gains no benefit. Our words show their benefit to those who hear, because we have written nothing to you outside the Law.
Nor have we sent you stolen treasure, but something from the seed and dough of the Holy Scriptures. Counterfeit silver is not accepted wherever it goes.
Old leaven is not kneaded into good flour, for worn-out wineskins cannot hold the strength of wine.
When a new patch is put on an old garment, it tears it. A vine that receives cultivation produces fruit, not sour grapes.
A heart as hard as rock dries up the seed. Any building set on sand is swept away by the rain and falls because of the wind.
Salt that has lost its flavor is eaten by a serpent. The fisherman throws the worthless fish out. The weeds are uprooted at their appointed time,
and the straw is separated from the wheat at the end. Worthless workers are ashamed when it is time for payment. And the foolish virgins whose oil has run out,
when the bridegroom comes, cannot buy any. The steward beats his fellow servants; his master comes and passes judgment on him.
The wicked servant hides his master's money; the one who gave it to him comes and settles accounts with him for the interest. And the doorkeeper who loves sleep,
at the time for keeping watch, is deprived of life. A wise king, while the army is still far away, sends envoys and asks for peace.
We have written these few reminders to you, our beloved. If anyone ridicules and mocks us, we do not blame him,
because he brings out the overflow of his heart and miscarries what his mind has conceived. Everyone gives birth from his own stores, produces, brings forth, and speaks.
Someone who has no gold—what can he give you from his treasury? A rich man who possesses all kinds of treasures brings some out and gives them to those who ask.
A poor man brings out tin and lead from what he owns and becomes involved in passing counterfeit money. Every tree brings forth its fruit in summer.
One that produces sour grapes is uprooted from the vineyard and becomes fuel to be burned in the fire. But the vine that bears good fruit is pruned by its owner, and he cultivates it further.
A vine that produces sour grapes comes from the planting of Sodom, whose grapes are bitter. Grapes are not gathered from thorns, nor figs from thistles,
because a good tree bears good fruit, and a bad tree bears bad fruit. A good tree cannot bear bad fruit,
nor can a bad tree bear good fruit. A good person brings out and speaks good things from the good treasures in his heart.
An evil person brings out and speaks evil things from the overflow of his heart, because the lips speak from the overflow of the heart, as our Savior taught and said.
For everyone brings out what he has and displays what he possesses. Consider a person who is full of confusion.
For there is no treasure greater than his. When peace comes, it removes strife, unrest ceases, and the Evil One is stripped of his treasure.
Our brothers, the world lacks nothing. It is full of every kind: the good and the evil, the rich and the poor,
the sweet and the bitter, the bright and the dark, [?] and sinners, the wicked and the unjust, the righteous and sinners,
the just and the unjust. Everything stands opposite its counterpart, and there is no perfection in this world, because the one who separates comes and separates the chaff and uproots the weeds.
But today the weeds are mixed with the wheat, and the good are mixed with the evil. The righteous are not separated from sinners,
nor the just from the unjust, nor the foolish from the wise. But at that time the master commands the harvest, and they gather the wheat and uproot the weeds.
The righteous are set apart for life, and the unjust go into darkness. The wise women enter with the bridegroom, and the foolish women are kept out.
The money is taken from the wicked servants, and the good servants inherit their talents. All who seek find what they asked for, and everyone who sows gathers the fruit of his labor.
But we are confident about you, our brothers, that you pursue peace and put away unrest, strife, and envy,
jealousy and division. For not everyone readily sees himself when he is behaving badly, just as he cannot see his own face.
For it seemed right to us, as far as we have been able at this time, to remind you of the conduct of those who came before: how good the diligent and the mature are,
and how evil are the fools who stir up unrest. You are children of peace. Love peace, so that you may receive a reward from the Lord of peace,
and share in the blessing that our Savior gave when he pronounced blessings on many. For he said, “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God.”
This letter was written in the month of Shebat, in the year six hundred and fifty-five of the reign of Alexander, son of Philip the Macedonian,
and in the thirty-fifth year of Shapur, king of Persia. May there be a good remembrance of the one who labored and wrote,
and also of the one who listens and accepts good advice, who pursues his course peacefully and does not stir up strife. For the children of strife are called the children of Cain,
but the children of peace are the brothers of Christ, children of the Father in heaven, who inherit the kingdom.
The Demonstration on Exhortation is finished.
The Demonstration on Distinctions between Foods
The minds of immature and uneducated people are greatly troubled about what enters the mouth, which cannot defile a person.
Those who are weak in these matters say this: God distinguished between unclean and clean foods and showed them to Moses his servant.
He made known to Moses which ought to be eaten and which ought to be regarded as unclean.
He instructed him about animals, birds, and the fish in the sea, according to their kinds. Now concerning these things, my dear friend, I will give you a brief explanation as far as I can:
foods bring no benefit to those who observe rules about them, nor do they cause any harm to those who eat them. For the holy mouth testified
that it is not what enters a person that defiles him, but what comes out of a person is what defiles him. And this is what our Savior said:
To take away the grounds of the Pharisees and Sadducees, because they boasted about ritual washings, purity, washing their hands, and distinguishing between foods.
Then he rebuked them and said to them, “Blind Pharisees, why do you wash the outside of the cup and dish, while inside it is full of wickedness and robbery?
You are like tombs, whitewashed on the outside and looking beautiful, but inside full of dead people’s bones and every kind of filth.”
He explained and showed them that their ritual washings and purifications did them no good, and he said to them:
“Evil thoughts arise in the heart, and those evil thoughts that arise in the heart—
they are what defile a person, not foods. For foods go into the stomach and from there are thrown out into the latrine.
A person is not defiled by them. For if all delicacies that are choice and pleasing to the palate, smell, sight, and taste—
if a person eats these, only his palate senses their pleasant flavors. From there his stomach receives them
and distributes their strength to all the arteries and limbs of the body. When the food goes down below, instead of a pleasant smell it changes and becomes a stench.
Instead of a good taste and a beautiful appearance, it changes to an ugly appearance and is thrown out into the latrine.
And if a person eats plain bread, which is neither beautiful in appearance nor pleasant in taste and has no appealing smell,
it travels along the same path within the person and gives strength to all his arteries and limbs. From there it is thrown out into the latrine.
It can happen that pleasant food turns into more of a stench than food that is not choice and pleasant. In these things there is neither sin nor righteousness.
The illustrious apostle also took away the grounds of those who boast about foods. For he said to those who were puffed up with this way of thinking,
who reject foods and make distinctions between them, “Foods do not commend us before God. For if we eat, we gain nothing,
and if we do not eat, we lose nothing.” For if a person eats every kind of provision and delicacy
and makes proper use of God’s creation without greed, receiving his gift in faith, he incurs no sin or wrongdoing.
But if he eats dust like a serpent, while the serpent’s gall bursts within him, he gains no benefit or advantage.
For all God’s creatures are good, and there is nothing among them to be rejected. They are sanctified by the word of God and by prayer.
My beloved, the apostle said this against the people of his own nation, when he saw that they regarded the foods of the Gentiles as unclean.
For the Israelites do not make use of anything at all among the foods that the Gentiles prepare, and they do not drink any wine that the Gentiles press.
For the pagan Gentiles offer sacrifices at every winepress and every threshing floor and invoke the names of their idols.
That is why the Israelites do not make use of their foods. This is the weak conscience.
The apostle took away the grounds of those who hold this view and said that all foods are sanctified by the word of God and by prayer.

For when someone makes use of God’s creatures, before he takes nourishment from them, he remembers, praises, blesses, and sanctifies the name of the Maker of those creatures, and prays. Then they are sanctified.
And the power of the evil one fled from them. The apostle also said, “If one of the pagans invites you to dinner and you wish to go, eat whatever he sets before you, for the sake of conscience.”
Concerning these things, my beloved, I will explain to you as much as I can: our holy God’s distinguishing between foods for the Israelites
was not intended to give them any righteousness. Rather, because of their gluttony and foulness, he devised this means for them, so that they would refrain from worship and sins
that they practiced in the land of Egypt. For in the beginning, when he made humankind, God commanded Adam and his descendants, and Noah and his offspring, as follows:
“See, I have given you animals and birds and all flesh. Pour out its blood on the ground and eat it, and let it be regarded by you like green plants.
Only you must not eat blood, but pour it out on the ground like water, because blood is life.” God gave these commands to those first generations,
and he did not distinguish between foods for them. For if there had been any sin or transgression of the law in these foods,
he would have distinguished unclean foods from clean ones for Adam and Noah from the beginning, just as he warned them and told them, “You must not eat blood,
but slaughter and eat any flesh, and let it be regarded by you like green plants.” He would also have commanded Abraham and his children not to use unclean food.
But we know that all the upright and righteous people who lived in the early generations down to Moses, who distinguished between foods for Israel—
all those generations used every kind of food that a person did not find repulsive, without sinning.
But he gave this command to the Israelites and distinguished between foods for them because the Israelites had turned aside to the worship of the Egyptians and abandoned the God of their fathers.
For the Egyptians worshiped bulls and calves. I will convince you of this.
For when Joseph’s brothers came to him, he gave orders to his steward and prepared a meal for them. When it was time to recline at the meal,

it is written that they served him separately, his brothers separately, and the Egyptians who ate with him separately, because the Egyptians could not eat a meal with the Hebrews, since it was an unclean thing to them.
For the Israelites had eaten every kind of flesh from the beginning, before they entered Egypt.
But the Egyptians did not eat the flesh of sheep and cattle, which were their gods. Also, when Jacob went down to Egypt, Joseph took five men from among his brothers
and presented them before Pharaoh. He instructed them, “When Pharaoh asks you and says to you, ‘What is your occupation?’
tell him, ‘Your servants are shepherds, and we are owners of livestock, both we and our fathers.’ When you tell him this, he will honor you,
because you are shepherds of what the Egyptians worship, and he will give you good pastureland, the land of Goshen.
And he will despise you, so that he will not take any of you and put you in charge of his work.” As it is written, “All shepherds are despised by the Egyptians.” And again it is written:
When Moses said before Pharaoh, “Let us go and sacrifice to the Lord our God in the wilderness,” Pharaoh said to him, “Worship the Lord your God in the land of Egypt.”
Moses said to him, “We cannot do this, because if we sacrifice the Egyptians’ animals before their eyes, they will stone us.”
And again it is written that the Lord also executed judgment on the gods of the Egyptians, when he destroyed the flocks of sheep and herds of cattle by hail and pestilence.
For the Egyptians kept flocks of sheep and herds of cattle for practical use, but they did not eat them, because they worshiped them.
But even to this day, the Egyptians’ food is pork, together with fish, which are abundant in their land, as the Israelites said
when they craved food: “We remember the fish we used to eat freely in Egypt, along with the strong-smelling onions, garlic, leeks, cucumbers, and melons.”
The Israelites followed the customs of the Egyptians, ate their food, and worshiped their gods.
And so that you may know that they practiced paganism in the land of Egypt and worshiped their gods: when the time came for Joshua son of Nun to die,
he summoned the Israelites and said to them, “Choose for yourselves today whom you will serve:
whether the gods your ancestors served beyond the River—Terah, the father of Abraham and the father of Nahor—or the gods you used to serve in the land of Egypt.
But I and my household worship the Lord God.” He went on to warn them: “Choose for yourselves today whom you will serve.”
They said to him, “We worship the Lord and serve him, because he is our God.” He said to them, “Be careful! Perhaps you will not be able to serve the Lord.”
They said, “We are able.” He said to them, “You are witnesses against yourselves that you have chosen for yourselves to serve the Lord.”
They said, “We are witnesses.” And to make it clear to you also that they used to worship sheep and cattle in Egypt, consider what happened when Moses delayed on the mountain.
They turned away from following the Lord and worshiped idols. They did not make any other image for themselves to worship, but the image of a calf,
something they had been accustomed to worship in the land of Egypt. They made sport and held a festival before the calf they had made.
Jeroboam son of Nebat also, when he led them astray, made a calf for them to worship, something they had worshiped in Egypt.
When the Holy One saw that they had still not been cleansed of the Egyptians’ leaven and remained in that pagan way of thinking,
he then commanded Moses to distinguish foods for them. He declared unclean for them the things that had been clean for them to eat in the land of Egypt.
He permitted them to eat the things they had worshiped in the land of Egypt and had not eaten. And because of their evil inclination,

he commanded that even the offerings they presented before him should come from the things they had worshiped, so that even if they did not want to eat them, they would eat the meat of sheep and cattle on account of their sacrifices.
Notice that although he designated many animals as clean for them, he did not command them to present offerings from all of them,
but only from sheep and cattle. Be convinced, then, my beloved, that Israel’s boasting about distinguishing foods is empty.
Tell me, then, scribe, debater, wise man of the people: if it brings uncleanness upon Israel to come into contact with and use something that the Law has declared unclean,
why did Samson the Nazirite, Israel’s champion, take honey from an unclean animal, from the carcass of a lion, and eat it, while it flowed over his hands?
He incurred no guilt or blame at all for this deed, nor is it written that he became unclean. And again, when he won a victory with a donkey’s jawbone
and piled up heaps of Philistines, he became thirsty and prayed before his God, saying, “Lord God, you have accomplished this great victory through the hand of your servant.
And now shall I die of thirst?” God heard Samson’s prayer and made water gush out for him from the donkey’s jawbone. He drank, and his thirst was relieved.
For if there had been any uncleanness or guilt in the donkey’s jawbone, since it was indeed unclean according to the Law, why would he have made water gush from the jawbone for his Nazirite to drink?
For if this is impurity, it should have sprung up for him from a rock, just as he brought water out of a rock for the Israelites in the wilderness.
Or from the ground, as he brought it out for Hagar, and Ishmael drank. But if there is impurity in food,
among all birds there are none more unclean and filthy than ravens, which used to carry bread and meat to the holy prophet Elijah while he was living by the brook Cherith.
And where else could the ravens have been carrying Elijah’s food from, if not Jerusalem?
The priests would set aside the portion due to him and faithfully give it to the ravens. They would take it and carry it to Elijah at the command of the Most High, his God.
And Elijah’s food was clean, though he received it from the mouths of ravens, birds that the Law declared unclean.

And know, my dear friend, that he distinguished foods for them to cut off their excuse for worshiping the calves, the objects of Egyptian worship. He commanded them to offer sacrifices from the very things they had worshiped in the land of Egypt.
For God had no need of sacrifices and offerings.

Rather, it was so that the requirement of offerings would restrain them from worshiping the gods of the nations when they entered among them and mingled with them, as they had worshiped the gods of the Egyptians when they entered Egypt and mingled with them.
For this reason he bound and restrained them by requiring them to present their offerings and slaughter their sacrifices before his altar. Yet although he warned them earnestly,
they turned away from following him, worshiped and served the gods of the nations, and corrupted their way, just as Moses said to them:
“I know that after my death you will utterly corrupt yourselves and turn aside from the way I commanded you, and many evils will befall you in the days to come.”
And to convince you that God had no need at all of sacrifices, offerings, incense, or fragrance, but that these were intended to restrain them:
when they turned aside and, using the sacrifices he had given them as a pretext, began sacrificing to idols, he then said to them through the prophet:
“Your many sacrifices are of no use to me, says the Lord.” And he said to them, “Incense is detestable to me.”
“My soul hates your new moons and your festivals.” David also said, “I do not eat the flesh of bulls,
and I do not drink the blood of young goats. Instead of these, offer thanksgiving as a sacrifice to God, and fulfill your vows to the Most High.
And when you have done this, call on me in the day of distress, and I will strengthen you, and you will glorify me.” And again it is written in the prophet, “I hate and despise your festivals,
and I will not smell the offerings at your solemn assemblies.” Again it is written, “Even if you bring me offerings, I will not look upon the abundance of your fattened animals.”
And again he said, “Did you offer sacrifices and offerings to me for forty years in the wilderness, Israelites?
And if you eat and drink, is it not you who eat and drink? says the Lord.” And Isaiah said:
“One who slaughters a lamb is like one who slaughters a dog, and one who offers a bull is like one who slaughters a man. One who offers frankincense is like one who offers pig’s blood,
and one who prays before me is like one who blesses idols.” And Samuel spoke to Saul when he heard the sound of the sheep and cattle that had come from the Amalekites:
“What is this sound that I hear?” Saul said to him, “The people spared the best of the sheep to sacrifice to the Lord your God.” And Samuel said to him:
“Look, obedience is better than sacrifices, and listening is better than the fat of fattened animals.” And again he said that the Lord does not desire the burnt offerings of sinners.
And again it is written: “The guilt of Eli’s household will never be atoned for by sacrifices and offerings.” And again it is written:
“The Lord takes no pleasure in rams, nor in vast quantities of oil. Instead of these, he has shown you, mortal, what is beneficial, what the Lord requires of you:
to practice justice, pursue faithfulness, and be ready to follow your God.” And when he rejected sacrifices and offerings in the days of Isaiah, he said:
“I will show you what I desire. Stop doing evil and learn to do good. Seek justice and do good to the oppressed.
Defend the cause of orphans and defend the cause of widows. When you have done these things, come, let us speak with one another, says the Lord.
Even if your sins are like scarlet, they will become white as snow; even if they are red like crimson, they will become like wool.” And Malachi said:
“Do not offer anything on my altar in vain, for I take no pleasure in you, says the Lord.” And Daniel said to Nebuchadnezzar:
“Redeem your sins through almsgiving and your wrongdoing through mercy toward the weak,” and not through sacrifices and offerings.
For he rejected Israel and rejected its offerings, as Jeremiah said: “Call them rejected silver, because the Lord has rejected them.”
And again he said: “Send them away from my presence, and let them go. If they say, ‘Where shall we go?’ tell them: ‘Those destined for the sword, to the sword; those destined for famine, to famine;
and those destined for captivity, to captivity.’” And again it is written that he will no longer look upon them. Isaiah also said: “Separate yourselves from them and call them unclean.”
Jeremiah also said: “I have abandoned my house; I have abandoned my inheritance. I have handed the beloved of my soul over to her enemies.” And again it is written:
“I gave the daughter of my people a certificate of divorce.” And again it is written: “The Lord has caused festivals and the Sabbath to be forgotten in Zion.”
And through the prophet Ezekiel he explained and showed them about their stubbornness. He gave them sacrifices and offerings so that perhaps, through these, they would refrain from their sins.
He told them earlier: “I gave them commandments and made judgments known to them, which a person will live by if he carries them out.” And again he said:
“I gave them commandments that were not good, and judgments by which they would not live. I defiled them through their gifts when they presented offerings.”

Be persuaded, then, you obstinate man, scribe of the Law and teacher of the people, now that the holy mouth has testified that the commandments and judgments given to you are neither beneficial nor good.
Why are you so brazen-faced and obstinate in debate? For look: it was because of your sins that he gave you offerings and prescribed distinctions between foods for you.
Which commandments and judgments did Ezekiel mean when he said that whoever carries them out will live by them? And which did he mean when he said: “I gave you commandments that were not good,
and judgments by which they would not live”? The life-giving commandments and judgments are those written above:
the just and righteous judgments that he set before them, the ten holy commandments that he inscribed with his own hands and gave to Moses to teach them.
But when they made themselves a calf and strayed from following him, then he gave them commandments and judgments that were not good:
offerings and purification for leprosy, discharges, menstruation, and childbirth; and the rule that no one should approach a dead person, a grave, bones, or those who have been killed;
and that a person should present an offering for every sin and for every human impurity. Concerning each one of these he said: “He will be unclean until evening,”
even if he bathes in water. Truly, under these written regulations, Israel does not have even a single day free from sins.
Instead, they spend all their days in sins and impurity, and they cannot be justified by the Law, as the apostle said:
“No one is justified by the Law. Rather, whoever does the things written in it will live by them.”
It is well known that no one can do these things or manage to keep them. Our Lord too, when he saw that they were burdensome, called out and said to us:
“Come to me, you who are weary and carry burdens, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, because my yoke is light and pleasant.”
We give thanks for the mercy that removed from us the harsh yoke and the heavy yoke. He gave us his own, which is restful and pleasant.
I have written these few reminders to you, my dear friend, concerning the pride, arrogance, and boasting of the Jewish people, who declare foods unclean and distinguish between them.
For they pride themselves on these three things: circumcision, keeping the Sabbath, and distinguishing between foods, along with other things.

About these three things I have written a little, according to what I have understood, and have explained them to you. About the other things, according to what God grants me, I will write from time to time and explain them to you.
End of the discourse on distinguishing between foods.
Demonstration concerning the nations that took the place of the people.
For the nations of every language had been called beforehand to the inheritance of the Most High, before Israel, as God said to Abraham:
“I have made you the father of a multitude of nations.” And Moses proclaimed and said, “They will call the nations to the mountain, and there they will offer righteous sacrifices.”
And in the Song of Witness he said to the people, “I will make you jealous through a people that is not a people, and through a foolish nation I will provoke you to anger.”
And our father Jacob testified concerning the nations when he blessed Judah and said to him, “The scepter will not depart from Judah,
nor an interpreter from between his feet, until the one comes to whom the kingdom belongs, and the nations will hope in him.” And Isaiah said:
“The mountain of the Lord’s house will be established at the head of the mountains and raised above the hills, and all the nations will look toward it.
Many nations will come from far away and say, ‘Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob.
He will teach us his ways, and we will walk in his paths.’ For the Law will go out from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem.
He will judge between the nations and rebuke all the distant nations.” And when he has judged and rebuked them, then they will accept discipline,
become peaceful, and be humbled out of their stubbornness. They will beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into sickles.
Nation will no longer take up the sword against nation, and they will no longer learn warfare. For in former times the nations that did not know God
used to fight with swords, spears, and javelins for plunder and oppression. But when Christ the Savior came,
he broke the bow of war and spoke peace to the nations. They beat their swords into plowshares and made their spears into sickles,
so that they might eat from the labor of their own hands and not from plunder. Again it is written, “I will give the nations a choice language,
so that they may all call upon the name of the Lord.” For in former times the nations did not have choice speech, nor did they call upon the name of the Lord.
For with their lips they praised the idols their hands had made, and they called on the names of their gods, not on the name of the Lord.
Again, the prophet Zechariah also said that many mighty nations would join themselves to the Lord. And the prophet Jeremiah proclaimed openly and plainly concerning the nations, saying:
“The nations will abandon their carved images and cry out and proclaim and say, ‘The false idols our fathers handed down to us are nothing.’”
Jeremiah proclaimed to his own people and said to them, “Stand at the roads, ask about the ancient paths, and see which road is good.
Walk in it.” But in their stubbornness they answered him, “We will not walk in it.” Again he said to them, “I have appointed watchmen over you so that you may listen to the sound of the trumpet.”
Again they said to him, “We will not listen.” They did this plainly and openly in the days of Jeremiah, when he proclaimed the word of the Lord to them.
They answered him, “As for the word you have spoken to us in the name of the Lord, we will not listen to you. Instead, we will do what we wish,
and everything that has come from our mouths, burning incense to other gods.” When he saw that they would not listen to him, he turned to the nations and said to them:
“Listen, nations, and take notice, assembly among them! Let the earth hear in all its fullness.” And when he saw that they brazenly opposed him
and answered him insolently, he then abandoned them, just as he prophesied and said: “I have abandoned my house; I have abandoned my inheritance.
I have given my dearly beloved into the hands of her enemies.” And in her place, a speckled bird became my inheritance—that is, the church from among the nations, gathered from every language.
And so that you may know that he truly abandoned them, Isaiah again said concerning them, “You have abandoned your people, the house of Jacob.”
He called them Sodomites and the people of Gomorrah, and brought in the nations in their place, giving them the name of the house of Jacob.
For Isaiah spoke and called the nations by the name of the house of Jacob, saying to them, “House of Jacob, come, let us walk in the light of the Lord.”
For the people of the house of Jacob were abandoned, and they became rulers of Sodom and the people of Gomorrah. Their father was an Amorite,
and their mother a Hittite. They changed and became a foreign vine, whose grapes are bitter grapes and whose clusters are bitterness to them.
Rebellious children and rejected silver; a vine of Sodom and a planting of Gomorrah; a vineyard that produced carob pods instead of grapes;
and a vine whose branches fire has consumed, which serves no purpose, is good for nothing, and is not wanted for any use. For he called two groups Jacob:

one that walks in the light of the Lord, and one that is abandoned. Instead of Jacob, those people were named rulers of Sodom, while the people from among the nations were called by the name of Jacob.
Again, the prophet said concerning the nations that they would offer offerings in place of the people. For he said, “My name is great among the nations,
and in every place they offer pure offerings in my name.” But concerning Israel the prophet said, “I take no pleasure in your offerings.”
Again he said, “Your sacrifices have not pleased me.” And Hosea also said concerning Israel, “They seek the Lord falsely.”
And Isaiah said that their heart was far from their God. For he said, “This people honors me with its lips, but its heart is far from me.”
And Hosea said, “Ephraim has surrounded me with falsehood, and the house of Israel and Judah with deceit, until the people of God came down.”
And which people? None other than the righteous and faithful people. For if he was speaking about Israel when he said, “They have surrounded me with falsehood and deceit,”
And concerning Ephraim: see, the sinful kingdom arose in Israel from Ephraim. For if the name of Judah had not been mentioned in that statement,
they would have gone away with the idea that Judah was the holy and faithful one who came down and joined himself to the Lord. But the prophet proclaimed clearly and plainly:
“Ephraim and Israel have surrounded me with falsehood,” because Jeroboam son of Nebat openly led them astray with the calf;
“and Judah with deceit,” because they worshiped idols deceitfully and secretly, as he also showed their uncleanness to Ezekiel.
Hosea proclaimed concerning them, describing them as a prostitute and an adulteress. For he said concerning the congregation of Israel, “Let her remove her prostitution from her face.”
And concerning the congregation of the house of Judah he said, “Let her remove her adultery from between her breasts.” And so that you may know that the prophet spoke about both congregations
and described them as a prostitute and an adulteress, he said after that statement, “Unless she removes her prostitution from her face and her adultery from between her breasts,
I will strip her naked and leave her as on the day she was born, and as on the day she came up from the land of Egypt.” And their two congregations:

one is Israel’s and one is Judah’s. Israel’s is the prostitute, and Judah’s is the adulteress. And the people from among the nations are the holy and faithful people who came down and joined themselves to the Lord.
Why did he say that they came down? It was because they came down from their pride. For Ezekiel also described them as Oholah and Oholibah.
And he called their two congregations the two branches of the vine that the fire consumed. David also proclaimed and said concerning the nations:

“The Lord will count the nations in the register.” And concerning the Israelites he prophesied and said, “Let them be erased from your book of life, and let them not be recorded with your righteous ones.”
But know, my dear friend, that the Israelites were recorded in the book of the Holy One, as Moses said before his God:
“Either forgive this people’s sin, or erase me from your book that you have written.” And he said, “Whoever has sinned against me, I will erase from my book.”
And when they sinned, David said concerning them, “Let them be erased from your book of life, and let them not be recorded with your righteous ones.”
And concerning the nations he said, “The Lord will count the nations in the register,” because the nations had not been entered in the book and the register. And see, my dear friend,
that the calling of the nations was marked out beforehand, before the calling of the people. For time after time they sinned in the wilderness. For he said to Moses:
“Leave me alone, so that I may wipe out this people and make you into a people greater and more excellent than they.” And because the time of the nations had not arrived,
and their savior was to be someone else, Moses did not agree to become the savior and teacher of the people from among the nations, who were greater and more excellent than the people of Israel.
For it was fitting that the Son of God should be named with this great and surpassing praise, as Isaiah said:
“It is too small a thing for you to be my servant, to restore the shoot of Jacob and raise up the tribe of Israel. Rather, I have made you a light to the nations,
so that you may show my salvation to the ends of the earth.” And again Isaiah proclaimed concerning the nations, “Listen to me, peoples,
and pay attention to me /and pay attention to me/, nations, because the law will go out from me, and my judgment is a light to the nations.” And David said:
“At the hearing of the ear, foreigners will obey me.” And these same foreigners “will grow weak and limp away from their paths.”
For the nations heard and limped away from the paths of worshiping images and idols.
And if they say that he called us foreign children, they themselves were not called foreigners, but children and heirs.
As Isaiah said, “I raised children and brought them up, but they rebelled against me.” And the prophet said, “Out of Egypt I called my son.”
And the Holy One said to Moses, “Say to Pharaoh, ‘Let my son go, so that he may serve me.’” And again he said, “Israel is my firstborn son.”
But it is the nations who listened to God, became lame, and were kept from the paths of their sins. And again Isaiah said:
“You will call nations that did not know you, and nations that do not know you will come to you and turn to you.” And again Isaiah said:
“Hear, nations, what I have done, and know my might, you who are far away.” And David said concerning the church and the assembly of the nations:
“Remember your congregation, which you acquired long ago.” And again David said, “Praise the Lord, all nations, and let the peoples praise his name.”
And again he said, “The kingdom belongs to the Lord, and he rules over the nations.” And again the prophet said, “In the last days,
I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh, and they will prophesy. No one will teach his fellow citizen or his brother, saying, ‘Know our Lord,’
because they will all know me, from their youngest to their oldest.” And concerning the children of Israel he said, “I will send a famine upon the land,
not a hunger for bread or a thirst for water, but for hearing the word of the Lord. They will come from west to east,
and from south to north, seeking the word of the Lord, but they will not find it, because it has departed from them.” Moses wrote beforehand concerning them:
