“When many troubles come upon you in the last days, you will say, ‘These troubles have come upon me because God is not among us.’”
As they said in the days of Ezekiel, “The Lord has abandoned the land, and the Lord no longer sees us.” And Isaiah said concerning them:
“Your wrongdoings have separated you from your God, and your sins have withheld good things from you.” And again he said:
“You will cry loudly in my ears, but I will not listen to you.” And concerning the people drawn from the nations, David said, “Clap your hands, all you nations,
and praise God with a voice of praise.” And again he said, “Hear this, all you nations, and listen, all inhabitants of the earth.”
Even long ago, everyone among the nations who pleased God was found more righteous than Israel. Jethro, a priest from among the nations, was blessed, both he and his offspring.

His dwelling became secure, and he set his nest on a cliff. And Joshua gave his right hand to the Gibeonites, who were from the unclean nations, and they entered and took refuge in the Lord’s inheritance.
They became gatherers of wood and drawers of water for the Lord’s congregation and altar. And when Saul sought to kill them, the heavens were held back from giving rain,
until Saul’s sons were slaughtered. Then the Lord turned toward the land and blessed his inheritance. And Rahab the prostitute, who received the spies,
received an inheritance in Israel, both she and her father’s household. And Obed-edom, from Gath of the Philistines—the ark of the Lord entered his house,
and it was honored in his care more than in all Israel. He and his household were blessed by the Lord. And Ittai the Gittite provided for David during his persecution,
and his name and his offspring were honored. And Ebed-melech the Cushite, a faithful eunuch, brought Jeremiah up from the pit,
when the children of Israel, his own people, had taken him captive. This is what Moses said concerning them: “The foreigner among you will rise above, while you will sink below.”
They took the prophet Jeremiah prisoner and lowered him into the deep pit. But Ebed-melech, a convert from Cush, brought Jeremiah up from the pit.
And Ruth the Moabite, from a people who provoked anger, came and joined the people of Israel. From her descendants arose a dynasty of kings,
from whom the Savior among the nations / of the nations was born. And Uriah the Hittite, from an unclean people, was a great man among David’s warriors.
Because David treacherously killed him in the war against the Ammonites, and desired his wife and took her, David received the sentence that the sword would never depart from his house.
And again Isaiah said about our Savior, “I have given you as a covenant to the people and a light to the nations.” How, then, did he become a covenant to the people?
It was because, from the time when the light and Savior of the nations came, Israel was restrained from worshiping idols.

And he became a true covenant for them. About this Moses said, “I will make you jealous through a people who are no people, and through a foolish people I will provoke you to anger.” They became jealous of us,
and because of us they do not worship idols, so that they will not be reproached by us, since we have abandoned idols and call what our ancestors left us falsehood.
They are angry, and their hearts are broken because we have entered and become heirs in their place. For this was the covenant that came to them:
that they should not worship other gods. Even though they did not accept him, he made them jealous through us, and he became light and life for us, as he proclaimed and said,
when he taught, “I am the light of the world.” And again he said, “Believe while you have the light, before darkness overtakes you.”
And again he said, “Walk in the light, so that you may be called children of the light.” And again it was said about him, “The light was shining in the darkness.”
He is the covenant that came to the world, and the light that enlightened all the nations and restrained them and kept them from crooked paths,
as it is written: “At his coming, the rugged ground will become smooth, and the difficult terrain a plain. The glory of the Lord will be revealed, and all flesh will see the life of God.”
I have written this brief reminder to you about the nations, because the Jews boast and say, “We are the people of God
and the children of Abraham.” But let us listen to John, who spoke to them when they boasted, “We ourselves are the children of Abraham.”
Then John said to them, “Do not be arrogant and say, ‘We have Abraham as our father,’
because God can raise up children for Abraham from these stones.” And our Savior said to them, “You are the children of Cain,
and not the children of Abraham.” And the apostle said, “The branches that sinned were broken off, and we were grafted in their places,
and we became sharers in the richness of the olive tree.” From now on, let us not boast and sin, lest we too be broken off, for we have indeed been grafted into the olive tree.
This is an utterance in the Spirit against the Jews, because they boast, “We are the children of Abraham, and we are the people of God.”
The Demonstration on the People and the Nations is finished.
A Demonstration to Show That Christ Is the Son of God
A comparison of statements in reply to the Jews who revile the people from the nations, because they say this: “You worship and serve a man who was born,
a human being who was crucified, and you call a human being God. And although God has no son, you say of him,
That this crucified Jesus is, they say, the Son of God. And they offer as proof that God said, “I, I am God, and there is no other besides me.”
And again he said, “You shall not worship another god.” “So then,” they say, “you are opposing God and calling a human being God.”
But concerning these things, my dear friend, I will explain them to you as far as I can and my limited ability allows: even if we grant them that he is a human being,
and we honor him and call him God and Lord, we are not calling him something foreign to him, nor have we given him an unfamiliar name,
one that they themselves have not used. Nevertheless, we are certain that Jesus our Lord is God, the Son of God, and King, the Son of the King,
Light from Light, Creator and Counselor, Guide and Way, Savior and Shepherd, Gatherer and Gate, Pearl and Lamp.
And he has been called by many names. But let us leave them all aside and demonstrate that he is the Son of God and is God, who came from God.
For the honored title of divinity has also been bestowed on righteous human beings, and they were found worthy to be called by it.
And the people in whom God delighted he called “my sons and my friends.” Moses, his friend and his beloved,
when he chose him and made him a leader, teacher, and priest for his people, he called a god. For he said to him, “I have made you a god to Pharaoh.”
And he gave him his priest as a prophet. He said, “Aaron your brother will speak for you with Pharaoh. You will be a god to him, and he will be your interpreter.”
It was not only to Pharaoh, who was wicked, that he made Moses a god; he also made Moses a god to Aaron, the holy priest.
Again, listen concerning our calling him the Son of God. They say, “Although God has no son, you make this crucified Jesus God's firstborn son.”
For he called Israel himself “my firstborn son” when he sent a message to Pharaoh through Moses and said to him, “Israel is my firstborn son.
I told you, ‘Let my son go so that he may serve me.’ If you are unwilling to let him go, look, I will kill your son, your firstborn.”
And through the prophet he also testified to this and rebuked them, saying to the people, “Out of Egypt I called him my son. Just as I called them,
so they went away, worshiped Baal, and offered incense to carved images.” And Isaiah said about them, “I raised children and brought them up,
but they rebelled against me.” And again it is written, “You are children of the Lord your God.” And concerning Solomon he said, “He will be a son to me,
and I will be a father to him.” We too call this Christ the Son of God, because through him we have come to know God,
just as he called Israel “my firstborn son,” and just as he said concerning Solomon, “He will be a son to me.” And we call him God,
just as he gave Moses his own name. And David also said about them, “I said, ‘You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High.’”
But when they failed to act rightly, he then said about them, “You will die like human beings, and you will fall like one of the rulers.”
For the title of divinity was given in the world as a great honor, and God bestowed it on whomever he pleased. Yet God's names are many and honored,
as when he revealed his names to Moses and said to him, “I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob.
This is my name forever, and this is how I am to be remembered from generation to generation.” And he called his name “I Am Who I Am,” “God Almighty,” “Lord,” and “Hosts.”
God was called by these names. And although the title of divinity is great and honorable, he did not withhold it even from his righteous ones.
And although he is the great King, he bestowed the great and honorable title of kingship on human beings, who are his handiwork, without begrudging it.
For through the mouth of his prophet, God called Nebuchadnezzar, the wicked king, “king of kings.” For Jeremiah said:
“Every nation and kingdom that does not put its neck under the yoke of Nebuchadnezzar, king of kings, my servant—I will punish that nation with famine, sword, and pestilence.”
And although he is the great King, he did not withhold the title of kingship from human beings. And although he is the great God, he did not withhold the title of divinity from people of flesh.
And although all fatherhood belongs to him, he also called human beings fathers. For he said to the congregation, “Your sons will take the place of your fathers.”
And although dominion belongs to him, he gave human beings authority over one another. And although bowing in homage belongs to him,
he granted it so that one person might honor another through it in the world. For even if a person bows before the unjust and the wicked,
and before those who deny his goodness, that person is not blamed by God. But concerning worship, he commanded his people, “You shall not bow down to the sun,
nor to the moon, nor to any of the hosts of heaven. Nor shall you desire to bow down to any creatures on earth.”
And see the goodness and compassion of our good Maker, who did not withhold from human beings the title of divinity, the title of homage, or the title of kingship,
or the title of dominion. For he is the Father of the creatures on the face of the world, and above all his creatures he honored, exalted, and glorified human beings,
because he formed them with his holy hands and breathed into them from his Spirit. And from the beginning he became a dwelling place for them.
He dwells in them and walks among them. For he said through the prophet, “I will dwell in them and walk among them.” And again the prophet Jeremiah also said,
“You are the Lord’s temple if you make your ways and your deeds good.” And long before, David said, “Lord, you have been our dwelling place throughout our generations,
before the mountains were conceived, before the earth went into labor, and before the world was established. From everlasting to everlasting, you are God.”
And how are you to understand this: that one prophet said, “Lord, you have been our dwelling place,” and another said, “I will dwell in them and walk among them”?
First he became a dwelling place for us, and afterward he dwelt in us and walked among us. To the wise, both statements are true and clear.
For David said, “Lord, you have been our dwelling place throughout our generations, before the mountains were conceived, and before the earth went into labor,
and before the world was established.” And you know, my beloved, that all the creatures above and below were created first,
and the human being last of them all. For when God planned to create the world with all its adornments, he first conceived Adam and fashioned him within his mind.
And after Adam was conceived in his thought, he then conceived the creatures, as he said, “Before the mountains were conceived and the earth labored in childbirth.”
For the human being is older and earlier than the creatures in conception, but in birth the creatures are older and earlier than Adam.
Adam was conceived and dwelt in God’s thought. And while he was held in conception within his mind, God created all the creatures by the word of his mouth.
And when he had completed and adorned the world, with nothing lacking in it, he then brought Adam forth from his thought and formed the human being with his hands.
And Adam saw the world prepared, and he gave him authority over everything he had made. It is like a man who has a son and wishes to hold a wedding feast for him.
He betroths a wife to him, builds him a house, and prepares and furnishes everything his son needs. Then he holds the wedding feast and gives his son authority over his house.
And after conceiving Adam, he brought him forth and gave him authority over his entire creation. Concerning this the prophet said, “Lord, you have been our dwelling place throughout our generations,
before the mountains were conceived, before the earth went into labor, and before the world was prepared. From everlasting to everlasting, you are the Lord.”
So that no one should suppose that there is another God, either before or afterward, he said, “From everlasting to everlasting.”
As Isaiah said, “I am the first, and I am the last.” And after God brought Adam forth from within his thought,
he formed him, breathed into him from his spirit, and gave him discerning knowledge, so that he could distinguish good from evil and know that God had made him. And through his knowing his Maker,
God took shape and was conceived within the human mind, and the human being became a temple for God his Maker, as it is written, “You are the temple of God.”
And he said, “I will dwell in them and walk among them.” But in human beings who do not know their Maker, he does not take shape within them,
nor does he dwell in them or become conceived in their minds. Rather, they are reckoned before him as animals and as the rest of the creatures.
For let the foolish be persuaded by these things that there is nothing strange in our calling Christ the Son of God. For look: all human beings—

he conceived them and brought them forth from his thought. And let them be reproved concerning the fact that the name of divinity also rests upon him, for he also bestowed the name “God” upon his righteous ones.
And concerning our bowing down to Jesus, through whom we have known God, let them be ashamed: they fall down, bow, and give honor even to wicked rulers from unclean nations.
And there is no blame in this, because God gave human beings this honor of bowing down, so that with it they might honor one another, including those who are greater and more honored than themselves.
For if they bow down to the wicked and honor them with the designation of worship—even those who in their wickedness deny the very name of God—
they should not bow down to them as to their Maker, as though they alone were without sins.
How much more ought we to bow down and give honor to Jesus, who turned our foolish minds away from all forms of worship belonging to empty error,

and taught us to worship, serve, and minister to the one God, our Father and Maker. And let them know that the kings of the world call themselves gods in the name of the great God, though they are deniers and cause others to deny him.
Yet people fall down and bow before them, serve them, and honor them as they do carved images and idols, without the law ever censuring them.
And there is no sin in it, just as Daniel bowed down to Nebuchadnezzar, who denied God and caused others to deny him, and was not censured. Joseph also bowed down to Pharaoh,
and it is not written that this was a sin for him. But we are certain that Jesus is God, the Son of God, and through him we have known his Father, and he has restrained us from all other worship.
Now we have nothing with which to repay the one who endured these things for us, except to repay him with the honor of worship in return for his suffering on our behalf.
Furthermore, we ought to acknowledge that this Jesus was promised beforehand through the prophets long ago and was called the Son of God. David said, “You are my Son,
and today I have begotten you.” Again he said, “In the splendor of holiness, from the womb, from of old, I have begotten you, O child.” And Isaiah said,
“A child has been born to us, and a son has been given to us. His authority rests upon his shoulder, and his name shall be called Wonder and Counselor, and God, the Mighty One of the ages.”
And ruler of peace, to increase his authority, and there is no end to his peace. Now tell me, [?], wise teacher of Israel:
Who is born and is named Child and Son, Wonder and Counselor, God, Mighty One of the ages, and Ruler of Peace?
“To increase his authority,” and he says that there is no end to his peace. For David taught us to call the Messiah the Son of God.
And we heard from Isaiah that we should call him God, whose authority was placed upon his shoulder, for he took up his cross and went out from Jerusalem.
And Isaiah also said that a child would be born: “Look, the virgin will conceive and give birth, and his name will be called Immanuel,” which means “Our God is with us.”
And if you say that the Messiah has not yet come, I will give you this too in answer to your contentiousness. For it is written that when he comes, the nations will hope in him.

Look, I, who am from the nations, have heard that the Messiah has come. And before he comes, I have already believed in him, and through him I worship the God of Israel. Will he perhaps blame me when he comes
because I have already believed in him before he comes? But, foolish man, the prophets do not allow you to say that the Messiah has not yet come.
Daniel rebukes you and says that after—after sixty-two weeks the Messiah will come and be killed.
And at his coming /at his coming/ the holy city will be destroyed, and its end will be in a flood. Until the completion of the things decreed, it will remain in devastation.
For you wait and hope that at the coming of the Messiah, Israel will be gathered through him from every region, and Jerusalem will be rebuilt and inhabited.
But Daniel testifies that when the Messiah comes and is killed, Jerusalem will be ruined and remain in devastation until the completion of the things decreed, forever.
And David said about the suffering of the Messiah: “They pierced my hands and my feet, and all my bones cried out. They looked and stared at me.”
“And they divided my clothes among themselves, and cast lots for my garment.” And Isaiah said: “Look, my servant will be known and revealed and exalted.”
“Just as many will be astonished at him, so his appearance is marred beyond that of a man, and his form beyond that of human beings.”
And he said that he would cleanse many nations, and kings would be astonished at him. And in the same passage he said: “He grew up like an infant before him,
and like a root from thirsty ground.” And at the end of the passage he said: “He is killed because of our sins and humbled because of our wrongdoing.
The punishment for our peace was upon him, and by his wounds we shall be healed.” By whose wounds were human beings healed? David was not killed,
for he died at a good old age and was buried in Bethlehem. And if they say this concerns Saul, Saul died in the mountains of Gilboa,
in the battle with the Philistines. And if they say that they pierced his hands and feet when they fastened his body to the wall of Beth-shan,
this does not apply to Saul. When Saul’s limbs were pierced, his bones did not feel his suffering,
because he was dead. And after Saul died, they hung his body and those of his sons on the wall of Beth-shan.
And when David said, “They pierced my hands and my feet, and all my bones cried out,” he said afterward in the passage: “O God, remain to help me,
and rescue my life from the sword.” For the Messiah was rescued from the sword, came up from within Sheol, lived, and rose on the third day.
And God remained to help him. But Saul called upon the Lord, and he did not answer him. He inquired through the prophets, but no answer was given to him.

He disguised himself, consulted the spirits of the dead, and learned from them. He was defeated before the Philistines and killed himself with his sword when he saw that the battle had overwhelmed him.
And David said about him in the verse, “I will proclaim your name to my brothers, and in the midst of the congregation I will praise you.” How can these things be fulfilled in Saul?
And David said again, “You did not allow your Holy One to see decay.” But all these things were fulfilled in Christ.
When he came to them, they did not receive him. They condemned him unjustly through false testimony, and he was hung on a tree by their hands.
They pierced his hands and feet with the nails they drove into him, and all his bones cried out. On that very day a great wonder occurred:
The light grew dark in the middle of the day, as Zechariah prophesied, saying, “The day will be known to the Lord, neither day nor night,
and at evening there will be light.” What day, then, was distinguished by the wonder that it was neither day nor night,
and at evening there was light, except the day on which they crucified him, when darkness came in the middle of the day and at evening there was light?
And again he said that that day would be cold and frosty. As you know, it was cold on the day they crucified him,
and they made themselves a fire to warm themselves, when Simon came and stood beside them. And again he said, “A spear will rise against the shepherd

and against the sheep, my friends. It will strike the shepherd, and the lambs of his flock will be scattered, and I will turn my hand against the little ones.” And David spoke again about his suffering:
“They put gall in my food, and for my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.” Again he said in the same passage, “They persecuted the one you struck,
and added to the pain of the slain one.” For they inflicted many additional things on him, including things that had not been written about him:
curses and insults that writing cannot even disclose, so vile were their insults.
But the Lord wished them to humble him and make him suffer. He was killed because of our wrongdoing and humbled because of our sins, and sin was laid upon his soul.
We worship these mercies and bend the knee before the majesty of his Father, who directed our worship toward him. We call him God, like Moses,
and firstborn and son, like Israel; and Jesus, like Joshua son of Nun; and priest, like Aaron; and king, like David;
and a great prophet, like all the prophets; and shepherd, like the shepherds who tended and led Israel. And he called us sons, as he said,
“Foreign sons will obey me.” He made us his brothers, as he said, “I will proclaim your name to my brothers.” And we became his friends,
as he said to his disciples, “I have called you my friends,” just as his Father called Abraham “my friend.” And he said to us, “I am the good shepherd,”
and the gate, the way, the vineyard, the seed, the bridegroom, the pearl, the lamp, the light, the king, God, the giver of life, and the Savior. And he was called by many names.
I have written this brief argument for you, my beloved, so that you may go out in the Spirit to confront the Jews concerning their assertion that God has no Son,
and concerning our calling him God, the Son of God, the King, and the Firstborn of all creation.
End of the discourse on the Son of God.
Demonstration against the Jews and on virginity and holiness.
I also want to explain to you, my dear friend, this matter that concerns me: this holy covenant, and the virginity and holiness in which we stand.
For because of their recklessness and the uncleanness of their bodies, the Jewish people take offense at it, and they unsettle and weaken the minds of childish and unlearned people,
who are caught and taken captive by the persuasiveness of their confusion. They say, “When God created Adam, he blessed him in this way and said to him,
‘Grow, multiply, have children, and fill the earth.’ He also spoke to Noah in the same way: ‘Multiply on the earth and have children on it.’ And he blessed Abraham and said to him,
‘Look at the heavens and count the stars, if you can count them.’ And he told him, ‘So shall your offspring be.’
And in the blessing / blessings he said to Israel, ‘There shall be no barren man or barren woman among you.’ And again he said, ‘There shall be no woman who miscarries or is barren in your land.’
Isaac was given to Abraham as a blessing, and Isaac prayed for Rebekah to bear children. He also blessed Jacob, that his offspring might multiply.
Hannah pleaded earnestly for Samuel, and the barren woman’s offspring increased through his birth. And all the righteous received children and blessing.
But you,” they say, “are doing something that God did not command: you have accepted a curse and increased barrenness.
You have prevented childbearing, the blessings of the righteous. You do not take wives, and the women do not become wives to men.
You have hated childbearing, the blessing given by God.” Concerning these statements, my dear friend, I will explain to you as well as I can.
For when God blessed Adam, he said to him, “Have children and multiply on the earth.” Indeed, he blessed them so that the world might be filled with them.
For his descendants were fruitful, but when they multiplied, they became corrupt and acted wickedly, until by their sins they grieved and distressed the spirit of their Creator.
And he said, “I regret that I made them.” In his outpoured wrath and severe judgment, he wiped them out with the waters of the flood.
Now tell me, [?] disputant of Israel: whom did Adam’s blessing benefit, when they corrupted their way and were wiped out by the waters of the flood?
Through that very natural union they became corrupt and were condemned, and the blessing was extinguished by the sins of the wicked. But Noah, with only a small number, not having multiplied,
built an altar and appeased the compassion of the Holy One. Noah, with his small number, was better than that entire corrupt generation, and from him a second world was established.
Again, Noah was blessed to multiply through childbearing, so that the world might be filled and humanity might increase. But when they multiplied, grew strong, and increased through childbearing,
they forgot God and worshiped carved idols—all the nations and languages that came from his offspring. They were reckoned as nothing before God,
like a drop from a bucket and like a slight tipping of the scales. Only the offspring of the righteous lived and were saved before God.
For how did the blessing help the ten generations before the [?]? And how did it benefit the people of Sodom, whose lives were destroyed by fire and sulfur?
The blessing was extinguished by the sins of the wicked. Or what benefit and advantage did the blessing bring to the six hundred thousand who came out of Egypt,
who perished in the desolate wilderness and angered the Holy One? And what advantage and benefit was there in the blessing of childbearing among the unclean nations whom Joshua destroyed?
Or how did the blessing benefit Israel—that his offspring should multiply like the stars—when war and the sword consumed them?
But to God, one person who does his will is more excellent and better known before his majesty than tens of thousands and thousands who are wicked.
Noah was distinguished and recognized before God above the ten corrupt generations that preceded him. And Abraham was esteemed before God
above the ten generations before him, and he also surpassed those who came after him. Isaac and Jacob, the children of the promise,
were good and more excellent in God's sight than all the Amorites among whom they lived. And Joseph was esteemed before God above all the wicked people in Pharaoh's household.
And Moses, the great prophet in Israel, was good and distinguished before God above the six hundred thousand whom he brought out of Egypt,
who distressed God by their rebelliousness and could not enter the promised land.
And concerning virginity and chastity, I will convince you that among that people—among that ancient people itself—it was lovingly held in higher esteem before God,
above abundant childbearing that proved unworthy. Moses, the man, the great prophet, the leader of all Israel, from the time his Lord spoke with him,
loved chastity and served the Holy One. He withdrew from the world and from fathering children, and remained by himself so that he might please his Lord.
Otherwise, show me what you have to say, wise interpreter of the people: that from the time God spoke with him—with Moses—he engaged in natural sexual intercourse.
And if you bring us a false argument, I will not be deceived by your confusion, for you seek to defile the holy man because of your own filthiness.
For if he had been engaging in sexual intercourse, he could not have served the majesty of his Lord, just as Israel could not receive the holy utterance
and the living words that the Holy One spoke with Moses on the mountain until he had sanctified the people for three days. Then the Holy One spoke with them.
For he said to Moses, “Go down to the people and sanctify them for three days.” And Moses told them plainly,
“Do not approach a woman.” And when they had sanctified themselves for these three days, then, on the third day, the Holy One appeared
with mighty radiance, great glory, a powerful voice, terrifying thunder, a mighty trumpet blast, and incessant flames,
and bright flashes of lightning. The mountains shook and the hills trembled, and the sun and moon departed from their courses. And Moses went up Mount Sinai
and entered the cloud and received the commandment. Moses saw the glorious radiance and was terrified and shook, and trembling seized him, because he saw the dwelling presence of the Most High,
which rested on the mountain—the great power of God's throne. When the myriads and thousands serve him, they cover their faces from his glorious radiance,
and they run and fly with their swift wings. They cry out, proclaim his holiness, and exalt his majesty. They are watchful and ready and swift in their movements,
splendid, lovely, beautiful, and delightful. They run, proclaim his holiness, and fulfill his command. They ascend and descend through the air like swift flashes of lightning.
For Moses spoke, and God answered him with a voice. On that day Israel stood trembling, in fear and shaking.
They fell on their faces and could not endure it. And they said to Moses, “Do not let God speak with us, lest we die.”
O idle one, you who struggle with these things and stumble! If Israel, with whom God spoke for only a single hour,
could not hear God's voice until they had sanctified themselves for three days, even though they neither went up the mountain nor entered the mighty cloud,
Moses, the man, the prophet, the bright eye of the whole people, who stood before God at all times and spoke with him mouth to mouth—
How could this have been possible amid marital intercourse? If God spoke with Israel after they had consecrated themselves for only three days,
how much more excellent and desirable are those who keep themselves holy and watchful all their days, ready and standing before God!
Will God not love them all the more, and will his Spirit not dwell in them, as he said, “I will dwell in them
and walk among them”? And Isaiah said, “Whom will I regard and dwell with, except the peaceful and humble person who trembles at my word?”
I will show you that a virgin is greatly esteemed and loved before God. For the Holy One commanded the priests, the sons of Aaron who minister before him,
that none of them should marry a widow, a divorced woman, or a woman defiled by prostitution.
Instead, he should marry a virgin from his own people, one who has not been defiled by another man. See that a widow is unclean compared with a virgin.
But if marital intercourse is superior to virginity and chastity, why was it necessary to warn Israel and consecrate them for those three days,
and only then speak with them? And why was it required that a priest marry a virgin and not approach a widow or a divorced woman?
And why did Moses restrain himself and abstain from his wife for forty years? Did he perhaps father other children
besides Gershom and Eliezer? This is how I consider the matter: would that Zimri had never been born, because of his sexual immorality,
on account of which twenty-four thousand of Israel fell in a single hour! And would that Achan had never been formed in his mother’s womb,
who brought the camp of Israel under a curse! And would that Eli had remained chaste, and Hophni and Phinehas had not been born to him,
who dishonored the priesthood and behaved greedily! And why did Samuel need sons who did not keep the law
and did not walk in his ways? There are many like these who would have been better off if they had neither fathered children nor been born themselves.
Moses loved chastity, and the Holy One loved him and showed him his glory. Joshua son of Nun loved virginity and lived in the tabernacle,
where the Holy One was served. Elijah excelled in virginity and lived in the wilderness, in mountains and in caves, and the Holy One raised him to the dwelling place of the holy ones,
where lovers of impurity have no authority. Elisha remained single and lived chastely, and God performed astonishing miracles through him.
Jeremiah also said, “I have not desired the day of man.” His Lord also commanded him, saying, “Do not take a wife for yourself,
and do not have sons or daughters.” But at this the Jew spoke up boldly: “That is why he commanded Jeremiah, ‘Do not take a wife for yourself,
and do not have sons or daughters in this place, because this is what the Lord says about the sons and daughters born in this place:
They will die the death of those stricken by famine.’ That,” he says, “is precisely why he told him, ‘Do not take a wife for yourself.’” You senseless people!
For anyone who holds this view: the very one who caused Jeremiah to receive mercy in the eyes of the king of Babylon would also, if he had fathered children,
have rescued them from sword and famine. Ezekiel’s Lord also showed him kindness and took away the delight of his eyes with a sudden blow,
removing and casting off from him an oppressive yoke. Otherwise, show me, teacher, that Joshua son of Nun took a wife and fathered children.
And explain to me also about Elijah and his disciple Elisha: what house of their own did they have in this world?
For look, they lived in the wilderness, in mountains, and in caves, in distress and persecution, and neither of them had a wife with him.
Their disciples attended to them. And see how, when Gehazi, Elisha’s disciple, turned his mind toward this world
and desired possessions, a wife, and children, Elisha said to him, “Is this the time to acquire possessions, vineyards, and olive trees? Now that you have done this,
let Naaman’s leprosy clothe Gehazi and all his descendants forever.” For if you convince me from the Scriptures about each of these things,
I will accept it from you. But whatever you invent out of your own mind and say, I will not listen to you, because you have sought to defile the holy one with your false persuasion.
As for the marital union that God has given in the world, far be it from us to regard it as something blameworthy, for it is written:
“God saw everything he had made, and look, it was very good.” Nevertheless, some things are superior to others. God created heaven and earth, and they are very good,
but heaven is superior to earth. He created darkness and light, and it is very good, but light is superior to darkness. He created night and day,
and it is very good, but day is superior to night. He created the sun and the moon, and it is very good, but the sun is superior to the moon.
He created the stars of heaven, and it is very good, but one star surpasses another in its brightness. He created Adam and Eve,
and it is very good, but Adam is superior to Eve. He created the marital union that brings children into the world, and it is very good, but virginity is superior to it.
While the earth was a virgin, it was not defiled, but after rain fell upon it, it sprouted thorns. Adam in his virginity was beloved and beautiful,
but after he brought forth Eve, he went astray and transgressed the commandment. The sons of Seth were beautiful in their virginity,
but when they mingled with the daughters of Cain, they were swept away by the waters of the flood. Samson was beautiful in his Nazirite state and his virginity,
but through his sexual immorality he ruined his Nazirite state. David was lovely in his youth, but through his desire for Bathsheba he transgressed the law
and broke three of the Ten Commandments: “Do not covet,” “Do not murder,” and “Do not commit adultery.” Amnon was beautiful in his virginity,

but because of his shameful desire for his sister, Absalom /Absalom/ killed him. Solomon was beautiful and splendid in his virginity, but in his old age, through his desire for women, his heart turned away from his God.
We have heard from the law that a man shall leave his father and his mother and cling to his wife, and they shall become one flesh. This is truly a great and excellent prophecy.
What father and mother does a man leave when he takes a wife? This is the meaning: while a man has not yet taken a wife, he loves and honors God his Father
and the Holy Spirit his Mother, and he has no other love. But when a man takes a wife, he leaves his Father and his Mother,
those mentioned above, and his mind becomes attached to this world. His mind, his heart, and his thought are drawn away from God into the world,
and he loves and cherishes it as a man loves the wife of his youth, and his love is separated from that of his Father and his Mother.
And he said that the two shall become one flesh. This is true, for just as a man and a woman become one flesh and one mind,
and his understanding and thought become detached from his father and mother, so also a man who has not yet taken a wife and remains single is of his Father, in one spirit and one mind.
I wrote to you, my dear friend, about virginity and holiness because I heard a Jewish man reproaching one of our brothers, a member of our church.
He said to him, “You are unclean because you do not marry women. But we are holy and superior because we have children and multiply offspring in the world.”
It was for this very reason that I wrote this explanation to you. However, I have already written to you and explained virginity and holiness to you
in the Demonstration on the Members of the Covenant: how beautiful and desirable virginity is, even though a person practices it with difficulty,
as our Lord said, “Not everyone can accept it, but only those to whom it is given.” And the apostle said, “Because of the distress in the world,
it is good for a person to remain as he is.” There is a great reward for this way of life, because we practice it by our own free choice,
and not under the constraint and compulsion of a commandment. Nor are we bound to it under the law. We have found its image and likeness in Scripture,
and we have seen that among the victorious there was found this likeness to the Watchers in heaven, and that on earth it was acquired as a gift.
This is a possession that, once lost, cannot be found, and no one can acquire it for money. Neither can someone who possesses it and loses it find it,
nor can someone who does not possess it attain it by running after it. Love this gift, my dear friend, for there is nothing like it in the whole world.
With what I have written to you, go out in the Spirit against the Jews, who in their foulness do not grasp the power of virginity and holiness.
The work on Virginity and Holiness is finished.
A Letter against the Jews concerning Their Claim That They Are Assured of Being Gathered Together
The voice of the Holy One was heard by Moses, and he sent him to bring his people out of Egypt, out of Pharaoh’s house, out of slavery to the Egyptians.
He told him to say to Pharaoh, “Israel is my son, my firstborn. I have told you to let my son go so that he may serve me.” And when he brought them out of Egypt,
with signs and wonders, with his mighty hand and his uplifted arm, and with great manifestations, he brought them across into the wilderness,
and led them there for forty years. He brought them into the promised land, brought them across the Jordan, and gave it to them as an inheritance,
destroying its inhabitants before them. They lived in it for four hundred and forty years, until Solomon built the temple,
and for four hundred years until the king of Babylon gained power over them. Because their sins had multiplied, he uprooted them and scattered them among every nation,
because they had not listened to his prophets whom he had sent to them. When they had been in Babylon for seventy years, he again remembered for their sake the covenant with their ancestors.
Through his prophets he proclaimed concerning them that they would come up from Babylon after seventy years. And when seventy years were completed, as Jeremiah had prophesied,
Daniel prayed and offered a petition that he would restore them from captivity and have mercy on them. The Lord stirred up the spirit of Cyrus,
and he sent a proclamation throughout his kingdom, declaring to them, “Who is left of all the Lord’s people? May his God be with him!
Let him return and go to Jerusalem in Judah.” But because they had mingled with the nations, and had built houses, planted, and acquired possessions in the land of their captivity,
they were not all willing to go up. Some of them went up, and some remained. And because God knew their evil inclination,
He did not force them to go up from Babylon. Rather, Cyrus king of Persia issued a proclamation to them without compulsion.
For even when he brought them up from Egypt through Moses, if Pharaoh’s oppression of them had not grown severe,
they would not have wanted to go up from Egypt. As they said to Moses when they were complaining against him in the wilderness, “This is what we told you in Egypt:
‘Leave us alone to serve the Egyptians, because we were better off in Egypt.’” See, even when they were suffering under slavery, they did not want to go up from Egypt,
until the Egyptians forced them to leave their land, when they saw that their firstborn had died and said, “We are all dying!”
And it is written that the Egyptians forced the people to leave their land. Likewise, if oppressors had gathered against them in Babylon, they would all have gone up.
I have written this to you because today they cherish an empty hope and say that it still remains for Israel to be gathered together,
because the prophet said, “I will leave none of them among the nations.” They say, “If all our people were gathered together, why are we scattered among every nation today?”
Concerning these things, my dear friend, I will persuade you as well as I can that Israel will never again be gathered together. For they rely on this:
“Look,” they say, “all the prophets gave Israel hope.” Listen, then, you who argue on Israel’s behalf: God is not subject to a law,
nor is there anyone above him who can accuse him over anything he does. For he said, “If I speak concerning a people and a kingdom, to build and to plant,
and afterward it does evil before me, I too will go back on my word and withhold from it the good that I promised it. I will destroy it for its injustice and its sins.

And if again I speak concerning a people and a kingdom, to build and to plant, and afterward to uproot and to tear down and to overthrow; and if again I speak concerning a people and a kingdom, to uproot and to tear down and to overthrow and to destroy,
and it does what is good before me, I too will turn away from it the evil that I declared against it.” Isaiah also said, “Woe to you who plunder, though you are not plundered,

and who act treacherously, though no one acts treacherously toward you! When you wish to plunder, you will be plundered; and when you wish to act treacherously, you will be treated treacherously.” In these matters no one can challenge God’s will.
I will write and show you that God never accepted their goodness, nor did Moses or any of the prophets. For Moses said to them,
“You have been rebellious before the Lord from the day I knew you.” Again he said, “They are a people devoid of judgment, and there is no understanding in them.”
Again he said, “They have angered me with their carved images and made me jealous with their objects of worship. I too will make them jealous through a people who are no people,
and through a foolish nation I will anger them.” Moses also said to them, “I know that after my death you will become utterly corrupt,
and you will turn aside from the way I commanded you, and many calamities will befall you in the latter days.
Look, even while I am still alive with you, you have rebelled against the Lord.” Hosea said, “I cut down the prophets and killed them by the word of my mouth.
Yet you, children of Israel, have not turned from your injustice since the days of your ancestors.” Again he said,
[to them,] “Your goodness is like a morning cloud and like dew that passes away early.” Again he said, “Woe to them, for they have wandered away from me!
I will bring disaster upon them.” Again he said, “They went to Baal-peor and dedicated themselves to shame.” Again he said,
“Their glory flew away from them like a bird. Even if they raise children, I will bereave them so that none remain among humankind, and I will put to death the beloved offspring of their wombs.”
And Jeremiah also said, “Call them rejected silver, because the Lord has rejected them.” And Hosea said, “I will drive them out of my house,
and I will no longer have mercy on them.” Now that he has said, “I will no longer have mercy on them,” what do they have to say?
And again he said, “The Lord has rejected them because they did not listen to him.” And again he said, “They will wander among the nations.” And again he said about them,
“As their land prospered, they multiplied altars and built high places.” And again he said, “Ephraim will receive shame, and Israel will be ashamed of its counsel.”
And again he said, “Ephraim has surrounded me with falsehood, and Judah and the house of Israel with deceit.” And again he said, “I have destroyed you, Israel. Who will help you?”
And again he said, “I gave you a king in my anger, and I took him away in my wrath.” And Micah said, “Do not hold your necks high,
and do not walk with an arrogant bearing.” And again he said, “Get up and go, because this was not my resting place.” And again he said,
“Those who see visions will be ashamed, and the diviners will be ashamed. They will all cover their lips, because God has not answered them.”
And why did he say about the diviners and those who see visions that they would be ashamed and cover their lips? For this is an affliction for which there is no cure.
For it is written in the law, “When there is a leper in Israel, he must cover his lips, and his clothes must be torn,
and his head must be uncovered. He must live outside the camp, and he must call himself unclean all the days that he has leprosy.”
For this reason, a prophet who proclaims falsehood with his lips receives the affliction of leprosy and covers his lips all his days.
He lives in shame like Uzziah, king of Judah. Because he wanted to seize the priesthood, leprosy came out from before the dwelling of the Holy One
and struck him on his forehead. He lived secluded in a house, ashamed all his days. And there was a great earthquake among all the people,
as Zechariah said: “You will flee as you fled from the earthquake that occurred in the days of Uzziah, king of Judah.”
And see how they have refused correction throughout their lives. For he said, “I struck you with scorching heat and hail, and the locust devoured many of your gardens,
yet you did not return to me, says the Lord.” And again he said, “I overthrew some among you, as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah.”
And he made known that they no longer have any hope: “Virgin Israel has fallen and will not rise again.” And again he said,
“She has been abandoned on the ground, and there is no one to raise her up.” And again he said, “There will be lamentation in all the streets, and in all the open places they will say, ‘Alas! Alas!’”
And he rejected them and cast them out of his presence. He said, “I hate and reject your festivals, and I will not smell the offerings at your solemn assemblies.”
And again he said, “I will take no pleasure in your offerings, and I will not look upon your fine fattened animals.” And again he said to them,
“Did you bring me sacrifices or offerings during the forty years in the wilderness, children of Israel?” And concerning his abandonment of them, Jeremiah said,
“I have abandoned my house; I have abandoned my inheritance.” And again he said, “I have given the daughter of my people a certificate of divorce.” And because they boast,
“We are the people of God,” the prophet cried out and said to them, “Look, you are like the Cushites to me, children of Israel.
Look, I brought the children of Israel up from the land of Egypt, the Philistines from Cappadocia, and Aram from Kir.”
And the eyes of the Lord of lords are on the sinful kingdom, and I will destroy it from the face of the earth. And know that he regarded them as Philistines.
And Jeremiah said about the congregation of Israel, “I planted you as a vine shoot, entirely from true seed, but you turned away and rebelled against me,
like a foreign vine.” And Moses said, “Their vine is from the vine of Sodom and from the planting of Gomorrah.
Their grapes are bitter grapes, and their clusters are bitter to them.” And David said, “You brought a vine out of Egypt.
You dug around it and planted its root.” And he said, “You destroyed nations and planted it.” And when they sinned, he said, “The boar from the forest has eaten it,
and the wild animals have grazed on it.” And Ezekiel said about the vine, “Fire has consumed its two branches, and its middle is scorched.” For he said,
“When the vine was undamaged, it was not fit to be made into anything. Now that fire has consumed it and it is scorched, how can it be made into anything?”
And Isaiah prophesied about the whole vineyard and said, “My beloved had a vineyard on a hilltop in fertile land. He cultivated it and surrounded it with a hedge,
and planted vine shoots in it. But when the vineyard produced carobs, he broke down its hedge, demolished its tower, and left it uncultivated.
He restrained his clouds from sending rain down on it.” And about the false prophets he said, “Woe to those who build Zion with bloodshed,
and Jerusalem with injustice.” And again he said about them, “From the prophets of Jerusalem, ungodliness has spread throughout the whole earth.”
And about the calling of the nations Isaiah said, “In the last days, the mountain of the Lord’s house will be established at the head of the mountains,
and raised above the hills. The nations will gather to it, and many nations will go and say, ‘Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord,
and to the house of the God of Jacob. He will teach us his ways, and we will walk in his paths.’ For the law will go out from Zion,
and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem.” And when the law went out from Zion, where indeed did it go? For he said, “He will judge between the nations,
and rebuke many nations far away.” And about them Isaiah said, “Separate yourselves from them and call them unclean,
because the Lord has rejected them.” And again the prophet said, “They rejected their good things like a moth-eaten patch.” And again he said,
“They will tremble because of their paths, and they will quake and be afraid before the Lord our God.” And again he said, “I will burn your gathered forces in smoke,
and the sword will devour your arrows.” And again he said, “Woe to the city of bloodshed, which is entirely full of lies, and in which destruction never ceases.”
And Micah said, “Judah has acted falsely, and defilement has been committed in Israel and Jerusalem, because Judah has defiled the Lord’s sanctuary.”
And he said, “You have turned aside from the way and caused many to stumble over the law. You have broken the covenant of Levi.
So I too have made you despised and humbled among every people, because you have not kept my ways.” And about the nations he said,
“I will give them instead a chosen language.” And about them Malachi said, “You have wearied the Lord with your words.” And again he said,
“You are the children of Jacob, yet you have not turned away from your wrongdoing, and since the days of your ancestors you have not kept my commandments.”
Now listen, my beloved: God delivered Israel only twice—once from Egypt, and the second time from Babylon.
That from Egypt was through Moses, and that from Babylon through Ezra, through the prophecy of Haggai and Zechariah. For Haggai said:
“Build this house, and I will take pleasure in it and be glorified in it, says the Lord.” And again he said, “Work, for I am with you,
and my Spirit remains among you. Do not be afraid, for this is what the Lord Almighty says: Once again I will shake heaven and earth,
and the sea and the dry land. I will shake all the nations, and they will bring the desirable things of all the nations, and I will fill this house with glory.
The later glory of this house will be greater than its former glory.” All these things were spoken in the days of Zerubbabel and in the days of Haggai and Zechariah.
They were urging the building of the house. And Zechariah said, “I have returned to Jerusalem with compassion, and I will place my house within it.”
And again he said, “The cities will be emptied of good things, and the Lord will build Zion and choose Jerusalem again.” And again he said:
“I have been intensely jealous for Zion and Jerusalem, and I am fiercely angry with the nations that are in turmoil.” And again he said:
“Jerusalem will be inhabited like open country because of the multitude of people and livestock within it. And I will be in it like a wall of bronze,
and I will be glory within it, says the Lord.” And again he said, “Ho! Ho! Flee from the land of the north, says the Lord,
for I have scattered you to the four winds of heaven. O Zion, escape, you who dwell with the daughter of Babylon!” And again he said:
“The Lord will inherit Judah as his portion in his holy land, and he will again take pleasure in Jerusalem.” And again he said:
“The hands of Zerubbabel laid the foundations of this house, and his hands will finish it.” Zechariah prophesied all these things,
and they were fulfilled and completed in the gathering of Israel from Babylon, not as they say, that Israel still awaits its gathering.
But listen, my dear friend, and I will convince you that Israel was delivered twice: once from Egypt, and the second time from Babylon.
For Isaiah said, “The Lord will stretch out his hand a second time to acquire the remnant of his people that remains, from the land of Assyria and from Egypt,
and from Tyre and Sidon, and from Hamath and the distant islands.” For if they still await being gathered and delivered,
why did Isaiah say, “The Lord will stretch out his hand a second time to acquire the remnant of his people that remains”? For if they still have a deliverance to come,
should not Isaiah have said, “The Lord will stretch out his hand a third time to acquire the remnant of his people,” rather than saying “a second time”?
Listen again, and I will explain to you the prayer that Daniel prayed before his God, pleading and imploring on behalf of his people, that they might return and come back from Babylon.
For Daniel was a greatly beloved man, to whom hidden things were revealed and the end was made known. Because he was a prophet, he built upon the words of the prophets.
For when his people were taken captive to Babylon, deceitful men arose among them and prophesied falsely and deceitfully.
They would say, “This is what the Lord says: Two years from now I will break the yoke of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon,
from the necks of all the nations.” Then, when Jeremiah heard the prophecy of the false prophets, he wrote a letter and sent it to Babylon:
“Do not listen to the false prophets among you, who hold you back and say, ‘Two years from now you will return from Babylon.’”
For this is what the Lord says: Build houses and live in them. Plant gardens and eat their fruit. Take wives for your sons.
And give your daughters in marriage to men. For only when seventy years have been completed for Babylon will you return from there.
Daniel, who was clothed with the Spirit, knew that Jeremiah’s prophecy was true. And when seventy years had been completed,
then he prayed, pleaded, and begged before his God, in the first year of Darius son of Ahasuerus, of Median descent,
who had become king over the kingdom of the Chaldeans. In the first year of his reign, I, Daniel, considered in the book the number of years.
And I saw that the word of the Lord, which Jeremiah the prophet spoke, was that seventy years would be completed for the devastation of Jerusalem.
I lifted my face before the Lord God to plead with prayer and supplication, with fasting, sackcloth, and ashes.
I prayed before the Lord my God, confessed, and said: Please, Lord, great and awesome God, who keeps the covenant and shows kindness to those who love him,
to those who keep his commandments: We have sinned and done wrong. We have acted wickedly and rebelled. We have turned aside from your commandments and your judgments.
We have not listened to your servants the prophets, who spoke in your name to our kings, our leaders, our ancestors, and all the people of the land.
Righteousness belongs to you, Lord, but shame belongs to us, as it does today—to the people of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem,
and to all Israel, those near and those far away, in all the lands where you scattered them because of the wrong they committed against you, Lord.
Shame belongs to us, to our kings, our leaders, and our ancestors, because we have sinned against you. Mercy and forgiveness of sins belong to the Lord God,
for we have rebelled against him. We have not obeyed the voice of the Lord our God by walking according to his law, which he set before us through his servants the prophets.
All Israel has transgressed your law, turned aside, and refused to obey your voice. You brought upon them the curses and afflictions
written in the law of Moses, the servant of God, because we sinned before him. He fulfilled his words that he spoke against us and against our judges who judged us,
bringing upon us a great disaster. Nothing like what happened in Jerusalem has been done anywhere under heaven, just as it is written in the law of Moses.
All this disaster you brought upon us, yet we did not pray before the Lord our God that we might turn from our sins and understand your faithfulness.
The Lord stirred up disaster and brought it upon us, for the Lord our God is righteous in all the deeds he has done, but we have not obeyed his voice.
And now, Lord our God, you who brought your people out of the land of Egypt with a mighty hand and an uplifted arm, and made a name for yourself that endures to this day:
We have sinned and acted wickedly. Lord, in keeping with all the righteousness you have shown us, may your fury and anger turn away from your city Jerusalem
and from your holy mountain. For because of our sins and the wrongdoing of our ancestors, your people have been scattered everywhere. Jerusalem has become an object of scorn to all the nations.
Now, God, listen to the prayer of your servant and to our supplication. Let your face shine upon your devastated sanctuary, for the sake of your name, Lord.
My God, incline your ear and listen. Open your eyes and see our ruins and our desolate places, and the city that bears your name.
We do not rely on our own righteousness as we pray before you, but on your abundant mercy. Lord, listen! Lord, have mercy on us!
Lord, listen and act! Do not delay, for your name’s sake, my God, because your name is invoked over your city and your people.
Then, when Daniel had finished his prayer, he said, “While I was still praying and confessing my sins and the sins of my people Israel,
and laying my plea before the Lord my God concerning the holy mountain of my God, while I was still speaking in prayer,
the man Gabriel, whom I had seen before, came flying swiftly down from heaven and approached me at the time of the evening offering.
He came and spoke with me and said to me, ‘Daniel, I have now come out to teach you so that you may understand. At the beginning of your prayer, a word went out, and I have come to tell you,
because you are greatly loved. Consider the word and understand the vision. Seventy weeks will rest upon your people and upon your holy city,
to bring transgressions to an end and finish sins, to forgive wrongdoing, to bring everlasting righteousness, and to fulfill the vision and the prophets,
and to anoint the Holy of Holies. Know and understand: from the issuing of the word to restore and rebuild Jerusalem until the coming of the Messiah, the king,
there will be seven weeks and sixty-two weeks. He will return and rebuild Jerusalem, its streets and its squares, until the completion of the time.
After sixty-two weeks, the Messiah will be killed and will have nothing. The holy city will be destroyed along with the king who comes.
The end will be with a flood, and until the end of the war, decreed destruction. He will strengthen a covenant for many,
one week and half a week. He will abolish sacrifice and offerings, and on the wings of defilement there will be destruction.’”
Now look, my dear friend, and consider the prayer that Daniel prayed and the vision that was explained to him. At the completion of seventy years of Jerusalem’s desolation,
he prayed and made confession in the first year of Darius. When he confessed his sins and the sins of his people Israel,
then Gabriel, the receiver of prayers, came to him and said to him, “At the beginning of your prayer, a word went out.” For this was the word that went out at the beginning of his prayer:
that the captives should return from Babylon. Daniel then considered what would happen to the people after their return. Then Gabriel said to him,
“Because you are greatly loved, I will show you what will happen to your people in the last days. Now consider the word and understand the vision.
Seventy weeks,” he said, “will rest upon your people and upon your holy city, to bring transgressions to an end and finish sins, to forgive wrongdoing,
to bring everlasting righteousness, to fulfill the vision and the prophets, and to anoint the Holy of Holies. Know and understand: from the issuing of the word
to restore and rebuild Jerusalem until the coming of the Messiah, the king, there will be seven weeks and sixty-two weeks. He will return and rebuild
Jerusalem, its streets and its squares, until the completion of the time. After sixty-two weeks, the Messiah will be killed and will have nothing.
The holy city will be destroyed along with the king who comes. The end will be with a flood, until the end of the war, decreed destruction.
He will strengthen a covenant for many, one week and half a week. He will abolish sacrifice and offerings, and on the wings of defilement there will be destruction.”
For he said to him, “Seventy weeks will rest upon your people and upon your holy city.” Seventy weeks are four hundred and ninety years,
from the time when Daniel prayed until Jerusalem was destroyed in its final destruction and would never be inhabited again.
And he said that in seven weeks he would return to rebuild Jerusalem. For when the captives came up under Ezra and began building the temple,
from the days of Cyrus and Darius they laid the temple’s foundations. But their enemies stopped them in the days of Darius and Artaxerxes
and other Persian kings, and would not allow them to build and finish it. I will show you the symbolic meaning of the matter.
For this is what is written in the prophet Zechariah: “I saw a lampstand with seven lamps on it, and seven openings for each of the lamps”—
forty-nine, which are seven weeks. And in the prophecy he said, “This is the word of the Lord concerning Zerubbabel: Not by might and not by strength,
but by the Spirit.” And earlier he said, “The hands of Zerubbabel laid the foundations of this temple, and his hands will finish it.”
Thus the entire time from the day the temple’s foundations were laid until its construction was finished was forty-nine years.
These are seven weeks out of the seventy. And this is the vision of the lampstand with seven lamps and their forty-nine openings.
And this is the word of the Lord that came concerning Zerubbabel: these forty-nine years. And after these seven weeks of the temple’s construction,
which took place in the days of Zerubbabel, Jerusalem then remained inhabited for sixty-two weeks—four hundred and thirty-four years.
And why did he say earlier, “Seventy weeks will rest upon your people and upon your holy city,”
while later there were seven and sixty-two, making sixty-nine in all? But further on he said,
“For a week and half a week he will put an end to sacrifice and offerings.” Here is one week out of the seventy in which sacrifice ceased.
This is how it was reckoned for them, like those seventy years when they lived in Babylon and the land rested during its captivity,
throughout the days of its desolation. So be convinced that after these weeks the Messiah came and was killed, to bring vision and prophets to their fulfillment.
Our father Jacob also said, when blessing Judah, “The scepter will not depart from Judah, nor the lawgiver from between his feet,
until he comes to whom the kingdom belongs.” Be convinced, my dear friend, and understand that the weeks have been completed, and visions and prophets have come to an end,
and kingship has ceased from Judah. For look: Jerusalem has been destroyed, its people have been scattered among every nation, and the Israelites live
without sacrifices and without an altar. Until the decreed things are completed, Jerusalem lies ruined and at rest in devastation.
The vineyard has been laid waste and has grown carob trees. Fire has consumed the vine’s two branches. The vineyard’s fence has been broken down,
its tower demolished, and its winepress destroyed. The silver has been rejected and is of no use. A certificate of divorce has been written for Jerusalem.
Now I have written this brief argument for you so that you may be at ease when circumstances require an answer, and so that the understanding of anyone who hears may be strengthened.
But one should not throw oneself into persuading the troublemakers, for they do not accept persuasion. Scripture has confined them
to not hearing and being persuaded, so that God may have mercy on everyone. For he said of them, “This people honors me with its lips,
but its heart is far from me.” And they said to Jeremiah, “As for the word you have spoken to us in the name of the Lord, we will not listen to you.”
Concerning these visions of Daniel, my dear friend, I have written to you according to what I have understood. But know that after Gabriel had explained to him what would happen to his people,
then, in the third year of Cyrus, a message was revealed to Daniel. He said that the message was true, and he pondered the vision with great effort.
He said, “I was mourning for three weeks. I ate no desirable food, and neither meat nor wine entered my mouth.”
Notice that Daniel saw this vision in the third year of Cyrus, on the twenty-fourth day of the first month,
which is Nisan, two years after he had issued a proclamation throughout his kingdom that the exiles should return to Jerusalem.
In the first year of Darius son of Ahasuerus, he prayed before God for the completion of the seventy years, in fulfillment of Jeremiah’s words.
As the matter indicates, the reign of Darius the Mede lasted one year, for when he killed Belshazzar, he became king in his place.
He exercised kingship only briefly, and Cyrus the Persian took it over. Why did Darius receive the kingdom first?
As the matter appears to us, it was so that the vision Daniel interpreted for Belshazzar would be fulfilled, when he told him, “This is the interpretation of the matter
and the reading of the inscription: Mene, Tekel, and Parsin. Mene: God has numbered your kingdom and brought it to an end. Tekel: You have been weighed in the balance and found wanting.
Peres: Your kingdom is divided and given to Media and Persia.” For this reason Darius came to the throne first, so that the vision would be fulfilled.
After him Cyrus the Persian received it, at the completion of the seventy years, at the time when Daniel prayed that the exiles would return through him,
as Isaiah prophesied about him: “He will build my city and release my exiles.” Cyrus himself said, “God has given us the kingdom of the earth
and has commanded me to build him a house in Jerusalem in Judah.” Notice that Daniel’s fast came after his prayer. He fasted for this reason:
because Jerusalem would remain inhabited for seventy weeks, and afterward would be destroyed and lie in ruin forever, until the completion of [?].
End of Against the Jews.
Demonstration on Providing for the Poor
This gift is great and glorious when it is found in a discerning person, when he gives to the needy from the labor of his own hands,
not from what he has plundered from others. As God said through the prophet, “This is my rest: give rest to the weary. This is the path of whoever listens.”
Again that prophet said, “This is the acceptable fast that God loves: when you share your bread with the hungry and bring the stranger into your house,
when you see someone naked and clothe him, and do not neglect your own flesh and blood.” Whoever does these things becomes like a joyful garden
and like a spring whose waters never fail. His righteousness goes before him, and he is gathered up in the glory of the Lord.
Moses, the great prophet of Israel, gave warnings and commands concerning the poor and afflicted, strangers and resident foreigners,
converts, orphans, and widows. For he said to Israel, “When you reap your harvest, do not reap your fields completely.
Nor, when you forget a sheaf, are you to return and take it. Instead, let it be for the poor, converts, orphans, and widows.”
And remember that you too were like this in Egypt. And he added: “When you harvest your vineyard, do not glean behind you.”
“Nor, when you beat your olive trees, are you to search through them afterward. Instead, let what remains belong to the foreigners and the poor among you. And when you do these things,” he says,
“the Lord your God will bless you in everything you undertake. You will eat old, well-aged produce, and you will clear out the old to make room for the new.”
/And again he said to them:/ “Look, I am bringing you into a good and fertile land, flowing with milk and honey, a land whose stones are iron,
and from whose mountains you will quarry copper; a land on which the eyes of the Lord God rest from the beginning of the year to the end of the year;
a land where you will not eat bread in poverty.” Although the land is so good and fertile, the poor do not disappear from it. And again he commanded them and said to them:
“For six years you shall sow your land and gather its produce, but in the seventh year you shall plow it and leave it alone, so that the poor among you may eat from it.
The wild animals shall eat what remains.” And he said to them: “In that seventh year you shall not harvest its vines or gather the gleanings.
Instead, they shall belong to the poor.” And because he knew their evil inclination, he said to them: “If you say, ‘What shall we eat in the seventh year,
since we neither sow nor gather produce?’” He said to them: “I will send you my blessings in the sixth year, and it will yield produce for three years:
the sixth, the seventh, and the eighth. And you will eat from the produce of the sixth year until the ninth year.”
And he carefully warned them: “The wages of a hired worker shall not remain with you overnight. Instead, give him his wages that very day,
so that he does not cry out to God against you and you become guilty of sin.” For when a hired worker’s wages remain with you overnight, your life may be taken from you that very night,
and the poor man will be cheated of his wages that are with you, for which he entrusted himself to you. Or he may die, and you will find no one there to claim his wages so that you can pay them.
David too was concerned for the poor and afflicted, the orphans and widows, and he appointed overseers throughout Israel
to feed and provide for the poor. And as he sang and offered praise before his God, he pronounced a blessing on those who feed the poor.
For he said: “Blessed is the one who cares for the poor; the Lord will rescue him in the day of trouble. The Lord will protect him and keep him alive and prosper him in the land.
He will not hand him over to his enemies, and in sickness he will support him on his bed of pain.” And again he said in another psalm:
“He has distributed freely and given to the afflicted, and his righteousness endures forever.” And again it is written: “Whoever gives /that whoever gives/ to the poor lends to God.”
And again he said: “Bind up your alms and place them in a treasury; they are better for you than all stored-up treasures.” And again it is written:
“Give to God from what he has given you.” And see that the giver of alms has begun to receive from the needy, so that through the needy his own need may be met when he shows mercy.
For it was within his power that there should be no needy person at all. But if he had done this, their reward from him through the needy
would have been lost through these things. The rich person gives to the poor person, and when the poor person receives, he gives thanks to the Lord of them both.
And when our Lord Jesus revealed an illustration of the judgment of the last day, when he separated people and placed them on his right and on his left, there he expressed gratitude to the good
and called them those blessed by his Father, who inherit his kingdom because they provided for the poor. For he said to those on his right:
Come, you who are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom that was prepared for you from the beginning. For I was hungry, and you gave me food.
I was thirsty, and you gave me a drink. I was naked, and you clothed me. I was a stranger, and you welcomed me. I was sick, and you visited me.
I was in prison, and you came to me. Then those righteous people did not understand the force of our Lord’s words.
They answered him, saying, “When did we see you, our Lord, in such need and do this for you?” Then he said to them:
“Whatever you did for one of these little brothers of mine, you did for me personally.” He turned toward those on his left and said to them:
“Go away from me, you who are cursed, into the fire prepared for the Evil One and his angels, because you did not do these things for me.”
Then those on his left also answered him, saying, “When, our Lord, did we see you in any of these conditions and not serve you?” He said to them:
“What you did not do for these needy people, you did not do for me personally either.” And the righteous, who served Christ through the needy,
went to eternal life, while the wicked went to fire and darkness because they had not provided for Christ through the poor.
Again, in another illustration, he spoke about a rich man who trusted in his possessions. When he had gathered abundant crops from his land,
he said to himself, “Look, many good things are stored up for you for many years.
My soul, rest, eat, and enjoy yourself.” God said to him, “You fool! Look, this very night your life will be demanded of you.
Whose will these things you have prepared be?” Afterward he said, “So it is with anyone who stores up treasures for himself but is not rich toward God.”
Again, he gave another illustration about the rich man who enjoyed his good things and met his ruin in Sheol, and the poor man who lay at his gate.
He yearned and longed to fill his stomach with what fell from that rich man’s table. And he said that no one gave him anything.
He said there that dogs used to come and lick his sores. For the rich man who enjoyed good things represents the people who ate and grew fat,
kicked, forgot the Lord, and insulted God, as it is written that the Israelites spoke against God and against Moses,
saying things that were not good. Moses called them rich when he said about them, “What people have their God near them,
as the Lord our God is, and have righteous laws and upright judgments?” Again he said to them:
“Look, you are entering the land of the Canaanites and taking possession of it. For you are entering houses you did not build,
vineyards and olive groves you did not plant, and dug cisterns you did not dig.
You will eat, be satisfied, live in luxury, and forget the Lord.” They had become rich through the many good things he gave them.
The poor man who lay at his gate is a likeness of our Savior. He yearned and longed to receive fruit from them
and bring it to the one who sent him, but no one gave him anything. As for his saying that dogs used to come and lick his sores,
the dogs that used to come are the Gentiles who lick our Savior’s wounds—his body, which they receive and place over their eyes.
For they are dogs with greedy appetites, and they do not know how to be satisfied. They cannot even bark.
But notice that these dogs that licked that poor man's sores were not greedy, because if they had been greedy,
they would have longed for the rich man's table, not to lick sores. It was about them that the prophet said,
"They are dogs with greedy appetites, and they do not know how to be satisfied." And David said, "They will howl like dogs and go around the city."
And at the end of the passage he said, "It happened that the rich man died and was buried, and he lay in torment.
The poor man also died, and the angels carried him to Abraham's embrace. The rich man lifted his eyes from within Sheol and from his torment,
and saw Abraham, with Lazarus in his embrace. He cried out loudly and said, 'My father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus to come and help me
and moisten my tongue because of the burning, for I am suffering terribly.' Abraham said to him, 'My son, remember that you received your good things during your life,
while Lazarus received his bad things. But today you have asked him, and he cannot help you, because there is a great chasm between us and you.
Those on your side cannot come to us, nor can those on our side come to you.' He said to him, 'If not, father, I ask you
to send him to my father's house, for I have five brothers. Let him go and warn them, so that they do not sin and come to this torment themselves.'
Abraham said to him, 'They have Moses and the prophets; let them listen to them.' He said to him, 'No, my father Abraham,
