but let someone from the dead go to them, and they will repent.' Abraham said to him, 'If they do not listen to Moses and the prophets,
they will not believe even if someone from the dead goes to them.'" As I said above, the rich man is the people,
and the poor man is our Savior, as it is written, "The Lord wished to humble him and make him suffer." And the apostle said, "For your sake the rich one became poor,
so that you might become rich through his poverty." And again he said, "He humbled himself and became obedient to the point of death—even death on a cross."
As for his saying that the rich man died, the prophet truly said about them, "The Lord God will put you to death,
and he will call his servants by another name." His servants are the people from the nations, and his calling them by another name
means that he called them Christians, that is, followers of the Messiah, and not rulers of Sodom and people of Gomorrah like them,
as the proclamation of the twelve apostles testifies to us: "It was there, in Antioch, that the disciples were first called Christians."
"The poor man also died," he says, "and the angels carried him to Abraham's embrace." As Mary said, "They have taken our Lord away, and I do not know where they have carried him."
Those angels said to Mary, "He has risen and gone to the one who sent him." And angels were serving him,
as it is said earlier in his Gospel: "Angels came down and were serving Jesus." And when he was born, angels were also praising God and saying,
"Glory to God in heaven, and good hope for humanity." And the angel Gabriel announced the good news of his birth. He himself said to his disciple Simon,
"Do you suppose that if I ask my Father for an army of heavenly angels, he will not give it to me?" And again he said to his disciples,
That you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God descending and ascending to the Son of Man.
I wrote these things to you because it is written that when the poor man died, the angels carried him to Abraham’s embrace. And when it says that they carried him to Abraham’s embrace,
that is the kingdom of heaven. And Abraham’s saying to the rich man, “There is a great chasm between us and you, and no one comes from you to us,
nor from us to you,” shows that after death and resurrection there is no repentance. The wicked do not repent and enter the kingdom,
nor do the righteous sin again and go to torment. This is the great chasm. And when he asked him to send someone to help him, but no one was sent to help him,
he showed by this that on that day no one helps his fellow. And when he said, “Let him go to my father’s house and proclaim to them that they should not sin,”
he told him, “They have Moses and the prophets; let them listen to them.” But he said, “Let someone from the dead go, and they will repent.”
This is well known: that people did not listen to Moses and the prophets, nor did they believe in Jesus, who rose from the dead.
Again, it is written that the sins of someone who has sinned are wiped away through almsgiving, as Daniel said to Nebuchadnezzar: “Redeem your sins through almsgiving,
and your wrongdoing through mercy toward the weak.” And the prophet said to the Israelites, “Because you oppressed the poor man and took choice offerings from him,
you will not live in the houses of cut stone that you built, and you will not drink the wine of the delightful vineyards that you planted.”
See how God cares for the poor. For Isaiah said, “The poor and needy seek water, but there is none,
and their tongues are dry with thirst. I, the Lord, will answer them, the God of Israel, and I will not abandon them. And because their tongues have dried up for lack of water,
I will open rivers in the mountains and springs in the valleys. I will place cedars, box trees, myrtles, and olive trees in the wilderness,
and I will set magnificent cypresses together in the plain.” For the poor and needy who seek water and find none are the people from the nations,
and the water is the teaching of the Holy Scriptures, for their tongues had dried up for lack of praise. And as for his saying, “I will open rivers in the mountains,
and springs in the valleys”: the mountains and valleys are human beings, the exalted and the humble, and rivers and springs flowed from them.
And he said, “I will place cedars, box trees, myrtles, and olive trees in the wilderness, and magnificent cypresses in the plain.” For the wilderness is the nations,
who formerly were like a desolate wilderness. The cedars, box trees, myrtles, and olive trees are the priests of the people,
and the holy covenant, who are magnificent in their branches, like these trees that are magnificent and thick with leaves in summer and winter.
And as for “I will set magnificent cypresses together in the plain”: from humble human beings came the message and teaching of the Spirit,
whose fragrance is sweet like that of a magnificent cypress, as the apostle said: “In every place we are a sweet fragrance to God.”
Job’s friends also said to him, when they were reproaching him during his trial, “Why has this happened to you?
Perhaps you sent a widow away empty-handed and weakened an orphan’s arm. You gave no water to the weary to drink, and you withheld bread from the hungry.
You took away the orphan’s dwelling and took the widow’s ox as a pledge. There is a man who sowed his land, and a violent master took it from him.”
Because you have done these things, snares have surrounded you, and sudden terror has shaken you. And when he heard these things from them,
he spoke out passionately in his own defense. For he said to them, “I was eyes to the blind and feet to the lame.
Those who were naked were warmed by the fleece of my sheep. I did not raise my hand against an orphan; rather, when I saw him at the gate, I helped him.
I did not send a widow away empty-handed, and I did not eat my bread alone; an orphan ate some of it. I broke the fangs of the wicked,
and I pulled the prey from between his teeth. I said that I would rescue the poor people.” And again he said, “I opened my door to the traveler.
I did not,” he said, “darken the widow’s eyes. For if I did not do these things, let my shoulder fall from its socket and my arm be broken from its joint.
Have mercy on me, have mercy on me, you my friends, because the hand of God has touched me. These things have not happened to me because of my sins.”
Our Lord gave particular instruction concerning the poor, saying to the host of the dinner, “When you give a banquet or a dinner, do not invite your friends or your relatives,
nor your rich neighbors, lest they too invite you and this become your repayment. But when you give one,
invite the poor, the common people, the blind, the disabled, and those who have nothing. Blessed are you because they have nothing with which to repay you.
Your repayment will be at the resurrection with the righteous.” And again he said, “Make friends for yourselves through this unrighteous wealth,
so that when it runs out, they may receive you into their eternal dwellings.” And who are the friends who have eternal dwellings,
and whom people acquire through unrighteous wealth? For the friends are God and his Christ, who have eternal dwellings.
For when someone gives to the poor from what he has, he satisfies the will of God and his Christ, as he said,
“This is my rest: give rest to the weary.” And our Lord said, “What you did for these people, you did for me myself.”
And he said, “Make friends for yourselves,” as Isaiah said, “Do not fear, my servant Jacob, offspring of Abraham my friend.”
And our Lord said to his disciples, “I have called you my friends, because I have made known to you everything I heard from my Father.”
These are the friends people acquire by giving to the poor, and in their eternal dwellings, the place where the righteous rest,
the tabernacle not made by hands and not belonging to these created things, as the apostle said. And again our Lord urged
those who provide for the poor and the afflicted. For he said, “Do not store up treasures for yourselves on earth, where thieves break in and steal,
and where moths invade and destroy. Instead, store up treasures /treasure/ for yourselves in heaven, treasure that does not run out, where no moth destroys
and no thieves steal. And where your treasure is, there your heart will also be.” Again the apostle also said,
concerning the apostles who came before him, “They instructed us only in this: that we should remember the poor. And I was eager to do this very thing.”
And our Lord said, “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” And concerning the rich he said,
“Woe to you rich people, because you have received what you asked for.” And who are the rich who received what they asked for, if not that former people, who asked for everything earthly?
and not those of heaven, like that rich man who gathered and increased his crops but was not rich toward God, and like the man who enjoyed every good thing
and received what he wanted here, but over there was not given what he asked for. And concerning the poor he said that theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
Are we to say that he meant everyone who is poor in this world's possessions? For there are poor people who have nothing
who are thieves, murderers, liars, and doers of hateful things contrary to the law. Does the kingdom of heaven belong to these people? Certainly not!
Rather, he gave the blessing upon the poor in spirit to those who fear God, those who consider their possessions nothing compared with the fear of their God,

but use them as something superfluous. There was wealthy Abraham, who humbled his spirit before his God, and Isaac and Jacob, the children of his promise, who walked in his footsteps and pleased their God
while they were wealthy. Job was a wealthy man among the people of the East, and when he was tested through his children and his possessions, he loved his God, who had given them to him,
and did not blaspheme God. For these are the people about whom the apostle said that they lived in love for strangers, those who welcomed angels.
Who, then, are these lovers of strangers, if not Abraham, Lot, Job, and other righteous people like them? And see, my dear friend,
how greatly these fathers loved strangers: when Abraham saw those angels, he took them for strangers,
and he ran to meet them and bowed before them, asking them to enter his tent and rest with him, so that the stranger might be blessed through hospitality.
And marvel greatly at this: a great man throws himself down, bows, pleads, and asks strangers to come to him for rest.
For it was Abraham's custom to welcome strangers into his home every day. When he saw those angels, he took them for poor strangers,
and ran to meet them and welcomed them as strangers, while their greatness was hidden from his eyes.
He himself stood beside them and served them, and he instructed Sarah to knead three measures of fine flour with her own hands,
generously providing a measure for each man, and with an overflowing measure, so that when he received his rewards, they would measure out to him in the same way.
And because he loved strangers, he received a reward and the promise that through his offspring all the nations would be blessed. Lot likewise welcomed strangers,
and he delivered him from Sodom, which hated strangers, as Ezekiel said: “This was the sin of Sodom and her companions:

she did not take the hand of the poor and needy. And when I saw these things in them, I overthrew them.” Also, when our Lord entered the house of Zacchaeus, the sinful tax collector, Zacchaeus said to him,
“Look, my Lord, I give half my possessions to the poor, and whatever I have defrauded anyone of, I repay fourfold.” And our Lord said to him, “Today salvation has come to this house.”
And to that rich man who came to our Lord and said to him, “What must I do to inherit eternal life?” our Lord said,
“Do not commit adultery, and do not steal. Honor your father and your mother, and love your neighbor as yourself.” The man said to him,
“I have done these things ever since I was a child. What do I still lack?” Then Jesus looked at him lovingly and said to him,
“You lack one thing. If you want to be perfect, go, sell everything you have and give to the poor. Take up your cross and follow me.”
When the man heard this, he became very sad and went home distressed, because he was very wealthy in possessions.
And Jesus said, “See how difficult it is for those who trust in their possessions to enter the kingdom of heaven.” And again he said:
“It is easier for a camel to enter through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God.” The apostle also spoke about this seed: “Whoever sows sparingly
will also reap sparingly, but whoever sows with blessings will reap blessings.” And let us not grow weary in doing good.
I have written this brief reminder to you, my beloved, about giving to the poor. Keep encouraging and persuading those who give
to sow before them the seed of life, as it is written: “Instruct a righteous person, and he will increase his learning.”
And keep urging everyone who loves the poor with these reminders, so that you too may have a share in his labor.
The discourse on providing for the poor is finished.
Demonstration on Persecution
I heard an insult and was grieved, as the unclean were saying, “This people, gathered from all nations, has no God.”
And the wicked say this: “If they have a God, why does he not exact vengeance for his people?” And the darkness thickened over me still more
when the Jews too were taunting us and exalting themselves over the members of our people. And it happened one day that I was challenged
by a man called a wise man of the Jews. He said, “Jesus, who is called your teacher, wrote to you:
‘If you have faith like a single mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, “Move,” and it will move away from before you,
and even be lifted up and fall into the sea, and it will obey you.’ So,” he said, “is there not one wise person among all your people whose prayer is heard,
who will ask God to make your persecutors leave you alone? For this,” he said, “is what is written for you in the passage: ‘There is nothing you will be unable to do.’”
When I saw that he was blaspheming and speaking far off the mark, my mind was troubled. I knew that he would not accept an explanation of the words he had quoted to me.
Then I too challenged him with passages from the Law and the Prophets, and said to him, “Do you believe
that God is with you even when you are scattered?” He assured me, “God is with us, because,” he said, “God said to Israel:
‘Even in the lands of their enemies, I have not abandoned them or annulled my covenant with them.’” And again I said to him:
“It is very good that I have heard from you that God is with you. In answer to your words, I too will speak to you. For the prophet Isaiah said to Israel,
as if from the mouth of his God: ‘If you pass through the sea, I am with you, and the rivers will not sweep you away. If you walk on fire, you will not be scorched,
and the flame will not burn you, because the Lord your God is with you.’ So is there not one righteous, good, and wise man among all your people
who can pass through the sea and live without drowning, and whom a river does not sweep away? Let him walk on fire, and let us see whether he is not scorched and whether a flame does not burn him.
And if you bring me an interpretation, I will not be persuaded by you, just as you do not accept from me an explanation of the words with which you challenged me.”
And again I asked him about another passage written in Ezekiel, where he says to Jerusalem, “Sodom and her daughters will be rebuilt as they were before.”
“And you and your daughters will be as you were before.” Now explain this statement to me. And he began speaking arrogantly and said to me:
“As for what God said to Jerusalem through the prophet, ‘Sodom and her daughters will be rebuilt as before,
and you and your daughters will be as you were before,’ this is the meaning of the statement: Sodom and her daughters will be inhabited as before,
and they will be subjected to Israel’s authority. And Jerusalem and her daughters will enjoy royal splendor as before.”
When I heard him uttering this arrogantly, he fell greatly in my esteem. And I said to him, “When the words of the prophets are spoken in anger,
is the whole pronouncement one of anger? Or is perhaps half of it anger and half mercy?” He said, “A pronouncement of anger is entirely filled with anger,
and there is no peace in it.” I said to him, “Now that you have assured me that there is no peace in that pronouncement of anger, listen without arguing,
and do not blaspheme. I will convince you about this statement. For from beginning to end, the whole pronouncement was spoken in anger.
For he said to Jerusalem, ‘As I live, says the Lord God, Sodom and her daughters have not done
what you and your daughters have done.’ And he said to her, ‘Be ashamed and bear your disgrace, for by your sins you have surpassed your sisters,
and they have proved more righteous than you.’ Now, since he said that Sodom and her daughters proved more righteous than Jerusalem and her daughters,
and Jerusalem surpassed Sodom in her sins, it cannot be that, when Israel is given this name, its dwelling will be in Sodom and Gomorrah.
For their vine comes from the vine of Sodom and from the planting of Gomorrah. Their grapes are bitter, and their clusters are gall to them.
Isaiah too called them rulers of Sodom and people of Gomorrah. For if Israel is gathered together, it is fitting that it should dwell in Sodom and Gomorrah,
with the rulers of Sodom and with the people of Gomorrah, beside the vine of Sodom and the planting of Gomorrah, to eat bitter grapes,
to pick clusters of gall, to eat wild gourds, to clothe itself in a spider’s web, and to make use of the vineyard’s wild grapes,
and to trade in rejected silver. And will Sodom and her daughters, who proved more righteous than Jerusalem, be rebuilt as before,
while Jerusalem, who surpassed Sodom in her sins, remains in her sins and rests upon destruction until the decreed judgments are completely fulfilled forever?
Ezekiel said, ‘This was the wrongdoing of Sodom and her daughters: they did not take the hand of the needy and the poor. And when I saw these things in them, I overthrew them.’
Consider and see that from the time Sodom was overthrown until Jerusalem was built, there were eight hundred and ninety-six years.
From the time Abraham received the good news from God through the angel, ‘At this time next year I will return to you, and Sarah your wife will have a son,’
from that time until Jacob entered Egypt there were two hundred years. And Jacob’s descendants were in Egypt for two hundred and five years,
making a total of four hundred and nineteen years from the time Isaac was conceived and Sodom was overthrown.
And from Israel’s departure from Egypt until Jerusalem was built on a grand scale by Solomon and the temple was built,
there were four hundred and eighty years. So all the years from Isaac’s conception and the overthrow of Sodom until the great building of Jerusalem,
There are 896 years. And from the great building of Jerusalem until the destruction of Jerusalem, there are 425 years.
The total number of years from the time of Sodom’s overthrow until Jerusalem was destroyed is 1,321.
For all these years Sodom and its daughter towns lay destroyed before Jerusalem did, and it has still not been inhabited, although it was more righteous than Jerusalem.
Now the total count of years from Sodom’s overthrow until the year 655 of the reign of Alexander, son of Philip the Macedonian:
2,076 years. And from the time Jerusalem was destroyed by the Babylonians until this present time:
955 years. And after the Babylonians destroyed it, Jerusalem was inhabited for those seventy weeks to which Daniel testified.
Then it suffered its final destruction at the hands of the Romans, never to be inhabited again, because it was consigned to destruction,
until the fulfillment of what has been decreed. Now the total number of years of Jerusalem’s first and final desolation:
465 years. And when you subtract from them the seventy years of Babylon, they amount to 395 years.
I have written this entire explanation for you because the Jews boast, “We are destined to be gathered together.” For if Sodom, whose wickedness was not as great as Jerusalem’s,
has still not been inhabited—and we say that it will never be inhabited—how will Jerusalem be inhabited, whose wickedness is greater than that of Sodom and its daughter towns?
For 2,076 years God has not had mercy on Sodom. Are we to say that he will have mercy on Jerusalem,
when it has been only 395 years since the day it was destroyed, according to the calculation written above? But as for what he said,
that Sodom and its daughter towns would be restored as they were before, and what he said to Jerusalem, “You and your daughter towns will be as you were before,”
this is the meaning of the statement: they will never be inhabited. For he also cursed the land against which the Lord was angry in this way:
“It shall not be sown or sprout, nor shall any vegetation grow in it. Instead, it shall be like Sodom and Gomorrah, against which the Lord was angry
and toward which he did not relent.” Be convinced, then, listener, that Sodom and its daughter towns will never be inhabited, but will be as they were before,
as at the time when they were not yet inhabited, and as at the time when the Lord was angry with them and did not relent toward them.
And Jerusalem and its daughter towns will be as they were before, as in the earliest time, when the mountain of the Amorites lay desolate,
on which Abraham built an altar when he bound his son Isaac upon it, and as it lay desolate when David bought the threshing floor from Araunah the Jebusite
and built an altar there. Understand and see that the mountain on which Abraham offered his son is the mountain of Jebus, which is Jerusalem.
And the site of the threshing floor that David bought from Araunah is the very place where the temple was built. Thus Jerusalem will lie desolate as it did before.
And understand that when Ezekiel prophesied this statement, Jerusalem was still inhabited in its greatness,
and those within it were rebelling against the king of Babylon. The statement that the prophet made about Jerusalem, he made in anger and reproach.
Understand and see, listener: if God had given hope to Sodom and its companion towns, he would not have overthrown them with fire and sulfur.
The sign of the last day of the world. Rather, he handed them over to one of the kingdoms to be disciplined, as it is written:
When Jeremiah gave the nations and kingdoms the cup of wrath to drink, he said concerning each of the cities:
“After they drink the cup, I will restore the captives of Elam, Tyre, Sidon, the Ammonites, and Moab,
/and Edom./” Concerning each of these kingdoms he said, “In the last days I will restore its captives.” And we see that Tyre is inhabited and prosperous,
after being forgotten for seventy years, after receiving payment for her prostitution, and after prostituting herself with all the kingdoms,
taking a harp, playing skillfully, and singing many songs. The land of Elam is also inhabited and prosperous. But concerning Babylon Jeremiah said:
“Babylon will fall and will not rise.” And look: to this day, and indeed forever, she remains in ruins. Concerning Jerusalem he also said:
“The virgin of Israel will fall and will never rise again. She has been abandoned on the ground, and there is no one to raise her.” For if the prophecy Jeremiah spoke concerning Babylon is true,
then the one concerning Jerusalem is also true and trustworthy. And Isaiah said to Jerusalem, “I will no longer be angry with you or rebuke you.”
Truly, he was no longer angry with her, nor did he ever rebuke her again, because in her ruined state he does not rebuke her, and she does not provoke him to anger.
As for their taunting us, saying, “You are persecuted and are not delivered,” let those who were continually persecuted be ashamed,
and who were delivered only after many years. They were enslaved in Egypt for two hundred and twenty-five years.
The Midianites enslaved Israel in the days of Barak and Deborah, and the Moabites ruled over them in the days of Ehud,
the Ammonites in the days of Jephthah, and the Philistines in the days of Samson, and also in the days of Eli and Samuel the prophet,
the Edomites in the days of Ahab, and the Assyrians in the days of Hezekiah. And the king of Babylon uprooted them from their land and scattered them.
Although he tested and disciplined them greatly, they did not improve, as he said to them: “In vain I struck your children, and they did not accept discipline.”
Again he said, “I cut down the prophets and killed them by the word of my mouth.” And to Jerusalem he said, “Be disciplined through pains and blows, Jerusalem,
lest my soul turn away from you.” But they abandoned him and worshiped idols, as Jeremiah said concerning them:
“Go to the distant islands, and send to Kedar. Examine carefully and see whether anything like this has happened: whether nations exchange their gods,
which are not gods. Yet my people have exchanged their glory for what is of no benefit. Be astonished at this, heavens; tremble and be greatly afraid, says the Lord,
because my people have committed two evils: they have abandoned me, the spring of living water, and have gone and dug cisterns for themselves,
broken /cracked/ cisterns that cannot hold water.” For the cracked cisterns are the worship of images and idols.
He calls on the heavens to be astonished because they worshiped the heavenly hosts. And the heavens receive punishment: they are rolled up like a scroll, and all their hosts fall away.
This entire discourse that I have written to you above, my dear friend, concerns a Jewish man who taunted the members of our people.
Nevertheless, as far as I am able to understand, I will show you concerning the persecuted that they received a good reward, while their persecutors fell under a curse and into disgrace.
Jacob was persecuted, and Esau was the persecutor. Jacob received the blessings and the birthright, and Esau was rejected from both.
Joseph was persecuted, and his brothers were the persecutors. Joseph was exalted, and his persecutors bowed down to him, and his dreams and visions were fulfilled.
The persecuted Joseph is a likeness of the persecuted Jesus. Joseph’s father clothed him in a multicolored tunic.
And Jesus’ Father clothed him in a body from the virgin. Joseph’s father loved him more than his brothers. And Jesus is his Father’s loved and cherished one.
Joseph dreamed dreams and saw visions / saw visions and dreamed dreams. And Jesus fulfilled the visions and the prophets.
Joseph was a shepherd with his brothers. And Jesus is the chief of shepherds. When Joseph’s father sent him to visit his brothers, they saw him coming,
and they plotted to kill him. And when Jesus’ Father sent him to visit his brothers, they said, “This is the heir. Come, let us kill him.”
Joseph’s brothers threw him into a pit. And Jesus’ brothers brought him down to the abode of the dead. Joseph came up from the pit.
And Jesus rose from the dead. After Joseph came up from the pit, he gained authority over his brothers. And after Jesus rose from the dead,
his Father gave him a great and exalted name, so that his brothers would submit to him, and his enemies are placed beneath his feet.
When Joseph made himself known to his brothers, they were ashamed and afraid and marveled at his greatness. And when Jesus comes at the last time, when he is revealed in his greatness,
his brothers who crucified him will be ashamed, afraid, and terrified before him. Joseph was sold into Egypt at Judah’s suggestion.
And Jesus was handed over to the Jews by Judas Iscariot. When Joseph’s brothers sold him, he gave them no answer.
And Jesus did not speak or give an answer to the judges who judged him. Joseph’s master unjustly handed him over to prison.
And Jesus’ own people unjustly condemned him. Joseph gave up two of his garments, one into the hands of his brothers and one into the hands of his master’s wife.
And Jesus gave up his garments, and the soldiers divided them among themselves. Joseph was thirty years old when he stood before Pharaoh
and became ruler of Egypt. And Jesus was about thirty years old when he came to the Jordan to be baptized, received the Spirit, and went out to preach.
Joseph supplied the Egyptians with bread. And Jesus supplied the whole world with his bread of life. Joseph married the daughter of a wicked and impure priest.
And Jesus brought near to himself the church from the unclean nations. Joseph died and was buried in Egypt. And Jesus died and was buried in Jerusalem.
Joseph’s brothers brought his bones up from Egypt. And Jesus’ Father raised him from the dead, and he took his body up with him to heaven, without its undergoing decay.
Moses too was persecuted, and Jesus was persecuted. When Moses was born, they hid him so that he would not be killed by his persecutors.
And when Jesus was born, they took him away to Egypt so that Herod, his persecutor, would not kill him. In Moses’ days, when he was born, children were being drowned in the river.
And at Jesus’ birth, children were being killed in Bethlehem and its surrounding territory. God said to Moses,
“The men who were seeking your life have died.” And the angel said to Joseph in Egypt, “Get up, take the child, and go to the land of Israel,
because those who were seeking to take the child’s life have died.” Moses brought his people out of slavery to Pharaoh.
And Jesus freed all the nations from bondage to Satan. Moses was brought up in Pharaoh’s house, and Jesus was brought up in Egypt, when Joseph took him there to escape.
Miriam stood on the riverbank while Moses floated on the water. And Mary gave birth to Jesus after the angel Gabriel brought her the good news.
When Moses slaughtered the lamb, the firstborn of the Egyptians were killed. And Jesus, the true Lamb, when they crucified him—
at his killing, the people who killed him died. Moses brought down manna for his people, and Jesus gave his body to the nations. Moses made bitter water sweet with a piece of wood.
And Jesus made our bitterness sweet through his cross, through the wood on which he was crucified. Moses brought down the Law for his people, and Jesus gave his covenants to the nations.
Moses defeated Amalek by spreading out his hands, and Jesus defeated Satan by the sign of his cross. Moses brought water out of the rock for his people.
And Jesus sent Simon Peter to carry his teaching among the nations. Moses removed the veil from his face, and God spoke with him.
And Jesus removed the veil from the faces of the nations so that they could hear and accept his teaching. Moses laid his hand on his messengers, and they received the priesthood.
And Jesus laid his hand on his apostles, and they received the Holy Spirit. Moses went up the mountain and died there, and Jesus went up to heaven and sat at his Father’s right hand.
Joshua son of Nun was also persecuted, and Jesus our Savior was persecuted. Joshua son of Nun was persecuted by unclean nations.
And Jesus our Savior was persecuted by a foolish people. Joshua son of Nun took the inheritance from his persecutors and gave it to his people.
And Jesus our Savior took the inheritance from his persecutors and gave it to foreign nations. Joshua son of Nun made the sun stand still in the sky.
And he took vengeance on the nations that persecuted him. And Jesus our Savior made the sun set at midday to shame the persecuting people who crucified him.
Joshua son of Nun divided the inheritance among his people, and Jesus our Savior promised to give the nations the land of the living. Joshua son of Nun spared the life of Rahab the prostitute.
And Jesus our Savior gathered the church, which had been a prostitute, and gave her life. Joshua son of Nun overthrew and brought down the walls of Jericho on the seventh day.
And with Jesus our Savior, on his seventh day, the Sabbath of God’s rest, this world will dissolve and fall. Joshua son of Nun stoned Achan, who stole some of what had been devoted to destruction.
And Jesus our Savior separated Judas from his fellow disciples because he stole some of the money belonging to the poor.
When Joshua son of Nun was dying, he laid a solemn charge on his people. And when Jesus our Savior ascended, he laid a solemn charge on his apostles.
Jephthah was also persecuted, and Jesus was persecuted. Jephthah’s brothers drove him out of his father’s house, and Jesus’ brothers drove him out and raised him up and crucified him.
Jephthah, who was persecuted, arose as leader of his people. And Jesus, who was persecuted, arose and became king of the nations. Jephthah made a vow.
And he offered his firstborn child as a sacrifice. And Jesus went up as a sacrifice to his Father on behalf of all the nations.
David was also persecuted, and Jesus was persecuted. David was anointed by Samuel to become king in place of Saul, who had sinned.
And Jesus was anointed by John to become high priest in place of the priests who transgressed the Law. David was persecuted after his anointing.
And Jesus was persecuted after his anointing. David first reigned over just one tribe, and afterward over all Israel.
And Jesus first reigned over the few who believed in him, and in the end he will reign over the whole world. David was thirty years old when Samuel anointed him.
And Jesus, when he was about thirty years old, received the laying on of hands from John. David took two daughters of the king as wives, and Jesus took two daughters of the king.
The congregation of the people and the congregation of the nations. David repaid his enemy Saul with kindness, and Jesus taught, “Pray for your enemies.”
David was God's heart, and Jesus was God's Son. David received the kingdom of Saul, his persecutor, and Jesus received the kingdom of Israel, his persecutor.
David wept in his laments over Saul, his enemy, when he died. And Jesus wept over Jerusalem, his persecutor, which was going to be destroyed.
David handed over the kingdom to Solomon and was gathered to his people. And Jesus handed over the keys to Simon and ascended and went to the one who sent him.
For David's sake, his descendants' sins are forgiven, and for Jesus' sake, the nations' sins are forgiven.
Elijah too was persecuted, and Jesus was persecuted. Elijah was persecuted by the murderous Jezebel, and Jesus was persecuted by the persecuting and murderous congregation.
Elijah shut the heavens against rain because of Israel's sins, and Jesus, at his coming, withheld the Spirit from the prophets,
because of the people's sins. Elijah destroyed the worshipers of Baal, and Jesus trampled Satan and his forces.
Elijah brought the widow's son back to life, and Jesus brought the widow's son back to life, along with Lazarus and the daughter of the synagogue leader.
Elijah fed the widow with a little bread, and Jesus fed thousands with a little bread. Elijah was taken up to heaven in a chariot,
and our Savior ascended and sat at his Father's right hand. Elisha received Elijah's spirit, and Jesus breathed into the faces of his apostles.
Elisha too was persecuted, and Jesus was persecuted. Elisha was persecuted by Ahab's son, the son of a murderer, and Jesus was persecuted by the murderous people.
Elisha prophesied, and there was plenty in Samaria. And Jesus said, “Whoever eats my body and drinks my blood lives forever.”
Elisha fed a hundred men with a little bread, and Jesus fed four thousand with five loaves, besides women and children.
Elisha made oil from water, and Jesus made wine from water. Elisha rescued a widow from her creditor, and Jesus rescued the indebted nations.
Elisha made iron float and wood sink, and Jesus raised us from our sunken state and sank our worthlessness. One dead man came to life on Elisha's bones,
and all the nations, who were dead in their sins, were cast upon Jesus' bones and came to life.
Hezekiah too was persecuted, and Jesus was persecuted. Hezekiah was persecuted and reviled by Sennacherib, his enemy, and Jesus was reviled by the foolish people.
Hezekiah prayed and defeated his enemy, and through Jesus' crucifixion our enemy was defeated. Hezekiah was king of all Israel,
and Jesus is king of all the nations. Because Hezekiah fell ill, the sun turned backward, and because Jesus suffered, the sun's light grew dark.
Hezekiah's enemies became dead bodies, and Jesus' enemies are cast down beneath his feet.
Hezekiah was from the family of the house of David, and Jesus was David's son in the flesh. Hezekiah said, “Let there be peace and truth in my days.”
And Jesus said to his disciples, “I leave you my peace.” Hezekiah prayed and recovered from his illness, and Jesus prayed and rose from the dead.
After Hezekiah recovered from his illness, years were added to his life. And Jesus, after—after his resurrection, received great glory.
After Hezekiah's life was extended, death gained power over him. But after Jesus rose, death will never again have power over him.
Josiah too was persecuted, and Jesus was persecuted. Josiah was persecuted, and Pharaoh the Lame killed him. Jesus was persecuted, and the people who had been crippled by their sins killed him.
Josiah cleansed the land of Israel of impurity. Jesus cleansed the whole earth and removed impurity from it.
Josiah honored and glorified the name of his God. Jesus said, “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it.” Josiah tore his clothes because of Israel's wickedness.
Jesus tore open the entrance of the holy temple because of the people's wickedness. Josiah said, “Great is the wrath that is coming upon this people.”
Jesus said that wrath would come upon that people, and they would fall by the sword. Josiah removed impurity from the holy temple.
Jesus drove the unclean merchants out of his Father's house. The daughters of Israel mourned and lamented over Josiah, as Jeremiah said:
“The daughters of Israel weep over Josiah.” The daughters of Israel wept and mourned over Jesus, as Zechariah said: “The land will mourn, family by family.”
Daniel too was persecuted, and Jesus was persecuted. Daniel was persecuted by the Chaldeans, a company of wicked men.
Jesus was persecuted by the Jews, a company of unjust men. The Chaldeans slandered Daniel.
The Jews slandered Jesus before the governor. They threw Daniel into the lions' den, but he was rescued and came up out of it victorious.
They lowered Jesus into the pit of the dwelling of the dead, but he came up, and death had no power over him. They thought that once Daniel fell into the pit, he would never come up again.
Of Jesus they said, “Now that he has fallen, he will never rise again.” Before Daniel, the mouths of the ravenous, destructive lions were shut.
Before Jesus, the mouth of death, which is ravenous and destroys human forms, was shut. They sealed Daniel's pit and guarded it carefully.
They carefully guarded Jesus' tomb, as they said, “Order that guards be posted at the tomb.” When Daniel came up, his slanderers were put to shame.
When Jesus rose, all those who crucified him were put to shame. The king who judged Daniel was deeply distressed because the Chaldeans had unjustly slandered him.
Pilate, Jesus' judge, was deeply distressed because he knew that the Jews were unjustly slandering him.
Through Daniel's prayer, the captives of his people came up from Babylon. Jesus prayed and brought back the captives of all the nations.
Daniel interpreted Nebuchadnezzar's dream and visions / visions and dreams. Jesus explained and interpreted the visions of the Law and the Prophets.
When Daniel explained Belshazzar's vision, he received the third rank of authority in the kingdom. When Jesus fulfilled the visions and the prophets,
his Father handed over to him all authority in heaven and on earth. Daniel saw wonders and spoke of hidden things. Jesus revealed hidden things and fulfilled what was written.
Daniel was taken away as a hostage on behalf of his people. Jesus' body was a hostage on behalf of all the nations. Because of Daniel,
the king's anger against the Chaldeans subsided, and they were not killed. Because of Jesus, his Father's anger against all the nations subsided,
and they were not killed and did not die because of their sins. Daniel petitioned the king and gave his brothers authority over the affairs of the province of Babylon.
Jesus petitioned God and gave his brothers, his disciples, authority over Satan and his power.
Daniel said of Jerusalem that it would remain in desolation until the decreed times. And Jesus said of Jerusalem that not one stone would be left upon another in it,
because it did not recognize the day of his greatness. Daniel saw the weeks decreed for his people, and Jesus came and fulfilled them.
Hananiah and his brothers were also persecuted, and Jesus was persecuted. Hananiah and his brothers were persecuted by Nebuchadnezzar, and Jesus was persecuted by the Jewish people.
Hananiah and his brothers fell into the fiery furnace, and it became cool as dew upon those righteous men. And Jesus descended into the realm of darkness,
broke its gates, and brought out its prisoners. Hananiah and his brothers came up out of the fiery furnace, and the flame burned their accusers.
And Jesus came to life and rose from the midst of darkness, and his accusers and those who crucified him will burn in the flame at the end.
When Hananiah and his brothers came up out of the furnace, King Nebuchadnezzar trembled and was terrified. And when Jesus rose from the dead,
the people who crucified him were terrified and trembled. Hananiah and his brothers did not worship the image of the king of Babylon, and Jesus kept the nations from worshiping lifeless images.
Because of Hananiah and his brothers, nations and languages praised God, who rescued them from the fire.
And because of Jesus, all nations and all languages praise the one who rescued his Son, so that he did not see corruption.
Fire had no power over the clothes of Hananiah and his brothers. And at the end, fire will have no power over the bodies of all the righteous who have believed in Jesus.
Mordecai too was persecuted, and Jesus was persecuted. Mordecai was persecuted by wicked Haman, and Jesus was persecuted by a rebellious people.
Through his prayer, Mordecai rescued his people from Haman's hands. And through his prayer, Jesus rescued his people from Satan's hands.
Mordecai was rescued from the hands of his persecutor, and Jesus was delivered from the hands of his persecutors. Because Mordecai sat down and put on sackcloth,
he saved Esther and his people from the sword. And because Jesus put on a body and humbled himself, he saved the church and her children from death.
Because of Mordecai, Esther found favor with the king, and she entered and took the place of Vashti, who had not done his will. And because of Jesus, the church found favor with God,
and she entered and became the king's in place of the synagogue, which had not done his will. Mordecai instructed Esther to fast, she and her young women,
so that she and her people might be rescued from Haman's hands. And Jesus instructed his church and her offspring, so that she and her children might be rescued from wrath.
Mordecai received the honor of Haman, his persecutor. And Jesus received great glory from his Father in return for his persecution by a foolish people.
Mordecai trod on the neck of Haman, his persecutor. And Jesus' enemies are being placed beneath his feet.
Haman proclaimed before Mordecai, “This is what shall be done for the man whom the king wishes to honor.” And Jesus' heralds came out from the people who persecuted him,
and said, “This is Jesus, the Son of God.” Mordecai's blood was exacted from Haman and his sons. And Jesus' persecutors took his blood upon themselves and upon their children.
These are the accounts I have written to you, my dear friend, about Jesus, who was persecuted, and the righteous who were persecuted,
so that those persecuted today, who are persecuted because of Jesus, who was persecuted, may be comforted. For he himself wrote to us and encouraged us personally.
For he said, “If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you.” And he said, “They persecute you because you are not of the world.”
Just as I was not of it. For he wrote to us beforehand: “Your fathers, your brothers, and your relatives will betray you,
and everyone will hate you because of my name.” He also taught us: “When they bring you before rulers and authorities,
and before kings who rule the world, do not consider beforehand what you will say or how you will defend yourselves.
I will give you words and wisdom that your enemies will be unable to overcome. For it is not you who speak,
but your Father’s Holy Spirit who speaks through you.” This is the Spirit who spoke through Jacob’s mouth with Esau, his persecutor,
and the Spirit of wisdom who spoke before Pharaoh through the mouth of the persecuted Joseph, and the Spirit who spoke through Moses’ mouth in all the wonders he performed in the land of Egypt,
and the Spirit of knowledge who was given to Joshua son of Nun when Moses laid his hand on him. The nations that persecuted him came to an end and perished before him.
And the Spirit who sang through the mouth of the persecuted David, through whom he sang and gave Saul, his persecutor, relief from the evil spirit, and the Spirit who clothed Elijah
and through him rebuked Jezebel and Ahab, his persecutor, and the Spirit who spoke through Elisha, so that he prophesied and informed the king, his persecutor,
about what would happen the next day, and the Spirit who blazed through Micaiah’s mouth when he rebuked Ahab, his persecutor, and said to him,
“If you return at all, the Lord has not spoken through me,” and the Spirit who strengthened Jeremiah, so that he stood boldly and through the Spirit rebuked Zedekiah,
and the Spirit who protected Daniel and his companions in the land of Babylon, and the Spirit who rescued Mordecai and Esther in the land of their captivity.
Listen, my dear friend, to these names of martyrs, confessors, and persecuted people. Abel was killed, and his blood cried out from the earth.
Jacob was persecuted, fled, and became a foreigner. Joseph was persecuted, sold, and fell into a pit. Moses was persecuted and fled to Midian.
Joshua son of Nun was persecuted and fought a war. Jephthah, Samson, Gideon, and Barak were also persecuted.
These are the ones about whom the blessed apostle said, “I have too little time to recount their victories.” David too was persecuted by Saul
and wandered among mountains, caves, and valleys. Samuel too was persecuted and mourned for Saul. Hezekiah too was persecuted and hemmed in by distress.
Elijah was persecuted and wandered in the wilderness. Elisha was persecuted and became a foreigner. Micaiah was persecuted and became a foreigner.
And Micaiah—and Micaiah [?]—was persecuted and ended up in prison. Jeremiah was persecuted, and they threw him into a muddy pit.
Daniel was persecuted and fell into the lions’ den. Hananiah and his companions too were persecuted and fell into the fiery furnace.
Mordecai, Esther, and their people were persecuted by Haman. Judas Maccabeus and his brothers were also persecuted
and endured disgrace. The seven brothers, sons of the blessed woman, endured torture under bitter scourging
and became confessors and true martyrs. Eleazar, old and advanced in years, was a good example: he confessed his faith and became a perfect martyr.
Great and outstanding was the martyrdom of Jesus. In suffering and confession he surpassed all who came before and after him.
And afterward, the faithful martyr Stephen, whom the Jews stoned. Simon and Paul too became perfect martyrs.
And James and John walked in the footsteps of their master, Christ. Others among the apostles also [?] confessed in place after place and proved to be true martyrs.
Our brothers in the West also suffered great distress in the days of Diocletian, and persecution came upon the whole church of God throughout their territory.
Churches were demolished and uprooted, and many confessors and martyrs confessed their faith. And he turned to them again in mercy after they had been chastened.
These things have happened in our own days too, because of our sins. But the things that are written have also been fulfilled, as our Savior said that these things were going to happen.
The apostle also said that this cloud of confession, our glory, is set over us too; in it many confess their faith and are killed.
The discourse on persecution is finished.
Demonstration on Death and the Last Times
The upright, the righteous, the good, and the wise do not fear or tremble before death, because of the great hope that lies before them.
They always remember death, their departure, and the last day, on which human beings will be judged. They know that death became king by a judicial decree,
because Adam transgressed the commandment, as the apostle said: “Death reigned from Adam until Moses,
even over those who had not sinned.” Thus it also passed upon all Adam’s descendants, just as it passed upon Adam.
And how did death reign from Adam until Moses? When God gave Adam a commandment, he warned him in this way, saying to him:
“On the day you eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, you will surely die.” And when he transgressed the commandment and ate from the tree, death became king over him
and over all his descendants. Even over those who had not sinned, death became king because of Adam’s transgression of the commandment.
And why did he say, “Death reigned from Adam until Moses”? Someone lacking knowledge supposes
that death ruled only from Adam until Moses. But let him understand from what he said: “It passed upon all human beings.”
Indeed, it passed upon all human beings, from Moses until the end of the world. But Moses proclaimed that its kingdom had been abolished.
For when Adam transgressed the commandment and death was decreed against his descendants, death supposed that it had imprisoned all human beings
and had become their king forever. But when Moses came, he proclaimed the resurrection, and death knew that its kingdom would be abolished.
For Moses said, “Let Reuben live and not die, and let him be counted.” And when the Holy One called to Moses from the bush,
he said to him, “I am the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.” When death heard this statement,
it trembled, feared, was terrified, and was thrown into confusion. It knew that it would not be king over Adam’s descendants forever. From the moment it heard God say to Moses,
“I am the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob,” death was at a loss, for it knew that God is king of the dead and the living,
and that Adam’s descendants were destined to come out of its darkness and rise in their bodies. And see how Jesus our Savior also repeated this statement to the Sadducees
when they were disputing with him about the resurrection of the dead. He said, “God is not the God of the dead, because they are all alive to him.”
And so that God might make Death know that his authority over all the children of the world does not last forever,
he took Enoch to himself in his beauty and made him free from death. He also raised Elijah to heaven, and Death had no power over him.
Hannah said, “The Lord puts to death and brings to life; he brings down to Sheol and raises up.” Moses also said, as though speaking from the mouth of his God,
“I put to death, and I bring to life.” And Isaiah the prophet also said, “Your dead will live, and their corpses will rise.
Those who sleep in the dust will awaken and praise you.” When Death heard all these things, astonishment seized him, and he sat in mourning.
And when Jesus, the slayer of Death, came and clothed himself in a body from Adam’s offspring, he was crucified in his body and tasted death. When Death perceived that he had come down to him,
he trembled in his place and was thrown into confusion at seeing Jesus. He shut his gates and was unwilling to receive him. Then Jesus broke his gates and entered his domain.
He began rescuing all of Death’s possessions. When the dead saw light in the darkness, they raised their heads from Death’s prison.
They looked intently and saw the radiance of Christ the King. Then the powers of Death’s darkness sat in mourning because Death had been brought low and stripped of his authority.
Death tasted the poison that would kill him. His hands grew weak, and he knew that the dead were coming to life and escaping from his bondage.
When Jesus distressed Death by rescuing his possessions, Death howled and cried out bitterly, saying, “Get out of my place, and do not enter it!
Who indeed is this who enters my place alive?” And while Death was crying out in terror because he saw that his darkness was beginning to disappear,
some of the righteous who had fallen asleep arose to ascend with Jesus. He made Death know that when he comes at the end of time, he will bring all the prisoners out from under his authority.
They will come out to him to see the light. Then, when Jesus had completed his ministry among the dead, Death expelled him from his place.
He could not bear for Jesus to remain there, and eating him gave him no pleasure as eating all the other dead had done. He had no power over the Holy One, nor was the Holy One given over to decay.
When Death had expelled him and he had left Death’s place, he left with him a poison, the promise of life, so that his authority would gradually be abolished.
It is like a man who takes deadly poison in food that is given to sustain life. When he realizes that he has taken deadly poison in his food,
he then vomits from his stomach the food mixed with deadly poison. But that poison has left its power in his limbs, so that gradually the structure of his body will break down and decay.
Jesus, who died, is the destroyer of Death. Through him life reigns, and through him Death is destroyed, so that Death is asked, “Where is your victory, Death?”
From now on, children of Adam, all of you over whom Death has reigned, remember death and keep life in mind. Do not transgress the commandment
as your first father did. O kings crowned with diadems, remember Death, who takes away the crowns placed on your heads
and himself becomes king over you until the time when you rise for judgment. O proud, lofty, and arrogant people, remember Death, who destroys pride,
loosens limbs, and separates joints. The body and its forms are given over to decay, and the lofty are brought low in death.
The bitter and harsh are buried in his darkness. He takes away all arrogance, and they decay and become dust until the judgment.
O rich people, remember Death, for when the time comes and you reach him, your wealth and possessions will be of no use to you there.
It sets no delicious food before you and prepares no desirable drink for you. There it destroys the bodies/body of the pampered who live proudly.
They cease their luxurious living and no longer remember it. There the worm consumes their bodies, and they wrap themselves in darkness over their fine clothes.
They do not remember this world at all, for death bewilders them when they descend to it and sit in the chamber and shadow of death.
They do not remember this world until the end comes and they rise for judgment. You robbers and oppressors, who deprive your neighbors, remember death!
Do not multiply your sins, because sinners do not repent in that place. Whoever seizes what belongs to his neighbor does not [?] his own.
He goes to a place where no one has any use for wealth. He comes to nothing and passes away from his honor, while his sins are kept for the day of judgment.
You who trust in this world, let this world be of little account in your eyes, because you are temporary residents and strangers in it.
You do not know the day when you will be taken away from it. For death comes suddenly and separates beloved children from their parents and carries them away.
It separates parents from their beloved children. It takes precious only children to itself, and their parents are deprived of them.
And they become despised. It separates dear friends, taking them to itself, and their loved ones weep sorrowfully over them.
It takes and confines with itself those whose beauty is desirable, to disfigure their features and destroy them. It takes those of splendid appearance to itself,
and they become dust until the judgment. It takes betrothed women away from their betrothed men and confines them in its bridal chamber, in its gloomy dwelling.
It takes betrothed men away and separates them from the virgins who are pledged to them and betrothed in their names, and who sit in bitter mourning for them.
It takes away and separates to itself all the handsome young men who thought they would not see death until old age.
It takes and gathers to itself beloved children only a few days old, whose parents have not yet had their fill of them.
It takes to itself the rich, those full of pride, and they leave their possessions like the waves of the sea.
It takes to itself skilled craftsmen who sustain the world with marvelous works. It takes to itself the clever and the wise,
and they become fools who cannot distinguish good from evil. It takes to itself the prosperous people of this world, and their affairs are ruined, never to be put right.
It takes to itself the mighty and the warriors, and their strength is brought low, grows weak, and comes to an end, though they had trusted that their strength would not diminish.
On the day of death, those weaker than they are gather up their bodies. And those who trust that at their death they will be buried with honor—
it may happen that dogs eat them. And those who trust that they will be buried in the place where they were born—
they do not know whether they will instead be gathered up in disgrace in the land of their captivity. And those who trust in their possessions, intending to leave them to their children—
it is hidden from them that their enemies will plunder them. Death takes to itself the valiant and the warlike, who had thought they would lay waste to much of the world.
Death takes those who adorn themselves with every desirable thing, and it happens that they are buried with a donkey's burial. Death rules over those not yet born,
and confines them with itself before they are born. Death takes to itself those honored because of their high status, and they are disgraced when they descend to it.
To his place, which is dark and has no light. He is not intimidated by kings wearing crowns, nor does he hide from the mighty and fierce who devastate countries.
Death shows no partiality to respected or honored people, nor does he accept bribes from the rich. Death does not despise the poor,
nor does he turn away from someone who has nothing. Death does not honor those who have conducted themselves arrogantly, and he makes no distinction between the good and the wicked.
He considers the old no more honorable than the young, and he makes those who have understanding thoughtless. Those who acquire possessions and run about and wear themselves out—
there with him they are stripped of their property. He leads slaves and their masters to himself alike,
and there masters are no more honored than their slaves. Small and great are there, and they do not hear the voice of the taskmaster.
The slave who is freed from his master pays no regard there to the one who used to enslave him. Death binds and imprisons the jailers with himself,
and the tormented prisoners. Through death the prisoners are released, and they no longer fear those who enslaved them.
Those who are arrogant fear death, while the afflicted wait to be taken away soon. All the rich tremble at death,
while the poor long for it so that they may rest from their labor. Death terrifies the mighty when they remember it,
while the sick wait for it so that through it they may forget their pains. The young in years also fear death,
because when it comes upon them, they leave their pleasures behind. But the elderly, advanced in years, pray for it—those who depend on their daily bread.
Peaceful people remember death, and they let go of anger and put aside hostility.
They live in this world as temporary residents and prepare provisions for the journey ahead of them. They think about the things above and meditate on the things above,
while the things before their eyes are of little account to them. They send their treasures to a place free from fear, a place where there are neither moths nor thieves.
The beloved citizens of that land live in this world as strangers, and they wait to be sent away from this world

and to go to the city, the dwelling place of the righteous. They discipline themselves in the place of their temporary residence, and they do not linger or become preoccupied in their temporary lodging.
Day after day their faces are turned upward, so that they may go to the rest of their fathers. They are like prisoners in this world,
and like hostages held for the king. They have no rest at all in this world, and there is no hope in it that lasts forever.
Those who acquire property do not enjoy it, and those who have children are grieved by death. Those who build cities are not allowed to remain in them,
and they run about and wear themselves out over something in which they are no different from fools. O senseless person, whose trust is in this world!

Remember, my beloved, reflect, and see in your mind: who from the former generations has been left in this world to remain forever? Death carried away the former generations—the mighty, the powerful, and the skilled.
Who acquired great possessions and took them with him when he departed? What is gathered from the earth returns into it, and a person departs stripped of his possessions.
Wise people who acquire property send some of it ahead of them, as Job said, “My witnesses are in heaven.” And he said,
“My brothers and my friends are with God.” Our Lord commanded those who possess property to make friends for themselves in heaven and also to store up treasures there.
You too, wise scribe, remember death, lest your heart become proud and you forget the sentence of judgment. Death has not spared the wise,
nor has it shown favor to the skillful. Death has taken wise scribes to itself, and they forget what they learned until the time comes when all the righteous rise.
In that place they forget this world. There they have no need, and they love one another with abundant affection.
There is no heaviness in their bodies, for they will fly lightly like doves to their windows. There they do not remember evil at all in their minds,
nor does anything impure enter their hearts. In that place there is no natural desire, and there they are free of all desires,
so that anger and obscenity do not enter their hearts. Everything that gives birth to sins is also removed from them. Love for one another burns in their hearts,
and no hatred at all is lodged within them. There they have no need to build houses, for they dwell in light, in the abodes of the holy.
They have no need of woven clothing, for they are wrapped in everlasting light. They have no need of food, for they recline at his table and are nourished forever.
The air there is delightful and splendid. Its light shines, beautiful and lovely. Beautiful trees are planted there, whose fruit never fails,
and whose leaves do not fall. Their branches are glorious and their fragrance sweet, and the soul never tires of their taste.
That place is spacious and without bounds. Its inhabitants see its distant reaches as though they were nearby. There the inheritance is not divided,
and no one says to another, “This is mine, and that is yours.” There they are not bound by greedy desire, nor do they quarrel there over remembrance.
There no one loves another out of excessive fear. Rather, they all love one another abundantly and in the same way.
There they do not take wives or bear children, and there is no distinction there between male and female.
Rather, they are all children of the Father in heaven, as the prophet said: “Do we not all have one Father? Has not one God created us?”
As for my statement that they do not take wives there and that there is no distinction between male and female, our Lord and his apostle taught us this. For our Lord said:
“Those who are worthy of that world and of the resurrection from the dead neither take wives nor become wives to husbands,
because they cannot die. Rather, they are like the angels in heaven and are children of God.” And the apostle said: “There is neither male nor female,
neither slave nor free, but you are all one in Jesus Christ.” For God separated Eve from Adam for the purpose of procreation,
so that she would become the mother of every living person. But in that world there is no female, just as in heaven there is neither female nor procreation nor any need for desire.
In that place there is no deficiency of any kind, but perfection and completeness. The old do not die, and the young do not grow old,
so that young men should take wives and father children in anticipation of growing old and dying, so that when the fathers die, the children may [?] in their place.
For all these things serve a purpose in this world. But in that place there is neither need nor deficiency,
nor desire, nor procreation, nor an end, nor destruction, nor death, nor annihilation, nor aging,
nor hatred, nor anger, nor jealousy, nor weariness, nor toil, nor darkness, nor night, nor falsehood.
There is no lack at all in that place. Rather, that place is full of light and life, mercy, fullness, and satisfaction,
renewal and love, and all the good promises, both those written down and those not recorded. For there is something there that the eye has not seen,
the ear has not heard, and the human heart has not conceived—something that cannot be expressed and that no human being can describe.
The apostle said, “What God has prepared for those who love him.” However much people may speak, they cannot express it.
They cannot describe what the eye has not seen. And as for what the ear has not heard, comparing it to anything the ear has heard and the eye has seen
is not a fitting way for them to speak. And what has not entered the heart—who dares to say that it resembles anything that has entered the heart?
But it is fitting for the speaker to use comparisons and call that place the dwelling of God, the place of life, the perfect place,
the place of light, the place of majesty, God's Sabbath, the day of rest, the rest of the righteous, the delight of the just,
the dwelling and abode of the righteous and holy, the place of our hope, the home of our firm confidence, the place of our treasure,
the place that erases our toil, removes our afflictions, and wipes away our sighs. These are the comparisons and names we should use for that place.
Again, death has taken to himself kings who founded cities and grew powerful in their pride. He has not spared the rulers of lands.
Death has taken and carried captive to himself the greedy, who are never satisfied and never say, “Enough!” He is greedier for them than they themselves were.
Death has taken plunderers to himself, and they are prevented, against their own will, from plundering their neighbors. Death has taken the unjust to himself,
and because of death they are prevented from doing wrong. Death has taken oppressors to himself, and the oppressed have rest until they go to him.
Death has taken to himself those who devour their neighbors. The mistreated and wronged have a little rest until they too are taken away and go there.
Death has taken those with many plans, and everything they intended is undone and brought to nothing. People plan many things,
but death comes upon them suddenly, and they are taken away and no longer remember anything they planned. Someone makes plans for many years,
unaware that tomorrow he will be no more. A human being exalts himself and boasts over his neighbor, but death comes upon him and puts an end to his boasting.
A rich man plans to add to his possessions, not knowing that even what he has acquired will not remain his. Death has taken all human beings to himself
and confined them in his abode until the judgment. He reigned even over those who had not sinned, because of the sentence Adam received for his sins.
Then the Giver of Life, the slayer of death, comes and ends death's authority over the just and the wicked. The dead rise at a mighty voice,
and death is emptied and stripped of all his captives. All Adam's descendants gather for judgment, and each person goes to the place prepared for him.

The resurrection of the righteous leads to life, while the resurrection of the wicked is handed over to death. The righteous who kept the commandment go on without coming to judgment on the day they rise,
as David asked, “Do not bring your servant into judgment.” Nor will their Lord terrify them on that day.
And remember that the apostle also said, “We will judge angels.” And our Lord said to his disciples, “You will sit on twelve thrones.”
And you will judge the twelve tribes of the house of Israel. Ezekiel also spoke about righteous men who would judge Oholah and Oholibah.
For he made it known that the righteous, who are destined to judge the wicked, do not themselves enter into judgment. And concerning what the apostle said, “We judge angels”—
listen, and let me convince you. For the angels who are judged by the apostles are priests who have transgressed the Law, as the prophet said:
“The lips of a priest preserve knowledge, and people seek the Law from his mouth, because he is the messenger of the mighty Lord.” The angels who are priests,
and from whose mouths the Law is sought, when they transgress the Law, will be judged at the end by the apostles and by priests who keep the Law.
The wicked will not stand in judgment, nor sinners in the assembly of the righteous. And just as the righteous, who are perfect in good deeds, do not enter into judgment to be judged,
so neither do the wicked whose sins are many and whose measure of guilt is overflowing. These are not required to come forward for judgment.
Instead, when they rise, they return to Sheol, as David said: “The wicked will return to Sheol,
and all the nations that forget God.” Isaiah also said: “All the nations are like a drop from a bucket,
and like dust on the scales. The islands will be cast away like dust, and all the nations are regarded by him as nothing.
He regards them as destined for destruction and desolation.” Now learn and be convinced that all the nations that do not know God their Maker
are regarded as nothing by God and do not approach his judgment. Instead, when they rise, they return to Sheol.
The rest of the whole world, who are called sinners, stand in judgment and are reproved. For those who have only a few faults [?],
the judge reproves and makes known to them that they have done wrong, and after judgment he gives them an inheritance of life. Understand what our Lord made known to us in his Gospel:
everyone receives his reward according to his labor. The one who received money and showed a profit, who made his mina and his talent amount to ten [?],
receives perfect life, lacking nothing. The one who made his mina and his talent into five minas received half of ten.
One was given authority over ten minas, and another over five. Understand and see that the profit of five is less than that of ten.
The workers who ask for wages are superior to those who receive them and remain silent. Those who labored all day receive their wages openly and without shame,
and confidently ask that more be added for them. Those who worked one hour receive their wages in silence, knowing that by grace they are shown mercy and live.
Those sinners whose sins are many are condemned by the court and go away to torment. From then onward, the judge has authority.

Listen again to the apostle, who said: “Everyone receives his reward according to his labor.” The one who labored little receives according to his toil, and the one who ran much is repaid according to his running.
Job also said: “Far be it from God to do wrong, and far be it from him to commit sin! For he repays a person according to his deeds,
and a man receives according to his ways.” The apostle also said: “One star surpasses another in its brightness. So it is also with the resurrection of the dead.”
Know, then, that even when people enter into life, one recompense surpasses another, and one glory surpasses another,
one reward is greater than another, one rank is higher than another, and one light is more beautiful in appearance than another. The sun surpasses the moon.
And the moon is greater than the stars that accompany it. Observe that the moon and the stars are also under the sun’s authority, and their light is swallowed up in the sun’s radiance.
But the sun has no authority alongside the moon and the stars, so that it does not abolish the night, which was separated from the day.
And when the sun was created, it was called a light. Observe that the sun, the moon, and the stars were all called lights, but one light surpasses another.
The sun dims the moon’s light, and the moon also darkens the light of the stars. And one star surpasses another in its light.
Take a lesson also from the things of this world: from laborers at their labor and hired workers who work alongside their companions.
One person hires another for a day’s wages, and that same day the worker receives the wages for his labor. Another is hired for a month,
and settles accounts and receives his wages at regular intervals. A day’s wages differ from a month’s, and a year’s wages exceed a month’s.
Take a lesson again from worldly authority: some please the king by their conduct and receive honor from those who hold power.
One receives a crown from the king to become governor of one of the provinces, while another is given villages under his authority by the king.
He is distinguished even in his clothing from someone of lower rank. Some receive presents and gifts, and one honor differs from another.
Another is given the honor by the king of becoming steward over the entire treasury. Another serves the king according to his lowly rank, and his entitlement is only his daily bread.
And I say that punishment for evil is not equal for everyone either. Whoever has committed much wickedness is severely tormented, while whoever has done wrong a little rather than much
is tormented a little. Some go into the outer darkness, where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth, while others fall into the fire, as they deserve.
It is not written that they gnash their teeth, nor that there is darkness there. Others fall into another place, where their worm does not die
and their fire is not quenched, and they become a spectacle to all humanity. Others have the door shut in their faces, and the judge says to them, ‘I do not know you.’
Understand that just as the reward for good deeds is not equal for everyone, neither is the punishment for evil deeds. People are not judged in one uniform way.
Rather, everyone receives recompense according to his deeds, because the judge is clothed in righteousness and shows no partiality.
And just as I have shown you how, in this world, one honor exceeds another, and how kings and worldly rulers grant these honors to those under their authority,
I will also show you this: just as kings have good gifts to give to those who honor them, so they also have prisons,
prisoners, chains, and shackles—bonds of every kind. One person commits a great offense against the king and is handed over to death without questioning.
Another commits an offense but does not deserve execution. He is imprisoned until he is tried and disciplined, and the king pardons his offense. There is another with whom the king is displeased,
and he is kept under guard outside the prison, at liberty, without chains or bonds. The person who is executed differs from the prisoner,
and one person’s punishment is greater than another’s, according to what his offense deserves. Now turn to our Savior, who said, ‘There are many dwelling places in my Father’s house.’
My dear friend, people with little understanding dispute about this matter that I am writing to you about, and they say:
‘Where is the place in which the righteous receive their good reward, and where is the place in which the torments are?’
in which evildoers receive punishment for their deeds. O mortal who thinks about these things, let me ask you, and tell me:
Who is Death, who is called Death, and what is Sheol, which is called Sheol? For it is written that when Korah and his companions rebelled against Moses,
the earth opened its mouth and swallowed them, and they went down alive to Sheol. So it was the mouth of Sheol that opened in the wilderness.
And David said, “Let the wicked return to Sheol.” We say that it is to the Sheol in which Korah and his companions were swallowed up
that the wicked return. For God has the power, if he wishes, to grant life as an inheritance in heaven, or on earth if it pleases him. Jesus our Lord said,
“Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” And to one of those who were crucified with him,
who believed in him, he swore, “You will be with me in the Garden of Eden.” And the apostle said that when the righteous rise, they fly upward to meet our Savior.
But we say this: what our Savior told us is true, that heaven and earth will pass away. And the apostle said,
“Hope that is seen is not hope.” And the prophet said, “The heavens will pass away like smoke, and the earth will wear out like clothing,
and its inhabitants will be like it.” And Job said about those who sleep in death, “Until the heavens wear out, they will not awaken or stir from their sleep.”
Be convinced by these things that this earth, in which human beings are sown, and the firmament above humankind—
this firmament set as a division between the highest heavens and the land of the living—these will pass away, wear out, and perish.
And God will make a renewal for humankind, and the heirs will inherit in the kingdom of heaven. If he grants them their inheritance on earth, it is called the kingdom of heaven;
and if in heaven, it is easy for him to do so. For even though the kings of the world each reside in their own place,
every place reached by a king’s authority is called his kingdom. And the bright sun, fixed in the firmament, spreads its rays everywhere.
Its dominion extends over sea and dry land. And see that the rulers of the world also have banquets and pleasures, and in every place and every city,
wherever they go, their banquets are with them. And wherever it pleases them, they make a prison. Prisoners.
For the sun makes its circuit in twelve hours, from east to west, and when it finishes its journey,
its light is concealed at night, and the night is not disturbed by its dominion. During the hours of the night, the sun circles on its swift course,
and returns and begins to travel as usual. And the sun that has been with you, O wise one, from your childhood to the end of your old age—
you do not know where it travels at night and makes its circuit to the place of its course. Must you investigate things that are hidden from you?
I have written these reminders for our brothers and our beloved ones, the children of the church of God, in every place, wherever these writings reach, for those who read them,
