so that they may also remember my lowly self in their prayers, and know that I too am sinful and deficient. But this is my faith,
which I set down and wrote earlier in these written chapters: faith is the foundation, and upon faith are deeds that befit it.
And after faith, I wrote about the two commandments of love. And after love, I wrote about fasting, explaining it and its practices.
After the piece on fasting, I wrote about prayer, its fruits and its works. After the piece on prayer, I wrote about war and what Daniel wrote about the kingdoms.

After the piece on war, I wrote an exhortation to the members of the covenant. After the piece on the members of the covenant, I wrote about repentance. After the piece on repentance, I wrote about the resurrection of the dead.
After the piece on the resurrection of the dead, I wrote about humility. After the piece on humility, I wrote about shepherds who teach. After the piece on shepherds, I wrote about circumcision,
in which the Jewish people boast. After the piece on circumcision, I wrote about Passover and the fourteenth day.
After the piece on Passover, I wrote about the Sabbath, in which the Jews take pride. After the piece on the Sabbath, I wrote an appeal concerning the dispute that arose in our days.
After the appeal, I wrote about foods, because the Jews declare them unclean. After the piece on foods, I wrote about the nations,
who entered and became heirs in place of the former people. After the piece on the nations, I wrote and made known that God has a Son.
After the piece on the Son of God, I wrote against the Jews who speak blasphemously about virginity. After the discourse on virginity,
I wrote again against the Jews who say, “We are destined to be gathered together.” After this discourse, I wrote about gifts to the poor.
After the piece on the poor, I wrote a demonstration concerning the persecuted. After the piece on the persecuted, I wrote, last of all, about death and the last times.
I wrote these twenty-two discourses according to the twenty-two letters. I wrote the first ten
in the year six hundred and forty-eight of the reign of Alexander, son of Philip the Macedonian, as is written at their conclusion. And these last twelve
I wrote in the year six hundred and fifty-five of the rule of the Greeks and Romans, which is the reign of Alexander, and in the thirty-fifth year of the Persian king.
I wrote these things according to what I understood. For if anyone reads these discourses and finds statements that do not agree with his understanding,
he should not mock. For what is written in these chapters was not written to suit the understanding of one person, nor to convince one reader,
but for the understanding of the whole church and the assurance of the whole community of faith. If he reads and listens with a receptive spirit, that is good. If not, I have this to say:
I wrote for receptive people, not for mockers. And if the reader also finds statements that we have expressed in one way,
and another wise person in another way, he should not be troubled by this. For everyone speaks to his hearers according to what he understands.
And I, who wrote these things, even if some of the statements do not agree with those of another speaker, nevertheless say this:
Those wise people have spoken well, and this is how it seemed right to me to speak. And if anyone speaks and instructs me on each point,
I will accept it from him without argument. Everyone who reads the earlier and later holy Scriptures, in both Testaments,
and reads with a receptive spirit, learns and teaches. But if he argues about something he does not understand, his mind does not accept instruction.
Rather, if he finds statements that are difficult for him and does not understand their meaning, he should say this: “What is written is well written,
but I have not grasped its meaning.” And if he asks discerning wise people who are practiced in learning about statements that are difficult for him,

when ten wise people give him ten interpretations of one statement, he should accept the one that pleases him. But he should not ridicule the wise people over an interpretation that does not please him.
For the word of God is like a pearl: whichever side you turn it toward, it has [?] a beautiful appearance. And remember, O student, what David said:
“I have learned from all my teachers.” And the apostle said, “Keep reading every scripture inspired by God. Examine everything, and hold on to what is good,
and flee from every evil thing.” For even if a person's days were to become as numerous as all the days of the world, from Adam until the end of time,
and he were to sit and meditate on the Holy Scriptures, he would not grasp the full force of the depth of their words. And no one can comprehend the wisdom of God,
as I wrote in the tenth discourse. But all speakers who do not draw from the great treasury—their words are despised and held in contempt.
For the king's image is accepted wherever it goes, but one that is counterfeit is rejected and not accepted.
And if someone says that these discourses are addressed to so-and-so, let him learn as a learner. He has not been commanded to trouble the speaker.
I too have written these things according to my limited ability, a human being descended from Adam and fashioned by the hands of God,
for I am a student of the Holy Scriptures. For our Lord said, “Everyone who asks receives, and whoever seeks finds,
and whoever knocks will have the door opened to him.” And the prophet said, “I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh in the last days, and they will prophesy.”
Therefore, as I wrote above, whoever reads should read with conviction and pray for the speaker, a brother of the community, so that through the supplication of the whole church of God,
his sins may be forgiven. And let the reader remember that it is written, “Let the one who hears the word share all good things with the one who teaches him.”
And again it is written, “The sower and the reaper will rejoice together.” And everyone receives his reward according to his labor. There is nothing hidden that will not be revealed to everyone.
The Demonstration on Death and the Last Times is finished.
Demonstration on the Grape.
I will write and explain to you, my dear beloved friend, the subjects you asked me about: the blessing hidden in the cluster of grapes,
because, on account of the blessed grape, the cluster was not handed over to destruction. For in the days of Isaiah, the owner of the cluster wanted to destroy it,
and he was told by a pronouncement that the cluster should not be destroyed, because there was a blessing in it. And you also asked me
whether righteous and upright people are to be found on earth at all times. I will explain to you that blessing which passed through all generations until its appointed time.
I will also explain to you the matter you asked me about: why the righteous were sometimes heard when they prayed, while at other times God did not hear them.
I will also write to you about the years of the earlier generations, reckoning each generation separately, until the time when Jerusalem was destroyed and grace was taken away from it,
and how the righteous carefully guarded the blessing that passed down from them, until the time when its transmission reached the nations through Jesus.
Now, investigating these matters is good for learning and understanding, but above all we ought to fear God with a pure heart, the giver of the pronouncements,
who wrote and set before us that those who fear God travel with great toil and much fear, through a narrow gate and along a constricted road.
First, then, my beloved, we ought to fear God's judgment, and the words and commandments of the Giver of Life, who said:
People will give an account on the day of judgment for every idle word they speak. And again it is written: “By your words you will be justified,”
“and by your words you will be condemned.” And again it is written: “People’s mouths bring them down.” And elsewhere it is written:
“The fool’s mouth makes a stumbling block for him.” And be troubled by the words of the teacher of the nations, who said: “We must all stand before the judgment seat of Christ,”
“so that each person may receive repayment in his body for what he previously did, whether good or evil.” And again he said:
“Save your lives with fear and trembling.” And again he added this warning to us: “It is a very fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.”
The blessed apostles also proclaimed: “We must enter the kingdom of God through great suffering.” And again he said: “The day of the Lord is terrifying,”
“and who can endure it? His wrath is fierce and burning. He will make the earth a wasteland and destroy its sinners from it.”
For because the first human being gave his obedience to the serpent, he received the curse as punishment: that he should become food for the serpent.
And the curse spread to all his descendants. For because he ate from the tree of knowledge, he was barred from the fruit of the tree of life,
so that he would not eat from it and live forever. And by this we know that, because the human being transgressed the commandment through the evil one’s deception,
and first took pride upon himself, seeking to become equal to his Maker, through the discernment of the knowledge he received, a barrier arose between him and the tree of life.
Because of the evil one’s deceit, he was barred from its fruit. And at the command of the Great One, the tree was fenced off with a terrifying spear and a revolving flame.
The human being himself, because he perceived and knew, could go toward that tree, but in his weakness he could not cross the barrier.
For this reason, this very tree of life, in its kindness, did not withhold itself from the needy, so that they might eat from it and live.
Then it lengthened its branches and spread out its boughs. It stretched its shoots above the barrier and graciously cast its fruit beyond the boundary
that surrounded it to guard it. And the children [?], because of the confusing and harmful knowledge, had previously been gripped by many scourges.
Through this means of healing, the pronouncement of the curse was lifted from them. And when the enemy perceived this, he was somewhat confounded in his mind,
and his schemes were thwarted. He became angry at the fruit and those who ate it, who received in their bodies the annulment of the curse.
And the wisdom of truth defeated the evil one’s deceit. Those who ate the fruit were preserved like a grape in a cluster.

And because of [?], the whole cluster was preserved until the time appointed by the Most High should be fulfilled, and so that the sentence against them—against the rest of the cluster—might be delayed.
But they did not wish to repent through the power of the blessing, so that they might ripen and become sweet instead of having the bitterness they had received,
and share in the sweetness of the fruit. The planting is cultivated through the cultivator’s wisdom, though for a long time it had been deprived of help
and of knowledge of the gift of healing. And when the door of the greeting of peace was opened, the darkness in the minds of many fled,
with the dawning of the light of understanding and the bearing of the fruits of the light-giving olive tree, in which is the sign of the mystery of life.
Through it Christians, priests, kings, and prophets are consecrated. It gives light to those in darkness, anoints the defiled, and brings the repentant near through its hidden mystery.
And those who press forward and draw near to him—his sweetness drips into their hidden ears, and they see with their eyes and hear with their ears.
They picture his likenesses through the perceptions of their thoughts, and eagerly strive to advance without delay. They stretch forward to go on and forget what is behind them.
And they are able to reach that hidden vision which they received when they tasted him, who pictured delights for them so that they might flee from the evil one.
Then they become the leaven of the righteous in this world, so that through them room may be given for repentance.
For their sake, sinners too are allowed to remain on earth, so that they may receive the promise and the sun of grace may shine upon them.
Because of the patience of the Good One, the weeds are preserved along with the wheat, lest the owner of the seed should wish, before the weeds have finished growing,
to order them uprooted, and harm should also come to the wheat when the weeds are cleared from among it. Rather, the rain that makes the good seed grow
also makes the weeds flourish, the seed of the evil one. The Good One has done this in his wisdom to bring to nothing the contrivance of the children of the evil one,
who posit two roots, one of good and one of evil. For if the rain that makes the wheat grow were harmful to the weeds, the seed of the evil one,
it would be clear that two natures were at work in creation. But the growth of both alike flourishes through rain, wind, and sunshine.
Created things bear witness to one Creator, whose creatures are governed by his command. For there are many good people in the world on behalf of the wicked,
for whose sake the outpouring of wrath is held back from them. But when the hedge around the wicked is breached and none of the good stands in it,
the measure of sins overflows and arouses the wrath of the Most High. Because of the wrath against the wicked, the chosen are caught in the smoke.
And when the sword is commanded to lay waste, it destroys sinners and righteous alike, because the righteous did not hurry to stand in the breach in the hedge.
As the prophet proclaimed: “I sought among my people a man who would build up the hedge and stand in the breach on behalf of the land, so that I would not destroy it, but I found none.”
And he had already shown this sign through the righteous of earlier generations. For the ten generations of Adam’s family were preserved during Methuselah’s lifetime.
At the very time he died, the flood came, and the world perished and was destroyed by wrath. But Noah was sheltered from the waters of the deluge,
so that a second world might spring from him. And during the lifetime of Noah, the man of rest, ten generations were preserved, from the flood onward.
When he had completed [?] and died, Abraham departed from Ur of the Chaldeans. In his patience, the Most High showed his mercy toward the Canaanites.
Since the measure of their sins was not yet full, he did not wish to destroy them. He brought Abraham’s descendants into Egypt and decreed slavery for the offspring of those who loved him,
so that the sins of the Amorites might reach their full measure, and his wonders might be displayed against those who enslaved them. And when he brought them out by his great power,
he showed them his wonders. In the wilderness he nourished them with the food of his holy ones and satisfied them with the bread of angels.
He made a spring flow for them in a waterless place. And when they embittered his spirit and angered him, Moses stood in the breach for his people.
And during the lifetime of Aaron, the high priest who made atonement and offered incense amid the wrath, their enemies did not gain power over them.
But at his death on Mount Hor, the Canaanite king of Geder, who lived in the south, attacked them. And during Moses’ lifetime they lacked nothing for their sustenance.
And at his death on Mount Nebo, the manna was withheld from them. When his people came out of Egypt, God brought them across the fearsome sea.
And when Pharaoh the oppressor drowned, Miriam took a tambourine in her hand and praised the Exalted One who had drowned them. And at the time when Miriam died,
there was no water for the people to drink. And in the days of King Hezekiah, they were delivered from two Assyrian kings.
And after the death of that righteous man, his sons were taken as hostages to the king of Babylon. And Josiah, the righteous king, cleansed the land of Israel of impurity.
He was gathered away before disaster came. After his death, Israel’s oppressors multiplied, and their enemies, the kings, uprooted them from their land.
And when the measure of sins overflowed, the prayer of the righteous was no longer heard. For the Holy One said to Jeremiah concerning that time:
“Even if Moses and Samuel were to stand before me, my soul would take no pleasure in this people. Instead, send them out of my presence, and let them go.
And if they say to you, ‘Where shall we go?’ tell them, ‘To the sword, captivity, famine, and pestilence.’ I will send four scourges upon them.”
And God also said to Ezekiel: “If I send a sword against a land and say, ‘Let a sword pass through the land,’ or send a wild beast,
and Noah, Job, and Daniel are in that land, as I live, says the Lord of lords, they will save neither son nor daughter.
Rather, by their righteousness they will save only themselves, and the land will be devastated.” This statement teaches us
that the prophet was distressed [?] when he prayed and was not heard. Therefore his Lord reassured him through the example of these three righteous men,
because a thought had arisen in his heart: “Why were Noah, Job, and Daniel heard, each in his own generation,
while he does not hear my prayer? Noah was heard, and the members of his household were saved with him from the wrath of the flood.
And Job prayed for his friends, and the Lord showed him favor, and they did not come under a curse. And the mystery was revealed to Daniel through his prayer,
and his companions were delivered from the king’s wrath. Even the wise men of Babylon, who were wicked, were saved and kept alive through Daniel’s prayer.”
When the prophet thought these things, the Good One reassured him in his kindness, as was his custom: “These three righteous men, each of whom I heard in his own generation—
if they were to stand before me at this time, not only would I not hear them on behalf of the wicked, but they would not even save a son or daughter.
Rather, by their righteousness they would save only themselves, and the land would be devastated.” Then the prophet was persuaded by his Lord’s reassurance.
Jeremiah the prophet also entertained a similar thought and said: “Why were Moses and Samuel heard, each in his own generation,
while the Lord has placed a covering before my prayer and does not hear it? For Moses stood in the breach for his people many times,
and they were not wiped out because of their sins. Samuel also made atonement for all Israel because they had asked for a king and rejected his kingship.”
And again the Good One, in his patience, persuaded Jeremiah the prophet: “Even if Moses and Samuel were to stand before me at this time, I would not hear them.”
Even in their own time, these righteous men, mighty in strength, were sometimes heard when they prayed, and at other times they prayed and were not answered.
Moses, the great prophet of all Israel, through whose accepted prayer his people were delivered from wrath many times,
And his prayer was sufficient for all Israel. But on another occasion, when he prayed, his prayer was not sufficient for his own self.
For he prayed with lamentation and pleaded that he might cross over and see the promised land. But his Lord said to him, “Enough for you! Do not speak to me again about this matter.
For I will not listen to you, because you rebelled against the word of my mouth and did not acknowledge my holiness at the waters of contention.”
O astonishing mysteries, that the righteous are not heard! For by not being heard, they are disciplined before the judgment,
so that they may not be condemned on the day of recompense. In this way Moses was disciplined because he rebelled: his prayer was not heard, and he did not enter the promised land.
I say, my brothers, with firm confidence, that at every time, from the beginning and forever, righteous and upright people are found on the earth.
As it is written, “No righteous person has departed from before the eyes of the Lord, and the world has not been left without upright people.” Our Savior testified to this:
“I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.” Christ came because he wanted sinners to become righteous.
For the healthy had no need of a physician, because they had no illness.
Nor were those who were full hungry for him, or thirsty so that they might drink and be refreshed. For he called out in this way: “Let everyone who is thirsty come and drink.”
And the prophet called out, “Ho, you who are thirsty, go to the water, and obtain milk and wine for yourselves without money and without payment.”
Wine brings joy, and milk nourishes. Concerning this the apostle said, “As to infants in Christ, I gave you milk to drink.”
This is the great mystery that the prophet proclaimed beforehand. For he said, “Let everyone who is thirsty go to the water.” And the one who fulfills the prophets said,
“Let everyone who is thirsty come and drink.” The prophet sent people to the spring, while the one who gives drink himself called them to drink. And the prophet proclaimed,
“Come near and drink wine and milk without payment,” from him whose eyes are red from wine and whose teeth are white from milk.
And not like the false prophets, who bite with their teeth and proclaim peace, but proclaim war against anyone who puts nothing into their mouths.
Nor do they resemble the wicked priests and lying prophets who teach for a fee and practice divination for money. They ate the sin of the people,
and gave themselves over to their wickedness. The priest became like the people because he did not rebuke the people for their sin, and the priest acted according to the people's sin.
But when the word reached the one who fulfills it, he proclaimed to his apostles, “Freely you received; freely give.” And the teacher of the nations built upon this after him:
“I proclaimed the good news of Christ to you free of charge.” And again he said, “I want to offer the good news without expense.”
And concerning what I wrote, that righteous and upright people are found on earth at every time, this is undoubtedly so.
For because of the righteous, the Good One makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good; and you send down your rain so that the wicked may be sustained.
For the righteous and upright are the salt of the earth, as our Savior said to his blessed apostles: “You are the salt of the earth.”
For if the salt loses its taste, the world quickly decays and is ruined. Just as the soul sustains the body, the righteous sustain the earth.
For when the soul departs, the body falls from its standing position and decays. The righteous on earth are like the eyes in the body.
For if it goes blind, the body becomes helpless and loses its beauty. It begins to stumble at noon as though it were night and cannot walk straight.
The righteous are a life-giving medicine in this world. If they were not in the world, the world would fall apart and be destroyed by wrath.
The world rejoices when the righteous are within it, like a garden with a spring of water. If the spring dries up, the garden’s fruit withers.
There is nothing in them to meet anyone’s needs or refresh the soul. Its vines, too, are uprooted and burned in the fire.
But when vines are found that make the farmer glad, they receive more cultivation and produce crops. The world is held together and preserved by the prayers of the righteous,
like dough by the power of yeast. The righteous are the guides of this world, just as a ship is guided by the skill of its sailors.
The ship encounters relentless waves and is tossed violently back and forth, while its wise pilots stand watchfully,
and bring the ship to a place of rest. If the ship has no wise pilots, it cannot make its way to the harbor.
The ship sinks, and its cargo is lost. If there are no upright people, the wicked perish; and if there are no righteous people, unbelievers receive no sustenance.
And if you, the listener, ask me, “Since there are righteous and upright people on earth, why is no prayer heard in an evil and distressing time?”
let the listener consider, without arguing, what I outlined for him above: Moses was a man, a great prophet, the leader of all Israel.
At various times his prayer brought forgiveness for all his people, yet at another time he was not heard even on his own behalf.
And consider someone greater than he: Jesus, the great Savior and Son of God. Because his acceptable prayer was heard, God was reconciled to his creation,
as the apostle said, “He reconciled us with his Father.” And when his hour came, he prayed, pleaded, and implored, although he had no need, and said,
“My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me.” Yet his prayer on his own behalf was not heard. For our benefit, our Savior was not heard.
It was fitting for him to die, to give us a pledge: he died as we do, killed death, rose and raised us, and promised us that we would live.
For if he had been heard when he asked to be spared from death while clothed in a body, who would have assured us of the resurrection? He gave us courage through his death,
and made us glad through his resurrection. In his wisdom, he showed fear of death for our benefit, so that we might be helped, plainly showing all human beings
the weakness of the body that he put on like ours. For if he had not been born as we are, death would have had no way to reach him.
And if there were nothing of his life-giving Spirit in us, he would not have given us the pledge of life, that we would rise as he did.
First he died our death, so that we might take courage through his death. Then he rose in great power, without weakness, having conquered death and come up from its domain.
We rejoice that our death is swallowed up in his life, and we have received the pledge of life through his death. If Christ had not died in a body taken from us,
he would have had no pledge to give us, so that we could confidently accept that we will live /that we will be alive/ after death.
But he fulfilled all the pledges in himself, and we have confidently received from him the pledge that we will live /that we will be alive/ after death.
We are not distressed at being born, because he was born as we are. Nor do we lose heart in our illnesses, because he too became ill as we do, grew weary, and even went hungry.
To teach us to fast, he was overcome by sleep, and he suffered and was tested in a weak body, so that he could help those who are tested.
Learn, understand, and convince yourself that the prayer of these two great prophets was not heard in their entreaty [?],
these glorious shepherds who prayed on their own behalf. For a testament does not take effect unless the one who wrote it dies.
For through Moses a testament was promised to the people of Israel, that he would give them the land of the Canaanites as an inheritance.
And through Jesus a testament was promised, that he would give the nations the land of the living. Moses died beyond the Jordan, and the testament promised to his people took effect.
And Jesus died in the land of death, and the testament promised to the nations took effect: he had promised to give them the land of the living.
His Lord showed Moses the promised land while Israel had not yet inherited it. And Jesus our Savior rose from the dead
and went to prepare for us the land he had promised, as he said to his apostles, “I am going to prepare a place for you,
and then I will come and take you with me, so that you too may be where I am.” He confirmed for us the promise that we would be with him.
He also showed his apostles ahead of time, when they asked him for a sign of his coming, when he took his three disciples,
Simon, James, and John: Simon Peter, the foundation of the church, and James and John, the firmly established pillars of the church.
He showed these three trustworthy witnesses a sign of his coming when his appearance was changed into the likeness of his coming, with Moses and Elijah beside him.
He encouraged the dead, whom he is going to bring to life, like Moses who appeared. And the living who remain until his coming are assured that they will be caught up to meet him,
like Elijah, who did not taste death and appeared beside him. For he made known to us that Moses, the great prophet,
and Jesus, the beloved Son, the firstborn [?], were heard when it was fitting, and through their prayers obtained forgiveness for a great many people.
At another time, however, their requests were denied, so that through this example many who pray and are not heard might be encouraged,
taking note of the example of these mighty heroes, so that when they pray and are not heard, they will not be distressed.
For they accept this in their minds and are reassured by the example of Moses, of our Savior, and of the prophets and righteous people of old.
Now be convinced and understand that there are righteous people on earth, and that the world is sustained because of the just. For the world stands by grace, as the prophet said,
“The world will be built by grace.” And this is the surpassing grace: righteous people never disappear entirely from the world or come to an end.
For if the righteous were gone from the world, when the measure of the sins of the wicked overflowed, the world would perish in wrath, and grace would be overcome
by justice, which demands judgment. This is why the just are left on earth, in a world of falsehood: so that, because of them, justice will not prevail
and enter the world, which stands by grace, to demand judgment in a place without judgment. The just are hidden in this world,
so that because of them it is not destroyed by wrath, like the grape that was hidden in the cluster. Because of that grape, the cluster was preserved for a long time.
For this is how we have heard the saying that the prophet proclaimed to the people: “Just as a grape is found in a cluster, and a man says to his companion,
“Do not destroy the cluster, because there is a blessing in it.” And he said, “So I will act for the sake of my chosen ones, and I will not destroy them all.”
“I will bring forth offspring from Jacob, and from Judah an heir to my holy mountain.” The cluster is the people of Israel, and the blessing within it was the Messiah, the King.
From the beginning, this seed was preserved in Adam, the first firstborn. Although he sinned, offspring of the righteous were preserved from him.
The blessing was preserved in Seth and in all his generations. And when all flesh corrupted its way upon the earth,
the blessing was preserved in the man of rest, Noah, who was found righteous and blameless in a corrupt generation. And the blessing was preserved in the wooden ark.
All the wicked perished in the wrath that was poured out, while the seed had been removed and taken away from them. And Noah and his sons came out of the ark.
The blessing was preserved in Shem, the father of the righteous. For the Spirit made this clear through the mouth of the man of rest, as he blessed his sons after the [?].
For he said, “May God enlarge Japheth, and may he dwell in Shem’s tent.” And he cursed Canaan, the offspring of Ham, who mocked his father, and he was deprived of the blessing.
This blessing passed down through ten generations, from Noah to Abraham. For he lived three hundred and fifty years after the flood.
His sons and daughters had children and multiplied during his lifetime. When they reached Babel, in the land of the Chaldeans, God confused the languages of the whole earth there.
Noah remained in Ur of the Chaldeans, dwelling there and preserving the blessing of the righteous for two hundred and ninety-two years after the flood.
Abraham was born in Ur of the Chaldeans, in the eight hundred and ninety-second year of Noah’s life,
a long time after the languages had been confused. And when Noah was nine hundred and fifty years old,
his time came to an end, and he died at a good old age. In the fifty-eighth year of Abraham’s life, Noah died in Ur of the Chaldeans.
Then Abraham left Ur of the Chaldeans and went to live in Haran for a short time. From Haran, God moved him to the land of Canaan,
the offspring of Ham, the cursed seed over whom slavery had been decreed. And when Abraham was a hundred years old,
in the four hundred and ninety-second year of the life of Shem, the father of the righteous, Isaac was born.
Shem lived for a hundred and twelve years after Isaac was born. Isaac fathered Jacob and Esau when he was sixty years old.
Shem lived for sixty-two years after Jacob and Esau were born. And Abraham died at the age of a hundred and seventy-five.
Shem lived for thirty-seven years after Abraham’s death. And Isaac was a hundred and thirty-seven years old
when he blessed his son Jacob, in whom the blessing of the righteous was hidden. Jacob was seventy-seven years old when he fled to Haran.
At the age of eighty-four, he married Leah and Rachel. And after a hundred and twelve years of Isaac’s life,
Shem died, in the fifty-second year of Jacob’s life. When Jacob was ninety-seven years old, God said to him,
“Return to the land of your fathers, and I will do good to you and be with you.” Jacob was ninety-seven years old when he returned from Haran,
and his father Isaac was a hundred and fifty-seven years old. Isaac lived for twenty-three years after Jacob returned from Haran.
In the forty-third year after he blessed him, and the twenty-third after he returned from Haran, he died at the age of one hundred and eighty.
Jacob went down to Egypt twenty years after the death of his father Isaac, and twenty-two years after his son Joseph was sold into Egypt,
sixty-eight years after the death of Shem. Jacob lived in Egypt for seventeen years and died at the age of one hundred and forty-seven,
fifty years after he came from Haran, and twenty-seven years after the death of his father Isaac. When Jacob died,
Joseph was fifty-six years old. The blessing was preserved in Judah, Jacob's son, before he entered Egypt.
Judah fathered Perez. When Jacob and Judah went down to Egypt, this blessing lay hidden in the loins of Perez.
Perez fathered Hezron, Hezron fathered Aram, and Aram fathered Amminadab. Amminadab fathered Nahshon, the leader of the people of Judah.
And Amminadab's [?] married Eleazar, the son of Aaron the priest, by whom Phinehas was born.
From Amminadab came the blessing of kingship and priesthood: leadership and kingship from Nahshon,
and priesthood from the offspring of Nahshon's sister, who bore Phinehas, who appeased God's anger through his zeal.
Shelah was born to Nahshon, and Shelah fathered Boaz. From Boaz came the rule of kings, through Boaz and Ruth the Moabite.
For this reason Boaz married Ruth the Moabite, so that Lot might share in the blessing of the righteous. From Ruth's offspring
came the family of the house of David, and from their descendants Christ the King was born. God did not leave unrewarded the hospitality of Lot,
Abraham's nephew, who left Haran with him. Because he welcomed strangers as his uncle Abraham did, God gave him a share in the blessing of the righteous,
through Ruth the Moabite, whom Boaz took as his wife. God also remembered Lot through Naamah the Ammonite, whom Solomon married,
and who bore King Rehoboam. For Solomon married many women: seven hundred noblewomen and three hundred concubines.
Yet it is not written that he had offspring by any of his thousand wives except Rehoboam, by Naamah the Ammonite,
who had become his wife during the lifetime of his father David. For when Solomon became king, Rehoboam was one year old.
Solomon reigned for forty years, and when Solomon died, Rehoboam became king at the age of forty-one.
Lot shared in the blessing of the righteous through Ruth the Moabite and Naamah the Ammonite, from the two tribes that descended from him.
Boaz fathered Obed, Obed fathered Jesse, and Jesse fathered David. This blessing was preserved in all the kings of the house of Judah,
from David to Jeconiah, through eighteen kings. David sinned, but through the blessing hidden within him, his wrongdoing was forgiven.
Solomon broke the law and abandoned his God. Yet because of the blessing hidden within him and his descendants, God said,
"I will make him great all his days." Folly led Rehoboam astray, but because of the blessing within him, God said,
"I will not tear the whole kingdom away from him, but I will give him a lamp in Jerusalem for the sake of David my servant." And Abijah, Rehoboam's son, sinned.
And because of the blessing within him, Jeroboam and his army were delivered into his hands. And in Asa the blessing of the righteous burned brightly.
He practiced righteousness, and God heard his prayer, and his enemies were delivered into his hands. And the blessing was preserved in Jehoshaphat.
He did what was good before the Lord. Jehoram sinned greatly, but because of the blessing he was preserved. He sinned, yet was not wiped out like the house of Ahab,
for he was a son-in-law of the house of Ahab, and Athaliah, the daughter of Omri king of Israel, led him astray. And the spark was preserved in Joash son of Ahaziah.
He was not killed with his brothers when Athaliah destroyed the royal offspring, after she saw that her son Ahaziah had been killed by Jehu son of Nimshi.

Joash sinned and shed innocent blood. He repaid the kindness of Jehoiada the priest with ingratitude and destroyed his offspring after him. Yet because of the blessing, his own offspring were preserved.
Amaziah arose and ruled the kingdom. He sinned with idols and worshiped other, foreign gods. Yet because of the blessing, his offspring were preserved.
Uzziah arose after him. He acted arrogantly against the priesthood and would not listen to it. And the Holy One struck him with the affliction of leprosy for all his days.
Jotham arose as king and sinned greatly. Yet because of the blessing, his offspring were saved. Ahaz arose as king and sinned greatly.
He worshiped dead gods and said, “You are my gods and my lords, and I worship you.” Yet because of the blessing, his offspring were preserved.
Hezekiah, a righteous king, arose over all Judah in Jerusalem. He prayed and pleaded before his God, and his prayer was heard.
It destroyed his enemies, and he gloriously served the blessing of the righteous that was within him. He became ill, prayed, and recovered from his illness.
And because there are some people, my beloved, who bring accusations against Hezekiah, asking why he was distressed during his illness that he was going to die,
since he had practiced great righteousness before his God, and saying, “What benefit did he gain from that extension of his life, since a blemish was placed on him during that extension,
because he boasted of his wealth before the envoys of the king of Babylon and did not glorify the name of his God, who had healed him of his illness?”
This was why Hezekiah, the righteous king, was distressed: he did not yet have a son, and the blessing of the righteous was hidden in his loins.
And this is what he said in his lament: “The blessing that has passed through all the former generations, from Adam down to me, through forty-six generations—
why has it not come forth from me? The spark has gone out with me! Look, now the cluster of grapes is being handed over to destruction.” While he reflected on these things and prayed mournfully,
Isaiah the prophet came to him and said to him, “This is what the Lord says: Look, I am adding to your years. You will live fifteen years.”
And he added fifteen years to his life. Then, in the eighteenth year of his reign and the third year of his added time, he fathered Manasseh.
For he reigned twenty-nine years: the first fourteen and the last fifteen. And the written saying was fulfilled:
“The righteous will prolong their days, but the years of the wicked will be shortened.” The years of the corrupt generation in the days of Noah were shortened,
as were those of the sinful kingdom of the house of Ephraim. But he added years to Hezekiah and also to Job. To Hezekiah he added fifteen years,
and for Job he doubled his years, his possessions, and his children. And if anyone argues that Job did not receive double in everything, let him be persuaded without argument.
For this is what is written: “God made Job’s latter condition greater than his former condition, and seven sons and three daughters were born to him.”
And his seven sons and his three daughters, the earlier ones and the later ones: when the time of resurrection comes in the world of the righteous, he will receive his children back twofold.
And while he was in this world, he received twice as much of all his possessions. The account makes us understand that God also gave him twice as many years.
As it is written, Job grew old, was full of days, and died. After his trial he lived a hundred and forty years,
and before his trial, seventy years. Thus the written statement was fulfilled in him: Job received twice as much of everything—
his years and his possessions in this world, and his sons and daughters in the world of the righteous. For the craftsman has authority over what he has formed, to increase it or diminish it.
And Manasseh, a wicked child, was born to a righteous man. He sinned more than all who preceded him. He came to the throne when he was twelve years old,
and he reigned for fifty-five years. Although he multiplied his sins and worshiped idols, his offspring were preserved because of the blessing.
And he fathered Amon. Amon became king and followed the ways of Manasseh. Because of the blessing within him, he ruled the kingdom.
And from him was born a righteous man, Josiah, whose memory is a blessing. He removed impurity from the land of Israel during his reign.
And because the people's sins were pressing on, he was gathered away before the calamity. [?] came upon the people in his days,
as Huldah the prophetess prophesied when he sent to her to inquire about the matter. She sent him this message: “This is what the Lord, the God of Israel, says:
‘Because your heart was broken and you grieved over the people's sins when you heard the words of the Law, look, I am gathering you to your ancestors,
and you will not see the calamity that is coming upon this people.’” And he was gathered away before the calamity, when Pharaoh the Lame, king of Egypt, killed him.
And his son Jehoahaz came to the throne. Because the blessing was not in him, he did not prosper in the kingship of the house of David.
He reigned for three months. Afterward Pharaoh the Lame, king of Egypt, took him away. He died in Egypt, and his memory was erased.
And Jehoiakim became king; the blessing of the righteous was hidden within him. In the third year of his reign, Nebuchadnezzar subjected him to tribute.
He took Daniel and his brothers away as hostages. And Jehoiakim served Nebuchadnezzar for eight years. When he multiplied his sins and rebelled,
Nebuchadnezzar killed him. They dragged him away and threw him outside the gates of Jerusalem, and he was buried with a donkey's burial. His son Jehoiachin became king after him.
And because the blessing of the righteous was hidden within him, he reigned for three months. When he rebelled against the king of Babylon, the Chaldean army came against him.
They took him away and went to Babylon. He was imprisoned in Babylon for thirty-seven years, while the blessing of the righteous was hidden within him.
And an impure people remained in Jerusalem. Zedekiah became king over them, over the remainder of the people.
And Jehoiachin fathered Shealtiel in Babylon. As long as the blessing was in Babylon, the Babylonians ruled the kingdom in peace and tranquility.
And when Shealtiel was born in the land of Babylon, the blessing of the righteous was hidden within him. Shealtiel fathered Zerubbabel.
Then, in the days of Zerubbabel, the exiles returned from Babylon through Ezra the scribe, during the reign of Cyrus the Persian.
And Zerubbabel was with the exiles and became their leader, as the prophet said: “Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah.”
And Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest. These are the two anointed ones who stood before the Lord of the whole earth.
When the blessing returned from Babylon to Jerusalem, the kingdom of the Babylonians came to an end, and Cyrus the Persian became king. After sixty-three years,
the blessing returned from Babylon to Jerusalem—from the time when Jehoiachin was taken captive until the captives returned through Ezra and Zerubbabel.
He fathered Abiud, and Abiud fathered Eliakim, and Eliakim fathered Azor, and Azor fathered Zadok, and Zadok fathered Achim.
And Achim fathered Eliud, and Eliud fathered Eleazar, and Eleazar fathered Matthan, and Matthan fathered Jacob.
And Jacob fathered Joseph, and Joseph was called the father of Jesus Christ. And Jesus was born of the virgin Mary,
from the offspring of the house of David, by the Holy Spirit, as it is written that Joseph and Mary his betrothed were both from the house of David.
And the apostle testified that Jesus Christ came from Mary, from the offspring of the house of David, by the Holy Spirit. Joseph was called the father of Jesus,
although he was not born from his seed. But the title of fatherhood was passed down from Adam to Joseph through sixty-three generations.
And the title of fatherhood was taken from Joseph and placed upon Christ. From Joseph he received the title of fatherhood,
and from John the title of priesthood. From Mary he put on a body and received the designation of birth. After sixty-two weeks,
Christ was born and was killed. And the berry of blessing was taken from the cluster, and the whole cluster was given over to destruction.
And the vineyard fell into ruin for lack of cultivation and produced carobs and bitter fruits. The vine was ruined, and the vine stock was uprooted.
Now receive the reckoning of these sixty-three generations, from Adam until Christ was born: Adam, Seth, Enosh, Kenan,
Mahalalel, Jared, Enoch, Methuselah, Lamech, Noah, Shem, Arpachshad, Shelah, Eber, Peleg, Reu, Serug, Nahor, Terah,
Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Judah, Perez, Hezron, Aram, Amminadab, Nahshon, Shelah, Boaz, Obed, Jesse, David,
Solomon, Rehoboam, Abijah, Asa, Jehoshaphat, Jehoram, Ahaziah, Jehoash, Amaziah, Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, Hezekiah,
Manasseh, Amon, Josiah, Jehoiakim, Jehoiachin, Shealtiel, Zerubbabel, Abiud, Eliakim, Azor, Zadok, Achim, Eliud,
Eleazar, Matthan, Jacob, Joseph, and Jesus the Son of God, who was born of the virgin Mary, and Joseph was called his father.
Now I will begin to show you the reckoning of the years, from Adam up to this very reckoning that I have set down and shown you. God created and brought forth Adam.
When Adam was one hundred and thirty years old, he fathered Seth. And Adam lived eight hundred years after he fathered Seth.
The total of his years was nine hundred and thirty years. Adam lived until the thirty-first year of the life of Lamech, who fathered Noah, and he died in the ninth generation.
And Seth lived one hundred and five years and fathered Enosh. And Seth lived eight hundred and seven years after he fathered Enosh.
The total of his years was nine hundred and twelve years. He lived until the one hundred and eightieth year of Lamech’s life, two years before Noah’s birth, and died in the eighth generation.
And Enosh lived ninety years and fathered Kenan. And Enosh lived eight hundred and fifteen years after he fathered Kenan.
His years totaled 905 years. Enosh lived until the seventy-ninth year of Noah’s life.
Until 521 years before the flood. He died in the eighth generation.
Kenan lived seventy years and fathered Mahalalel. After he fathered Mahalalel, Kenan lived 840 years.
His years totaled 910 years. Kenan lived until the 179th year of Noah’s life.
Until 421 years before the flood. He died in the seventh generation.
Mahalalel lived sixty-five years and fathered Jared. After he fathered Jared, Mahalalel lived 830 years.
His years totaled 895 years. Mahalalel lived until the 214th year of Noah’s life.
Until 386 years before the flood. He died in the sixth generation.
Jared lived 162 years and fathered Enoch. After he fathered Enoch, Jared lived 800 years.
His years totaled 962 years. Jared lived until the 378th year of Noah’s life.
Until 222 years before the flood. He died in the fifth generation.
Enoch lived sixty-five years and fathered Methuselah. After he fathered Methuselah, Enoch pleased God for 300 years.
His years totaled 365 years. In the three-hundredth year of his son Methuselah, and in the 113th year of Lamech’s life,
sixty-nine years before Noah’s birth, 669 years before the flood, God transferred him to the land of the living, in the third generation.
Methuselah lived 187 years and fathered Lamech. After he fathered Lamech, Methuselah lived
782 years. His years totaled 969 years.
Methuselah lived until the six-hundredth year of Noah’s life. After his death, Noah entered the ark. The flood came at the very time when the righteous man died.
He saw Adam for 151 years, and Shem for ninety-seven years. He died in the third generation, and the world perished in wrath.
Lamech lived 182 years and fathered Noah. After he fathered Noah, Lamech lived 595 years.
His years totaled 777 years. Lamech lived until the 596th year of the life of his son Noah,
four years before the flood. His father Methuselah lived four years after him, and then the flood came.
Lamech saw Adam for sixty-eight years. He died after four years [?] before the flood, in the second generation.
Noah was born eighty-six years after the death of Adam, the firstborn, the first, who fathered Seth.
He was born nine years before the death of Seth, who fathered Enosh. In the seventy-ninth year of Noah’s life,
Enosh, who fathered Kenan, died. In the 179th year of Noah’s life, Kenan, who fathered Mahalalel, died.
In the two hundred and fourteenth year of Noah’s life, Mahalalel, who fathered Jared, died. In the three hundred and seventy-eighth year of Noah’s life,
Jared, who fathered Enoch, died. In the sixty-ninth year before Noah was born, Enoch was taken away, and his death was not found.
Six hundred and sixty-nine years before the flood. In the six hundredth year of Noah’s life, Methuselah died, and afterward the flood came.
In the five hundred and ninety-sixth year of Noah’s life, Lamech, Noah’s father, died, four years before his father Methuselah.
Noah was six hundred years old when he entered the ark, in the very year that Methuselah died. Noah was inside the ark,
he and his household, from the seventeenth day of the second month until the twenty-seventh day of the second month of the following year,
twelve months and ten days. Then Noah and his sons came out of the ark. After the flood Noah lived
three hundred and fifty years, and he died in the fifty-eighth year of Abraham’s life. He was born in the seventy-ninth year of Enosh’s life,
and died in the fifty-eighth year of Abraham’s life. He saw eighteen generations, those before him and those after him.
At one hundred years old, Shem fathered Arpachshad, two years after the flood. After fathering Arpachshad, Shem lived five hundred years.
His years totaled six hundred years. He died in the one hundred and twelfth year of Isaac’s life,
and in the seventy-second year of Jacob’s life. Shem was born ninety-eight years before the flood.
He was born in Methuselah’s time and died in Jacob’s time. He saw sixteen generations, those before him and those after him.
Arpachshad lived thirty-five years and fathered Shelah. After fathering Shelah, Arpachshad lived
four hundred and three years. His years totaled four hundred and thirty-eight years.
He died in the one hundred and forty-seventh year of Abraham’s life and in the forty-seventh year of Isaac’s life, in the tenth generation.
Shelah lived thirty years and fathered Eber. After fathering Eber, Shelah lived
four hundred and three years. His years totaled four hundred and thirty-three years.
He died in the sixty-second year of Jacob’s life and in the one hundred and twenty-second year of Isaac’s life, in the tenth generation.
Eber lived thirty-four years and fathered Peleg. After fathering Peleg, Eber lived
four hundred and thirty years. His years totaled four hundred and sixty-four years.
He died in the one hundred and twenty-fifth year of Jacob’s life, five years after Isaac died, in the tenth generation.
Peleg lived thirty years and fathered Reu. After fathering Reu, Peleg lived two hundred and nine years.
His years totaled two hundred and thirty-nine years. He died in the forty-eighth year of Abraham’s life, in the sixth generation.
Reu lived thirty-two years and fathered Serug. After fathering Serug, Reu lived two hundred and seven years.
His total lifespan was 239 years. He died in the seventy-eighth year of Abraham’s life, three years after Abraham left Haran, in the fifth generation.
Serug lived thirty years and fathered Nahor. After he fathered Nahor, Serug lived two hundred years.
His total lifespan was 230 years. He died in the 101st year of Abraham’s life, in the first year after Isaac was born, in the fifth generation.
Nahor lived twenty-nine years and fathered Terah. After he fathered Terah, Nahor lived 119 years.
His total lifespan was 148 years. He died in the forty-ninth year of Abraham’s life, in the 939th year of Noah’s life,
in the 339th year after the flood. Noah lived eleven years after Nahor died, and he died in the third generation.
Terah lived seventy years and fathered Abraham. After he fathered Abraham, Terah lived 135 years.
His total lifespan was 205 years. He died in the 135th year of Abraham’s life,
in the thirty-fifth year of Isaac’s life, five years before Isaac married Rebekah, the daughter of Bethuel. He died in the third generation.
Abraham lived one hundred years and fathered Isaac. After he fathered Isaac, Abraham lived seventy-five years.
His total lifespan was 175 years. He died in the fifteenth year of Jacob’s life. He died in the third generation.
Isaac lived sixty years and fathered Jacob. After he fathered Jacob, Isaac lived 120 years.
His total lifespan was 180 years, and he died in the 120th year of Jacob’s life, twenty-three years after Jacob returned from Haran,
eleven years after Joseph was sold into Egypt, ten years before Jacob went down to Egypt. He died in the fourth generation.
Jacob was seventy-seven years old when his father Isaac blessed him. At eighty-four years old, he married Leah and Rachel, the daughters of Laban.
Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun were born to him by Leah; and Joseph and Benjamin by Rachel;
and Gad and Asher by Bilhah, Rachel’s maidservant; and Dan and Naphtali by Zilpah, Leah’s maidservant. These are Jacob’s twelve sons.
Jacob died at 147 years old, seventeen years after he went down to Egypt. He died in the fourth generation.
From Adam until Noah entered the ark, there were 1,651 years, according to what is written in the book of Genesis.
From the time Noah left the ark until the time God established a covenant with Abraham, there were 387 years,
according to what is written in the book of Genesis. And from the promise to Abraham until Jacob entered Egypt,
there were 205 years. The Israelites were in Egypt for 225 years.
From the promise to Abraham until the people left Egypt, there were 430 years, as Paul the apostle testifies, saying:
“A covenant that had previously been established/confirmed by God—the law, which came 430 years later,
cannot set it aside and nullify the promise.” From Adam until [?], there were 1,651 years.
From the flood until the people left Egypt, there were 817 years.
Moses led the people in the wilderness for 40 years. Joshua son of Nun led the people for 25 years.
Judah and Othniel son of Kenaz led the people for 48 years.
Eglon king of Moab subjugated the people for 18 years. Ehud [?] led the people for 80 years.
Jabin [?] subjugated Israel for 20 years. Deborah and Barak led the people for 40 years.
The Midianites subjugated Israel for seven years. Gideon led the people for 40 years.
Abimelech son of Gideon led the people for 60 years. Tola son of Puah led the people for 23 years.
Jair led the people for 22 years. The Philistines and Ammonites subjugated Israel for 18 years.
Jephthah [?] led the people for six years. Ibzan led the people for seven years. Elon led the people for ten years.
Abdon [?] led the people for eight years. The Philistines subjugated Israel for 40 years.
Samson led the people for 20 years. Eli led the people for 40 years.
After Eli, the ark was in the house of Abinadab in Gibeah for 20 years. Samuel led the people for 30 years.
Saul led the people for 40 years. These years of the leaders amount to 655.
However, in the Book of Kings it is written as follows: In the 480th year after the Israelites departed from the land of Egypt,
up to the fourth year of Solomon’s reign, when he began to build the house of God. This is how the years were calculated, and the first calculation does not agree with the latter.
David reigned for 40 years. Solomon reigned for 40 years. Rehoboam reigned for 17 years.
Abijah reigned for three years. Asa reigned for 41 years. Jehoshaphat reigned for 25 years.
Jehoram reigned for eight years. Ahaziah reigned for one year. Athaliah reigned for six years. Joash reigned for 40 years.
Amaziah reigned for 23 years. Uzziah reigned for 52 years. Jotham reigned for 16 years.
Ahaz reigned for 16 years. Hezekiah reigned for 29 years. Manasseh reigned for 55 years.
Amon reigned for two years. Josiah reigned for 31 years. Jehoahaz reigned for three months.
Jehoiakim reigned for 11 years. Jehoiachin reigned for 100 days. Zedekiah reigned for 11 years.
These years of the kings amount to 455 years, six months, and ten days. In the third year of Jehoiakim’s reign,
Nebuchadnezzar went up to Jerusalem and subjected the nation to tribute. Israel remained in Jerusalem, subject to tribute,
for 29 years under Jehoiakim and 11 under Zedekiah. Jerusalem remained desolate for 50 years.

Seven weeks of years; and the land rested during its sabbaths while they were in the land of their enemies, because it had not kept its sabbath rest during their sabbaths while they were living in it.
At the end of seventy years, Cyrus the Persian issued a proclamation throughout his kingdom and announced their return. And after the return,
Israel lived in Jerusalem for seventy weeks, as Daniel prophesied. These weeks amount to four hundred and ninety years.
After the killing of the anointed king, Jerusalem was destroyed, never to be inhabited again. And until the completion of the things decreed,
it remained in ruin. The protective covering was removed from the cluster of grapes, and the cluster was handed over to destruction. The people were emptied of grace.
From Jesus the blessing flowed to the nations. For he said to the Jews, “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you
and given to a people that produces fruit.” And to us he said, “I am with you until the end of the world.” Again he said, “You are in me,
and I am in you.” And the apostle testified, “If anyone among you does not have the Spirit of God in him, he does not belong to him.”
Again he said, “You are the temple of God, and the Spirit of Christ dwells in you.” And the prophet said, “I will dwell in them and walk among them.”
He himself encouraged us not to fear the trials that come upon us. He said to us, “If they listened to my word and kept it, they will also keep yours.
And if they persecuted me, they will persecute you too.” Again he said to us, “You are not of the world, just as I am not of it.”
And he said, “If you were of the world, the world would love its own.” Now that we have received these commands from Jesus, who gives us life,
we cannot walk outside the paths in which he walked. If they persecuted Christ, they will persecute us too. If they hated Christ, they will hate us too.
If they bound Christ, they will bind us too. If they struck Christ on his cheeks, they will strike us too. If Christ suffered, we too will suffer.
For great is the gift of the Good One to us. Although our sins do not distress him, he wishes us to be righteous. And although our good deeds do not help him,
he urges us to please him. When we are unwilling to ask him, he is angry with us. At all times he calls to us, “Ask and receive,
and when you seek, you will find.” For his wealth satisfies those in need. No one says, “I have received enough,” when receiving from his glorious treasury.
He delights in those who ask him. At all times he calls to us, “Ask and receive, and when you seek, you will find,” and he delights in those who persist in receiving from him.
Whoever has tasted his wealth needs to receive from him again. For who is like him, who says, “Ask and receive,” and is angry with us when we do not ask him?
Even when we did not ask him, he sent us his gift, the like of which had never been found among us. He sent Christ as a human being to mock the evil one and his forces,
and to drive the condemned power away from us. He sent the innocent one to us to be tried and condemned, so that the guilty might be acquitted through the trial of the innocent one.
He sent the mighty one in the likeness of our weakness, to strengthen our frailty against the power of the evil one. He put on a body made of dust and drew it to his own nature.
He hid within us salt that dissolves corruption, so that when the serpent wishes to approach and eat it, it will recoil from the salt, which it cannot eat.
He sent his innocent Son to us to die as we die, so that death might be put to shame through him. Great is the gift of the Good One, which he gave to the lowly.
What greater thing than his Son should he have given us? When we were more sinful than we are now, he sent this gift to us.
When we are justified, what will he give us but life with the one who came to us—he who did not spare his Son, but sent him to humiliation?
Wonderful and great is his gift to us. For the King left his own land to bring about our healing, and lived under the conditions of a weak body, being born like us,
and suffering humiliation beyond ours. He endured all these things for us, and we received his gift as a pledge of our life. This is what I have to say:
God had no gift to send us greater than this. And when he came, he took a pledge from us and went to his own land.
He said to us, “You are in me, and I am in you.” And the apostle said, “He raised us up and seated us with him in heaven.”
The beginning of our resurrection is the body he put on from us. He freed it from bondage and raised it up to himself, and confirmed his promises to us that we would be with him.
He said plainly, “Where I am, you too will be.” So let us rejoice in the hostage taken from among us, who sits in glory with the glorious King.
Great is the Good One’s gift to us: a hostage from among us has been taken by a king like himself, who made him his friend and guardian of the border.
This is the son of Adam, the body from Mary, which was taken from among us to the land of life.
The weak body became mighty and received glory greater and more wonderful than the glory Adam cast off in his degradation.
We rejoice in you, beloved Child, because you opened a road for us to the land we desire. We thank you, physician of our pains,

because you placed your Spirit within us as medicine for our bodies. We worship you and your exalted Father, who raised us up in you and called us to himself. Through you we give thanks for the mercy that sent you,
because he wanted us to live through the death of his only Son. Through you we praise the One who exists of himself, who set you apart from his own being and sent you to us.

We exalt you, who dwell in his holiness; [?] our bodies, through the pledge we have received. With our mouths let us give thanks, as far as we are able, to the Power who came to give life to the weak.
My beloved, let us rouse ourselves every day to offer praise through the Son to the Father who sent him. Let us rejoice in his gift, so that he too may rejoice in us.
Through him let us give thanks to his Father, so that he too may give thanks for us. Let us ask for a gift from the treasury that is in need, for its need is this: to give life to those in need.
For great and glorious is his gift to us: he asks for praise from insignificant people, although even when we do not praise him, he is glorious.
And when we do not exalt him, he is exalted. For he needs to give and wants us to ask, so that through our requests he may give the life he promised,
and we may live with his only Son. It is his to give, and ours to ask. He has life, and it is for us to flee from death. He has life,
and he has called us to receive it. He has grace, and it lies in our hands to flee from evil. He has life, and light is with him,
and he has warned us to flee from the darkness of death. For no one can reach the limit of his treasures, and no one can understand the depth of his wisdom.
O good and kind One, open the door to our requests, listen to our prayer, and hear our petition,
as your beloved taught us: “Keep praying, and do not grow weary.” Again he repeated his warning to us: “Pray that you may not enter into temptation.”
Again he wrote to us so that we might know your kindness, and said, “There is nothing you ask God for in your prayer that he will not give you.”
Even now, it is not because of our good deeds or in reliance on our righteousness that we pray before you.
But act for the sake of your mercy, for you are good and kind. For we pray before you as guilty people.
And you, being good and kind, hear our prayer. We pray before you as weak people; and you, the mighty one, do not withhold our requests.
For our hands and our hearts are stretched out toward you, to ask and seek grace from you. Gladden our minds by hearing our petition; let our senses be awakened to ask with confidence.
Open our ears to the prayer of your words, and let the eyes of our hearts reach upward toward you. Hear our prayer and accept our petition.
Grant our desire. Listen and hear our voice. See our subjection, and have pity on your people in their time of distress. Hasten your mercy and show your mighty power.
Do not discipline us in your anger or rebuke us in your wrath. We are your people, formed by your hands, the work of your fingers. You created us in your image.
You made us in your likeness; you formed us with your hands. Your spirit is within us. Do not be angry forever, and do not stand far away. When we were wandering, you saved us.
When we were scattered, you gathered us. When we were in darkness, you enlightened us. When we were imprisoned, you brought us out. When we were captives, you rescued us.
When we were bound, you released us from the confining pit. When we had no hope, you called us to hope in you. When we were sinners, you desired that we should be made righteous.
When we had not asked you, you sent us your only Son. By his blood you redeemed us; through him we came to know you. You sent him to us when we had not called upon you.

You laid our wrongdoing upon him when we had not asked you. You brought him down to Sheol when we had not pressed you. You humbled him for our sake while we were provoking you to anger. You saved us through his suffering,
when our wrongdoing was great before you. And now too, as we plead, as we worship, as we give thanks, and as we praise your mercy through him,
hear our prayer and accept our petition. See our disgrace and listen to our humiliation. Let your soul grieve over your plundered people, over your house that lies in ruins,

over your altars that have been overturned, over your priests who have been devastated, over your religious community that is persecuted, over your books that have been sealed shut, over our scattering,

and over our being plundered. Our shame has become great. Our people have been scattered. Our blood has been shed. The members of our religious community have been stripped naked. Have pity on our humiliation, our disgrace, and our shame.
Whom shall we ask to hear our prayer? To whom shall we go? For see, we belong to you. You have disciplined us in your anger; claim us in your mercy. We are distressed.
Do not neglect us when we lose hope. Do not delay in responding to our humiliation and disgrace, as your prophet pleaded when he was distressed like us and said,
“Do not take me away in your patience.” Hear our prayer as you heard Moses, your friend, and let our enemies be repaid like Pharaoh the oppressor.
Listen to our petition, as you heard Joshua, when Amalek was destroyed and his memory was wiped out. You are the God of those who came before and those who come after.
You heard Moses and drowned Pharaoh. You answered Aaron, and the plague was stopped. You turned away your anger through the zeal of Phinehas.
You helped Joshua son of Nun, and his enemies were put to shame. You answered Samson in the time of his humiliation, and avenged him upon the Philistines who provoked you to anger.
You vindicated David against Saul, his persecutor, and gave him justice against Absalom, who troubled him. Samuel made atonement before you for his people,
and you showed your greatness against those who rejected your kingship. You gave justice to Elijah when he was persecuted, and through his prayer the prophets of Baal were destroyed.
Micaiah was protected by your abundant mercy, and his persecutor fell and died in battle. You showed your wonders among Elisha’s oppressors,
when they entered Samaria and came to know your greatness. You answered Hezekiah when he was hemmed in by distress, and you showed your mighty power against Sennacherib and his army.
You heard Asa and helped Jehoshaphat, and you swiftly took vengeance on all his oppressors. You heard Jonah from the depths of the sea,
and from the belly of the fish, and from the waves that surrounded him. You answered Daniel when he was thrown into the pit, and rescued him from the mouths of lions.
You helped Hananiah and his brothers inside the fiery furnace, and the flame burned up their accusers. You answered Mordecai and Esther in their distress,
and you delivered your people, and Haman the persecutor was put to shame. You brought Jeremiah up from the muddy pit and granted him favor before the king of Babylon.
Have mercy, Lord, on your people in their bondage. Have mercy, Lord, on our plea, and hear our prayer. Our sanctuary lies in ruins,
and our house of worship is desolate. Our priests are devastated, and our heads are covered. Our virgins are humiliated, and our community is scattered.
Have mercy, Lord, have mercy on the poor, the strangers, and the displaced, who have no rest and no resting place to lay their heads.
The roads are deserted, and the paths are no longer used. Our eyes have grown dim, and our hearts are sick. Hear our prayer and accept our plea.
Though we have acted wickedly and provoked you, have mercy for the sake of your great name. We have no other source of trust, no hope and no rest apart from you.
For the heavens are yours, and the earth is yours. The day is yours, and the night is yours. You created the sun and the moon.
The seas praise you with their waves, for you fixed their boundaries, and they obey your command. The sea is bound by the sand and carries out your will.
All beings look to you and wait for you. Your right hand provides for all your creatures, and nothing can resist your will.
The lights of the sky are yours. Winds and storms praise your name. The wild animals look to you,
as do the birds of the sky and the fish of the sea. Rise to help us with your great power, so that all the nations on the face of the earth may know
that there is no one like you and none besides you. Pharaoh said of you, “Who is God?” And you drowned him like a crab in the dreadful sea.
Sennacherib considered you like the gods of the nations, but you made him an object of astonishment and showed your greatness. You helped Mattathias when he was zealous for you,
and you answered Judas and Simon and his brothers. You helped them in the wondrous battles you fought through their hands.
Let your compassion be stirred, and let your mercy be revealed. Leave a remnant of your plundered people. Restore your house in our days.
Lift up our heads, bowed down by our wickedness. Accept the offering of our people, and let our prayer be pleasing to you. Let the closed gates be opened,
and let the overturned altars be set upright. Let our plundered people be gathered together and rejoice in the restoration of your house. Let the blood of the righteous cry out to you,
and may you take pleasure in them as in the fragrance of spices. Have mercy, Lord. Have mercy on the purity of your community, which has fallen into the hands of the wicked,
who rejoice over our downfall. You are accustomed, our King, to showing your mercy, and we are accustomed at all times to asking for your compassion.
We appeal to you, trusting in your kindness. Your grace is not withheld even from the wicked. You make your sun rise on the good and the wicked,
and you send down your rain on the righteous and the unjust. For we know that you are always accustomed to hearing those in distress.
For time after time you have answered prisoners, helped the persecuted, strengthened the weak, lifted up the lowly, and rescued the displaced.
You rescued the plundered, released the prisoners, gave light to those in darkness, fed the hungry, and enriched the poor.
In every generation, we know that you have done these things for your servants. You yourself have made known to us: “I am the first, and I am the last.”
You are the God of the first and the last, for both worlds belong to you, along with all who have existed and all who are yet to come.
To whom shall we go, that he may hear us? To whom shall we look, that he may help us? For whom shall we wait, that he may save us? To whom shall we pray, that he may receive our petition?
We are yours, and you are our God. Far be it from you to let the blood of the righteous, shed unjustly, be covered up.
Instead, let it be laid on a bare rock, so that wrath may rise over it for vengeance. Far be it from you to withhold your compassion in your anger.
For your goodness is never overcome by our wickedness, nor is your mercy withheld because of our wrongdoing. Your nature is not corrupted because of us.
Your name is Good. Show your goodness: your goodness toward us, and your justice toward our adversaries. Both are found with you and are in your hands.
We worship you, the self-existent one, who created us from nothing, formed us in the image of your likeness, and breathed into us from your spirit of life.
You placed us in the world as inhabitants before you. Our death and our life are in your hands. What are human beings before you?
They are like steam rising from a pot, like dust carried away by a whirlwind, like an evening shadow, and like a morning cloud;
like passing dust and like a flower that withers. If you will it, we exist; if you do not will it, we do not exist. If you look at the earth, it trembles;
and if you turn your face away, its inhabitants perish. Your will sustains all your creatures, and your command governs all natures.
The sun rises at your word and makes its circuit throughout your creation by your will. The moon changes marvelously,
and you appointed it to distinguish the seasons. You arranged the lights in the firmament, and they adorn all creation. The winds blow by your will,
and from time to time they display their strength. They churn up the sea and shake the mountains; then again, at your command, they bring relief to your creation.
A bird swims in the air /in the air/ and travels along its paths as though along a well-trodden road. So too do the fish of the sea in their own realm.
When fish come up into the air, they die, and when a bird falls into the sea, it suffocates. Whatever has existed and exists belongs to you, and all natures were distinguished by you.
We praise you, though you are clothed in glory. We give you thanks, though you have no need. We exalt you from the lowest depths,
while your dwelling is in the highest heavens. Your will is above heaven, and your command is beneath the earth. Hands did not make you,
nor did our fingers toil over you. We pictured you in our hearts and imagined you in our minds. Our thought saw you, and we called you God. We named you Father because you brought us into being,
and King and God because you called us. We tried to define you, but could not do so fully. We compared you, but you have no likeness. Your appearance is hidden, and your power is great.
Your greatness is concealed, and creation depends on you. The abundant waters are contained /you have measured them/ in the hollow of your hand. You weighed the lofty mountains on a balance,
and the hills on scales. The earth is long, broad, and spacious, yet its dimensions are enough only for a footstool for your feet. You measured the dust of the earth in your fist.
Heaven is your throne, yet it cannot contain you. Though your name is great and your works are mighty, you have made your greatness small enough to fit our language.
Our mouth has room for you, and you have dwelt within us. You dwell among the righteous, and there is ample room for you. Your greatness has entered a little heart.
You have made us temples, a dwelling for your glory, and have called us your sanctuary. Your greatness has walked among us, as you announced beforehand through the mouths of your prophets:
“I will dwell among them and walk among them.” You dwell among the gentle; you reside among the humble. You rest among the gentle and good; you delight in the repentant.
You look upon the upright and rejoice in the poor. You borrow from the needy like a man who lacks something. There is no end to your mercy.
There is no measure to your grace. All our mouths cannot do you justice; all our tongues are insufficient for you. When a human being reaches his limit, he stops.
However far he stretches his mind, it is not enough. If he raises his thought above heaven, he finds himself walking on the earth. And if his thought descends into the depths,
in a little while he returns to his earth, and his meditation ceases. What is above heaven? Who can explain it? What lies beneath the earth?
There is no telling. By what is the firmament stretched out, or from what are the heavens suspended? On what does the earth rest, or by what is the deep held in place?
From Adam until now, we have understood little. We know only this: there is one God, one Messiah of his, one Spirit, and one faith,
and one baptism. It does us no good to speak beyond this. If we speak, we fall short; if we investigate, we suffer harm.
Many have lost the way, abandoned the path, and walked in the wilderness, on a road full of stumbling blocks. They conceived and devised destructive words.
They prophesied falsehood and abandoned God. Those who wanted to understand became undiscerning, their understanding darkened, groping in gloom.
O son of Adam, dust from the earth, who persists in a way of thinking that leads to destruction! Your mind has given birth to other gods.
Your thought has fashioned something that does not befit it. You have not ascended above; you are bound to the earth. You have not descended below to know what is there.
You imagined and spoke, though you had not seen it. You have become a liar, speaking falsehood and deceit. I will ask you; tell me:
The sun that you have seen—what is its substance? Does it have a soul? Does it have knowledge? Or does it have discernment?
If you believe what I tell you, this is how it is: the sun and moon are like fire and water, which neither perceive nor discern.
