Whatever you give to fire, it does not reject it, nor does it recoil from what is foul and repulsive. It does not know whoever honors it, nor does it recognize whoever despises it.
Water is the same, for it is a created thing without discernment. The sun, moon, and stars, the winds, lightning, and clouds,
and fire and water—all these are created things with courses to follow. They were made from the beginning to serve the world.
As they follow their courses, they have no discernment. Fire consumes dung and rottenness and does not say, “Enough!” For this is its nature.
The sun shines on corpses and mud, blazing in its strength without discernment. Water sweeps away every kind of impurity,
and mixes [?] the filth of the mud, having no awareness of its own. All these works of heaven and earth
were made to serve the world, without souls. Even the earth, which stands still—when he wishes, he shakes it from its foundations.
Know this, human being who does not understand: God's will sustains everything, and nothing is outside his will.
But we, who know that God is one, should give thanks, worship, praise, exalt, honor, sanctify, and glorify his greatness through Jesus his Son, our Savior, who chose us for himself.
He brought us near to himself, and through him we came to know him, and became his worshipers, his people, his church, and his holy assembly.
Glory and honor to the Father, to his Son, and to his living and holy Spirit, from the mouths of all who praise him above and below, forever and ever. Amen and amen.
At the head of all good deeds, this is required before God: that a person believe that God is one, and, along with faith, keep the commandments.
If someone professes that God is one but breaks his commandments and does not carry them out, that person does not truly believe that God is one.
As the teacher of the nations said, “They profess to know God, but by their deeds they deny him.” Isaiah also said:
“This people honors me with its lips, but its heart is far from me.” And David said, “With their mouths they bless, but in their hearts they curse.”
And how do they profess to know God but deny him by their deeds? If someone believes that God is one but does not do what God commanded,
that person does not truly believe that God is one. God commanded, “Keep my commandments and carry them out.” And whoever does not keep God's commandments—
it is clear that he has denied God, because he does not truly believe in the Lord who gave the commandments. God said, “Do not murder, and do not commit adultery,
and do not steal, and do not give false testimony. Honor your father and your mother. And do not do to your neighbor what you yourself hate.”
For whoever believes that God judges murderers does not murder, and whoever murders does not truly believe that God exists.
And whoever believes that God judges adulterers does not commit adultery, and whoever commits adultery does not truly believe that God exists.
And whoever believes that God judges thieves does not steal, and if someone steals, that person does not truly believe that God exists. All the commandments are like this.
Our Life-giver commanded further, “Do not swear a false oath; whoever does so will be condemned at the judgment.” How can someone who truly believes that God is one swear by him and lie?
See: whoever breaks any of these commandments has clearly denied God. But someone who swears and lies under oath is especially wicked before God.
For our Savior commanded with a solemn warning in his teaching, “Do not swear by heaven, because it is God's throne.” For if you swear falsely by heaven,
how will you lift your eyes to heaven and make requests of the one who dwells in heaven? “And do not swear by the earth, because it is the footstool beneath his feet.”
Otherwise, if you swear falsely by the earth, it may tremble beneath you whenever you pray upon it, because you have sworn falsely by the footstool of God's feet.
“Nor should you swear by Jerusalem, because it is the city of the great King.” Otherwise, if you swear falsely by the place of worship,
you will be ashamed to stand there to pray, and your prayer will not rise from the house by which you lied, nor will it be acceptable. He also says, “Do not swear by your head,
because you cannot make a single hair on it black or white.” Otherwise, if you swear falsely by your head,
you dishonor your head, over which your Lord's name has been invoked. As the apostle said, “The head of a man is Christ.” You who swear falsely by your head,
if [?] you truly believe in the three great and glorious names invoked over your head—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—when you received the seal of your life,
if you truly believe in baptism, do not swear falsely by your head. Know that you have no authority to swear by your head. Rather, he says, “Let your word be ‘Yes, yes,’ and ‘No, no.’”
And he said that anything beyond these comes from the evil one. For swearing falsely by God is worse than all the sins that human beings commit.
If someone breaks one of God's commandments, he stands and prays and asks God, in the hope that he may forgive him.
But someone who swears by God himself and lies—from whom can he ask forgiveness? How can he appeal to God, whom he has made out to be a liar? How can he pray to God, to whom he has not been faithful?
For the kings of Israel committed great and grievous sins. Some of them abandoned God and worshiped idols.
Some committed adultery with their neighbors' wives; they also murdered and committed sexual immorality. Yet they were not reproached as severely as those who swore and lied were charged.
Nebuchadnezzar, the wicked king, into whose hands the whole earth had been delivered, when the people of Israel were delivered into his hands,
took some of them as hostages to Babylon. He left them and their kings in their own land under an agreement without an oath.
When they pledged to him, saying, "We will serve you," Jehoiakim made an agreement with him without oaths. Afterward he rebelled and broke his word, and when he broke his word, he was killed.
He appointed his son Jehoiachin as king after him. Jehoiachin made an agreement with him without oaths, saying, "I will not rebel," but he broke his agreement.
He rebelled against the king of Babylon. Then Nebuchadnezzar sent men, bound him in chains, and took him to Babylon.
There he remained in prison for thirty-seven years. And he appointed his uncle Zedekiah as king.
Then Nebuchadnezzar considered the matter and took counsel: "How can I leave him as king and know that he will not rebel?" His advisers said to him,
"Ask the priests who know the law." So Nebuchadnezzar summoned the priests and said to them, "How can I know that you will serve me and will not rebel?"
They said to him, "We and our king swear by the God of Israel, and we establish an agreement through an offering that is presented on the altar."
Then Nebuchadnezzar said, "I will make you swear by the God of Israel, so that if you swear falsely by him, he will deliver you into my hands.
I will not make you swear by the gods of Babylon." Then King Zedekiah, the priests, and the officials brought a calf.
They laid their hands on the calf's head and slaughtered it. The priests took some of the calf's blood and poured it around the altar.
They offered its fat on the altar as a pleasing aroma. They took the calf and cut it in two, and the officials of Judah passed between its halves,
along with the priests and the teachers of the people, and King Zedekiah with them. They established an agreement with an oath by the God of Israel, saying, "We will not rebel."
Nebuchadnezzar trusted them. But afterward they broke their oaths sworn by the God of Israel and rebelled against the king of Babylon.
At that time Jeremiah and Ezekiel were prophesying to them: Jeremiah in Jerusalem, and Ezekiel among the captives in Babylon.
When they broke their oath and rebelled, Jeremiah the prophet called out to them: "O men of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem,
and King Zedekiah and all Judah, serve the king of Babylon and live! Do not break the oaths you have sworn.
Remember the calf that you cut in two and between whose halves you passed." But they did not listen to the prophet.
When he repeatedly called out to them, they seized him and threw him into a muddy pit. Some of them said, "Come, let us strike him on the tongue, and let us not listen to anything he says."
Ezekiel also sent word to them from Babylon: “Do not break the oaths you have sworn by the God of Israel.” But they did not listen to him.
When they did not listen to him, he said in his prophecy: “As I live, says the Lord of lords, Zedekiah, who has dealt falsely with the God of Israel and despised my oaths
and broken my covenant—I will bring it upon his head.” Jeremiah called out and warned them: “Serve the king of Babylon and live, so that this city will not become a ruin.”
Again they did not listen to him. When they broke their oaths and did not listen to the prophets, the army of the Chaldeans came against them and surrounded Jerusalem,
from the ninth year of Zedekiah until the eleventh year. Even while they were rebelling, Jeremiah kept telling them,
“Go out to the king of Babylon, and live rather than die.” But they did not listen to him, and the city remained in distress for a long time,
while the Chaldeans besieged it for nineteen months, from the tenth day of the tenth month of the ninth year, which is January,
until the fifth month of the eleventh year, which is August. The city was captured on the ninth day of the fifth month, and the Chaldeans entered Jerusalem.
They burned the house of God, by whom they had sworn falsely, and tore down the altar on which they had offered up the smoke of the oath, from the calf of the oaths [?].
/of the oath/ And they took all the utensils used in the service of the house of the God of Israel. They burned the houses of the nobles who had sworn falsely.
The priests went out into captivity and went to Babylon. When Zedekiah fled and left the city, the Chaldean army overtook him in the plain of Jericho.
They bound him in chains, along with the nobles who had sworn with him, and brought him to the king of Babylon in the land of Hamath. It is written that he pronounced judgment on him
and said to him: “Why did you break the oaths sworn by the God of Israel? Now I will bring it upon your head.” He blinded his eyes and bound him in chains.
He slaughtered his sons before his eyes and slaughtered the nobles who had sworn falsely. He took him in chains to Babylon, and he remained there until the day he died.
He destroyed Jerusalem because of the false oath. Their kingdom was given to Nebuchadnezzar, who believed in the God who demands an accounting for oaths sworn by him.
For this reason our Life-giver warned us: “Do not swear by yourselves.” For the Lord does not acquit anyone who swears falsely by his name, lest someone who trains his mouth to swear oaths
stumble at every turn because he has trained his mouth to swear, and his tongue has become a passageway for oaths. We know, my dear friends,

that many people among our brothers have sworn falsely, have coerced others and made them swear, and have killed themselves and put their companions to death, transgressing the commandment that our Savior taught.
We have no confidence in this world, and everything in it is built on sand. The world and its affairs do not endure.
Its delights fly away on swift wings. Human beings enter it naked and leave it just as they came into it.
Those who pursue wealth do not secure it, for it is taken from them and given to others. Those who have children do not rejoice in them,
for it happens that they bring them bitterness: some through death and some through captivity, while those who remain dishonor their parents.
Those who gain friends should not rely on them, for they quickly turn like a wheel. Those who build and plant should not rejoice greatly in these things,
for their enemies seize their possessions. They see them, and their souls are tormented over their labor, which has become the property of others.
Those who build cities and establish villages sometimes find that they are not allowed to remain in them, because their enemies take them captive.
They become strangers to the land where they were born. They betroth women and hope to rejoice, but within a short time they die and pass away.
Their betrothed women belong to others, whose names they have never called. They run and wear themselves out and store up treasures.
After their death, these belong to others. Their companions enjoy their good things, while their own hands cannot reach their possessions.
And women who hurry about making preparations and expect to rejoice in their clothes—after only a short time,
those clothes are torn over their dead. This is the building set on sand, and there is no assurance that it will endure forever.
Our treasure is in the place promised to us, and where our treasure is, there let our thoughts be. Nothing is greater than the fear of God.
A person who keeps his commandments is praised. Many are called wise, but there is no wisdom like the fear of God.
I have written this brief reminder for you, my dear friend: what you requested of me, and also what you did not ask me, so that you may be enriched and I may be helped.
The giver rejoices, and the receiver gives praise. Whoever sows in hope awaits the harvest. Cultivated land into which seed falls yields fruit and brings joy to the farmer.
Whoever has something and gives asks and receives. Whoever has something and withholds it becomes deprived. Whoever received money and showed a profit
receives praise, authority, and ten minas. But what the other hid was taken from him, and he was sent to the place of lazy servants.

Whoever gives from what he has received suffers no lack himself. Whoever asks and receives from his master's treasury—his master calls him to receive. And let the one who receives give to you as he has received.
I wrote this letter to you, my dear friend, in the month of Ab, in the year six hundred and fifty-six of the reign of Alexander, son of Philip the Macedonian,

and in the thirty-sixth year of Shapur, king of Persia, who carried out the persecution, in the fifth year since the churches were uprooted, in the year when the great slaughter of the martyrs took place in the land of the East,
after I had written these first twenty-two chapters, arranged according to the letters, one after another. Read, learn, and remember your dear friend.
The Demonstration on the Blessing That Passed through the Righteous and through All the Former Generations is finished.
The copying into this book of all the letters of Mar Jacob, the Persian Sage, is finished.
They number twenty-two, arranged according to the alphabet, and one on the cluster of grapes. Glory to the Father, to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.
[?] concerning [?] you took me [?] in you. Open to me the spiritual senses of your mind,
and show me something of what you have understood from the Holy Scriptures, so that my deficiency may be supplied by you and my hunger satisfied by your teaching,
and my thirst relieved from your flowing spring. For there are many things in my mind that I wish to ask you,
but I am keeping them all with me, so that when I come to you, you may satisfy me concerning every matter.
But before everything else, I want you to write and explain to me this matter that presses upon me: concerning our faith, what it is,
what its foundation is, on what building it rises, and by what things it is established,
and how [?] and its completion, and what deeds it requires. For I have only believed.
That there is one God who made heaven and earth from the beginning. He adorned the world with its furnishings, and he made humankind in his image.
He is the one who accepted Abel’s offering. He took Enoch away because of his goodness, and he sheltered Noah because of his righteousness.
He chose Abraham because of his faith, and he spoke with Moses because of his humility. He also spoke through all the prophets.
He also sent his Messiah into the world. For, my brother, I believe that these things are so. Therefore, my brother,
I ask you to write to me and show me what deeds are required for this faith of ours, and set my mind at rest.
